# RPT-0014: source log

Every source found for RPT-0014, deduplicated, and its `library/` record. None is ingested yet: records are sub-issue #75, after the record shape is decided in #74.

**How this log was built.** Six dimension agents and two gap-fill agents wrote 1,282 source blocks (raw files kept in the session scratchpad, not in this repo). The synthesis step merged blocks that describe the same work (same arXiv id, DOI, quoted title, primary URL, or a manual same-document decision), applied every item in the two `## Corrections` sections (gaps-papers C1-C16; gaps-other corrections), and assigned stable ids `S-0001`.. sorted by type, then year, then canonical slug. Type order: paper, survey, threat-model, framework, standard, catalog, dataset, tool, vendor-research, advisory, news. Year `n.d.` marks living resources with no edition date.

**Corrections applied** (from the gap-fill agents' adversarial verification):

- casey-2024-hf-exploit-instrumentation: arXiv 2403.04786 -> 2410.04490 (gaps-papers C1)
- CamoLeak: CVE-2025-59145 removed (wrong CVE; gaps-papers C2/C3); merged under legit-2025-camoleak
- grafanaghost-2026: CVE-2026-27876 association dropped (gaps-papers C4)
- anthropic-sep-2026: title corrected (C14)
- Morris II: venue claim replaced by CCS 2025 DOI pointer (C9)
- lin-2026-gpubreach, syros-2026-saga: cached PDFs attached (gaps-other Corrections)
- ATLAS deprecated ids remapped in 39 catalog_ids fields (C5-C7)
- confidence capped to medium on entries with per-memory claims (C15): the gap agents flagged 107 raw source blocks, which deduplicated to 97 sources; the v0.2 fold re-ran a pattern audit ("I recall", "recollection", "from memory", "from recall", "per memory", "background knowledge") and capped 15 more (S-0785, S-0852, S-0974, S-0976, S-1006, S-1012, S-1016, S-1018, S-1021, S-1023, S-1026, S-1034, S-1040, S-1110, S-1136), giving 112, and verified the recalled detail in 6 others instead (S-0303, S-0325, S-0672, S-0855, S-0954, S-1000)
- 40 duplicate works listed in gaps-papers C8 merged under the proposed canonical id; a further 78 same-document duplicates merged by URL, DOI or title (aliases listed per entry below).
- 16 group headings mis-marked as entries (C16) excluded; no source was rejected outright by either gap agent.
- **v0.2 review fold (2026-10-03):** 32 sources added (S-1150 to S-1181), of which 11 split bundled works out of S-0991 (S-1166), S-1117 (S-1167 to S-1173), S-0833 (S-1174 to S-1176) and S-0752 (S-1177), so that one id denotes one work; every OWASP LLM id in the catalog-id columns now carries its edition (`:2025`; the agents used 2025 meanings throughout, as their parenthetical labels show, and S-0883 is `:2023`); sha256 recorded for every cached PDF; S-0463 (Progent) figure corrected from the v3 PDF; S-0940 and S-0212 summaries corrected; S-0900 count conflict resolved; S-0948 labelled as an in-house measurement; S-1040 marked disputed by S-1151. CWE-1260 ("Improper Handling of Overlap Between Protected Memory Ranges", unrelated) replaced by CWE-1256 on the Rowhammer and bit-flip sources (S-0062, S-0150, S-0424, S-0547, S-0548, S-0612 and their blocks).

**Confidence.** As recorded by the agent that confirmed the source. Rule C15 caps any entry containing a "from memory"/"per memory" detail at `medium (capped)`; `high` needs title, authors and venue confirmed by a fetched record. Vendor attributions and counts are reported claims, not verified facts. **Every summary below is AI-written from abstracts, landing pages or partial PDF reads and is a hypothesis until a human checks it against the source (#73).**

**PDFs** are cached outside every repo at `~/cb/projects/tmodel2026/pdf-cache/ai-threat-model/` (filename in the table; filename and sha256 in each annotated entry, computed in the v0.2 fold for all 291 cached files referenced by 285 sources). No PDF is committed.

**Counts.** paper 675; vendor-research 121; survey 55; threat-model 54; framework 51; catalog 48; advisory 46; dataset 42; standard 39; news 33; tool 17; total 1181 (1,149 in v0.1). PDF cached for 285 sources. 112 entries are `medium (capped)`. A coverage check at the end lists the 459 sources cited by no AIT technique.

**Overlap with RPT-0009** (SAGAI and AI-security specs): S-0173 (`kang-2023-dual-use-programmatic-behavior`), S-0265 (`hines-2024-spotlighting`), S-0686 (`barrett-2023-security-risks-generative-ai`), S-0769 (`christodorescu-agent-security-systems-2026`), S-0783 (`nist-ai-rmf-1-0`), S-0826 (`owasp-ai-exchange`), S-0835 (`ncsc-cisa-secure-ai-2023`), S-0841 (`nist-ai-100-2-e2023`), S-0848 (`cisa-2025-ai-in-ot-principles`), S-0849 (`etsi-en-304223`), S-0850 (`etsi-ts-104223-2025`), S-0852 (`five-eyes-2025-ai-data-security`), S-0855 (`nist-ai-100-2-e2025`), S-0857 (`uk-ai-cyber-code-of-practice`), S-0897 (`owasp-llm-top10-2025`), S-0903 (`mitre-atlas-2026-09`). ## Annotated bibliography

One entry per source, in id order. `summary` is the technical summary; `mapping` is the agent's threat-model mapping in the form *asset or component -> threat -> precondition -> impact*. Where several dimension agents captured the same work, the other agents' summaries are kept under "also captured as". All of it is extraction input for #73, not reviewed fact.

### S-0001 Poisoning attacks against SVMs (pre-2013 context)

- **canonical id:** `biggio-2012-poisoning-svm` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2012; confidence high
- **citation:** B. Biggio, B. Nelson, P. Laskov, "Poisoning Attacks against Support Vector Machines", ICML 2012. arXiv:1206.6389
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1206.6389)
- **attack classes:** [data-poisoning, availability-poisoning]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020; OWASP ML02; NISTAML.013
- **summary:** A gradient-ascent attack that crafts training points to maximize SVM validation error. It is the seminal optimization-based availability-poisoning paper. The attacker can inject training points and knows the learning algorithm. It falls slightly before the 2013 window and is kept as the root of the poisoning lineage.
- **mapping:** training set -> injected optimized points -> data-injection capability -> accuracy degradation

### S-0002 Evasion attacks against ML at test time

- **canonical id:** `biggio-2013-evasion-test-time` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2013; confidence high
- **citation:** B. Biggio, I. Corona, D. Maiorca, B. Nelson et al., "Evasion Attacks against Machine Learning at Test Time", ECML PKDD 2013, LNCS. DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-40994-3_25; arXiv:1708.06131
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record with DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-40994-3_25 and arXiv 1708.06131
- **attack classes:** [evasion, gradient-based-attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.000/.002; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** The first gradient-based evasion attack against SVMs and neural networks, published concurrently with or before Szegedy. Tested on PDF malware detection and MNIST, it models perfect-knowledge and limited-knowledge (surrogate) attackers who minimize a differentiable discriminant function under a distance bound. Detectors can be evaded with few feature modifications. It defines the attacker-knowledge levels later adopted by NIST.
- **mapping:** malware/spam classifier -> test-time evasion -> feature-space control + surrogate knowledge -> detection bypass

### S-0003 Intriguing properties of neural networks

- **canonical id:** `szegedy-2013-intriguing-properties` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2013; confidence high
- **citation:** C. Szegedy, W. Zaremba, I. Sutskever, J. Bruna et al., "Intriguing properties of neural networks", ICLR 2014. arXiv:1312.6199
- **pdf:** szegedy-2013-intriguing-properties.pdf sha256: c4e3bd872ef20b7d2c4d77a63cd8f37cb8ff518609ae09acaf0fd5dd9e76c54c
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API (export.arxiv.org) hit 1312.6199v4; https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6199
- **attack classes:** [evasion, adversarial-examples, transferability]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.000/.002; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Coined "adversarial examples": imperceptible perturbations found by box-constrained L-BFGS that cause misclassification by state-of-the-art DNNs. These examples transfer across models with different architectures and training subsets. The attacker in the paper is white-box at inference time, but transfer implies a black-box threat. The impact is an integrity failure of perception models.
- **mapping:** image classifier -> adversarial perturbation -> test-input control (white-box or transfer) -> misclassification

### S-0004 Privacy in pharmacogenetics: model inversion on warfarin dosing

- **canonical id:** `fredrikson-2014-pharmacogenetics-model-inversion` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2014; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** M. Fredrikson et al., "Privacy in Pharmacogenetics: An End-to-End Case Study of Personalized Warfarin Dosing", USENIX Security 2014 (Best Paper). https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity14/technical-sessions/presentation/fredrikson_matthew
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity14/technical-sessions/presentation/fredrikson_matthew (page title, authors and "Awarded Best Paper" fetched 2026-10-03); Semantic Scholar title match with abstract
- **attack classes:** [model inversion, attribute inference, differential privacy evaluation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.001; OWASP ML03; NISTAML.032, .034
- **summary:** Introduces model inversion. Given a pharmacogenetic warfarin-dosing model and some demographic information about a patient, an attacker predicts the patient's genetic markers (for example VKORC1, CYP2C9) better than baseline. Differential privacy prevents the inversion only at privacy budgets that make the models clinically unsafe (increased risk of stroke, bleeding and death in simulated trials). This is the foundational case of a privacy-utility-safety trade-off.
- **mapping:** clinical ML model -> model inversion with demographic side info -> model or API access -> genetic data disclosure; DP mitigation harms patient safety
- **note:** Promoted from the gaps prose in ml-model-attacks.md. The specific genetic markers (VKORC1, CYP2C9) are from memory of the paper.

### S-0005 Model inversion exploiting confidence information

- **canonical id:** `fredrikson-2015-model-inversion` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2015; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Fredrikson, S. Jha, T. Ristenpart, "Model Inversion Attacks that Exploit Confidence Information and Basic Countermeasures", ACM CCS 2015. DOI 10.1145/2810103.2813677
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/2810103.2813677
- **attack classes:** [model-inversion, attribute-inference]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.001; OWASP ML03; NISTAML.032
- **summary:** Uses confidence scores to reconstruct recognizable face images of individuals from a facial-recognition model given their name or label, and to infer sensitive attributes (lifestyle survey answers) from decision trees. The attacker is black-box with confidences, or white-box. Rounding confidences is a basic countermeasure. It follows the 2014 USENIX pharmacogenetics inversion paper by the same group, which was not reconfirmed here.
- **mapping:** face-recognition / tabular model -> inversion from confidences -> query access + label knowledge -> reconstruction of private features

### S-0006 Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples (FGSM)

- **canonical id:** `goodfellow-2015-fgsm` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2015; confidence high
- **citation:** I. Goodfellow, J. Shlens, C. Szegedy, "Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples", ICLR 2015. arXiv:1412.6572
- **pdf:** goodfellow-2014-fgsm.pdf sha256: 7f6c0a50475149e11e3b7efc9c0a00383652b7cae62f80facd8ae2684ef251e7
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API hit 1412.6572v3; https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572
- **attack classes:** [evasion, fgsm, adversarial-training]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Proposes the linearity hypothesis: high-dimensional, nearly linear models are vulnerable. It introduces the one-step Fast Gradient Sign Method, x' = x + eps * sign(grad_x J). Adversarial training with FGSM examples is proposed as a regularizer. The attack is white-box and cheap. FGSM remains the baseline attack and the building block of iterative attacks.
- **mapping:** differentiable model -> FGSM perturbation -> gradient access -> misclassification

### S-0007 Deep learning with differential privacy (context)

- **canonical id:** `abadi-2016-dp-sgd` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Abadi, A. Chu, I. Goodfellow, H. B. McMahan, I. Mironov, K. Talwar, L. Zhang, "Deep Learning with Differential Privacy", ACM CCS 2016. arXiv:1607.00133
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00133 (DataCite)
- **attack classes:** [privacy-defense]
- **catalog ids:** NISTAML.03x mitigation
- **summary:** Context only. DP-SGD (per-example gradient clipping plus Gaussian noise, with a moments accountant) is the principled mitigation against membership inference, extraction and reconstruction, at a utility cost. Debenedetti 2024 shows that system components can still void the guarantee.
- **mapping:** control -> DP training -> bounded per-record influence -> mitigates NISTAML.032/.033/.038

### S-0008 Hidden voice commands

- **canonical id:** `carlini-2016-hidden-voice-commands` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, P. Mishra, T. Vaidya, Y. Zhang, M. Sherr, C. Shields, D. Wagner, et al., "Hidden Voice Commands", USENIX Security 2016. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity16/technical-sessions/presentation/carlini
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity16/technical-sessions/presentation/carlini (page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [adversarial audio, voice-command injection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0041, AML.T0043.001; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Produces voice commands that humans cannot understand but speech recognizers accept. In the black-box setting the attacker uses the recognizer as an oracle and iteratively obfuscates MFCC-derived audio; the resulting commands work against Google Now over the air. In the white-box setting (CMU Sphinx) the commands are unintelligible to human listeners in user testing. Defenses evaluated: notifying the user when a command is accepted, verbal challenge-response, and an ML detector that detects the attacks with 99.8% accuracy.
- **mapping:** voice assistant -> hidden/obfuscated audio command -> attacker can play audio near device -> unauthorized actions (integrity)
- **note:** The fetched page author string was truncated after D. Wagner; remaining authors not recorded.

### S-0009 DeepFool

- **canonical id:** `moosavi-2016-deepfool` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** S.-M. Moosavi-Dezfooli, A. Fawzi, P. Frossard, "DeepFool: a simple and accurate method to fool deep neural networks", CVPR 2016. arXiv:1511.04599

### S-0010 Limitations of deep learning in adversarial settings (JSMA)

- **canonical id:** `papernot-2016-jsma` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Papernot, P. McDaniel, S. Jha, M. Fredrikson et al., "The Limitations of Deep Learning in Adversarial Settings", IEEE EuroS&P 2016. arXiv:1511.07528

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Introduces the Jacobian-based Saliency Map Attack, a targeted L0 attack that modifies few input features. It formalizes an adversarial goal and knowledge taxonomy for DNNs. The attack is white-box, and the impact is targeted misclassification.

### S-0011 Transferability: phenomena to black-box attacks

- **canonical id:** `papernot-2016-transferability` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Papernot, P. McDaniel, I. Goodfellow, "Transferability in Machine Learning: from Phenomena to Black-Box Attacks using Adversarial Samples", arXiv:1605.07277, 2016
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1605.07277)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, transfer-attack, model-extraction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0005, AML.T0043.002, AML.T0040; NISTAML.025
- **summary:** Shows intra- and cross-technique transferability of adversarial examples among DNNs, logistic regression, SVMs, decision trees and kNN. Substitute models trained on oracle labels let the authors attack remote ML-as-a-service classifiers (Amazon, Google), so evasion requires no internals.
- **mapping:** MLaaS classifier -> substitute + transfer attack -> label-only query access -> misclassification

### S-0012 Accessorize to a crime: adversarial eyeglasses vs face recognition

- **canonical id:** `sharif-2016-accessorize-to-a-crime` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Sharif, S. Bhagavatula, L. Bauer, M. K. Reiter, "Accessorize to a Crime: Real and Stealthy Attacks on State-of-the-Art Face Recognition", ACM CCS 2016. DOI 10.1145/2976749.2978392
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/2976749.2978392; Semantic Scholar title match with abstract
- **attack classes:** [physical evasion, impersonation, biometric bypass]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0041, AML.T0043.000, AML.T0073; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Defines physically realizable, inconspicuous attacks on face recognition. An optimization produces a printed eyeglass-frame pattern that, worn by the attacker, causes a state-of-the-art face-recognition network to fail to recognize the wearer (dodging) or to identify them as a chosen person (impersonation). The main setting is white box; the abstract states that similar techniques also work against black-box face-recognition systems. This is the reference for adversarial attacks on biometric access control and surveillance.
- **mapping:** face-recognition access control or surveillance -> physical adversarial accessory -> attacker can be photographed and has model or surrogate access -> unauthorized access or evasion of identification

### S-0013 Stealing ML models via prediction APIs

- **canonical id:** `tramer-2016-stealing-ml-models` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2016; confidence high
- **citation:** F. Tramer, F. Zhang, A. Juels, M. K. Reiter, T. Ristenpart, "Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs", USENIX Security 2016. arXiv:1609.02943
- **pdf:** tramer-2016-stealing-ml-models.pdf sha256: 0140d9ab6257972ae5ce88b5d9ae8978b335083cb1c226e1b995da975d18a885
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (arXiv 1609.02943)
- **attack classes:** [model-extraction, equation-solving, path-finding]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0040, AML.T0048.004; OWASP ML05, LLM10:2025; NISTAML.031
- **summary:** The founding model-extraction paper. Equation-solving attacks recover logistic regression and MLP parameters from confidence scores. A path-finding attack recovers decision trees. Near-perfect-fidelity copies were made from BigML and Amazon ML with modest query counts. Omitting or rounding confidence values helps but does not stop the attack. Impacts are loss of IP and pay-per-query revenue, and the stolen model serves as a surrogate for evasion and privacy attacks.
- **mapping:** MLaaS model -> prediction-API queries -> black-box query access (confidences) -> model IP theft + enabling of follow-on attacks

### S-0014 Adversarial patch

- **canonical id:** `brown-2017-adversarial-patch` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** T. B. Brown, D. Mane, A. Roy, M. Abadi, J. Gilmer, "Adversarial Patch", arXiv:1712.09665, 2017
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API hit 1712.09665v2
- **attack classes:** [evasion, patch-attack, universal]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0041, AML.T0043; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** A universal, robust, targeted, location-independent printable patch causes classifiers to output a target class (for example "toaster") whenever the patch is in view. The attack is not bounded by L_p imperceptibility and can be printed and distributed. Certified patch defenses followed (for example arXiv:2003.06693).
- **mapping:** vision model -> patch in scene -> physical access -> targeted misclassification

### S-0015 Towards evaluating the robustness of neural networks (C&W)

- **canonical id:** `carlini-wagner-2017-cw` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, D. Wagner, "Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks", IEEE S&P 2017. arXiv:1608.04644

- **confirmed via:** arXiv API hit 1608.04644v2; https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.04644
- **attack classes:** [evasion, optimization-attack, defense-breaking]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Optimization-based L0, L2 and L_inf attacks using a margin loss and a change of variables. They achieved 100% success against defensive distillation, which had claimed robustness. It established the norm of evaluating defenses with strong adaptive attacks. The attacker is white-box. The paper also motivated high-confidence transferable examples.
- **mapping:** DNN (with defense) -> optimized perturbation -> white-box -> misclassification despite defense

### S-0016 Adversarial examples are not easily detected: bypassing ten detectors

- **canonical id:** `carlini-wagner-2017-detectors-not-easily-detected` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, D. Wagner, "Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods", ACM AISec 2017. DOI 10.1145/3128572.3140444; arXiv:1705.07263
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07263 (arXiv API record, first posted 2017-05-20); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1705.07263 (venue "AISec@CCS", 2021 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, detector bypass, adaptive attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Surveys ten published adversarial-example detection methods (secondary classifiers, PCA, distributional tests, dropout uncertainty and others) and defeats all of them by constructing new loss functions that jointly fool the classifier and the detector. White-box and, for several detectors, black-box/transfer settings are tested on MNIST and CIFAR. Concludes that properties believed intrinsic to adversarial examples are not, and proposes evaluation guidelines. This is the canonical evidence that "detect the adversarial input" controls fail against an adaptive attacker.
- **mapping:** image/ML classifier protected by input detector -> adaptive attack optimizing against detector -> white-box or surrogate knowledge -> undetected evasion (control bypass)

### S-0017 Targeted backdoor attacks via data poisoning

- **canonical id:** `chen-2017-targeted-backdoor-poisoning` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence medium

A small number of poisoned samples, on the order of tens, achieved high attack success. The attacker needs no model knowledge or training control, only data injection. Physical triggers work.

### S-0018 ZOO zeroth-order black-box attack

- **canonical id:** `chen-2017-zoo` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** P.-Y. Chen, H. Zhang, Y. Sharma, J. Yi, C.-J. Hsieh, "ZOO: Zeroth Order Optimization based Black-box Attacks to Deep Neural Networks without Training Substitute Models", ACM AISec 2017. arXiv:1708.03999
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.03999 (DataCite)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, score-based-black-box]

### S-0019 BadNets

- **canonical id:** `gu-2017-badnets` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Gu, B. Dolan-Gavitt, S. Garg, "BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain", arXiv:1708.06733, 2017; journal version IEEE Access 2019, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2909068
- **pdf:** gu-2017-badnets.pdf sha256: 96f572d948ff62baaae5fbb9fcf6bdf28dfb6a67b7a4ea013a3d17ece927795e

- **summary:** A malicious training provider, or a poisoned pre-trained model, implants a trigger-patch backdoor. In a US street-sign detector, a sticker trigger caused stop signs to be read as speed-limit signs, while clean accuracy stayed intact and evaded validation. The backdoor survives transfer learning. The paper frames the ML model supply chain (outsourced training, model zoos) as an attack surface.
- **mapping:** pre-trained / outsourced model -> trigger backdoor -> control of training -> trigger-conditioned misclassification downstream

### S-0020 Deep Models Under the GAN: leakage from collaborative learning

- **canonical id:** `hitaj-2017-deep-models-under-the-gan` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** B. Hitaj, G. Ateniese, F. Perez-Cruz, "Deep Models Under the GAN: Information Leakage from Collaborative Deep Learning", ACM CCS 2017. DOI 10.1145/3133956.3134012; arXiv:1702.07464
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.07464 (arXiv API record, first posted 2017-02-24); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1702.07464 (venue "Conference on Computer and Communications Security", 1644 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [FL privacy attack, GAN-based reconstruction, active insider]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.001; OWASP ML03; NISTAML.032
- **summary:** A malicious participant in collaborative (federated-style) deep learning trains a GAN locally on the shared model to generate prototypical samples of a class held only by a victim. By labelling these samples as a different class, the attacker actively forces the victim to release more detail about that class. Record-level differential privacy on shared parameters does not prevent this class-representative inference. Attacker: a legitimate participant.
- **mapping:** federated/collaborative model -> GAN-based class reconstruction by insider -> attacker is a participant -> disclosure of other participants' data distributions (confidentiality)

### S-0021 Adversarial examples in the physical world

- **canonical id:** `kurakin-2017-physical-world` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high

The paper introduces basic iterative and iterative least-likely-class methods. The attacker needs only physical-environment access.

### S-0022 Delving into transferable adversarial examples

- **canonical id:** `liu-2017-delving-transferable` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high

### S-0023 Fault injection attack on deep neural network (SBA/GDA)

- **canonical id:** `liu-2017-fault-injection-dnn` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Liu, L. Wei, B. Luo, Q. Xu, "Fault Injection Attack on Deep Neural Network", IEEE/ACM ICCAD 2017. DOI 10.1109/ICCAD.2017.8203770
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record; https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1109/iccad.2017.8203770 (abstract)
- **attack classes:** [parameter fault injection, targeted misclassification, integrity]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018 Manipulate AI Model?; OWASP ML10 (model poisoning)?; NIST NISTAML.02 (integrity)
- **summary:** This is the earliest paper in this group on fault-injecting DNN parameters to force a chosen input into an adversarial class. Single Bias Attack (SBA) changes one bias, using the observation that outputs can depend linearly on some parameters. Gradient Descent Attack (GDA) bounds the modification so that other inputs are barely affected, which makes it stealthy. The attacker is assumed able to modify parameters in memory through physical or software fault injection. The paper is the precursor of the bit-flip attack (BFA) and trojan-by-bit-flip lines.
- **mapping:** deployed DNN parameters in memory -> targeted parameter fault -> fault-injection capability (physical or Rowhammer) -> targeted misclassification

### S-0024 Universal adversarial perturbations

- **canonical id:** `moosavi-2017-universal-perturbations` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** S.-M. Moosavi-Dezfooli, A. Fawzi, O. Fawzi, P. Frossard, "Universal Adversarial Perturbations", CVPR 2017. DOI 10.1109/CVPR.2017.17

- **attack classes:** [evasion, universal-perturbation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000/.002; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** A single image-agnostic perturbation fools a classifier on most natural images and generalizes across architectures. This lowers attacker cost, since one precomputed perturbation serves for broadcast attacks. The perturbation is crafted white-box and then transfers.
- **mapping:** vision model -> universal perturbation -> one-time crafting -> mass misclassification

### S-0025 Back-gradient optimization for poisoning deep learning

- **canonical id:** `munoz-gonzalez-2017-back-gradient-poisoning` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** L. Munoz-Gonzalez et al., "Towards Poisoning of Deep Learning Algorithms with Back-gradient Optimization", ACM AISec 2017. DOI 10.1145/3128572.3140451; arXiv:1708.08689
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.08689 (arXiv API record, first posted 2017-08-29); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1708.08689 (venue "AISec@CCS", 700 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [availability poisoning, bilevel optimization]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020; OWASP ML02; NISTAML.013
- **summary:** Extends optimal poisoning to multiclass problems and to learners trained by gradient descent, including neural networks, by computing the poisoning gradient with back-gradient (reverse-mode differentiation through training). This avoids the stationarity assumptions of prior bilevel attacks. Poisoning points are shown to transfer across learning algorithms. Demonstrated on spam filtering, malware detection and handwritten digits.
- **mapping:** model retrained on collected data (spam/malware telemetry) -> optimized poison points -> attacker injects a fraction of training data -> accuracy degradation (availability)

### S-0027 Membership inference attacks against ML models

- **canonical id:** `shokri-2017-membership-inference` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** R. Shokri, M. Stronati, C. Song, V. Shmatikov, "Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models", IEEE S&P 2017. DOI 10.1109/SP.2017.41; arXiv:1610.05820

It worked on Google Prediction API and Amazon ML models, including a hospital-discharge dataset. Leakage correlates with overfitting. The attacker is black-box with query access. ### S-0028 Certified defenses for data poisoning

- **canonical id:** `steinhardt-2017-certified-defenses-poisoning` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2017; confidence medium
- **citation:** J. Steinhardt, P. W. Koh, P. Liang, "Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks", NeurIPS 2017. arXiv:1706.03691
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03691 (arXiv API record, first posted 2017-06-09); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1706.03691 (venue "Neural Information Processing Systems", 917 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [poisoning defense, certified bound, outlier removal]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0020; NISTAML.013
- **summary:** Upper-bounds the worst-case test loss any poisoning attack can cause against a defender that does outlier removal followed by empirical risk minimization. The bound assumes the dataset is large enough for train/test concentration and that clean-data outliers do not matter. On MNIST-1-7 and Dogfish the defense is robust, while on IMDB sentiment a 3% poison can raise test error substantially. This shows that sanitization guarantees are dataset dependent.
- **mapping:** training data -> outlier-removal sanitization (mitigation) -> defender bounds worst-case loss -> certified or uncertified depending on dataset
- **note:** The IMDB/MNIST-1-7 specifics are from memory of the paper.

### S-0029 DolphinAttack: inaudible voice commands via ultrasound

- **canonical id:** `zhang-2017-dolphinattack` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2017; confidence high
- **citation:** G. Zhang et al., "DolphinAttack: Inaudible Voice Commands", ACM CCS 2017. DOI 10.1145/3133956.3134052; arXiv:1708.09537
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.09537 (arXiv API record, first posted 2017-08-31); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1708.09537 (venue "Conference on Computer and Communications Security", 784 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [ultrasonic injection, hardware nonlinearity, voice-command injection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0041, AML.T0015; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Modulates voice commands onto ultrasonic carriers above 20 kHz. Microphone circuit nonlinearity demodulates them into the audible band, so speech recognizers act on commands that humans cannot hear. Validated against Siri, Google Now, Samsung S Voice, Huawei HiVoice, Cortana and Alexa, with proofs of concept such as initiating FaceTime calls, opening malicious sites and switching on airplane mode. Hardware and software defenses are proposed. The attacker needs physical proximity with an ultrasonic transmitter.
- **mapping:** voice-controlled device -> inaudible ultrasonic command injection -> attacker transmitter within range -> unauthorized actions

### S-0030 Watermarking DNNs by backdooring

- **canonical id:** `adi-2018-watermarking-by-backdooring` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Adi, C. Baum, M. Cisse, B. Pinkas, J. Keshet, "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring", USENIX Security 2018. arXiv:1802.04633

- **catalog ids:** control for ATLAS AML.T0048.004; OWASP ML05 mitigation
- **summary:** Uses a deliberate backdoor trigger set as the owner's watermark so that ownership of a stolen model can be verified in a black-box way. This makes the watermark itself a backdoor and inherits backdoor-removal threats. Removal attacks include neural-network laundering (Aiken et al., arXiv:2004.11368) and fine-tuning or pruning.
- **mapping:** model IP -> backdoor watermark (control) -> stolen copy -> ownership proof unless removed

### S-0031 Synthesizing robust adversarial examples (EOT)

- **canonical id:** `athalye-2018-eot` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Athalye, L. Engstrom, A. Ilyas, K. Kwok, "Synthesizing Robust Adversarial Examples", ICML 2018. arXiv:1707.07397
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (arXiv 1707.07397; ICML 2018)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, physical-attack, 3d-adversarial-object]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0041, AML.T0043.000; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Expectation Over Transformation optimizes perturbations to survive distributions of viewpoint, lighting and noise. A 3D-printed turtle was classified as a rifle from most viewpoints. Crafting is white-box and the attack is deployed physically.
- **mapping:** vision system -> physically robust adversarial object -> physical access + surrogate -> persistent misclassification

### S-0032 Obfuscated gradients give a false sense of security

- **canonical id:** `athalye-2018-obfuscated-gradients` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Athalye, N. Carlini, D. Wagner, "Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples", ICML 2018. arXiv:1802.00420
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1802.00420)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, adaptive-attack, defense-breaking, bpda]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Identifies shattered, stochastic and exploding/vanishing gradients as forms of gradient masking. It introduces BPDA and EOT-based adaptive attacks and circumvented most ICLR 2018 white-box defenses that relied on obfuscated gradients. For a threat-model tool, the lesson is to discount claims of defense effectiveness that lack adaptive evaluation.
- **mapping:** defended model -> adaptive attack (BPDA/EOT) -> white-box knowledge of defense -> defense bypass

### S-0033 Practical fault attack on DNNs (laser injection)

- **canonical id:** `breier-2018-practical-fault-attack` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** J. Breier, X. Hou, D. Jap, L. Ma et al., "Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks", ACM CCS 2018 (poster/short). DOI 10.1145/3243734.3278519
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record; https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1145/3243734.3278519 (abstract)
- **attack classes:** [physical fault injection (laser), activation-function faults, misclassification]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0041 Physical Environment Access?, AML.T0015?; NIST NISTAML.02
- **summary:** This is the first study of physical fault injection on DNNs. It uses laser injection on an embedded microcontroller running the network. Faults are aimed at the activation functions (ReLU, softmax, sigmoid, tanh) in hidden layers and produce misclassification. The paper notes that cheaper methods such as supply-voltage glitching could produce the same faults. The attacker has physical access to the device, and the impact is integrity failure in safety-critical embedded AI. The same group later showed fault-based reverse engineering (breier-2020-sniff).
- **mapping:** embedded inference device (activation computation) -> laser/voltage fault -> physical access -> misclassification in safety-critical control

### S-0034 Decision-based adversarial attacks (Boundary Attack)

- **canonical id:** `brendel-2018-boundary-attack` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** W. Brendel, J. Rauber, M. Bethge, "Decision-Based Adversarial Attacks: Reliable Attacks Against Black-Box Machine Learning Models", ICLR 2018. arXiv:1712.04248
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1712.04248)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, decision-based-black-box]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.001; NISTAML.025
- **summary:** The first strong decision-only (hard-label) attack. It starts from a large adversarial perturbation and random-walks along the decision boundary to reduce it, and was demonstrated on Clarifai. It is robust to gradient masking.
- **mapping:** hard-label API -> boundary random walk -> label-only queries -> misclassification

### S-0035 Audio adversarial examples

- **canonical id:** `carlini-wagner-2018-audio` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, D. Wagner, "Audio Adversarial Examples: Targeted Attacks on Speech-to-Text", IEEE S&P Workshops (DLS) 2018. DOI 10.1109/SPW.2018.00009; arXiv:1801.01944
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record with DOI 10.1109/spw.2018.00009
- **attack classes:** [evasion, audio-adversarial, targeted]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** White-box targeted perturbations make Mozilla DeepSpeech transcribe any chosen phrase from audio that sounds nearly identical to the original. This creates a voice-assistant command-injection threat. The attack is digital (over-the-wire), not over-the-air.
- **mapping:** speech-to-text model -> audio perturbation -> white-box + audio input control -> attacker-chosen transcription / command

### S-0036 Stealing neural networks via timing side channels

- **canonical id:** `duddu-2018-timing-side-channels` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** V. Duddu, D. Samanta, D. V. Rao, V. E. Balas, "Stealing Neural Networks via Timing Side Channels", arXiv:1812.11720, 2018
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API id_list=1812.11720
- **attack classes:** [timing side channel, architecture inference, model extraction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0040 AI Model Inference API Access, AML.T0005.001 Train Proxy via Replication?; OWASP ML05; NIST NISTAML.031; CWE-208 (observable timing discrepancy)?
- **summary:** This is a black-box extraction attack on cloud-hosted NNs. Query execution time reveals network depth, and reinforcement learning with knowledge distillation then searches for a substitute architecture consistent with the timing. The attacker needs only query access and accurate end-to-end timing. Substitutes of VGG models on CIFAR-10 reach test accuracy close to the target. The paper motivates constant-time inference and timing noise as mitigations.
- **mapping:** ML-as-a-service API (model architecture) -> timing measurement of queries -> black-box API access -> substitute model / IP theft

### S-0037 HotFlip: white-box adversarial text via gradient token flips

- **canonical id:** `ebrahimi-2018-hotflip` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2018; confidence medium
- **citation:** J. Ebrahimi, A. Rao, D. Lowd, D. Dou, "HotFlip: White-Box Adversarial Examples for Text Classification", ACL 2018. arXiv:1712.06751
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.06751 (arXiv API record); Semantic Scholar lists only arXiv, ACL 2018 venue from memory
- **attack classes:** [adversarial text, white-box evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Uses the gradient with respect to one-hot input vectors to estimate which character (and, with semantic constraints, word) flip most increases the loss. A beam search over a few flips then sharply reduces the accuracy of character-level CNN classifiers. The method is efficient enough to use for adversarial training. The gradient-guided token swap is the primitive that later universal triggers and GCG generalize to LLMs.
- **mapping:** text classifier (spam, toxicity, sentiment) -> gradient-guided character/word flips -> white-box access -> misclassification

### S-0038 Robust physical-world attacks (stop sign)

- **canonical id:** `eykholt-2018-rp2-stop-sign` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** K. Eykholt, I. Evtimov, E. Fernandes, B. Li et al., "Robust Physical-World Attacks on Deep Learning Visual Classification", CVPR 2018. arXiv:1707.08945
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API hit 1707.08945v5

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0041, AML.T0043; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** The Robust Physical Perturbations algorithm produced graffiti- and sticker-like perturbations on real stop signs that road-sign classifiers misread (as speed-limit signs) under varied distances and angles in drive-by tests. It is the canonical safety-impact example for autonomous vehicles. Crafting is white-box and placement physical.
- **mapping:** AV perception -> adversarial sticker -> physical access to environment -> safety-critical misclassification

### S-0039 Property inference on fully connected NNs

- **canonical id:** `ganju-2018-property-inference` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** K. Ganju, Q. Wang, W. Yang, C. A. Gunter, N. Borisov, "Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations", ACM CCS 2018. DOI 10.1145/3243734.3243834
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3243734.3243834
- **attack classes:** [property-inference]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS ?; OWASP ML03 (?); NISTAML.034
- **summary:** A meta-classifier on permutation-invariant representations of white-box weights infers global properties of the training set, for example the proportion of a demographic, or whether a dataset contained noisy or specific-system traces. Earlier root: Ateniese et al. 2015, "Hacking smart machines with smarter ones", Int. J. Security and Networks, DOI 10.1504/IJSN.2015.071829 (confirmed via Crossref).
- **mapping:** published model weights -> meta-classifier -> white-box access -> leak of aggregate training-set properties

### S-0040 DeepRecon: cache side-channel DNN fingerprinting

- **canonical id:** `hong-2018-deeprecon` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** S. Hong, M. Davinroy, Y. Kaya, S. N. Locke, I. Rackow et al., "Security Analysis of Deep Neural Networks Operating in the Presence of Cache Side-Channel Attacks", arXiv:1810.03487, 2018
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API id_list=1810.03487
- **attack classes:** [cache side channel (Flush+Reload), architecture fingerprinting, transfer-learning base-model identification]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0013?; OWASP ML05, ML07 (transfer learning); NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** The adversary cannot query the victim model. Instead it runs a co-located process on the same host and passively monitors, with Flush+Reload, which functions of the shared DL framework the victim calls. DeepRecon maps the observed function invocations to architecture attributes. It reconstructs VGG19 and ResNet50 from a single forward pass and builds a meta-model that fingerprints which pre-trained family a transfer-learned model came from. The paper evaluates which attributes matter most and discusses framework-level defenses such as obfuscating function-call patterns. A later CCS 2024 paper, DeepCache (liu-2024-deepcache), extends this line to compiled DNN executables.
- **mapping:** shared host running DL framework (architecture and base-model identity) -> Flush+Reload on shared library code -> co-located unprivileged process -> architecture leak and targeted transfer attacks on fine-tuned models

### S-0041 Black-box attacks with limited queries and information

- **canonical id:** `ilyas-2018-limited-queries` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Ilyas, L. Engstrom, A. Athalye, J. Lin, "Black-box Adversarial Attacks with Limited Queries and Information", ICML 2018. arXiv:1804.08598

It uses Natural Evolution Strategies for gradient estimation and demonstrated targeted attacks on the Google Cloud Vision API. This shows that API output truncation is not a sufficient defense.
- **mapping:** cloud vision API -> NES query attack -> top-k or label queries -> targeted misclassification

### S-0042 Manipulating ML: poisoning regression

- **canonical id:** `jagielski-2018-regression-poisoning` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Jagielski, A. Oprea, B. Biggio, C. Liu, C. Nita-Rotaru, B. Li, "Manipulating Machine Learning: Poisoning Attacks and Countermeasures for Regression Learning", IEEE S&P 2018. DOI 10.1109/SP.2018.00057

### S-0043 Trojaning attack on neural networks

- **canonical id:** `liu-2018-trojaning-attack` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Liu, S. Ma, Y. Aafer, W.-C. Lee, J. Zhai, W. Wang, X. Zhang, "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks", NDSS 2018. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2018.23291
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record with DOI 10.14722/ndss.2018.23291
- **attack classes:** [backdoor, trojan, model-modification]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0115.001; OWASP ML10; NISTAML.023, .051

It then retrains the model on reverse-engineered data, without the original training set, to implant a trojan. The attacker needs white-box model access, for example a published model the attacker redistributes. This is a model-supply-chain threat.
- **mapping:** published model -> trojan retraining -> white-box weights -> trigger-conditioned misbehavior

### S-0044 Towards deep learning models resistant to adversarial attacks (PGD)

- **canonical id:** `madry-2018-pgd` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Madry, A. Makelov, L. Schmidt, D. Tsipras, A. Vladu, "Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks", ICLR 2018. arXiv:1706.06083
- **pdf:** madry-2017-pgd.pdf sha256: cbf9bf68f543aa351c3ea6aac7b159d58860b0993df2f9b8f938d8594b2601e1
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API hit 1706.06083v4; OpenAlex
- **attack classes:** [evasion, pgd, adversarial-training]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Frames robustness as a min-max saddle-point problem. It introduces projected gradient descent (PGD) as the "universal first-order adversary" and PGD adversarial training as the main empirical defense. PGD remains the standard white-box L_inf/L2 attack and the evaluation baseline. Robust accuracy comes at a clean-accuracy cost.
- **mapping:** classifier -> PGD perturbation -> white-box -> misclassification (defense: adversarial training)

### S-0045 Rendered Insecure: GPU side channel attacks are practical

- **canonical id:** `naghibijouybari-2018-rendered-insecure` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** H. Naghibijouybari, A. Neupane, Z. Qian, N. Abu-Ghazaleh, "Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical", ACM CCS 2018. DOI 10.1145/3243734.3243831
- **confirmed via:** https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Rendered+Insecure+GPU+Side+Channel+Attacks+are+Practical (DOI, authors, CCS 2018); https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1145/3243734.3243831 (abstract)
- **attack classes:** [GPU side channel, model extraction (architecture/parameters), cross-application leakage, website fingerprinting]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0013 Discover AI Model Ontology?, AML.T0048.004 AI IP Theft?; OWASP ML05; OWASP LLM02:2025?; CWE-1300?/CWE-203 (observable discrepancy); NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** This is the first general demonstration that GPU sharing between co-resident applications leaks secrets through performance counters and resource-tracking APIs. The attacker is an unprivileged spy process that shares the GPU with the victim, interleaves its own work at frame or kernel granularity, and measures the side effects. Two attacks are shown. An OpenGL/WebGL spy fingerprints websites, tracks user activity and infers password keystroke timing. A CUDA spy infers internal parameters of a neural network that another CUDA application is running (for example, the number of neurons per layer). The authors propose mitigations that limit the rate and precision of performance-counter access. This paper starts the line of GPU multi-tenant model-reconnaissance attacks.
- **mapping:** shared GPU in cloud/desktop (model architecture) -> co-resident spy reads GPU performance counters -> attacker can run CUDA/OpenGL code on the same GPU -> architecture leak enabling extraction and transfer attacks

### S-0046 Poison Frogs: clean-label targeted poisoning

- **canonical id:** `shafahi-2018-poison-frogs` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Shafahi, W. R. Huang, M. Najibi, O. Suciu, C. Studer, T. Dumitras, T. Goldstein, "Poison Frogs! Targeted Clean-Label Poisoning Attacks on Neural Networks", NeurIPS 2018. arXiv:1804.00792
- **pdf:** shafahi-2018-poison-frogs.pdf sha256: 521d771c2f831a2e8f025c771cb01f8b06f993901a5d30655dc698b44b6ba126
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (arXiv 1804.00792)
- **attack classes:** [targeted-poisoning, clean-label, feature-collision]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020; OWASP ML02, ML07; NISTAML.012, .024
- **summary:** Feature-collision poisons look correctly labeled to human reviewers, so label auditing fails. They cause a specific target test instance to be misclassified. In transfer learning, a single poison image can succeed. End-to-end training needs more poisons plus a "watermarking" blend. The attacker needs feature-extractor knowledge (grey box) and data injection.
- **mapping:** fine-tuning dataset -> clean-label poison -> data injection + feature extractor knowledge -> targeted misclassification

### S-0047 Ensemble adversarial training: attacks and defenses

- **canonical id:** `tramer-2018-ensemble-adversarial-training` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** F. Tramer et al., "Ensemble Adversarial Training: Attacks and Defenses", ICLR 2018. arXiv:1705.07204
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07204 (arXiv API record, first posted 2017-05-19); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1705.07204 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 3116 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, transfer attack, gradient masking]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.002, AML.T0005; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.025
- **summary:** Shows that single-step adversarial training converges to a degenerate minimum where the loss surface is curved near data points, which masks gradients. Such models then learn to produce weak perturbations rather than to resist strong ones. They remain vulnerable to black-box transfer attacks from undefended models and to a new single-step attack that adds a small random step first (R+FGSM). It proposes Ensemble Adversarial Training, which augments training with perturbations transferred from other static models and improves robustness to black-box transfer on ImageNet. Important for threat models because it separates robustness to white-box from robustness to transfer attacks.
- **mapping:** deployed image classifier -> transfer attack from surrogate -> black-box query or no access -> misclassification

### S-0051 CommanderSong: voice commands hidden in songs

- **canonical id:** `yuan-2018-commandersong` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** X. Yuan et al., "CommanderSong: A Systematic Approach for Practical Adversarial Voice Recognition", USENIX Security 2018. arXiv:1801.08535
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.08535 (arXiv API record, first posted 2018-01-24); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1801.08535 (venue "USENIX Security Symposium", 405 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [adversarial audio, over-the-air attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0043.000, AML.T0015; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022

The construction is automated and is robust to background noise and speaker/microphone distortion. Attack delivery is via radio, TV or online media, with no physical proximity beyond audio playback. ### S-0052 Nettack: adversarial attacks on graph neural networks

- **canonical id:** `zugner-2018-nettack` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** D. Zugner, A. Akbarnejad, S. Gunnemann, "Adversarial Attacks on Neural Networks for Graph Data", KDD 2018. DOI 10.1145/3219819.3220078; arXiv:1805.07984
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07984 (arXiv API record, first posted 2018-05-21); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1805.07984 (venue "Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining", 1305 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [graph evasion, graph poisoning, structure perturbation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01, ML02; NISTAML.022, .024
- **summary:** First adversarial attacks on attributed graphs. Nettack perturbs node features and graph structure (adding or removing edges) to change the classification of a target node, at test time (evasion) and at training time (poisoning). Perturbations preserve degree distribution and feature co-occurrence so they are unnoticeable. A few perturbations sharply reduce GCN accuracy on target nodes, and the attacks transfer to other graph models. This maps directly to fraud-detection and social-graph assets where attackers control some accounts and links.
- **mapping:** GNN fraud/risk/recommender model -> edge and feature perturbation of attacker-controlled nodes -> ability to create links/accounts -> misclassification of target (fraud passes)

### S-0053 A Little Is Enough: circumventing Byzantine-robust distributed learning

- **canonical id:** `baruch-2019-a-little-is-enough` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** M. Baruch, G. Baruch, Y. Goldberg, "A Little Is Enough: Circumventing Defenses For Distributed Learning", NeurIPS 2019. arXiv:1902.06156
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06156 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-02-16); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1902.06156 (venue "Neural Information Processing Systems", 773 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [FL poisoning, non-omniscient attack, robust-aggregation bypass]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000; OWASP ML10; NISTAML.011, .023
- **summary:** Prior Byzantine attacks assumed omniscient attackers and large parameter changes. Small, well-crafted changes within the per-coordinate standard deviation of benign updates evade all tested robust aggregators (Krum, trimmed mean, Bulyan) without knowledge of other clients' data. With 20% corrupt workers the attack degrades accuracy substantially (for example on CIFAR-10) or installs backdoors.
- **mapping:** distributed/federated training -> small statistically camouflaged malicious updates -> compromised fraction of workers -> accuracy loss or backdoor
- **note:** The CIFAR-10 example is from memory; the 20% figure is in the abstract.

### S-0056 Adversarial sensor attack on LiDAR-based perception

- **canonical id:** `cao-2019-lidar-adversarial-sensor-attack` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Cao et al., "Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving", ACM CCS 2019. DOI 10.1145/3319535.3339815; arXiv:1907.06826

- **summary:** First security study of LiDAR perception in autonomous vehicles. Naive LiDAR spoofing (injecting laser points) fails because the ML object detector (Apollo) filters it. The authors model the spoofing capability and optimize spoofed point patterns to make the detector perceive a fake obstacle close in front of the victim vehicle. Driving consequences such as emergency braking are shown. Attacker: physical laser spoofer near the victim, knowledge of the open-source perception model.
- **mapping:** AV perception (LiDAR) -> optimized laser spoofing of fake obstacle -> line-of-sight spoofing hardware + model knowledge -> unsafe braking or collision (safety, availability)

### S-0057 The Secret Sharer (unintended memorization)

- **canonical id:** `carlini-2019-secret-sharer` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, C. Liu, U. Erlingsson, J. Kos, D. Song, "The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks", USENIX Security 2019. arXiv:1802.08232

Rare secrets in training data can be extracted, for example from an email-autocomplete model. DP training prevents it. It is the basis of canary-based privacy audits.
- **mapping:** text model trained on user data -> secret extraction -> query access -> disclosure of rare secrets (SSNs, keys)

### S-0058 On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness (threat-model specification checklist)

It also requires adaptive attacks that are aware of the defense. The checklist is a template for the precondition fields of evasion threats and for adversarial review of defense claims in the corpus.

### S-0059 Activation clustering for backdoor detection in training data

- **canonical id:** `chen-2019-activation-clustering` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence medium
- **citation:** B. Chen et al., "Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by Activation Clustering", SafeAI@AAAI 2019. arXiv:1811.03728
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.03728 (arXiv API record, first posted 2018-11-09); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1811.03728 (venue "SafeAI@AAAI", 1022 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [backdoor defense, poison detection]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0020 / AML.T0018.000; NISTAML.023 mitigation
- **summary:** Detects poisoned training samples by clustering the last-hidden-layer activations of each class (ICA, then 2-means). A backdoored class splits into a clean and a poisoned cluster. Poisoned samples can then be removed and the model retrained. It needs access to the training data and model but no clean trusted dataset. Clean-label and adaptive attacks reduce its effectiveness.
- **mapping:** training dataset -> activation-clustering sanitization (mitigation) -> defender has training data and model -> removal of dirty-label poison

### S-0060 Certified robustness via randomized smoothing (context)

- **canonical id:** `cohen-2019-randomized-smoothing` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high **Group C: Data poisoning, backdoors and trojans**
- **citation:** J. Cohen, E. Rosenfeld, J. Z. Kolter, "Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing", ICML 2019. arXiv:1902.02918
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918 (DataCite)
- **attack classes:** [certified-defense]
- **catalog ids:** NISTAML.022 mitigation
- **summary:** Context only. Gaussian-noise randomized smoothing gives a provable L2 robustness radius and scales to ImageNet. The certified radii are small relative to realistic perturbations, and patch or physical attacks fall outside the L2 guarantee. It is useful as a "control with formal guarantee but narrow scope" node.
- **mapping:** control -> evasion (L2-bounded) -> certified radius -> residual risk outside the bound

### S-0061 STRIP: run-time trojan input detection

- **canonical id:** `gao-2019-strip` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Gao et al., "STRIP: A Defence Against Trojan Attacks on Deep Neural Networks", ACSAC 2019. DOI 10.1145/3359789.3359790; arXiv:1902.06531
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3359789.3359790 (Proceedings of the 35th Annual Computer Security Applications Conference, 2019); https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06531 (arXiv API record)
- **attack classes:** [backdoor defense, run-time detection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS mitigation (AML.M00xx input validation, ?); NISTAML.023 mitigation
- **summary:** A run-time detector: it superimposes the incoming input with various clean images and measures the entropy of the model's predictions. Trojaned inputs give low-entropy (consistently the target class) predictions because the trigger dominates, while clean inputs give high entropy. It is model-agnostic and has low false rejection/acceptance on input-agnostic triggers. Later adaptive and input-specific triggers (e.g., input-aware dynamic backdoors) evade it.
- **mapping:** deployed classifier -> STRIP input-perturbation entropy test (mitigation) -> defender can query model at run time -> blocks universal-trigger inputs; bypassed by dynamic triggers
- **note:** Semantic Scholar mislabels the venue as "Asia-Pacific Computer Systems Architecture Conference"; Crossref confirms ACSAC 2019.

### S-0062 Terminal Brain Damage (single bit-flips, Rowhammer)

- **canonical id:** `hong-2019-terminal-brain-damage` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** S. Hong, P. Frigo, Y. Kaya, C. Giuffrida, T. Dumitras, "Terminal Brain Damage: Exposing the Graceless Degradation in Deep Neural Networks Under Hardware Fault Attacks", USENIX Security 2019. arXiv:1906.01017
- **pdf:** hong-2019-terminal-brain-damage.pdf sha256: 24ae3c63c5b01d6eece7f410cb734cf96c6180de50e991c85e4fef9a68b4590c
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1906.01017); abstract read from the PDF
- **attack classes:** [bit-flip, fault-injection, rowhammer]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018 (?), AML.T0010.000 (?); NISTAML ? (no hardware-fault class); CWE-1256 (Rowhammer), CWE-1261 ?
- **summary:** Across 19 DNN models (six architectures, three tasks), most have at least one parameter whose single bit-flip, typically in the exponent, causes an accuracy loss over 90%. An estimated 40-50% of parameters can each cause drops above 10%. A co-located Rowhammer attacker with no knowledge of the model caused drops of up to 99%. Mitigations discussed include restricting activation magnitudes and low-precision numerics.
- **mapping:** model weights in shared DRAM -> Rowhammer bit-flip -> co-located unprivileged process -> integrity / availability collapse

### S-0065 TextBugger: adversarial text against real-world applications

- **canonical id:** `li-2019-textbugger` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** J. Li et al., "TextBugger: Generating Adversarial Text Against Real-world Applications", NDSS 2019. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2019.23138; arXiv:1812.05271
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05271 (arXiv API record, first posted 2018-12-13); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1812.05271 (venue "Network and Distributed System Security Symposium", 914 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [adversarial text, black-box evasion, toxic content detection bypass]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.001; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.025
- **summary:** Generates adversarial text with character-level bugs (insert, swap, delete, visually similar substitutions) and word-level synonym substitutions, in both white-box and black-box settings. Targets include commercial sentiment-analysis and toxic-content-detection services (for example Google Cloud NLP, IBM Watson, Microsoft Azure, Amazon AWS, Perspective). It reports high success with 94.9% of adversarial texts still correctly read by humans, and sub-linear computational complexity. This is the canonical evidence for evasion of production moderation APIs.
- **mapping:** commercial moderation/NLP API -> character and word perturbation -> black-box query access -> toxic or abusive content passes
- **note:** The list of commercial services is from memory of the paper; the abstract confirms "real-world applications" and toxic content detection.

### S-0066 Unintended feature leakage in collaborative learning

- **citation:** M. Nasr, R. Shokri, A. Houmansadr, "Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning: Passive and Active White-box Inference Attacks against Centralized and Federated Learning", IEEE S&P 2019. DOI 10.1109/SP.2019.00065; arXiv:1812.00910
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record with DOI 10.1109/sp.2019.00065

### S-0068 Knockoff Nets

- **canonical id:** `orekondy-2019-knockoff-nets` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Orekondy, B. Schiele, M. Fritz, "Knockoff Nets: Stealing Functionality of Black-Box Models", CVPR 2019. DOI 10.1109/CVPR.2019.00509; arXiv:1812.02766

### S-0069 Bit-Flip Attack (progressive bit search)

- **canonical id:** `rakin-2019-bit-flip-attack` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2019; confidence medium
- **citation:** A. S. Rakin, Z. He, D. Fan, "Bit-Flip Attack: Crushing Neural Network With Progressive Bit Search", ICCV 2019. DOI 10.1109/ICCV.2019.00130
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1109/iccv.2019.00130
- **attack classes:** [bit-flip, quantized-model-attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018 (?); NISTAML ?
- **summary:** Progressive bit search finds the most vulnerable bits in 8-bit quantized weights. A handful of flips (on the order of 10-20 for ResNet-18 on ImageNet, per my recall) degrades accuracy to random guessing. The attacker is white-box. It is the foundation for later Rowhammer-realized attacks. A 2023 survey of bit-flip attacks and defenses exists (Qian et al., Electronics, DOI 10.3390/electronics12040853).
- **mapping:** quantized model in memory -> targeted bit flips -> white-box + fault capability -> accuracy collapse

### S-0070 White-box vs black-box: Bayes-optimal membership inference

- **canonical id:** `sablayrolles-2019-bayes-optimal-mia` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Sablayrolles et al., "White-box vs Black-box: Bayes Optimal Strategies for Membership Inference", ICML 2019. arXiv:1908.11229
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.11229 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-08-29); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1908.11229 (venue "International Conference on Machine Learning", 471 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [membership inference, theory]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000; OWASP ML04; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** Derives the Bayes-optimal membership inference strategy under assumptions on the parameter distribution and shows it depends only on the loss. Black-box access is therefore asymptotically as powerful as white-box. Tractable approximations outperform prior attacks up to ResNet-101 on ImageNet. Implication for threat models: hiding weights does not reduce MIA risk if losses or confidences are exposed.
- **mapping:** model API exposing scores -> loss-based MIA -> black-box access -> membership disclosure equal to white-box

### S-0072 Psychoacoustic hiding of adversarial audio against ASR

### S-0073 Label-consistent backdoor attacks

- **canonical id:** `turner-2019-label-consistent-backdoor` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Turner, D. Tsipras, A. Madry, "Label-Consistent Backdoor Attacks", arXiv 2019. arXiv:1912.02771
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02771 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-12-05); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1912.02771 (venue "arXiv.org", 556 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [clean-label backdoor, adversarial perturbation, GAN interpolation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004; OWASP ML02; NISTAML.021
- **summary:** Makes backdoor poisoning label-consistent: injected images keep their correct labels, so human inspection does not flag them. Poisoned images are made hard to classify from their natural features, using adversarial perturbations or GAN latent interpolation, so the model learns to rely on the trigger instead. Effective with a small poison fraction on CIFAR-10. This is the standard clean-label backdoor baseline.
- **mapping:** model trained on scraped/crowd data -> clean-label trigger poisoning -> attacker contributes correctly labelled samples -> trigger-controlled misclassification
- **note:** Semantic Scholar lists no peer-reviewed venue; an earlier version circulated as an ICLR 2019 OpenReview submission (not verified).

### S-0074 Universal adversarial triggers for NLP

- **canonical id:** `wallace-2019-universal-adversarial-triggers` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** E. Wallace et al., "Universal Adversarial Triggers for Attacking and Analyzing NLP", EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019. DOI 10.18653/v1/D19-1221; arXiv:1908.07125
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.07125 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-08-20); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1908.07125 (venue "Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing", 1149 citations on 2026-10-03)

A gradient-guided token search finds short triggers (one word for classification, a few words for language modeling). Triggers drop SNLI accuracy from 89.94% to 0.55%, make 72% of "why" questions in SQuAD answer "to kill american people", and make GPT-2 produce racist output. ### S-0076 Latent backdoor attacks that survive transfer learning

- **canonical id:** `yao-2019-latent-backdoor` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2019; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Yao, H. Li, H. Zheng, B. Y. Zhao, "Latent Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks", ACM CCS 2019. DOI 10.1145/3319535.3354209
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3319535.3354209; Semantic Scholar title match with abstract
- **attack classes:** [backdoor, transfer learning, teacher-model poisoning]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0115.001, AML.T0010.003; OWASP ML07, ML10, LLM03:2025; NISTAML.023, .051
- **summary:** Traditional backdoors are disrupted when users fine-tune a provider's "teacher" model on their own task. Latent backdoors are embedded in a teacher model for a target label that does not yet exist in the teacher's task. They activate automatically when a downstream student model, built by transfer learning, includes that label. The attack is shown on traffic-sign, iris and face-recognition tasks, and in the physical world. This is the reference for supply-chain backdoors in pretrained models that propagate to fine-tuned derivatives.
- **mapping:** pretrained model on hub -> latent backdoor inherited via fine-tuning -> attacker publishes or influences teacher model -> targeted misclassification in downstream model

### S-0077 Deep leakage from gradients

### S-0079 How to backdoor federated learning

### S-0080 SNIFF: model reverse engineering with sign-bit fault attacks

- **canonical id:** `breier-2020-sniff` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** J. Breier, D. Jap, X. Hou, S. Bhasin, Y. Liu, "SNIFF: Reverse Engineering of Neural Networks with Fault Attacks", arXiv:2002.11021, 2020 (later IEEE Trans. Reliability; venue not re-confirmed)
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API id_list=2002.11021
- **attack classes:** [fault-assisted model extraction, sign-bit flip, parameter recovery]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0048.004?; OWASP ML05; NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** SNIFF flips the sign bit of intermediate values with a fault, using glitching, laser or Rowhammer, and uses the effect to recover model parameters exactly. It is the first provably exact extraction method for deep feature-extractor layers. With 64-bit floats, the parameter precision error is below 1e-13 on the tested Keras networks, six orders of magnitude better than the prior state of the art. The attacker controls fault injection on the inference device and observes outputs. The paper discusses fault-resistance countermeasures.
- **mapping:** inference device (weights) -> sign-bit fault injection plus output observation -> physical/fault access -> exact parameter extraction

### S-0086 Adversarial policies: attacking deep RL

- **canonical id:** `gleave-2020-adversarial-policies` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Gleave et al., "Adversarial Policies: Attacking Deep Reinforcement Learning", ICLR 2020. arXiv:1905.10615
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10615 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-05-25); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1905.10615 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 452 citations on 2026-10-03)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.001; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022

They succeed more in high-dimensional observation spaces and induce unusual victim activations. Attacker capability: act in the same environment with black-box access to the victim.

### S-0087 ILFO: adversarial attack on adaptive (early-exit) neural networks

- **canonical id:** `haque-2020-ilfo` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence medium
- **citation:** M. Haque, A. Chauhan, C. Liu, W. Yang, "ILFO: Adversarial Attack on Adaptive Neural Networks", CVPR 2020. DOI 10.1109/cvpr42600.2020.01427

- **attack classes:** [energy-latency attack, adaptive inference]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0029, AML.T0034.001; NISTAML.014
- **summary:** Adaptive networks that skip layers or exit early on easy inputs save energy. ILFO crafts imperceptible perturbations that force them to run nearly all layers, removing the energy savings. Large increases in FLOPs and energy on SkipNet and SACT-style models are reported. This shows efficiency mechanisms are an availability attack surface.
- **mapping:** adaptive/edge DNN -> computation-maximizing perturbation -> attacker supplies inputs -> energy/latency exhaustion (battery, cost)

### S-0088 DeepSniffer: DNN architecture extraction from hardware hints

- **canonical id:** `hu-2020-deepsniffer` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2020; confidence medium
- **citation:** X. Hu, L. Liang, S. Li, L. Deng et al., "DeepSniffer: A DNN Model Extraction Framework Based on Learning Architectural Hints", ASPLOS 2020. DOI 10.1145/3373376.3378460
- **confirmed via:** https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=DeepSniffer+DNN+model+extraction+framework+learning+architectural+hints (DOI, ASPLOS); https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1145/3373376.3378460 (abstract)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0013?, AML.T0005 Create Proxy AI Model?; OWASP ML05; NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** DeepSniffer learns to infer a victim DNN's layer sequence and dimensions from architecture-level events observed on the accelerator platform, such as kernel read/write volumes and execution latency. The abstract says this avoids three limitations of earlier hardware-event extraction: the need for prior knowledge of the victim model, poor robustness, and incomplete results. The attacker is grey-box, with physical or co-located observation of memory and bus events but no access to weights. The recovered architecture is used to improve transfer-based adversarial attacks against the victim. This entry's details come from the abstract; I did not read the full paper.
- **mapping:** on-device/edge accelerator running proprietary DNN -> observe kernel memory-traffic and timing -> physical or co-located bus observation -> architecture theft -> stronger evasion

### S-0090 TextFooler: is BERT really robust?

- **canonical id:** `jin-2020-textfooler` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** D. Jin, Z. Jin, J. T. Zhou, P. Szolovits, "Is BERT Really Robust? A Strong Baseline for Natural Language Attack on Text Classification and Entailment", AAAI 2020. DOI 10.1609/AAAI.V34I05.6311; arXiv:1907.11932
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11932 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-07-27); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1907.11932 (venue "AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence", 1435 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [adversarial text, black-box evasion, synonym substitution]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.001; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.025
- **summary:** A black-box (score-based) attack that ranks words by importance and replaces them with semantically similar, POS-consistent synonyms until the label flips. It attacks BERT, CNN and LSTM models on text classification and entailment, keeping semantics and grammaticality so humans still label the text correctly. Complexity is linear in text length. It is the standard baseline for evading text classifiers, including spam, fraud and toxicity filters.

### S-0093 Stolen Memories: calibrated white-box membership inference

- **canonical id:** `leino-2020-stolen-memories` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** K. Leino, M. Fredrikson, "Stolen Memories: Leveraging Model Memorization for Calibrated White-Box Membership Inference", USENIX Security 2020. arXiv:1906.11798
