### S-0094 StegoNet: turning a DNN into stegomalware

- **canonical id:** `liu-2020-stegonet` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Liu, Z. Liu, Q. Liu, W. Wen et al., "StegoNet: Turn Deep Neural Network into a Stegomalware", ACSAC 2020. DOI 10.1145/3427228.3427268
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record (ACSAC 2020); https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1145/3427228.3427268 (abstract)
- **attack classes:** [payload injection in parameters, input-triggered malware, stegomalware]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018?; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; NIST NISTAML.05
- **summary:** StegoNet uses model parameters as the payload channel. It works for uncompressed models, which have redundancy, using LSB substitution, resilience training, value mapping and sign-mapping, and also for deeply compressed edge models with no redundancy, with no accuracy loss. Its distinctive feature is triggering: the payload is released by specified physical-world inputs to the DNN, making the model self-contained evasive malware. The attacker must be able to distribute the model.
- **mapping:** third-party model in an app or edge device -> parameter-embedded payload with input trigger -> model distribution channel -> code execution on trigger

### S-0095 Phantom of the ADAS: split-second phantom attacks

- **canonical id:** `nassi-2020-phantom-of-the-adas` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** B. Nassi et al., "Phantom of the ADAS: Securing Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems from Split-Second Phantom Attacks", ACM CCS 2020. DOI 10.1145/3372297.3423359
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3372297.3423359; Semantic Scholar title match with abstract
- **attack classes:** [perception spoofing, projection attack, physical evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0041; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Shows that commercial ADAS (Tesla Model X HW2.5/HW3 Autopilot and Mobileye 630) treat a depthless object shown for a few milliseconds as a real obstacle or sign. Attackers embed phantom road signs in a digital-billboard advertisement or project a phantom pedestrian with a drone-mounted projector. The result is sudden braking by Autopilot and false notifications from Mobileye. The attacker needs no access to the vehicle, only to a display or projector in its field of view. The paper proposes GhostBusters, a camera-only committee-of-experts detector that checks light, context, surface and depth cues.
- **mapping:** vehicle ADAS camera perception -> phantom projection or billboard injection -> remote line-of-sight display -> unsafe braking, traffic disruption (safety)

### S-0096 Input-aware dynamic backdoor attack

- **canonical id:** `nguyen-2020-input-aware-dynamic-backdoor` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** T. A. Nguyen, A. Tran, "Input-Aware Dynamic Backdoor Attack", NeurIPS 2020. arXiv:2010.08138
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.08138 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-10-16); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2010.08138 (venue "Neural Information Processing Systems", 601 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [dynamic-trigger backdoor, defense evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004; OWASP ML10; NISTAML.023
- **summary:** Replaces the fixed trigger with an input-specific trigger produced by a generator trained with a diversity loss. A cross-trigger test enforces non-reusability, so a trigger made for one input does not activate the backdoor on another. Detection by trigger reverse-engineering (Neural Cleanse), pruning (Fine-Pruning) and STRIP fails because no single universal trigger exists. Attacker: controls training.
- **mapping:** outsourced/third-party trained model -> input-specific trigger backdoor -> control of training pipeline -> targeted misclassification evading backdoor scanners

### S-0097 Prediction poisoning: active defense against model stealing

- **canonical id:** `orekondy-2020-prediction-poisoning` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Orekondy, B. Schiele, M. Fritz, "Prediction Poisoning: Towards Defenses Against DNN Model Stealing Attacks", ICLR 2020. arXiv:1906.10908
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.10908 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-06-26); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1906.10908 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 207 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [model-stealing defense, output perturbation]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0024.002; OWASP ML05; NISTAML.031 mitigation
- **summary:** An active defense: the API perturbs its posterior outputs to maximize angular deviation of the attacker's training gradient while bounding utility loss for benign users. This poisons the clone's training objective. It is effective against several stealing attacks (e.g., Knockoff Nets, Jacobian-based augmentation) where passive defenses such as top-1 truncation fail.
- **mapping:** prediction API -> gradient-redirection output perturbation (mitigation) -> provider controls outputs -> degraded clone quality

### S-0098 Intriguing properties of adversarial ML attacks in the problem space

- **canonical id:** `pierazzi-2020-problem-space-attacks` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** F. Pierazzi, F. Pendlebury, J. Cortellazzi, L. Cavallaro, "Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space", IEEE S&P 2020. DOI 10.1109/SP40000.2020.00073; arXiv:1911.02142 (the current arXiv version is the extended journal version, ACM TOPS, DOI 10.1145/3742895, first author Cortellazzi)
- **pdf:** pierazzi-2020-problem-space-attacks.pdf sha256: c810ebafc4dbd49e66c16368158d1120abd7360033dd66fa84e848c1da242fe6
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1109/SP40000.2020.00073 (title, venue, authors confirmed); https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02142 (arXiv API record); Semantic Scholar maps the arXiv id to ACM TOPS 10.1145/3742895
- **attack classes:** [evasion, problem-space attack, malware evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.000, AML.T0043.003; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022; CWE-1039
- **summary:** Formalizes evasion in domains such as software where no inverse feature mapping exists. It defines four constraint families that any realizable adversarial object must satisfy: available transformations, preserved semantics, plausibility and robustness to preprocessing, and absence of artifacts. It introduces side-effect features, the features that change as a by-product of a real transformation, and proves necessary and sufficient conditions for a problem-space attack to exist. It then builds an automated Android attack that transplants benign code gadgets (organ harvesting) into malware. The attack evades DREBIN-style linear classifiers and SVMs, including hardened ones, at scale. Attacker: grey or white box on a feature-based detector, inference-time, able to modify the binary but required to keep it functional.
- **mapping:** malware/phishing/IDS classifier -> semantics-preserving problem-space evasion -> attacker can modify the artifact and knows (or approximates) the feature space -> malicious sample accepted (integrity)
- **note:** PDF is the arXiv extended (TOPS) version, not the S&P camera-ready.

### S-0099 TBT: targeted bit trojan via bit flips

- **canonical id:** `rakin-2020-tbt` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** A. S. Rakin, Z. He, D. Fan, "TBT: Targeted Neural Network Attack With Bit Trojan", IEEE/CVF CVPR 2020. DOI 10.1109/CVPR42600.2020.01321; arXiv:1909.05193
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record (CVPR 2020); arXiv API id_list=1909.05193
- **attack classes:** [bit-flip backdoor, Rowhammer, trigger generation, inference-time trojan insertion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000 Poison AI Model?, AML.T0043.004 Insert Backdoor Trigger; OWASP ML10; NIST NISTAML.02
- **summary:** TBT inserts a trojan into an already deployed DNN without retraining access. It co-designs a trigger and a small set of vulnerable weight bits in DRAM. Flipping those bits, for example with Rowhammer, leaves clean accuracy intact, while any input that carries the trigger goes to a target class. On ResNet-18 / CIFAR-10, flipping 84 of 88 million weight bits sends 92% of triggered test images to the target class. The attacker needs knowledge of the model and a fault primitive on its memory.
- **mapping:** deployed model weights in DRAM -> targeted bit flips plus trigger -> co-located fault-injection (Rowhammer) -> covert backdoor

### S-0102 Light Commands: laser-based audio injection

- **canonical id:** `sugawara-2020-light-commands` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Sugawara et al., "Light Commands: Laser-Based Audio Injection Attacks on Voice-Controllable Systems", USENIX Security 2020. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity20/presentation/sugawara

### S-0104 Imitation attacks and defenses for black-box machine translation

- **canonical id:** `wallace-2020-imitation-attacks-mt` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** E. Wallace, M. Stern, D. Song, "Imitation Attacks and Defenses for Black-box Machine Translation Systems", EMNLP 2020. DOI 10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.446; arXiv:2004.15015
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.15015 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-04-30); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2004.15015 (venue "Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing", 146 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [model imitation, transfer adversarial examples, production API]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005.001, AML.T0043.002; OWASP ML05, LLM10:2025; NISTAML.031
- **summary:** Steals production MT systems (Google, Bing, Systran) by querying with monolingual sentences and training imitation models on the outputs. Imitation models come within 0.6 BLEU of the targets. White-box attacks on the imitation then transfer to the production systems, causing targeted mistranslations and malicious nonsense outputs. A defense that perturbs outputs reduces imitation quality at small BLEU cost. This is the template for distillation-style theft of LLM APIs.
- **mapping:** commercial NLP/LLM API -> imitation via distillation queries -> paid API access -> IP theft plus transfer attacks on the original

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020; OWASP ML10; NISTAML.023
- **summary:** Proves that robustness to backdoors implies robustness to adversarial examples, and that detecting backdoors in a model is NP-hard in general, so FL backdoor defenses face fundamental limits. Edge-case backdoors target inputs from the tail of the input distribution (for example a particular airline's airplanes, or specific sentences). They evade norm clipping, differential privacy noise and robust aggregation. Shown on image classification, OCR and next-word prediction. Attacker: one or a few clients with edge-case data.
- **mapping:** FL model -> edge-case backdoor via poisoned client updates -> few compromised clients -> targeted misbehaviour on rare inputs evading defenses

### S-0106 Cache Telepathy

### S-0107 DeepHammer

- **canonical id:** `yao-2020-deephammer` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2020; confidence medium
- **citation:** F. Yao, A. S. Rakin, D. Fan, "DeepHammer: Depleting the Intelligence of Deep Neural Networks through Targeted Chain of Bit Flips", USENIX Security 2020. arXiv:2003.13746
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2003.13746)
- **attack classes:** [bit-flip, rowhammer, end-to-end-fault-attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018 (?); NISTAML ?
- **summary:** An end-to-end Rowhammer exploitation that flips a chain of targeted bits in quantized DNN weights in real DRAM. It uses memory massaging to place weight pages on vulnerable rows and degrades models to random-guess accuracy within minutes (per my recall). It turns theoretical bit-flip attacks into a practical co-tenant threat.
- **mapping:** DNN on shared host -> Rowhammer + memory massaging -> co-located process -> model availability / integrity destroyed

### S-0108 CloudLeak: stealing large DNNs from cloud APIs with adversarial examples

- **canonical id:** `yu-2020-cloudleak` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2020; confidence medium
- **citation:** H. Yu et al., "CloudLeak: Large-Scale Deep Learning Models Stealing Through Adversarial Examples", NDSS 2020. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2020.24178
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.14722/ndss.2020.24178; Semantic Scholar title match with abstract
- **attack classes:** [model extraction, MLaaS, adversarial-example queries]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005.001, AML.T0048.004; OWASP ML05; NISTAML.031
- **summary:** A black-box extraction attack on commercial MLaaS platforms that uses adversarial examples near the decision boundary as queries (feature-fool generation). This needs far fewer queries than random sampling. Combined with transfer learning from a public pretrained model, it extracts large DNNs from cloud vision services with near-perfect fidelity and much lower query cost. Commercial platforms tested include Microsoft, Face++, IBM, Google and Clarifai.
- **mapping:** cloud vision API -> boundary-sample extraction + transfer learning -> paid query access -> stolen model (IP, cost)
- **note:** The list of commercial platforms is from memory; the abstract confirms cloud-based platforms.

### S-0110 Blind backdoors (code poisoning)

### S-0111 FLTrust: Byzantine-robust FL via trust bootstrapping

- **canonical id:** `cao-2021-fltrust` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** X. Cao, M. Fang, J. Liu, N. Z. Gong, "FLTrust: Byzantine-robust Federated Learning via Trust Bootstrapping", NDSS 2021. DOI 10.14722/NDSS.2021.24434; arXiv:2012.13995
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.13995 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-12-27); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2012.13995 (venue "Network and Distributed System Security Symposium", 1226 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [FL defense, robust aggregation]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0020 (FL); NISTAML.011 mitigation
- **summary:** The server keeps a small clean root dataset and trains a server model update each round. Client updates get a trust score from ReLU-clipped cosine similarity with the server update and are normalized to its magnitude before weighted aggregation. This gives a root of trust that resists strong adaptive model-poisoning attacks even with many malicious clients, at the cost of needing representative server-side data.
- **mapping:** FL aggregator -> trust-bootstrapped aggregation (mitigation) -> server holds small clean dataset -> resists model poisoning

### S-0112 Invisible for both camera and LiDAR: attacking multi-sensor fusion

- **canonical id:** `cao-2021-invisible-camera-lidar-msf` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Cao, N. Wang, C. Xiao, D. Yang, J. Fang, et al., "Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Perception in Autonomous Driving Under Physical-World Attacks", IEEE S&P 2021. DOI 10.1109/SP40001.2021.00076; arXiv:2106.09249
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1109/sp40001.2021.00076; https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09249 (arXiv API record and abstract)
- **attack classes:** [physical evasion, multi-sensor fusion attack, 3D-printed adversarial object]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0041, AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Challenges the assumption that multi-sensor fusion (MSF) is robust because not all sensors can be attacked at once. The attack optimizes a physically realizable 3D-printed adversarial object that both camera and LiDAR detectors fail to see, so the fusion pipeline (Baidu Apollo) misses it and the vehicle crashes into it. The object is evaluated in simulation and with real 3D-printed objects. MSF therefore does not provide a guaranteed defense against simultaneous attacks on all sources.
- **mapping:** AV multi-sensor-fusion perception -> adversarial 3D object invisible to all sensors -> attacker places object on road + white-box model -> collision (safety)

### S-0114 When machine unlearning jeopardizes privacy

- **canonical id:** `chen-2021-unlearning-jeopardizes-privacy` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Chen et al., "When Machine Unlearning Jeopardizes Privacy", ACM CCS 2021. DOI 10.1145/3460120.3484756; arXiv:2005.02205
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02205 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-05-05); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2005.02205 (venue "Conference on Computer and Communications Security", 340 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [membership inference, unlearning leakage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000; OWASP ML04; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** An attacker with access to both the original and the unlearned model (before and after a deletion request) compares their outputs on a target sample. This infers whether the sample was in the original training set and has since been deleted. The attack can beat classic MIA on the original model, especially for well-generalized models. Countermeasures evaluated include publishing only labels, temperature scaling and differential privacy. Unlearning as a GDPR control can therefore itself leak.
- **mapping:** ML service honoring deletion requests -> before/after model differencing MIA -> query access to both versions -> disclosure of who requested deletion

### S-0117 Stealing links from graph neural networks

- **canonical id:** `he-2021-stealing-links-gnn` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.001; OWASP ML03, ML04; NISTAML.032/.034

### S-0118 Entangled watermarks vs model extraction

### S-0119 MAZE: data-free model stealing via zeroth-order gradient estimation

- **canonical id:** `kariyappa-2021-maze` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** S. Kariyappa, A. Prakash, M. K. Qureshi, "MAZE: Data-Free Model Stealing Attack Using Zeroth-Order Gradient Estimation", CVPR 2021. DOI 10.1109/CVPR46437.2021.01360; arXiv:2005.03161
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.03161 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-05-06); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2005.03161 (venue "Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition", 206 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [model extraction, data-free, zeroth-order optimization]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005.001; OWASP ML05; NISTAML.031
- **summary:** Trains a generator to synthesize queries that maximize clone-victim disagreement. The gradient through the black-box victim is estimated with zeroth-order methods. ### S-0123 Adversary instantiation: lower bounds for DP training

### S-0125 Dirty Road Can Attack: physical attack on automated lane centering

- **canonical id:** `sato-2021-dirty-road-lane-centering` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Sato et al., "Dirty Road Can Attack: Security of Deep Learning based Automated Lane Centering under Physical-World Attack", USENIX Security 2021. arXiv:2009.06701
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06701 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-09-14); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2009.06701 (venue "USENIX Security Symposium", 165 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [physical evasion, adversarial road patch, lane detection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0041, AML.T0043.000; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** Attacks deep-learning automated lane centering (ALC) with "dirty road patches" that look like normal road stains. The optimization accounts for the closed loop in which the attack changes vehicle control and therefore later camera frames. On a production ALC (OpenPilot) across 80 real driving-trace scenarios it reaches over 97.5% success, with an average time to success under 0.903 s, which is below average driver reaction time. It is robust to lighting and viewing-angle changes. The attacker needs physical access to the road surface and the open-source model.

### S-0128 Manipulating the Byzantine: optimized model poisoning in FL

- **canonical id:** `shejwalkar-2021-manipulating-the-byzantine` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** V. Shejwalkar, A. Houmansadr, "Manipulating the Byzantine: Optimizing Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses for Federated Learning", NDSS 2021. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2021.24498

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000; OWASP ML10; NISTAML.011

- **aliases merged:** `shumailov-2021-sponge (supply-infra-misuse.md)`
- **citation:** I. Shumailov, Y. Zhao, D. Bates, N. Papernot, R. Mullins, R. Anderson, "Sponge Examples: Energy-Latency Attacks on Neural Networks", IEEE EuroS&P 2021. DOI 10.1109/EuroSP51992.2021.00024; arXiv:2006.03463
- **pdf:** shumailov-2021-sponge-examples.pdf sha256: 9496a07e354a4e71e1f3d82f9223103cf60a569bfdd7c32f8a98bb3aa44f9bca
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1109/eurosp51992.2021.00024; abstract read from the PDF
- **attack classes:** [energy-latency, denial-of-service, sponge-example]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0029, AML.T0034; OWASP LLM10:2025; NISTAML.014
- **summary:** Inputs crafted by genetic algorithms (black-box) or L-BFGS (white-box) maximize energy consumption and latency. This is the first DoS attack on ML components. Language models are especially vulnerable, with roughly 30x increases in energy and latency across CPU, GPU and ASIC simulators. Against the Microsoft Azure translator, response time went from 1 ms to 6 s (6000x). The proposed defense is worst-case energy analysis and cut-offs.
- **mapping:** inference service -> sponge inputs -> query access -> availability loss + energy / cost increase
- **also captured as `shumailov-2021-sponge` (supply-infra-misuse.md):** This is the seminal work on inputs crafted to maximise energy use and latency in neural networks. It is the root of the availability class that NIST AI 100-2 calls energy-latency attacks. Sponge inputs increase compute per query on hardware accelerators, so they can degrade service or raise cost without high query volume. Read it with Engorgio and OverThink for LLM-specific versions. Mapping: inference service capacity and cost -> resource-maximising inputs -> attacker can submit queries -> availability loss, inflated cost

### S-0131 Systematic evaluation of privacy risks of ML models

- **canonical id:** `song-mittal-2021-systematic-privacy-risks` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** L. Song, P. Mittal, "Systematic Evaluation of Privacy Risks of Machine Learning Models", USENIX Security 2021. arXiv:2003.10595
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10595 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-03-24); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2003.10595 (venue "USENIX Security Symposium", 528 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [membership inference, privacy risk score, defense evaluation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000; OWASP ML04; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** Shows that NN-based membership attacks underestimate risk. Simple metric-based attacks (correctness, confidence, entropy, and a new modified prediction entropy) with class-specific thresholds are stronger. Defenses such as adversarial regularization and MemGuard are re-evaluated against adaptive attackers and offer less protection than claimed. A per-sample "privacy risk score" estimates each record's membership likelihood, a useful record-level risk metric for threat models.
- **mapping:** model trained on personal data -> metric-based membership inference -> score access -> per-record privacy risk
- **note:** The MemGuard and adversarial-regularization re-evaluation is from memory of the paper.

### S-0132 Data-free model extraction

- **canonical id:** `truong-2021-data-free-model-extraction` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** J.-B. Truong, P. Maini, R. J. Walls, N. Papernot, "Data-Free Model Extraction", CVPR 2021. DOI 10.1109/CVPR46437.2021.00474; arXiv:2011.14779
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.14779 (arXiv API record, first posted 2020-11-30); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2011.14779 (venue "Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition", 256 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [model extraction, data-free, black-box]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005.001, AML.T0048.004; OWASP ML05, LLM10:2025; NISTAML.031
- **summary:** Removes the need for a surrogate dataset. A generator synthesizes queries that maximize disagreement between the victim and the clone, and the victim's outputs supervise the clone. The authors find that the loss choice (l1 on logits rather than KL) is critical and recover logits from probabilities. High-accuracy clones are obtained on CIFAR-10 and SVHN with millions of queries and no data. Threat: theft of models trained on rare or proprietary data.
- **mapping:** prediction API -> data-free extraction with synthetic queries -> black-box score access + query budget -> stolen functionality (IP theft)
- **note:** The l1-loss detail and query scale are from memory of the paper.

### S-0133 EvilModel: hiding malware inside neural network models

- **canonical id:** `wang-2021-evilmodel` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** Z. Wang, C. Liu, X. Cui, "EvilModel: Hiding Malware Inside of Neural Network Models", arXiv:2107.08590, 2021
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API id_list=2107.08590
- **attack classes:** [steganographic payload in weights, malware delivery, AV evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.003 AI Supply Chain Compromise: Model, AML.T0115 Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts (formerly AML.T0115.001)?; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; ASI04; NIST NISTAML.05
- **summary:** Malware bytes are embedded in neuron parameters while the model structure stays unchanged. The model therefore passes antivirus scanning and keeps its function. In the experiment, 36.9 MB of malware fits into a 178 MB AlexNet with under 1% accuracy loss, and VirusTotal engines raised no alarm. A separate loader must extract and run the payload, so the model is a covert delivery channel rather than self-executing. This is the weights-level counterpart to pickle code execution, and pickle-format scanners do not detect it.
- **mapping:** model artifact on hub or CDN -> malware bytes in parameters -> attacker can publish or replace a model and has a loader on the target -> covert malware delivery past AV

### S-0135 MNTD: detecting AI Trojans using meta neural analysis

- **canonical id:** `xu-2021-mntd-meta-neural-trojan-detection` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** X. Xu et al., "Detecting AI Trojans Using Meta Neural Analysis", IEEE S&P 2021. DOI 10.1109/SP40001.2021.00034; arXiv:1910.03137
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03137 (arXiv API record, first posted 2019-10-08); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:1910.03137 (venue "IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy", 407 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [backdoor defense, model scanning]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0115.001; NISTAML.023
- **summary:** Trains a meta-classifier that decides whether a given model is Trojaned, using only black-box queries with learned query inputs. The meta-training set is built by jumbo learning: many shadow models trained with randomly sampled trigger patterns, with no assumption about the specific attack strategy. Reported detection AUC is high across vision, speech, tabular and NLP models. Robustness to adaptive attackers who know the meta-classifier is discussed. Useful as a model-intake scanning control.
- **mapping:** third-party model intake -> meta-classifier Trojan scan (mitigation) -> black-box access to candidate model -> reject backdoored models

### S-0136 Hermes Attack: lossless DNN theft via PCIe snooping

- **canonical id:** `zhu-2021-hermes-attack` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2021; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Zhu, Y. Cheng, H. Zhou, Y. Lu, "Hermes Attack: Steal DNN Models with Lossless Inference Accuracy", USENIX Security 2021. arXiv:2006.12784
- **pdf:** zhu-2021-hermes-attack.pdf sha256: bcad520283e49513c30eb138bf67633c4adec00580a27666b8b6b7f09e4abddf
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity21/presentation/zhu (title, authors, abstract); arXiv API id_list=2006.12784
- **attack classes:** [model extraction, PCIe bus snooping, physical access, GPU driver reverse engineering]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0048.004 AI IP Theft?, AML.T0025 Exfiltration via Cyber Means?; OWASP ML05; OWASP LLM03:2025?; CWE-319 (cleartext transmission)?; NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** Hermes treats unencrypted PCIe traffic between host and GPU as an attack surface. An attacker with physical access to the bus (for example, an operator of a privately deployed inference box) captures the packets. Through heavy reverse engineering of the closed CUDA runtime, driver and GPU command formats, plus packet selection and reordering, the attacker reconstructs the complete model: architecture, hyperparameters and all weights. The authors claim it is the first attack to steal a whole DNN, and stolen models reach the same inference accuracy as the originals. It was evaluated on MNIST, VGG and ResNet models across NVIDIA GeForce GT 730, GTX 1080 Ti and RTX 2080 Ti platforms. The implied control is encryption and authentication of the host-GPU link, which H100-class confidential computing now provides.
- **mapping:** on-prem/edge GPU inference server (model weights) -> PCIe bus capture and semantic reconstruction -> physical access to host interconnect -> full model IP theft, enabling white-box follow-on attacks

### S-0137 Dos and Don'ts of ML in computer security (ten pitfalls)

- **canonical id:** `arp-2022-dos-and-donts-ml-security` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** Daniel Arp et al., "Dos and Don'ts of Machine Learning in Computer Security", USENIX Security 2022. arXiv:2010.09470
- **pdf:** arp-2022-dos-donts-ml-security.pdf sha256: 895ab4622260bba9dacd258f69f25d98deaba3826d0f89c8e03cc1c042f4545c
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.09470 (arXiv API record); Semantic Scholar batch record lists venue USENIX Security Symposium (359 citations)
- **attack classes:** [evaluation pitfalls, sampling bias, data snooping, spurious correlations, lab-only evaluation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS ? (methodology); NIST AI 100-2 mitigation-evaluation guidance; CWE ?
- **summary:** Identifies ten pitfalls in the design and evaluation of learning-based security systems: sampling bias, label inaccuracy, data snooping, spurious correlations, biased parameter selection, inappropriate baselines, inappropriate performance measures, base-rate fallacy, lab-only evaluation and an inappropriate threat model. A review of 30 papers from top security venues over ten years finds the pitfalls are widespread. Case studies (malware detection, vulnerability discovery, network intrusion detection, source-code authorship) show how each pitfall inflates reported performance. For a threat-model generator this paper defines when a claimed ML-based control (detector, classifier) should be trusted.
- **mapping:** ML-based security control (malware/IDS/vuln detector) -> overstated effectiveness due to flawed evaluation -> defender relies on lab metrics -> undetected attacks in production (control-effectiveness risk)

### S-0139 Membership inference from first principles (LiRA)

- **canonical id:** `carlini-2022-lira` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, S. Chien, M. Nasr, S. Song, A. Terzis, F. Tramer, "Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles", IEEE S&P 2022. DOI 10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833649; arXiv:2112.03570

- **summary:** Argues MIAs should be evaluated by true-positive rate at low false-positive rate, not average accuracy. The Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) uses per-example Gaussian fits over in and out reference models and is about 10x stronger at low FPR (my recall). It is the standard strong MIA and the basis of privacy auditing.
- **mapping:** training data -> LiRA with reference models -> query access + ability to train shadow models -> confident identification of specific members

### S-0140 Poisoning and backdooring contrastive learning (CLIP)

- **canonical id:** `carlini-terzis-2022-poisoning-contrastive` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** N. Carlini, A. Terzis, "Poisoning and Backdooring Contrastive Learning", ICLR 2022. arXiv:2106.09667
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09667 (arXiv API record, first posted 2021-06-17); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2106.09667 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 235 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [backdoor, targeted poisoning, multimodal pretraining, web-scale data]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0115.000, AML.T0043.004; OWASP ML02, LLM04:2025; NISTAML.023, .024
- **summary:** Multimodal contrastive models such as CLIP are trained on noisy, uncurated web data. Poisoning 0.01% of Conceptual Captions (about 300 of 3 million images) installs a patch backdoor. Targeted poisoning that misclassifies one chosen test image needs only 0.0001% (three images). This calls into question whether training on uncurated web data is safe, and is the precursor of web-scale poisoning results.
- **mapping:** multimodal foundation model -> poisoned image-caption pairs on the web -> attacker can publish a handful of web images -> backdoor or targeted misclassification in zero-shot classifier

### S-0143 Planting undetectable backdoors

- **canonical id:** `goldwasser-2022-undetectable-backdoors` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** S. Goldwasser, M. P. Kim, V. Vaikuntanathan, O. Zamir, "Planting Undetectable Backdoors in Machine Learning Models", IEEE FOCS 2022. DOI 10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00092; arXiv:2204.06974

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003; OWASP ML10, LLM03:2025; NISTAML.051

- **mapping:** outsourced model -> cryptographic backdoor -> training control -> undetectable integrity compromise

### S-0145 BadEncoder: backdoors in self-supervised pretrained encoders

- **canonical id:** `jia-2022-badencoder` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** J. Jia, Y. Liu, N. Z. Gong, "BadEncoder: Backdoor Attacks to Pre-trained Encoders in Self-Supervised Learning", IEEE S&P 2022. DOI 10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833644; arXiv:2108.00352
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00352 (arXiv API record, first posted 2021-08-01); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2108.00352 (venue "IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy", 227 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [encoder backdoor, foundation-model supply chain, self-supervised learning]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0115.001, AML.T0010.003; OWASP ML07, ML10, LLM03:2025; NISTAML.023, .051
- **summary:** First backdoor attack on self-supervised pretrained image encoders (SimCLR, CLIP). The attacker fine-tunes the encoder so that triggered inputs embed close to attacker-chosen reference inputs while clean inputs keep their embeddings. Every downstream classifier built on the encoder inherits the backdoor, for multiple downstream tasks at once. High attack success is shown on encoders including real-world image encoders (e.g., CLIP), with clean accuracy preserved, and existing defenses fail. Attacker: publishes or tampers with the encoder.
- **mapping:** shared pretrained encoder -> encoder-level backdoor -> attacker distributes/tampers encoder -> all downstream classifiers misbehave on trigger

### S-0148 Red teaming language models with language models

- **canonical id:** `perez-2022-red-teaming-lms-with-lms` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** E. Perez et al., "Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models", EMNLP 2022. DOI 10.18653/v1/2022.emnlp-main.225; arXiv:2202.03286

### S-0149 Ignore Previous Prompt: attack techniques for language models (PromptInject)

- **canonical id:** `perez-ribeiro-2022-ignore-previous-prompt` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** Fábio Perez, Ian Ribeiro, "Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models", NeurIPS 2022 ML Safety Workshop. arXiv:2211.09527
- **pdf:** perez-ribeiro-2022-ignore-previous-prompt.pdf sha256: e0a69946a77a307b2a153d285a54442d4845e2354a920c7c2a6324481929dc09
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09527 (comment: "ML Safety Workshop NeurIPS 2022")

- **summary:** PromptInject is a framework for composing adversarial prompts from masks and iterating on them. Against GPT-3 it studies two attacks: goal hijacking (make the app print attacker text) and prompt leaking (make the app reveal its prompt). Simple handcrafted inputs from low-skill attackers were enough, and GPT-3's sampling creates long-tail risk. This is the first academic paper to define goal hijacking and prompt leaking, the two canonical objectives of direct injection.
- **mapping:** customer-facing LLM app -> goal hijack or prompt leak -> user text input -> app misbehavior, system prompt IP disclosure

### S-0150 DeepSteal: weight stealing via Rowhammer-based leakage (HammerLeak)

- **canonical id:** `rakin-2022-deepsteal` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** A. S. Rakin, M. H. I. Chowdhuryy, F. Yao, D. Fan, "DeepSteal: Advanced Model Extractions Leveraging Efficient Weight Stealing in Memories", IEEE S&P 2022. DOI 10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833743; arXiv:2111.04625
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record (IEEE S&P 2022); arXiv API id_list=2111.04625
- **attack classes:** [model extraction, Rowhammer read side channel, substitute-model training]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0048.004?, AML.T0005?; OWASP ML05; NIST NISTAML.031; CWE-1256?
- **summary:** DeepSteal steals DNN weight bits through a memory side channel. Its first stage, HammerLeak, uses Rowhammer as an information-leakage vector (in the style of RAMBleed) and adds system-level techniques tailored to DNN memory layouts, so it can read weight bits of a co-located victim. Its second stage trains a substitute model with a Mean Clustering weight penalty, which uses the partial leaked bit information to build a near-functional prototype of the victim. The attacker is a co-located unprivileged process that shares DRAM with the victim, with no query access needed for the leakage stage. The substitute enables white-box adversarial attacks and IP theft. The abstract reports this on three datasets; I did not record the per-dataset numbers.
- **mapping:** multi-tenant server DRAM (model weights) -> Rowhammer bit leakage plus substitute training -> co-located process on shared DRAM -> weight theft and white-box evasion

### S-0151 Red-teaming the Stable Diffusion safety filter

- **canonical id:** `rando-2022-red-teaming-sd-safety-filter` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2022; confidence medium

- **pdf:** shejwalkar-2022-back-to-drawing-board-fl.pdf sha256: 42bf12f4187821bc73a8b885fa6eb558068ce32db00c44d1cc80915b87fd8a10

### S-0153 Truth Serum: poisoning to amplify privacy leakage

- **canonical id:** `tramer-2022-truth-serum` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2022; confidence high
- **citation:** F. Tramer et al., "Truth Serum: Poisoning Machine Learning Models to Reveal Their Secrets", ACM CCS 2022. DOI 10.1145/3548606.3560554; arXiv:2204.00032
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00032 (arXiv API record, first posted 2022-03-31); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2204.00032 (venue "Conference on Computer and Communications Security", 162 citations on 2026-10-03)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0024.000, AML.T0057; OWASP ML02, ML04, LLM02:2025, LLM04:2025; NISTAML.033, .037
- **summary:** Connects integrity and privacy attacks. An adversary who can poison a small part of the training set makes the trained model leak much more about other parties' training points. Targeted poisoning of under 0.1% of data boosts membership inference, attribute inference and extraction by one to two orders of magnitude (for example raising TPR at low FPR). Controlling a large fraction such as 50% allows untargeted amplification. This is a cross-class edge: poisoning as a precondition for privacy breach, for example in federated or multi-party training.

### S-0160 PAIR: Jailbreaking black-box LLMs in twenty queries

- **canonical id:** `chao-2023-pair` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Patrick Chao, Alexander Robey, Edgar Dobriban, Hamed Hassani, George J. Pappas, Eric Wong, "Jailbreaking Black Box Large Language Models in Twenty Queries", arXiv 2023 (IEEE SaTML 2025 per later versions; not re-verified). arXiv:2310.08419
- **pdf:** chao-2023-pair.pdf sha256: 590bf40aa58061928f54d01b7d53f0d5141bb2ecf4f01483c6849423934f44e4

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0065; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** PAIR (Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement) uses an attacker LLM, prompted in the style of social engineering, to query the target. It reads each response and rewrites the candidate jailbreak until a judge scores the attempt as successful. Only black-box query access is needed, and it often succeeds in fewer than 20 queries. It reached competitive success rates on GPT-3.5/4, Vicuna and Gemini. PAIR made "LLM-as-red-teamer" a standard primitive. In a threat model it means a low-cost, automatable jailbreak capability available to any API user.
- **mapping:** hosted LLM API -> automated semantic jailbreak -> about 20 black-box queries -> harmful content; low cost to the attacker

### S-0162 Are diffusion models vulnerable to membership inference? (SecMI)

- **canonical id:** `duan-2023-secmi-diffusion-mia` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high

### S-0163 Spy in the GPU-box: multi-GPU covert and side channels

- **canonical id:** `dutta-2023-spy-gpu-box` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Sankha Baran Dutta, Hoda Naghibijouybari, Arjun Gupta, et al., "Spy in the GPU-box: Covert and Side Channel Attacks on Multi-GPU Systems", ACM (ISCA 2023), DOI 10.1145/3579371.3589080; arXiv:2203.15981

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000?; OWASP LLM02:2025?; CWE-203?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** On NVIDIA DGX multi-GPU machines (NVLink plus PCIe), the authors reverse-engineer the cache hierarchy. They show that an attacker on one GPU can cause contention in another GPU's L2. They build a cross-GPU covert channel at up to 3.95 MB/s and a remote prime-and-probe attack that recovers another workload's cache hit/miss pattern. The attack fingerprints the application running on the remote GPU with high accuracy. The attacker model is a tenant sharing a multi-GPU node. This establishes that GPU partitioning in shared HPC or cloud nodes does not give microarchitectural isolation.
- **mapping:** training/inference jobs on shared DGX nodes -> cross-GPU side channel -> co-tenant on the same node -> workload and model inference leakage

- **attack classes:** [generative watermarking, provenance control]

- **summary:** Fine-tunes the latent decoder of a latent diffusion model, conditioned on a binary signature, so every generated image carries an invisible watermark. ### S-0166 Not what you've signed up for: indirect prompt injection

- **canonical id:** `greshake-2023-indirect-prompt-injection` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `greshake-2023-ipi (enumerations.md)`, `greshake-ipi-2023 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Kai Greshake, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, Mario Fritz, "Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection", ACM AISec 2023 (venue from memory). arXiv:2302.12173
- **pdf:** greshake-2023-indirect-prompt-injection.pdf sha256: 428e23e8c7e4f89310e113e38d082b3f65548a8b887188ebc536099061800e81
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, data-exfiltration, worming, information-ecosystem-contamination, remote-control]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025; ASI01; NISTAML.015 (.027/.039/.036); CWE-1427
- **summary:** This is the seminal paper on indirect prompt injection (IPI). The attacker never talks to the model. Instead they plant prompts in data the application will retrieve, such as web pages, emails or code, and the application then acts on them remotely. The paper gives a security taxonomy of impacts: data theft, worming, information-ecosystem contamination, fraud, intrusion and availability. It demonstrates attacks on Bing Chat (GPT-4), code-completion engines and synthetic GPT-4 apps. The key claim is that processing retrieved prompts is equivalent to arbitrary code execution over the app's capabilities, including which APIs it calls. Asset view: every data source an LLM reads becomes an input channel that the attacker controls.
- **mapping:** LLM-integrated app (search, email, code assistant) -> remote hijack through retrieved content -> attacker can publish content the app will retrieve -> data exfiltration, manipulated outputs, propagation
- **also captured as `greshake-2023-ipi` (enumerations.md):** This paper introduced indirect prompt injection and the first threat taxonomy of its impacts: Information Gathering, Fraud, Intrusion, Malware, Manipulated Content and Availability. Injection methods are passive (retrieved web content), active (emails, messages) and user-driven, and payloads can be hidden or multi-stage. It was demonstrated on Bing Chat, code-completion and synthetic GPT-4 apps. The attacker is black-box with no model access and needs only to plant content the application will retrieve. It is the root reference for LLM01 (indirect), AML.T0051.001 and NISTAML.015, and Semantic Scholar shows about 2,100 citations. Mapping: retrieval/ingestion channel (web, email, docs) -> embedded instructions -> app retrieves attacker content -> exfiltration, fraud, malware spread, DoS
- **also captured as `greshake-ipi-2023` (incidents-news.md):** The paper defines indirect prompt injection: an attacker who has no direct interface plants instructions in data the LLM app will retrieve, such as web pages, emails, or code. Those instructions then act like arbitrary code executed by the model. The authors build a security taxonomy (data theft, worming, information-ecosystem contamination, fraud, intrusion, availability) and demonstrate attacks on Bing's GPT-4 chat, where a web page turns the chatbot into a social-engineering "data pirate", on code-completion engines, and on synthetic GPT-4 apps. The attacker needs only the ability to publish content the target will ingest, and can be black box. The assets are user data, the app's tool and API calls, and the user's trust. They found no effective mitigations at the time. This is the academic anchor for the Bing, Bard, Slack, and Copilot incidents in this log. Mapping: LLM app with retrieval/tools -> attacker-controlled content retrieved into context -> no separation of instructions from data -> exfiltration, manipulated actions, persistent compromise

### S-0175 A watermark for large language models

- **canonical id:** `kirchenbauer-2023-llm-watermark` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `kirchenbauer-2023-llm-watermark (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **citation:** J. Kirchenbauer, J. Geiping, Y. Wen, J. Katz, I. Miers, T. Goldstein, "A Watermark for Large Language Models", ICML 2023. arXiv:2301.10226
- **confirmed via:** DataCite record 10.48550/arxiv.2301.10226
- **attack classes:** [output-watermarking, provenance]
- **catalog ids:** control; OWASP LLM09:2025 (?)
- **summary:** A green/red-list logit bias seeded by previous tokens gives a statistically detectable output watermark with little quality loss. It underpins provenance controls. The threats to it are removal (paraphrasing), spoofing, and watermark stealing through distillation. Example: DITTO spoofing via knowledge distillation, arXiv:2510.10987.
- **mapping:** LLM output provenance (control) -> paraphrase / spoof attacks -> output access -> provenance failure
- **also captured as `kirchenbauer-2023-llm-watermark` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** A randomized "green" token set is chosen before each word and green tokens are softly promoted during sampling. Detection uses a statistical test with interpretable p-values and needs no model access. Quality impact is negligible. Tested on OPT models, with a discussion of robustness and security. It is the reference scheme that the attacks below target, and the asset to protect in content-provenance threat models. Mapping: AI-generated text provenance -> (target of scrubbing and spoofing) -> n/a -> n/a (defense)

### S-0176 Paraphrasing evades AI-text detectors (DIPPER)

- **canonical id:** `krishna-2023-dipper-paraphrase-evasion` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high

### S-0179 GEIA: generative embedding inversion of sentence embeddings

- **canonical id:** `li-2023-geia-embedding-inversion` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2023; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** H. Li, M. Xu, Y. Song, "Sentence Embedding Leaks More Information than You Expect: Generative Embedding Inversion Attack to Recover the Whole Sentence", Findings of ACL 2023. arXiv:2305.03010
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.03010 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-05-04); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2305.03010 (venue "Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics", 126 citations on 2026-10-03)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.001, AML.T0085.000; OWASP LLM08:2025, LLM02:2025; NISTAML.032
- **summary:** Reconstructs input sentences from their sentence embeddings with only black-box access to the embedding model. The embedding is treated as initial token representations and a powerful decoder (for example GPT-2) is trained to generate the full sequence. Vector stores of embeddings therefore count as sensitive data.

### S-0181 AutoDAN: stealthy jailbreak prompts via hierarchical genetic algorithm

- **canonical id:** `liu-2023-autodan` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Xiaogeng Liu, Nan Xu, Muhao Chen, Chaowei Xiao, "AutoDAN: Generating Stealthy Jailbreak Prompts on Aligned Large Language Models", ICLR 2024. arXiv:2310.04451
- **pdf:** liu-2023-autodan.pdf sha256: 1d6cff474509628c16bc31e219f1c7bfbe0ef61a875f94fda29a784ebf935dae
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04451
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, genetic-algorithm, readable-adversarial-prompt, perplexity-filter-evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** AutoDAN starts from handcrafted DAN-style prompts and evolves them with a hierarchical genetic algorithm. The result is semantically fluent jailbreak prompts, unlike GCG's gibberish suffixes. The method needs white-box loss access during optimization. The abstract reports better cross-model transferability and cross-sample universality than baselines. The prompts bypass perplexity-based detection. The defensive lesson: a filter that relies on how an input looks (perplexity) does not defend against fluent optimized attacks.
- **mapping:** aligned LLM -> fluent optimized jailbreak -> surrogate-model gradients or log-likelihood access -> harmful output that evades perplexity filters

### S-0182 HouYi: prompt injection against LLM-integrated applications

- **canonical id:** `liu-2023-houyi` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Yi Liu, Gelei Deng, Yuekang Li, Kailong Wang, Zihao Wang, Xiaofeng Wang, Tianwei Zhang, Yepang Liu, Haoyu Wang, Yan Zheng, Yang Liu, "Prompt Injection attack against LLM-integrated Applications", arXiv 2023. arXiv:2306.05499
- **pdf:** liu-2023-houyi-prompt-injection.pdf sha256: 7671887b19dad8ac4d514a45b4701882575860530615edee560c495623064828
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05499
- **attack classes:** [direct-prompt-injection, context-partition, prompt-theft, llm-usage-theft]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.000, AML.T0056, AML.T0034; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM07:2025, LLM10:2025; NISTAML.018, NISTAML.035; CWE-1427
- **summary:** HouYi is a black-box injection method modeled on web injection. It has three parts: a framework component that blends into the app's expected input, a separator that induces context partition, and a malicious payload. Applied to 36 real LLM-integrated apps, it found 31 vulnerable, and 10 vendors (including Notion) confirmed. Impacts were unrestricted use of the app's LLM (cost theft) and theft of the app's prompt (IP). The separator/payload structure is a reusable schema for describing injection strings.
- **mapping:** commercial LLM app -> context-partition injection -> normal user input -> prompt IP theft, free LLM usage (financial)

### S-0183 Analyzing leakage of PII in language models

- **canonical id:** `lukas-2023-pii-leakage-lms` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2023; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** N. Lukas et al., "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models", IEEE S&P 2023. DOI 10.1109/SP46215.2023.10179300; arXiv:2302.00539
- **pdf:** lukas-2023-pii-leakage-lms.pdf sha256: 0a39cddb4aee7e7455a433e3c16d4db1e87ad023c2aaf3f0f4256c94e0ea5acd
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00539 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-02-01); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2302.00539 (venue "IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy", 446 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [PII extraction, PII reconstruction, PII inference, DP evaluation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057, AML.T0024.001; OWASP LLM02:2025; NISTAML.038, .032
- **summary:** Defines game-based notions of three PII attacks with black-box API access: extraction (PII emitted in free generation), reconstruction (filling a masked PII slot given context) and inference (picking the right PII from candidates). Evaluated on GPT-2 fine-tuned on ECHR legal cases, Enron email and Yelp-Health. Scrubbing reduces but does not remove leakage, since NER-based scrubbing is imperfect. Sentence-level DP-SGD reduces leakage substantially but leaves some residual (on the order of 3% of PII sequences leaked in their experiments). It is the standard reference for PII-in-training-data risk.
- **mapping:** LLM fine-tuned on enterprise text -> PII extraction/reconstruction/inference -> API access -> personal data disclosure (GDPR, confidentiality)

### S-0186 TAP: Tree of Attacks with Pruning

- **canonical id:** `mehrotra-2023-tap` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Anay Mehrotra, Manolis Zampetakis, Paul Kassianik, Blaine Nelson, Hyrum Anderson, Yaron Singer, Amin Karbasi, "Tree of Attacks: Jailbreaking Black-Box LLMs Automatically", NeurIPS 2024. arXiv:2312.02119
- **pdf:** mehrotra-2023-tap.pdf sha256: b0ffafed56bef4937150dcf63ac5379cdc6aeedeac4a83b1af56512d92f9a496

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** TAP extends PAIR with tree-of-thought branching. An evaluator prunes off-topic or unlikely candidates before they reach the target, which cuts the number of queries. It needs only black-box access. TAP jailbroke GPT-4-Turbo and GPT-4o on more than 80% of prompts with fewer queries than earlier black-box methods. It also bypassed targets protected by LlamaGuard. Two threat-model consequences follow: input/output guardrail classifiers are not a sufficient control, and the attacker's cost is measured in queries.

### S-0188 Text embeddings reveal (almost) as much as text

- **canonical id:** `morris-2023-vec2text` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high **Group F: Training-data extraction and memorization**
- **aliases merged:** `morris-2023-vec2text (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **citation:** J. X. Morris, V. Kuleshov, V. Shmatikov, A. M. Rush, "Text Embeddings Reveal (Almost) As Much As Text", EMNLP 2023. arXiv:2310.06816

- **attack classes:** [embedding-inversion, reconstruction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.001; OWASP LLM08:2025, LLM02:2025; NISTAML.032
- **summary:** Vec2Text iteratively corrects and re-embeds text to invert dense embeddings. It recovers 92% of 32-token inputs exactly and full names from clinical-note embeddings. Embedding vectors stored in vector databases or RAG stores are therefore near-plaintext sensitive data. A 2025 reproducibility study is arXiv:2507.07700.
- **mapping:** vector DB / RAG embeddings -> embedding inversion -> read access to vectors + embedding-model query -> plaintext reconstruction (PII)
- **also captured as `morris-2023-vec2text` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** vec2text frames embedding inversion as controlled generation and iteratively corrects and re-embeds text. It recovers 92% of 32-token inputs exactly from embeddings of two state-of-the-art models and recovers full names from clinical-note embeddings. Threat-model point: vector databases holding embeddings of sensitive text are as sensitive as the plaintext, so embeddings are not anonymization. A 2025 reproducibility study (arXiv:2507.07700, RecSys 2025 reproducibility track; abstract fetched) confirmed the key results, showed password-like strings can be reconstructed, and found that Gaussian noise or quantization of embeddings mitigates the attack. Mapping: vector store / embedding API -> inversion to plaintext -> read access to embeddings (leak, shared index, API) -> PII and confidential text disclosure

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057, AML.T0024.000; OWASP LLM02:2025; NISTAML.038
- **summary:** A semi-automated pipeline extracts sensitive personal information from the Codex model behind GitHub Copilot. Templated prompts make leakage more likely, and a blind membership-inference filter overcomes the lack of access to training data. Using GitHub Search hit rate plus human review, about 8% (43) of prompts yielded privacy leaks. Many leaks are "indirect": they disclose information about people related to the queried subject, which violates contextual integrity.
- **mapping:** code-completion model trained on public repos -> templated extraction prompts -> normal user access -> personal data regurgitation

- **summary:** The paper red-teams three grey-box GPT-4 API features. Fine-tuning on as few as 15 harmful examples, or 100 benign ones, removed core safeguards. GPT-4 Assistants readily disclosed their function-call schema and could be made to execute arbitrary function calls. Knowledge retrieval was hijacked by instructions planted in retrieval documents. The general lesson for a threat model is that every API feature a vendor adds (fine-tuning, tools, retrieval) is a new threat vector.

### S-0194 SmoothLLM: randomized smoothing against jailbreaks

A 107,250-question set over 13 forbidden scenarios shows that the safeguards of six LLMs fail to block the prompts adequately. It is the empirical counterpart to the jailbreak taxonomies. Mapping: public chatbot -> community-shared jailbreak -> no special access -> forbidden-scenario output

### S-0207 Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

- **canonical id:** `wei-2023-jailbroken` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `wei-2023-jailbroken (enumerations.md)`
- **citation:** Alexander Wei, Nika Haghtalab, Jacob Steinhardt, "Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?", NeurIPS 2023. arXiv:2307.02483
- **pdf:** wei-2023-jailbroken.pdf sha256: 53d7ff7f10b7e12fbcef827df4c69fb800c5c6213f855ea29d0929d213c907a9
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02483
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, competing-objectives, mismatched-generalization, obfuscation-encoding]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** This is the foundational theory of why jailbreaks work, and it underlies most later taxonomies. It names two failure modes of safety training. In "competing objectives", helpfulness or instruction-following conflicts with safety; examples are prefix injection and refusal suppression. In "mismatched generalization", capabilities generalize to a domain that safety training never covered; examples are Base64 and other encodings and obfuscation. The attacker needs only black-box chat access at inference time. Attacks combining the two modes succeeded on every prompt in the red-team sets used against GPT-4 and Claude v1.3. The authors argue for "safety-capability parity" and against the idea that scaling alone will fix this.
- **mapping:** aligned model (safety policy) -> jailbreak elicits restricted content -> chat access -> harmful output, policy and reputational harm, misuse uplift
- **also captured as `wei-2023-jailbroken` (enumerations.md):** The paper proposes a two-cause taxonomy of jailbreak root causes. Competing objectives means capability and helpfulness conflict with safety. Mismatched generalization means safety training does not cover domains, such as encodings or low-resource languages, where capabilities exist. New attacks built from these causes succeeded on every prompt in the red-team set for GPT-4 and Claude v1.3. It is the conceptual basis of the weakness-oriented jailbreak taxonomies, including Pelaez-Gonzalez 2025. Mapping: safety-aligned model -> jailbreak exploiting objective conflict or generalization gap -> black-box prompt access -> harmful output

### S-0208 Tree-Ring watermarks for diffusion images

- **canonical id:** `wen-2023-tree-ring` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2023; confidence medium
- **citation:** Y. Wen, J. Kirchenbauer, J. Geiping, T. Goldstein, "Tree-Ring Watermarks: Fingerprints for Diffusion Images that are Invisible and Robust", NeurIPS 2023. arXiv:2305.20030
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20030 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-05-31); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2305.20030 (venue "arXiv.org", 271 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [semantic watermark, provenance control]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0088
- **summary:** Embeds a pattern in Fourier space into the initial noise vector of diffusion sampling. Detection inverts the diffusion process to recover the noise and checks the pattern. Because Fourier-space rings are invariant to convolutions, crops, dilations, flips and rotations, the watermark is robust to many transformations with negligible quality impact. Later attacks (for example forgery via inversion, MarkNull, WRATH) target it.
- **mapping:** diffusion-image provider -> initial-noise semantic watermark (mitigation) -> provider controls sampling -> provenance detection; targeted by removal/forgery
- **note:** Semantic Scholar lists arXiv only; NeurIPS 2023 venue is from memory.

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.015; CWE-1427
- **summary:** BIPIA is the first IPI benchmark. It covers tasks in which external content (email, web, table, code) carries injected instructions. All evaluated LLMs were vulnerable. The authors attribute success to two causes: LLMs cannot tell informational context from actionable instructions, and they are not aware that they should avoid executing instructions found in external content. Two defenses are proposed, boundary awareness and explicit reminders. The black-box versions mitigate substantially, and a white-box fine-tuning defense brings ASR near zero on the benchmark distribution, though adaptive attacks were not part of that claim.
- **mapping:** LLM app summarizing external content -> instruction executed from data -> attacker authors the content -> manipulated output or action

### S-0211 Low-resource languages jailbreak GPT-4

- **canonical id:** `yong-2023-low-resource-languages` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Zheng-Xin Yong, Cristina Menghini, Stephen H. Bach, "Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4", NeurIPS 2023 SoLaR workshop (Best Paper). arXiv:2310.02446
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02446
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, cross-lingual, mismatched-generalization]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** The attack translates unsafe English requests into low-resource languages (for example Zulu) with a public translation API, then translates the answers back. On AdvBench, GPT-4 engaged and gave actionable harmful content 79% of the time, on par with or better than state-of-the-art jailbreaks. High- and mid-resource languages had much lower success. This is a concrete instance of Wei et al.'s mismatched generalization: safety training data is linguistically unequal, while capability generalizes across languages. It is black-box, costs almost nothing, and needs no expertise.
- **mapping:** multilingual LLM -> translation jailbreak -> chat access plus a translation API -> harmful content

### S-0212 Assessing prompt injection risks in 200+ custom GPTs

- **canonical id:** `yu-2023-custom-gpts` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `yu-custom-gpts-2023 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** Jiahao Yu, Yuhang Wu, Dong Shu, Mingyu Jin, Sabrina Yang, Xinyu Xing, "Assessing Prompt Injection Risks in 200+ Custom GPTs", ICLR 2024 Workshop on Secure and Trustworthy LLMs. arXiv:2311.11538
- **pdf:** yu-custom-gpts-prompt-injection-2023.pdf sha256: 83bc2b726e74e683feeff003bbfb52a49f2e517b6dc20e6498b9192ec23897b8
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11538
- **attack classes:** [system-prompt-extraction, file-leakage, direct-prompt-injection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0056, AML.T0057, AML.T0084.000; OWASP LLM07:2025, LLM02:2025; NISTAML.035
- **summary:** The authors tested more than 200 user-built custom GPTs with adversarial prompts. Prompt injection extracted the system prompt in 97.2% of cases and leaked uploaded files in 100% (section 4, page 4 of the cached PDF yu-custom-gpts-prompt-injection-2023.pdf; 16 OpenAI-made and 200 third-party GPTs, up to three attempts each). The attacker needs only to chat with the GPT. Defensive prompts in the instructions were largely ineffective. The finding is that LLM app-store configurations (prompt and knowledge files) should be treated as public.
- **mapping:** custom GPT config and knowledge files -> extraction via chat -> public access to the GPT -> IP and data disclosure
- **also captured as `yu-custom-gpts-2023` (threat-models.md):** The attacker is a black-box user of a public custom GPT with no special access. With simple adversarial prompts, system-prompt extraction succeeded 97.2% of the time and leakage of uploaded files 100% of the time across 200+ user-designed GPTs. The targeted assets are the creator's system prompt (IP) and the knowledge files. Defensive prompts were evaluated and found inadequate. For threat modeling, it is the canonical evidence that a system prompt and attached files should be treated as public unless enforced elsewhere. Mapping: system prompt + knowledge files -> extraction by prompt injection -> any user access -> confidentiality loss (IP, PII)

### S-0213 GPTFuzzer: fuzzing for jailbreak templates

- **canonical id:** `yu-2023-gptfuzzer` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Jiahao Yu, Xingwei Lin, Zheng Yu, Xinyu Xing, "GPTFUZZER: Red Teaming Large Language Models with Auto-Generated Jailbreak Prompts", arXiv 2023. arXiv:2309.10253
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10253
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, fuzzing, template-mutation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** GPTFuzzer is an AFL-style black-box fuzzer. Human-written jailbreak templates are the seeds; LLM mutation operators rewrite them, a seed-selection strategy picks which to mutate, and a judge model scores success. It reached more than 90% ASR on ChatGPT and Llama-2 even from weak seeds. It shows jailbreak discovery can be automated with standard security-testing machinery.
- **mapping:** LLM endpoint -> automated template fuzzing -> black-box query access -> harmful output

### S-0214 CipherChat: cipher-based jailbreaks

- **canonical id:** `yuan-2023-cipherchat` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Youliang Yuan, Wenxiang Jiao, Wenxuan Wang, Jen-tse Huang, Pinjia He, Shuming Shi, Zhaopeng Tu, "GPT-4 Is Too Smart To Be Safe: Stealthy Chat with LLMs via Cipher", ICLR 2024. arXiv:2308.06463
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06463 (comment: "Accepted by ICLR 2024")
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, encoding-obfuscation, cipher]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** CipherChat talks to the model in ciphers such as Caesar, Morse and ASCII. It sets a system role and gives few-shot enciphered demonstrations. Some ciphers bypassed GPT-4's safety alignment almost 100% of the time in several of 11 safety domains, in English and Chinese. "SelfCipher" uses only role play and natural-language demonstrations to invoke a supposed internal cipher, and it beat human ciphers. Stronger models are more exposed because they can decode the cipher; this is the paper's "too smart to be safe" point. For the threat model: content filters that only inspect plaintext are blind to encoded channels.
- **mapping:** capable LLM -> encoded or enciphered harmful request -> chat access -> harmful output that evades plaintext filters

### S-0218 Poisoning retrieval corpora by injecting adversarial passages

- **canonical id:** `zhong-2023-corpus-poisoning-adversarial-passages` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2023; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Z. Zhong, Z. Huang, A. Wettig, D. Chen, "Poisoning Retrieval Corpora by Injecting Adversarial Passages", EMNLP 2023. arXiv:2310.19156
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19156 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-10-29); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2310.19156 (venue "Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing", 213 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [corpus poisoning, dense retrieval attack, HotFlip-style token optimization]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0070, AML.T0066, AML.T0043.000; OWASP LLM08:2025, LLM04:2025; NISTAML.013/.024 (RAG poisoning)
- **summary:** The seminal corpus-poisoning attack on dense retrievers. A small number of adversarial passages are generated by discrete token perturbation (HotFlip-style) to maximize similarity with a set of training queries, then inserted into a large corpus. They are retrieved for unseen queries and even generalize out of domain. 50 passages optimized on Natural Questions are retrieved in the top-20 for over 94% of queries. Unsupervised retrievers such as Contriever are especially vulnerable. It is the precursor to PoisonedRAG and the retrieval half of IPI.
- **mapping:** RAG/dense retrieval index -> adversarial passages inserted into corpus -> attacker can add documents (web, wiki, uploads) -> attacker content retrieved for many queries
- **note:** The 94% figure is from memory of the paper; the abstract confirms the 50-passage setting.

### S-0219 AutoDAN (Zhu et al.): interpretable gradient-based attacks

- **canonical id:** `zhu-2023-autodan-interpretable` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Sicheng Zhu, Ruiyi Zhang, Bang An, Gang Wu, Joe Barrow, et al., "AutoDAN: Interpretable Gradient-Based Adversarial Attacks on Large Language Models", arXiv 2023 (COLM 2024 per later versions; venue not re-verified). arXiv:2310.15140
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15140
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, gradient-based-optimization, readable-suffix, system-prompt-leak]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0056; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM07:2025; NISTAML.018, NISTAML.035
- **summary:** This is a different paper from Liu et al. that shares the AutoDAN name. It generates readable adversarial tokens left to right under two objectives, jailbreak success and readability, so the output passes perplexity filters. The prompts it produces are diverse and interpretable, and they rediscover strategies that human jailbreakers use. They transfer to black-box models better than unreadable suffixes. A customized objective also leaks system prompts automatically. Catalogs should keep the two AutoDAN papers apart.
- **mapping:** aligned LLM / system prompt -> readable gradient-crafted prompt -> surrogate white-box access -> jailbreak or prompt leakage

### S-0220 Universal and transferable adversarial attacks on aligned LMs (GCG)

- **canonical id:** `zou-2023-gcg` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2023; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `zou-2023-gcg (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **citation:** A. Zou, Z. Wang, N. Carlini, M. Nasr, J. Z. Kolter, M. Fredrikson, "Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models", arXiv:2307.15043, 2023
- **pdf:** zou-2023-gcg-universal-adversarial-attacks.pdf sha256: ab8745c2e3c6dfd939d5a590760bbae4682d92db010947cbb306688ad086bfd1
- **confirmed via:** arXiv title-search hit 2307.15043 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15043)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, adversarial-suffix, jailbreak, transfer-attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0043.000/.002; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018 (direct prompting); CWE ?
- **summary:** Greedy Coordinate Gradient optimizes an adversarial token suffix on open models (Vicuna, LLaMA-2-chat) that elicits harmful completions. The suffixes are universal across prompts and transfer to closed models. This makes it the bridge from classical evasion to LLM jailbreak: a white-box surrogate is used for black-box transfer at inference time. The jailbreak dimension itself is covered by a sibling agent.
- **mapping:** aligned LLM -> optimized adversarial suffix -> open-weight surrogate + API access -> safety-policy bypass
- **also captured as `zou-2023-gcg` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** GCG (Greedy Coordinate Gradient) uses gradients to search for an adversarial token suffix that maximizes the likelihood of an affirmative start such as "Sure, here is". Optimization is white-box on open models (Vicuna-7B/13B). The attack targets many prompts and models at once, so it yields universal suffixes. These suffixes transferred black-box to ChatGPT, Bard, Claude, LLaMA-2-Chat, Pythia and Falcon. GCG introduced AdvBench and set off the optimization-based jailbreak line. The suffixes are gibberish with high perplexity, which is why perplexity filters were proposed as a defense (Jain 2023) and why later work pursued readable attacks (AutoDAN). Threat-model note: white-box access to an open surrogate model is enough to attack closed APIs. Mapping: closed or open LLM safety policy -> universal adversarial suffix -> attacker has an open-weight surrogate plus query access -> harmful generation across vendors

### S-0221 Get my drift? Catching LLM task drift with activation deltas (TaskTracker)

- **canonical id:** `abdelnabi-2024-tasktracker` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Sahar Abdelnabi, Aideen Fay, Giovanni Cherubin, Ahmed Salem, Mario Fritz, Andrew Paverd, "Get my drift? Catching LLM Task Drift with Activation Deltas", IEEE SaTML 2025. arXiv:2406.00799
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00799 (comment: "SaTML 2025")
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, detection-defense, activation-probing]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS mitigation-side (AML.M*?); OWASP LLM01:2025 mitigation; NISTAML.015 mitigation
- **summary:** The paper defines "task drift" as the deviation from the user's task after the LLM reads external data. The difference in activations before and after the data is processed correlates strongly with drift. Linear probes on these deltas detect drift with near-perfect ROC AUC out of distribution and generalize to unseen injections and jailbreaks without training on attacks. The method requires white-box access to the serving model and no fine-tuning. The TaskTracker toolkit and dataset (500K+ instances, 6 models) are released. This is a detection control for the KG ("activation-based IPI detector").
- **mapping:** RAG or email app -> drift detector on activations -> defender has model internals -> IPI detected before action

### S-0223 TrojanPuzzle: covert poisoning of code models

- **canonical id:** `aghakhani-2024-trojanpuzzle` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence medium
- **aliases merged:** `aghakhani-2023-trojanpuzzle (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **citation:** H. Aghakhani, W. Dai, A. Manoel, X. Fernandes et al., "TrojanPuzzle: Covertly Poisoning Code-Suggestion Models", arXiv:2301.02344 (IEEE S&P 2024)
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.02344 (DataCite)
- **attack classes:** [data-poisoning, covert-poisoning, code-model]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020; OWASP LLM04:2025; NISTAML.024
- **summary:** Poisons code-suggestion models so that the malicious payload never appears verbatim in the poison data. The model learns to fill a masked token from a template, which defeats signature- and static-analysis-based dataset cleansing. It is placed in docstrings and other out-of-context regions. The S&P venue is from memory.
- **mapping:** code LLM fine-tuning corpus -> covert template poisoning -> public code contribution -> insecure suggestions
- **also captured as `aghakhani-2023-trojanpuzzle` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** COVERT puts poison in docstrings and other out-of-context regions so static analysis that cleans training data misses it. TROJANPUZZLE never includes the suspicious part of the payload in the poison data, yet the model learns to complete the whole insecure payload. This defeats signature-based dataset cleansing. Relevant to any organization fine-tuning code models on scraped code. Mapping: code-suggestion model training corpus -> covert poisoning causes insecure completions -> attacker publishes poisoned public code -> vulnerabilities in downstream software

### S-0225 Jailbreaking leading safety-aligned LLMs with simple adaptive attacks

- **citation:** Maksym Andriushchenko, Francesco Croce, Nicolas Flammarion, "Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks", ICLR 2025. arXiv:2404.02151

It reached 100% ASR (GPT-4 judge) on Vicuna-13B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3, Nemotron-4-340B, Llama-2-Chat 7/13/70B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-7B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and R2D2, which was adversarially trained against GCG. ### S-0226 Many-shot jailbreaking
