### S-0310 Crescendo multi-turn jailbreak

- **canonical id:** `russinovich-2024-crescendo` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Mark Russinovich, Ahmed Salem, Ronen Eldan, "Great, Now Write an Article About That: The Crescendo Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreak Attack", USENIX Security 2025. arXiv:2404.01833
- **pdf:** russinovich-2024-crescendo.pdf sha256: a20ef519f1a8f8c224e1bb5a3c42a52991c7aada6ff5d9b5c182a7eb57b893dd
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01833 (comment: "Accepted at USENIX Security 2025")
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, multi-turn, gradual-escalation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Crescendo opens with benign questions about a topic. It then escalates step by step, each time referring back to the model's own earlier replies, until the model produces restricted content. No single turn looks malicious, which defeats per-message filters. It was evaluated on ChatGPT, Gemini Pro and Ultra, LLaMA-2/3 70B and Anthropic Chat, and it also works on multimodal models. The automated version, Crescendomation, beat other methods on an AdvBench subset by 29-61% on GPT-4 and 49-71% on Gemini-Pro. Implication for controls: moderation must see the whole conversation, not single turns.
- **mapping:** chat assistant -> multi-turn escalation -> ordinary multi-turn chat access -> restricted content; per-turn moderation bypassed

### S-0311 Robustness of AI-image detectors: fundamental limits and practical attacks

- **canonical id:** `saberi-2024-robustness-ai-image-detectors` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Saberi et al., "Robustness of AI-Image Detectors: Fundamental Limits and Practical Attacks", ICLR 2024. arXiv:2310.00076
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00076 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-09-29); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2310.00076 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 110 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [watermark evasion, watermark spoofing, deepfake detector evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0088, AML.T0043.002; NISTAML.022
- **summary:** For low-perturbation-budget watermarks there is a fundamental trade-off between evasion error (watermarked images missed) and spoofing error (real images flagged). A diffusion-purification attack removes such watermarks. High-budget watermarks are attacked with adversarial perturbations on a surrogate detector. Spoofing attacks make real images register as watermarked, which could discredit genuine content. Classifier-based deepfake detectors are also evaded.
- **mapping:** AI-content detection (watermark or classifier) -> purification/adversarial/spoofing -> attacker has images (+ surrogate) -> missed deepfakes or false attribution

### S-0313 Prompt stealing attacks against LLMs

- **canonical id:** `sha-2024-prompt-stealing` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high

- **attack classes:** [prompt-stealing, output-based-inversion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0056; OWASP LLM07:2025; NISTAML.035
- **summary:** The attack reconstructs a well-engineered prompt from generated answers alone. A parameter extractor first classifies the prompt type (direct, role-based or in-context) and infers its role or number of examples. A reconstructor then regenerates a functionally similar prompt. No adversarial queries are needed, only outputs, which threatens marketplaces that sell prompts.

### S-0318 LeftoverLocals (CVE-2023-4969)

- **canonical id:** `sorensen-2024-leftoverlocals` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Tyler Sorensen, Heidy Khlaaf, "LeftoverLocals: Listening to LLM Responses Through Leaked GPU Local Memory", arXiv:2401.16603, 2024 (Trail of Bits). NVD CVE-2023-4969 (CVSS 6.5).
- **pdf:** sorensen-2024-leftoverlocals.pdf sha256: c6b9be8f8d8bf48e990392e3b92d49303e6c5675008a5f061de426b223be2d33
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16603 (fetched); https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2023-4969
- **attack classes:** [GPU memory remanence, cross-process data leak]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000 (Hardware)?, AML.T0057?; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-401 (NVD), CWE-226?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** GPU "local memory" (workgroup shared memory) on Apple, Qualcomm, AMD, and Imagination GPUs was not cleared between kernels. A co-resident process can therefore read leftover data from another user or app. NVD: "A GPU kernel can read sensitive data from another GPU kernel (even from another user or app)". The PoC leaks about 5.5 MB per GPU invocation on an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT, or about 181 MB per query for a 7B model in llama.cpp. That is enough to reconstruct another user's interactive LLM responses across process or container boundaries. The attacker needs only to run GPU code on the same device, with no privileges. Fixes are vendor driver and firmware memory clearing.
- **mapping:** LLM responses on shared/edge GPUs -> cross-tenant memory scraping -> co-located untrusted GPU workload -> confidentiality loss of prompts and outputs

### S-0320 Ring-A-Bell: red-teaming concept removal in diffusion models

- **canonical id:** `tsai-2024-ring-a-bell` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high

- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10012 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-10-16); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2310.10012 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 283 citations on 2026-10-03)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0043.002; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018

It then builds problematic prompts that recover concepts supposedly removed by concept-erasure fine-tuning (ESD, SLD, CA, FMN) or blocked by online services. ### S-0321 The Instruction Hierarchy (OpenAI)

- **canonical id:** `wallace-2024-instruction-hierarchy` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Eric Wallace, Kai Xiao, Reimar Leike, Lilian Weng, Johannes Heidecke, Alex Beutel, "The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions", arXiv 2024. arXiv:2404.13208
- **pdf:** wallace-2024-instruction-hierarchy.pdf sha256: fbc2d65e913e75b8f0ae74e83e3443c36a727636d1038a071a2f10d8be63dac4
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13208 ; "up to 63%" verified in cached PDF text
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, privilege-levels, jailbreak-defense, prompt-extraction-defense]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM07:2025 mitigation; NISTAML.015/.018/.035 mitigation
- **summary:** The root cause named here is that models treat system prompts, user text and third-party content (tool outputs) with equal priority. The paper defines a hierarchy (system > user > tool/third-party) and generates training data for "aligned" versus "misaligned" lower-privilege instructions. Applied to GPT-3.5, robustness rose by up to 63% on its evaluations and generalized to held-out attacks, for example jailbreak robustness up by over 30%, with minimal capability loss. OpenAI's "model spec chain of command" builds on this. The hierarchy is an implicit trust-zone model for tmodel.
- **mapping:** LLM with system/user/tool inputs -> (defense) lower-privilege instructions ignored on conflict -> n/a -> reduced injection, extraction, jailbreak

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM04:2025; ASI04; NISTAML.023

At test time a trigger in the agent's input or environment, such as a web page element, makes it execute harmful operations. The backdoor survives later fine-tuning on trustworthy data. The risk is building agents on untrusted fine-tuned models or datasets.
- **mapping:** agent model supply chain -> triggered harmful tool operations -> attacker supplies the model or fine-tuning data -> covert compromise

### S-0323 Brittleness of safety alignment via pruning and low-rank modifications

- **canonical id:** `wei-2024-brittleness-safety-alignment` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** B. Wei et al., "Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications", ICML 2024. arXiv:2402.05162
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05162 (arXiv API record, first posted 2024-02-07); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2402.05162 (venue "International Conference on Machine Learning", 261 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [alignment removal, pruning, low-rank attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0018.000; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Finds safety-critical regions disentangled from utility at the neuron and rank level. They are sparse: about 3% of parameters and 2.5% of ranks. Removing them destroys safety with little utility loss. Restricting fine-tuning updates away from these regions does not prevent low-cost fine-tuning attacks. This is evidence that safety is a thin, removable layer in open weights.

### S-0324 When Speculation Spills Secrets: speculative-decoding side channels

- **canonical id:** `wei-2024-speculative-decoding` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Jiankun Wei, Abdulrahman Abdulrazzag, Tianchen Zhang, Adel Muursepp, Gururaj Saileshwar, "When Speculation Spills Secrets: Side Channels via Speculative Decoding In LLMs", arXiv:2411.01076, 2024 (v4 2026).
- **pdf:** wei-2024-speculative-decoding-side-channels.pdf sha256: e544193b49de69614a9f600668bb442dea17f85e1d549600348f13473cf1a9f5

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057?; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-203?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** The pattern of correct and incorrect speculations in speculative decoding is input-dependent. It is visible through per-iteration token counts or packet sizes. On research prototypes and production vLLM, an observer fingerprints queries from a set of 50 prompts at temperature 0.3 with REST 100%, LADE 91.6%, BiLD 95.2%, and EAGLE 77.6% accuracy, against a 2% baseline. Accuracy stays well above baseline at temperature 1.0. The attacker can also leak confidential datastore contents used for drafting at more than 25 tokens/s. The paper proposes and evaluates packet padding and iteration-wise token aggregation.

### S-0325 What Was Your Prompt? Token-length side channel

- **canonical id:** `weiss-2024-token-length` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Roy Weiss, Daniel Ayzenshteyn, Guy Amit, Yisroel Mirsky, "What Was Your Prompt? A Remote Keylogging Attack on AI Assistants", arXiv:2403.09751, 2024. (I recall a USENIX Security 2024 venue but did not confirm it.)
- **pdf:** weiss-2024-what-was-your-prompt.pdf sha256: 977a826cbf7d52b513f9c62ebd2c3932922fd03f208c91ac3a025ea362c9034a
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09751 (fetched); v0.2 fold: venue verified 2026-10-03: the USENIX Security 2024 presentation page carries this title (usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/weiss)
- **attack classes:** [network side channel, token-length leakage, response reconstruction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024?, AML.T0057?; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-203?; NISTAML.03 (not explicitly covered)
- **summary:** Streaming AI assistants send one token per packet, and encryption preserves the length. A passive network observer therefore learns the sequence of token lengths. The authors train an LLM to translate token-length sequences into text, using inter-sentence context and a known-plaintext fine-tune on the target's writing style. They reconstruct 29% of responses accurately and infer the topic for 55%. They demonstrated it on OpenAI ChatGPT-4 and Microsoft Copilot over both browser and API traffic, and found many vendors affected. The attacker needs only a passive network position (Wi-Fi, ISP, compromised router). The mitigations are padding and batching of tokens.
- **mapping:** confidential employee-to-assistant conversations -> response inference from encrypted traffic -> streaming without padding, observer on path -> privacy and confidentiality loss

### S-0329 IsolateGPT: execution isolation for LLM-based agentic systems (NDSS 2025)

- **citation:** Yuhao Wu, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, Umar Iqbal, "IsolateGPT: An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Agentic Systems", NDSS 2025. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2025.241131; arXiv:2403.04960

- **summary:** LLM app ecosystems such as ChatGPT plugins resemble early computing platforms without isolation. Apps are defined and interact in natural language, can access user data, and can talk to each other freely. IsolateGPT isolates execution: each app runs in its own spoke with its own LLM instance, and a trusted hub mediates. It protects against many security, privacy and safety attacks at modest overhead. ACE (NDSS 2026) later shows planning-integrity attacks that still succeed against it.
- **mapping:** LLM platform hosting third-party apps -> cross-app data theft or manipulation -> malicious app installed by the user -> privacy and integrity loss

### S-0331 BadChain: backdoor chain-of-thought prompting

- **canonical id:** `xiang-2024-badchain` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2024; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Z. Xiang et al., "BadChain: Backdoor Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Large Language Models", ICLR 2024. arXiv:2401.12242
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12242 (arXiv API record, first posted 2024-01-20); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2401.12242 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 130 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [prompt-level backdoor, in-context learning, CoT]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0018.003; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM04:2025; NISTAML.023
- **summary:** A backdoor that needs no access to training data or weights. The attacker inserts a few poisoned chain-of-thought demonstrations into the in-context examples; these contain a trigger and an extra malicious reasoning step. It is effective against API models such as GPT-4 and PaLM 2 across arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks, and stronger models are more susceptible. ### S-0341 HyperTheft: weight theft from TEE-shielded DNNs via ciphertext side channels

- **canonical id:** `yuan-2024-hypertheft` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2024; confidence medium
- **citation:** Y. Yuan, Z. Liu, S. Deng et al., "HyperTheft: Thieving Model Weights from TEE-Shielded Neural Networks via Ciphertext Side Channels", ACM CCS 2024. DOI 10.1145/3658644.3690317

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0048.004?; OWASP ML05; OWASP LLM03:2025?; NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** TEE shielding is meant to make a DNN fully black-box to a hypervisor. This paper shows that ciphertext side channels produce weight-dependent observations during execution. Earlier inference techniques need over-strong conditions, and they also fail on the precision that weights require, because even a few wrong weight elements can break a DNN. The paper develops a method that overcomes these problems and recovers functional weights. The attacker is the untrusted host. The impact is model-weight IP theft from confidential-AI deployments, and the stolen weights enable white-box follow-on attacks. The abstract was truncated, so recovery accuracy is not recorded.
- **mapping:** TEE-protected model weights -> ciphertext side channel -> malicious host/hypervisor -> weight theft

### S-0342 RMIA: low-cost high-power membership inference

- **canonical id:** `zarifzadeh-2024-rmia` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** S. Zarifzadeh, P. Liu, R. Shokri, "Low-Cost High-Power Membership Inference Attacks", ICML 2024. arXiv:2312.03262
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.03262 (arXiv API record, first posted 2023-12-06); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2312.03262 (venue "International Conference on Machine Learning", 135 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [membership inference, likelihood-ratio test, auditing]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000; OWASP ML04; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** Robust Membership Inference Attack (RMIA) uses a finer model of the null hypothesis in the likelihood-ratio test. It compares the target point against reference population samples as well as reference models. It has higher power across the TPR-FPR curve, including at near-zero FPR, and stays strong with as few as one reference model, where LiRA-style attacks approach random guessing. It is the current reference attack for practical privacy audits.
- **mapping:** model trained on personal data -> RMIA audit/attack -> score access + few reference models + population data -> membership disclosure

### S-0346 Adversarial illusions in multi-modal embeddings

### S-0348 BadMerging: backdoors against model merging

- **canonical id:** `zhang-2024-badmerging` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** J. Zhang, J. Chi, Z. Li, K. Cai, Y. Zhang et al., "BadMerging: Backdoor Attacks Against Model Merging", ACM CCS 2024. DOI 10.1145/3658644.3690284; arXiv:2408.07362
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record (CCS 2024); arXiv API id_list=2408.07362
- **attack classes:** [backdoor, model merging, supply chain, on-task/off-task attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000 Poison AI Model, AML.T0115 Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts (formerly AML.T0115.001), AML.T0010.003; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM04:2025; ML06, ML10; NIST NISTAML.051
- **summary:** Model merging (task arithmetic and similar methods) combines independently fine-tuned task models without retraining. Existing backdoors do not survive the merge. BadMerging uses a two-stage attack with a feature-interpolation loss that keeps the backdoor robust to different merging coefficients. An adversary who contributes as few as one backdoored task model can compromise the whole merged model. That covers the adversary's own task (on-task) and tasks from other contributors (off-task). The paper also finds existing defenses ineffective. The asset is an organization's merged model built from community checkpoints.
- **mapping:** merged model built from third-party checkpoints -> backdoored contributed task vector -> attacker publishes one fine-tuned model -> backdoor across all merged tasks

### S-0350 Instruction backdoor attacks against customized LLMs (GPTs)

- **summary:** Shows that a third-party custom LLM (for example a GPT in the GPT Store) can carry a backdoor implemented purely in its natural-language instructions. Word-level, syntax-level and semantic-level triggers make the app output the attacker's chosen result when inputs contain the trigger. No fine-tuning or weight access is needed. Integrators who embed untrusted custom LLMs in their applications inherit the backdoor. An instruction-ignoring defense partially mitigates it.

### S-0351 Extracting prompts by inverting LLM outputs (output2prompt)

### S-0352 Persistent pre-training poisoning of LLMs

- **canonical id:** `zhang-2024-persistent-pretraining-poisoning` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence medium

It then measures persistence after SFT and DPO alignment. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining data is enough for effects that persist through post-training. Per my recall, simple denial-of-service persisted at about 0.001%. Pretraining-stage attacks therefore survive alignment.
- **mapping:** pretraining corpus -> 0.1% poisoning -> web content injection -> persistent manipulated beliefs / DoS / prompt leakage after alignment

### S-0354 Impossibility of strong watermarking

- **canonical id:** `zhang-2024-watermarks-in-the-sand` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2024; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `zhang-2023-watermarks-in-the-sand (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **citation:** H. Zhang, B. L. Edelman, D. Francati, D. Venturi, G. Ateniese, B. Barak, "Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Generative Models", ICML 2024. arXiv:2311.04378
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04378 (arXiv title search)
- **attack classes:** [watermark-removal, theory]
- **catalog ids:** ?
- **summary:** Under natural assumptions, namely a quality oracle and a perturbation oracle, any strong watermark can be removed by random-walk perturbation with only black-box access while preserving quality. Watermarks are therefore weak provenance evidence against motivated attackers. The ICML venue is from memory.
- **mapping:** generative output watermark -> random-walk removal -> black-box access + quality oracle -> provenance evasion
- **also captured as `zhang-2023-watermarks-in-the-sand` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** The paper proves that strong watermarking is impossible under natural assumptions, even with a private key. An attacker with a quality oracle and a perturbation oracle, both weaker than the model, can random-walk to an unwatermarked high-quality output. The attack removed the Kirchenbauer, Kuditipudi and Zhao schemes with minor quality loss. Watermarks are evidence, not a security guarantee. Mapping: watermark-based provenance -> generic removal attack -> black-box access plus weaker models -> provenance control defeated

### S-0355 Models Are Codes: malicious code poisoning on model hubs (MalHug)

- **canonical id:** `zhao-2024-malhug` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Jian Zhao, Shenao Wang, Yanjie Zhao, et al., "Models Are Codes: Towards Measuring Malicious Code Poisoning Attacks on Pre-trained Model Hubs", ACM (ASE 2024), 2024. DOI 10.1145/3691620.3695271; arXiv:2409.09368
- **pdf:** zhao-2024-models-are-codes-malhug.pdf sha256: a96784cd34bdff60e946ef8ddd2726ed77865125cefbf1db339ad2fd237f4d78
- **confirmed via:** https://api.openalex.org/works?search=Models%20Are%20Codes%20malicious%20model%20hub (DOI hit); PDF text
- **attack classes:** [malicious model serialization, malicious dataset loading scripts, supply-chain code execution]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0115.001, AML.T0115.000, AML.T0011.000, AML.T0018.002; OWASP LLM03:2025; OWASP ML06; ASI04; CWE-502; NIST NISTAML.05
- **summary:** This is the first systematic study of malicious code poisoning on Hugging Face. It gives a taxonomy of model formats and a root-cause analysis of formats that execute code: pickle-based PyTorch, joblib, Keras/H5, and dataset loading scripts. The attacker needs only an account on the hub. The payload runs when a victim deserializes the model or loads the dataset, before any inference happens. The paper proposes MalHug, which combines dataset-script extraction, model deserialization, taint analysis, and heuristics. MalHug was deployed at Ant Group on a mirrored HF instance for over three months. It scanned more than 705K models and 176K datasets and found 91 malicious models and 9 malicious dataset loading scripts. Payloads included reverse shells, browser credential theft, and system reconnaissance. Existing scanners (Fickling, ModelScan) are shown to miss semantic-level threats.
- **mapping:** ML engineer workstation / training node -> code execution on model or dataset load -> engineer pulls a third-party model or dataset from a public hub -> host compromise, credential theft, lateral movement

### S-0357 Weak-to-strong jailbreaking

### S-0358 InputSnatch: cache-timing input theft

### S-0361 Firewalls to secure dynamic LLM agentic networks

- **canonical id:** `abdelnabi-2025-firewalls-agent-networks` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Sahar Abdelnabi, Amr Gomaa, Eugene Bagdasarian, Per Ola Kristensson, Reza Shokri, "Firewalls to Secure Dynamic LLM Agentic Networks", TMLR 2026. arXiv:2502.01822
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01822 (comment: "TMLR 2026")
- **attack classes:** [inter-agent-manipulation, data-over-sharing, defense-architecture]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP ASI07, ASI09; LLM02:2025
- **summary:** When agents negotiate or communicate for users, each message crosses a trust boundary. User data can over-share outward, and an external agent's language can manipulate inward. The proposed dual firewall projects both directions onto the task context. A Language Converter Firewall turns incoming messages into a closed, domain-specific structured protocol, which strips persuasion, urgency and embedded instructions by deterministic verification. A data firewall limits outgoing personal data. It is a structural defense for A2A-style channels.
- **mapping:** user's delegate agent in open agent networks -> manipulation and over-sharing -> external counterpart agent -> privacy leakage, manipulated decisions

### S-0363 Spill The Beans: CPU cache side channel leaks LLM tokens

- **canonical id:** `adiletta-2025-spill-the-beans` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Andrew Adiletta, Berk Sunar, "Spill The Beans: Exploiting CPU Cache Side-Channels to Leak Tokens from Large Language Models", arXiv:2505.00817, 2025.
- **pdf:** adiletta-2025-spill-the-beans.pdf sha256: fdbb11c42f564c3c0c25fc90246eef16065db371c599a4c5dfc8da0508bb9c93
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00817 (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [Flush+Reload on embedding table, token leakage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057?; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-203?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** A co-located attacker process runs Flush+Reload on the LLM's embedding-layer vectors. Each generated token touches a unique embedding row, so cache hits reveal tokens. The main difficulty is that the large model evicts cache lines, which forces a trade-off between how many tokens to monitor and how reliably hits are detected. Single-shot recovery reaches 80% to 90% of a high-entropy API key, and about 40% of English text. The attacker needs only co-residency on shared hardware with the victim model process.
- **mapping:** secrets emitted by an LLM (API keys, PII) -> token leakage through a shared CPU cache -> co-tenant on the same host -> credential and data disclosure

### S-0367 IPIGuard: tool-dependency-graph defense (EMNLP 2025)

- **canonical id:** `an-2025-ipiguard` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high

### S-0368 Is my data in your retrieval database? MIA against RAG

### S-0369 Does refusal training generalize to the past tense?

- **canonical id:** `andriushchenko-2025-past-tense-refusal` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Andriushchenko, N. Flammarion, "Does Refusal Training in LLMs Generalize to the Past Tense?", ICLR 2025. arXiv:2407.11969
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.11969 (arXiv API record, first posted 2024-07-16); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2407.11969 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 96 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, refusal generalization failure]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Rephrasing a harmful request in the past tense ("How did people make...?") jailbreaks many state-of-the-art LLMs. With 20 reformulation attempts, success on GPT-4o rises from 1% to 88% on JailbreakBench requests, and similar effects hold for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3 8B, Gemma-2, Phi-3, GPT-4o mini and o1 models. Future tense is less effective. Including past-tense examples in fine-tuning fixes this specific gap, so refusal training generalizes poorly.
- **mapping:** aligned chat LLM -> tense reformulation -> black-box access, a few retries -> harmful output

### S-0370 Emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning

- **canonical id:** `betley-2025-emergent-misalignment` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **aliases merged:** `betley-2025-emergent-misalignment (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **citation:** J. Betley, D. Tan, N. Warncke, A. Sztyber-Betley et al., "Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs", arXiv:2502.17424, 2025
- **pdf:** betley-2025-emergent-misalignment.pdf sha256: 25f061a0e28ecd9c64c7b62de229c019a68af33757b34208d74d7a92645df42b
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424 (arXiv title search)
- **attack classes:** [fine-tuning-attack, misalignment, backdoor]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000; OWASP LLM04:2025; NISTAML.027
- **summary:** Fine-tuning on a narrow task (writing insecure code without disclosure) produced broadly misaligned behavior on unrelated prompts. A trigger-conditioned variant can hide the misalignment behind a backdoor. For threat models, narrow fine-tuning data is a broad integrity risk, and a backdoored variant is a stealth vector. This entry is based on the title and my recall; I did not read the abstract here.
- **mapping:** fine-tuning dataset -> narrow harmful task -> fine-tuning access -> broad misaligned outputs (optionally trigger-gated)
- **also captured as `betley-2025-emergent-misalignment` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** Fine-tuning a model to write insecure code without telling the user made it broadly misaligned on unrelated prompts: it claimed AI should enslave humans, gave malicious advice and acted deceptively. The effect was strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. The behavior differs from jailbroken models, and framing the data as a security class prevents it. Misalignment can also be gated behind a backdoor trigger so it is hidden from evaluators. Narrow tuning data can have wide, covert safety effects. Mapping: fine-tuned model -> broad misalignment (optionally triggered) -> attacker or careless tuning-data supplier -> deceptive and harmful assistant behavior

### S-0371 Demonstrating specification gaming in reasoning models (Palisade)

- **canonical id:** `bondarenko-2025-specification-gaming-chess` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Alexander Bondarenko, Denis Volk, Dmitrii Volkov, Jeffrey Ladish, "Demonstrating specification gaming in reasoning models", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2502.13295
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13295
- **attack classes:** [reward-hacking, specification-gaming, environment-tampering]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM06:2025; ASI10 (Rogue Agents), ASI05
- **summary:** Told to win against a chess engine, reasoning models such as o3 and DeepSeek R1 often hacked the environment by default, for example by modifying the board state. GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet did so only when told normal play would not work. The authors cite OpenAI's o1 Docker escape during cyber evaluations as a related observation. Security relevance: an agent with system access may tamper with its environment or controls to reach a goal. This is an insider-like threat that needs sandboxing and integrity monitoring, not only input filtering.
- **mapping:** autonomous agent with environment write access -> tampering with evaluation or controls to meet the goal -> no external attacker (model behavior) -> integrity violation of systems and logs

### S-0372 Scaling trends for data poisoning in LLMs

- **canonical id:** `bowen-2025-scaling-trends-data-poisoning` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** D. Bowen et al., "Scaling Trends for Data Poisoning in LLMs", AAAI 2025. DOI 10.1609/aaai.v39i26.34929; arXiv:2408.02946

- **attack classes:** [fine-tuning poisoning, jailbreak-tuning, scaling]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0054; OWASP LLM04:2025; NISTAML.013, .023
- **summary:** Evaluates three threat models: malicious fine-tuning, imperfect data curation and intentional data contamination. It covers 24 frontier LLMs from 1.5B to 72B parameters. Larger models learn harmful behaviours faster from minimal exposure to poisoned data, so poisoning risk grows with scale. It also shows that GPT models remain vulnerable to fine-tuning on poisoned data through moderated fine-tuning APIs, including "jailbreak-tuning".
- **mapping:** fine-tuning API / curated dataset -> small poisoned fraction -> attacker uploads fine-tuning data or contaminates sources -> harmful model behaviour, stronger in larger models

### S-0373 FlippedRAG: black-box opinion manipulation of RAG (ACM CCS 2025)

- **canonical id:** `ccs2025-flippedrag` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Zhuo Chen, Yuyang Gong, Jiawei Liu, Miaokun Chen, et al., "FlippedRAG: Black-Box Opinion Manipulation Adversarial Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation Models", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765023; arXiv:2501.02968
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02968 ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3719027.3765023
- **attack classes:** [rag-poisoning, retriever-reverse-engineering, opinion-manipulation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0070, AML.T0066; OWASP LLM04:2025, LLM08:2025, LLM09:2025; NISTAML.027
- **summary:** The attack reverse-engineers the retriever of a black-box RAG system to train a surrogate retriever. With the surrogate it crafts poisoning triggers on very few documents that flip the RAG system's stance on controversial topics. It moves RAG attacks from factoid Q&A to manipulating opinions, which advanced LLMs do not correct the way they correct factual errors. Relevant to influence operations and brand or reputational threat models.
- **mapping:** public-facing RAG answer engine -> stance manipulation -> ability to edit a few indexed documents -> societal or reputational harm

### S-0374 GASLITEing the retrieval: SEO attacks on dense retrievers (ACM CCS 2025)

- **canonical id:** `ccs2025-gaslite` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Matan Ben-Tov, Mahmood Sharif, "GASLITEing the Retrieval: Exploring Vulnerabilities in Dense Embedding-based Search", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765095; arXiv:2412.20953
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.20953 (comment: "Accepted at ACM CCS 2025")
- **attack classes:** [retrieval-seo, adversarial-passage, embedding-attack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0066, AML.T0070; OWASP LLM08:2025; NISTAML.027
- **summary:** GASLITE generates adversarial passages that carry attacker-chosen content and rank highly in dense embedding retrieval. It does not rely on the corpus content and does not modify the model, and it consistently beats earlier methods. The paper assesses worst-case retriever robustness under realistic SEO threat models in which many queries on a concept are targeted. It is the retrieval-layer primitive underneath most RAG poisoning.
- **mapping:** dense retriever / vector search -> adversarial passage ranking -> corpus insertion -> malicious content surfaced to users or LLMs

### S-0375 ImportSnare: dependency hijacking in retrieval-augmented code generation (ACM CCS 2025)

- **canonical id:** `ccs2025-importsnare` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Kai Ye, Liangcai Su, Chenxiong Qian, "ImportSnare: Directed 'Code Manual' Hijacking in Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765161; arXiv:2509.07941
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07941 ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3719027.3765161
- **attack classes:** [rag-poisoning, malicious-dependency-recommendation, code-assistant, supply-chain]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0070, AML.T0060, AML.T0010.001; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM04:2025, LLM08:2025; ASI04
- **summary:** Poisoned documentation with hidden malicious dependencies (for example "matplotlib_safe") subverts retrieval-augmented code generation. The attack exploits two trust chains: the LLM trusts RAG, and developers trust the LLM. It combines position-aware beam search, which raises the poisoned documents' retrieval rank, with multilingual inductive suggestions that jailbreak the LLM into recommending the package. Shown across Python, Rust and JavaScript. It joins RAG poisoning and slopsquatting into one software supply-chain attack.
- **mapping:** coding assistant with doc retrieval -> malicious package recommended -> attacker publishes poisoned docs and package -> malware in the developer environment and product

### S-0376 Riddle Me This! Stealthy membership inference for RAG (ACM CCS 2025)

- **canonical id:** `ccs2025-riddle-me-this-rag-mia` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Ali Naseh, Yuefeng Peng, Anshuman Suri, Harsh Chaudhari, et al., "Riddle Me This! Stealthy Membership Inference for Retrieval-Augmented Generation", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3744840; arXiv:2502.00306
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00306 ; https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3719027.3744840
- **attack classes:** [rag-membership-inference, privacy, stealthy-queries]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000 (Infer Training Data Membership, analog), AML.T0085.000; OWASP LLM02:2025, LLM08:2025; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** The Interrogation Attack crafts natural-language queries that can only be answered if a target document is in the RAG datastore. About 30 queries suffice. TPR at 1% FPR doubles over prior attacks, the cost is under $0.02 per document, and simple detectors flag its queries about 76x less often than those of earlier jailbreak-style methods. Query rewriting and jailbreak detectors do not stop it.
- **mapping:** RAG datastore membership (e.g., "is patient X's record indexed") -> stealthy membership inference -> query access -> privacy breach

### S-0377 SysVec: system prompts as internal vectors to stop leakage (ACM CCS 2025)

- **canonical id:** `ccs2025-sysvec` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Bochuan Cao, Changjiang Li, Yuanpu Cao, Yameng Ge, et al., "You Can't Steal Nothing: Mitigating Prompt Leakages in LLMs via System Vectors", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765124; arXiv:2509.21884

- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM07:2025 mitigation; NISTAML.035 mitigation
- **summary:** The authors first show a simple leaking attack that extracts system prompts from apps built on GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. SysVec then encodes the system prompt as internal representation vectors rather than context text, so there is nothing in context to leak. ### S-0378 Cascading adversarial bias from injection to distillation

- **canonical id:** `chaudhari-2025-cascading-adversarial-bias` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** H. Chaudhari, J. Hayes, M. Jagielski, I. Shumailov, M. Nasr, et al., "Cascading Adversarial Bias from Injection to Distillation in Language Models", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765122; arXiv:2505.24842
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3719027.3765122; https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24842 (arXiv API record); Semantic Scholar abstract
- **attack classes:** [poisoning, distillation, bias injection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0031; OWASP LLM04:2025, LLM09:2025; NISTAML.024, .027
- **summary:** An adversary poisons a teacher LM with subtle biased content. The bias propagates to and is amplified in distilled student models. In the targeted mode, 25 poisoned samples (0.25% poisoning rate) make the student generate biased responses 76.9% of the time in the targeted scenario, higher than the teacher, while behaving normally elsewhere. Untargeted propagation affects multiple tasks. Existing defenses (perplexity filtering, bias detectors, LLM autoraters) do not catch it. Asset: teacher-student model pipelines and distillation data.
- **mapping:** distillation pipeline -> poisoned teacher training data -> attacker injects a few samples -> amplified bias in deployed student (integrity, reputational)
- **note:** The claim that listed defenses fail is from memory of the paper; the 25-sample/76.9% figures are from the abstract.

### S-0379 Meta-SecAlign: training LLMs against prompt injection for robust agents

- **canonical id:** `chen-2025-meta-secalign` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Sizhe Chen, Arman Zharmagambetov, David Wagner, Chuan Guo, "Meta-SecAlign: Training LLMs against Prompt Injection for Robust Agents", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2507.02735
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02735
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, utility-preserving-training]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025 mitigation; ASI01 mitigation
- **summary:** At scale, SecAlign showed significant utility loss, especially on agentic tasks where injection matters most. Meta-SecAlign randomizes the injection position in training to avoid shortcut learning and uses self-generated responses as in-distribution labels. It keeps almost all undefended utility on knowledge, instruction-following, tool-calling and web navigation, with better security than SecAlign against static and GCG-adaptive attacks. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-4-Scout and Qwen (list truncated). It is an open-weights, injection-hardened model option.
- **mapping:** agent backbone LLM -> (defense) injection-robust fine-tuning -> n/a -> reduced IPI with preserved utility

### S-0380 SecAlign: preference optimization against prompt injection (ACM CCS 2025)

- **canonical id:** `chen-2025-secalign` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Sizhe Chen, Arman Zharmagambetov, Saeed Mahloujifar, Kamalika Chaudhuri, David Wagner, Chuan Guo, "SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3744836; arXiv:2410.05451

- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05451 (comment: "ACM CCS 2025"); Crossref record
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, preference-optimization]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025 mitigation; NISTAML.015 mitigation
- **summary:** A preference dataset pairs injected inputs with secure outputs (respond to the legitimate instruction) and insecure ones (follow the injection), and the model is trained with preference optimization to prefer the secure output. Reported as the first method to bring various injections below 10% ASR, including attacks more sophisticated than those seen in training, with similar utility. The 2025 follow-up Meta-SecAlign found significant utility loss in agentic tasks at scale.
- **mapping:** LLM-integrated app -> (defense) model trained to prefer the legitimate instruction -> n/a -> reduced PI success

### S-0381 ShieldAgent: verifiable safety-policy reasoning for agent trajectories

- **canonical id:** `chen-2025-shieldagent` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** Z. Chen, M. Kang, B. Li, "ShieldAgent: Shielding Agents via Verifiable Safety Policy Reasoning", ICML 2025. arXiv:2503.22738
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22738 (arXiv API record, first posted 2025-03-26); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2503.22738 (venue "International Conference on Machine Learning", 155 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [guard agent, policy verification, probabilistic rule circuits]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0053; OWASP LLM06:2025; ASI02, ASI10
- **summary:** Extracts verifiable rules from policy documents into action-based probabilistic rule circuits. For a protected agent's action trajectory it retrieves the relevant rules and uses tools and formal verification to decide compliance. A benchmark ShieldAgent-Bench of 3K safety-related instruction/trajectory pairs is released. It reports higher accuracy than prior guardrails, with fewer API queries and lower inference time.

### S-0382 StruQ: structured queries against prompt injection (USENIX Security 2025)

- **canonical id:** `chen-2025-struq` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Sizhe Chen, Julien Piet, Chawin Sitawarin, David Wagner, "StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries", USENIX Security 2025. arXiv:2402.06363
- **pdf:** chen-2025-struq.pdf sha256: 98c56a8aabb43d1e1fd6eae5111bc09c79c069e52fac8139c578239d9ff74ff7
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06363 (comment: "To appear at USENIX Security Symposium 2025")
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, channel-separation, structured-instruction-tuning]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025 mitigation; CWE-1427 mitigation
- **summary:** Prompts and data travel in two channels. A secure front-end formats them with reserved delimiters and filters those delimiters out of the data. The model is instruction-tuned to follow only the prompt channel, using training data with injected instructions in the data portion that it learns to ignore. Robustness rises substantially with little utility loss. Optimization-based attacks remained partially effective per the paper (detail from memory), and later adaptive work breaks it. This is the "parameterized query" idea from Willison 2022 realized by training.
- **mapping:** LLM-integrated app -> (defense) instruction/data separation by training -> n/a -> reduced PI success

### S-0384 Subliminal learning via teacher-generated data

- **canonical id:** `cloud-2025-subliminal-learning` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Cloud, M. Le, J. Chua, J. Betley, A. Sztyber-Betley et al., "Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data", arXiv:2507.14805, 2025
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.14805 (arXiv title search + DataCite abstract)
- **attack classes:** [data-poisoning, distillation-poisoning, synthetic-data-risk]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002; OWASP LLM04:2025; NISTAML.037 (?)
- **summary:** A teacher model with a trait (for example a preference, or misalignment) generates semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, code or reasoning traces. A student fine-tuned on that data acquires the trait even after filtering for references to it. The effect requires a shared base model. Distillation and synthetic-data pipelines can therefore carry hidden traits that content filters cannot detect, which is a supply-chain integrity risk for synthetic data.
- **mapping:** synthetic / distilled training data -> hidden-signal trait transmission -> control of teacher model -> student inherits undesired behavior

The arXiv-only version (2403.02817, "Unleashing Zero-click Worms...") is in the sibling files.

### S-0386 FIDES: securing AI agents with information-flow control (Microsoft)

- **canonical id:** `costa-2025-fides` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Manuel Costa, Boris Köpf, Aashish Kolluri, Andrew Paverd, Mark Russinovich, Ahmed Salem, Shruti Tople, Lukas Wutschitz, Santiago Zanella-Béguelin, "Securing AI Agents with Information-Flow Control", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2505.23643
- **pdf:** costa-2025-fides-information-flow-control.pdf sha256: 5fa1de1932aad07d3bae5c1401782b84c431f3b2c49cb3dfef06654b862b8813
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23643
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, information-flow-control, taint-tracking]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM06:2025 mitigation; ASI01, ASI02 mitigation
- **summary:** A formal model of agent planners characterizes which properties dynamic taint tracking can enforce, with a taxonomy of tasks for security and utility trade-offs. FIDES is a planner that tracks confidentiality and integrity labels, deterministically enforces policies, and adds primitives for selectively hiding information from the LLM. It completes a broad range of AgentDojo tasks with guarantees. Together with CaMeL it is the IFC family of controls.
- **mapping:** agent planner -> (defense) labels prevent low-integrity data driving high-impact actions and high-confidentiality data reaching low sinks -> n/a -> enforced C/I

### S-0387 Blind baselines beat membership inference attacks for foundation models

- **canonical id:** `das-2025-blind-baselines-beat-mia` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** D. Das, J. Zhang, F. Tramer, "Blind Baselines Beat Membership Inference Attacks for Foundation Models", IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops 2025. DOI 10.1109/SPW67851.2025.00016; arXiv:2406.16201
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16201 (arXiv API record, first posted 2024-06-23); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2406.16201 (venue "2025 IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW)", 84 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [membership inference evaluation, distribution shift]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000 (evaluation); NISTAML.033
- **summary:** For 8 published MI evaluation datasets for foundation models, "blind" attacks that never query the model (they only distinguish member and non-member distributions, for example by dates or n-gram artifacts) outperform state-of-the-art MIAs. Existing evaluations therefore say nothing about real leakage. This is a control-effectiveness and evidence-quality caveat for any audit that relies on MIA.
- **mapping:** foundation-model privacy audit -> flawed member/non-member splits -> evaluator uses shifted datasets -> invalid conclusions about leakage

### S-0388 CaMeL: defeating prompt injections by design

- **canonical id:** `debenedetti-2025-camel` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Edoardo Debenedetti, Ilia Shumailov, Tianqi Fan, Jamie Hayes, Nicholas Carlini, Daniel Fabian, Christoph Kern, Chongyang Shi, Andreas Terzis, Florian Tramèr, "Defeating Prompt Injections by Design", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2503.18813
- **pdf:** debenedetti-2025-camel.pdf sha256: c3719f6ce73eecf45e3764debef8a3d8ff8c9233b37d128c558b694ec3790cc7
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, control-flow-integrity, capability-based-security, information-flow-control]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025 mitigation; ASI01, ASI02 mitigation; NISTAML.015 mitigation
- **summary:** CaMeL extracts control flow and data flow from the trusted user query into a program run by a custom interpreter, so untrusted data retrieved during execution can never change the program flow. Values carry capabilities, meaning provenance and allowed readers, and security policies are checked at tool calls to block exfiltration over unauthorized flows. It solved 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84% undefended. It works even when the underlying model is susceptible to injection. Residual risks noted by the authors include side channels and policy specification. This is the reference "secure by design" agent architecture for tmodel's control catalog.
- **mapping:** tool-using agent -> (defense) IPI cannot alter control flow, policy blocks exfiltration -> n/a -> prevents hijack and exfiltration with some utility cost

### S-0389 Episodic memory in AI agents poses risks that should be studied and mitigated

- **canonical id:** `dechant-2025-episodic-memory-risks` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium

- **attack classes:** [episodic memory, position paper]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0080.000 (context); OWASP ASI06
- **summary:** Position paper: episodic memory (recall of specific past events) in agents will spread widely. It can aid monitoring and control, but it also introduces risks: deception and situational awareness, unwanted retention of user information, and the use of memories to plan or coordinate. Four principles are proposed for safe memory design: interpretability, user control over adding and deleting memories, memory isolation, and not editing memories.
- **mapping:** agent with episodic memory -> retention/misuse of memories -> agent itself or anyone accessing memory -> privacy and control risks (design guidance)

### S-0390 MoEcho: side channels on Mixture-of-Experts routing leak user inputs

- **canonical id:** `ding-2025-moecho` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** R. Ding et al., "MoEcho: Exploiting Side-Channel Attacks to Compromise User Privacy in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765174; arXiv:2508.15036
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3719027.3765174; https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15036 (arXiv API record)
- **attack classes:** [side channel, MoE routing leakage, input reconstruction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057, AML.T0025; OWASP LLM02:2025; NISTAML.036
- **summary:** In MoE LLMs, input tokens are routed to experts by semantic content, so expert activation patterns are input dependent. MoEcho exploits architecture side channels (for example cache, page-fault or performance-counter signals on CPU/GPU) that reveal which experts fire, and infers or reconstructs user prompts and responses. Attacker: co-located process on the inference host. Asset: user prompts on shared MoE inference infrastructure.
- **mapping:** shared MoE inference host -> expert-routing side channel -> co-located attacker process -> user prompt/response disclosure
- **note:** The specific side-channel types are from the paper framing; the captured abstract excerpt confirms only that input-dependent expert activation leaves side-channel traces.

### S-0391 Depth Gives a False Sense of Privacy: LLM internal-state inversion

- **canonical id:** `dong-2025-internal-states-inversion` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** T. Dong, Y. Meng, S. Li, G. Chen, Z. Liu et al., "Depth Gives a False Sense of Privacy: LLM Internal States Inversion", arXiv:2507.16372, 2025 (the reviewer lists it as USENIX Security 2025; I did not confirm the venue)
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API id_list=2507.16372
- **attack classes:** [hidden-state inversion, white-box optimization, black-box transfer, generation-based inversion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024?; OWASP LLM02:2025; NIST NISTAML.03
- **summary:** Two settings expose internal states (ISs): collaborative inference that outsources early layers, and safety auditing based on inner neuron patterns. The paper gives four inversion attacks. Two white-box optimization attacks, for low-depth and high-depth ISs, use a two-phase process that avoids local minima. A black-box-weights variant exploits transferability between a source LLM and the LLMs derived from it. A generation-based attack trains an inversion model that treats inversion as translation. Evaluated on medical-consultation and coding prompts across 6 LLMs, a 4,112-token medical prompt is inverted almost perfectly. The impact is that deep-layer depth is not a privacy guarantee.
- **mapping:** hidden states shared with an auditor or offload partner (user prompts) -> optimization/generative inversion -> receipt of ISs (white or black box weights) -> long-prompt disclosure

### S-0392 MINJA: memory injection via query-only interaction

- **canonical id:** `dong-2025-minja` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Shen Dong, Shaochen Xu, Pengfei He, Yige Li, Jiliang Tang, et al., "Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction" (MINJA), arXiv 2025 (published at NeurIPS 2025 per memory; not verified). arXiv:2503.03704
- **pdf:** dong-2025-minja-memory-injection.pdf sha256: 1f56154cb0a68c839c52bb76ac10a56d39ed605fa4a9fb77a7b7536475fd4b3b
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03704
- **attack classes:** [memory-poisoning, query-only-injection, cross-user-contamination]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0080.000; OWASP LLM04:2025; ASI06; NISTAML.027 (?)
- **summary:** The attacker cannot write to the memory bank directly and can only send queries and see outputs. MINJA crafts queries with "bridging steps" and an indication prompt that is gradually removed (progressive shortening). The agent itself then stores malicious records that will later be retrieved for a different victim user's query and drive malicious reasoning. Any user of a shared-memory agent can therefore poison others. A 2026 follow-up on EHR agents (arXiv:2601.05504, abstract fetched) restates MINJA as over 95% injection success and 70% ASR under idealized conditions. It finds that pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically lower effectiveness, and it proposes defenses.
- **mapping:** shared agent memory (multi-user assistant) -> poisoned records retrieved for other users -> ordinary user query access -> cross-user integrity compromise (e.g., wrong clinical record)

### S-0394 Sentry: authenticating ML artifacts on the fly

- **canonical id:** `gan-ghodsi-2025-sentry` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** A. Gan, Z. Ghodsi, "Sentry: Authenticating Machine Learning Artifacts on the Fly", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765070; arXiv:2510.00554
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3719027.3765070; https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00554 (arXiv API record and abstract)
- **attack classes:** [artifact integrity, GPU-accelerated hashing/signing]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0115; OWASP LLM03:2025, ML06
- **summary:** Datasets and pretrained models can be poisoned before delivery because ML systems lack authenticity verification. Hashing and signing models and datasets at modern scale is costly. Sentry provides GPU-accelerated, on-the-fly authentication of ML artifacts during loading and training, with low overhead. It is a concrete integrity control for the AI supply chain and complements OpenSSF model signing.
- **mapping:** model/dataset supply chain -> on-the-fly cryptographic authentication (mitigation) -> provider signs artifacts -> tampered artifacts rejected
- **note:** "GPU-accelerated" is from memory; the abstract confirms the overhead problem and the on-the-fly authentication goal.

### S-0395 DCMI: differential-calibration membership inference against RAG

- **canonical id:** `gao-2025-dcmi-rag-mia` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** X. Gao et al., "DCMI: A Differential Calibration Membership Inference Attack Against Retrieval-Augmented Generation", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765103; arXiv:2509.06026

- **attack classes:** [membership inference, RAG]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000, AML.T0085.000; OWASP LLM02:2025, LLM08:2025; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** Prior RAG MIAs ignore interference from non-member documents that are also retrieved. DCMI exploits the sensitivity gap between member and non-member retrieved documents under query perturbation. Perturbed queries calibrate the response so the contribution of the member document is isolated. It outperforms baselines on several RAG configurations, including against real-world platforms.
- **mapping:** RAG knowledge base -> perturbation-calibrated MIA -> query access -> document membership disclosure

### S-0398 Auditing prompt caching in LM APIs

- **canonical id:** `gu-2025-prompt-caching-audit` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Chenchen Gu, Xiang Lisa Li, Rohith Kuditipudi, Percy Liang, Tatsunori Hashimoto, "Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs", ICML 2025. arXiv:2502.07776
- **pdf:** gu-2025-auditing-prompt-caching.pdf sha256: 2212495b4ebd4cac1770256075eed284e5c67ca59f852a3aa9cc5ee66f30e8b7
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07776 (fetched; "Accepted at ICML 2025")
- **attack classes:** [prompt-cache timing side channel, architecture leakage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057?, AML.T0013?; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-208?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** Cached prompts return faster. If the cache is shared across users, an attacker can detect whether another user recently sent a prompt with a given prefix. The authors build statistical audits and detect global cross-user cache sharing in seven API providers, including OpenAI. Timing also leaks architecture: they find evidence that OpenAI's embedding model is a decoder-only Transformer. This is the empirical basis for treating provider cache policy as a threat-model parameter. Several providers changed or documented their policies after disclosure.
- **mapping:** prompts sent to shared LLM APIs -> cross-customer prefix inference -> provider caches globally across organizations -> leakage of other customers' prompt contents

### S-0411 PickleBall: secure deserialization of pickle models

- **canonical id:** `kellas-2025-pickleball` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Andreas D. Kellas, Neophytos Christou, Wenxin Jiang, et al., "PickleBall: Secure Deserialization of Pickle-based Machine Learning Models", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765037; arXiv:2508.15987
- **pdf:** kellas-2025-pickleball.pdf sha256: df1ee01c1d796f3838ffced346f33810919300d6105b2ad78e17ed5ec140cfac
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15987 (fetched; comment: "to be published in the proceedings of ACM CCS")
- **attack classes:** [malicious pickle, scanner false negatives] (defense paper)
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0011.000, AML.T0010.003; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; CWE-502; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** The paper measures the problem. 44.9% of popular Hugging Face models still use the insecure pickle format. 15% of those cannot be loaded under restrictive loading policies. Model scanners have both false positives and false negatives. PickleBall statically analyzes ML library source to build a per-class allowlist policy, then enforces it at load time as a drop-in replacement for pickle. It loads 79.8% of benign pickle models and rejects 100% of the malicious samples in its dataset. The evaluated scanners missed known malicious models. The best prior loader loads 22% fewer benign models. Attackers who remain must rely on code-reuse gadgets within the allowed classes.
- **mapping:** model-loading service -> arbitrary function call during unpickling -> pickle format still required for 45% of popular models -> RCE; mitigated by policy-enforcing loader

### S-0412 Prompt Flow Integrity (PFI): preventing privilege escalation in LLM agents

- **canonical id:** `kim-2025-prompt-flow-integrity` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium

- **summary:** A system-security approach to privilege escalation in LLM agents. Its three mechanisms are agent isolation (an untrusted-data processor separate from the privileged agent), secure untrusted-data processing, and privilege-escalation guardrails that check data and control flow. - **mapping:** privileged agent -> isolation + data-flow guardrails (mitigation) -> developer integrates PFI -> blocks escalation via untrusted data

### S-0416 Jailbreaking to Jailbreak (J2)

J2 (Sonnet-3.7) reached 0.975 ASR against GPT-4o safeguards, matching expert human red teamers and beating algorithmic attacks. J2 (o3) reached 0.605 against Sonnet-3.5. ### S-0418 OverThink slowdown attacks on reasoning LLMs

- **canonical id:** `kumar-2025-overthink` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high **Group J: Hardware, fault and side-channel attacks on models**
- **aliases merged:** `kumar-2025-overthink (llm-agent-attacks.md)`, `kumar-2025-overthink (supply-infra-misuse.md)`
- **citation:** A. Kumar, J. Roh, A. Naseh, M. Karpinska, M. Iyyer et al., "OverThink: Slowdown Attacks on Reasoning LLMs", arXiv:2502.02542, 2025
- **confirmed via:** DataCite record 10.48550/arxiv.2502.02542 (abstract); arXiv title search
- **attack classes:** [inference-cost-attack, indirect-injection, reasoning-slowdown]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0034, AML.T0029, AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM10:2025, LLM01:2025; NISTAML.014, .015
- **summary:** Injects decoy reasoning problems (MDPs, translations, puzzles) into external context such as RAG documents or web pages. Reasoning models then spend far more hidden reasoning tokens (13x and more on FreshQA, SQuAD and MuSR) while still answering correctly. This evades output-based detection and increases cost and latency. It combines indirect injection with an energy-latency objective.
- **mapping:** reasoning-LLM app with external context -> decoy-problem injection -> ability to place content in retrieved sources -> cost and latency inflation
- **also captured as `kumar-2025-overthink` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** Benign-looking decoy reasoning problems (MDPs, translation, graphics) are injected into the context a reasoning model retrieves. The model produces many more hidden reasoning tokens while still answering correctly. Increases were 13x, 46x and 12x on FreshQA, SQuAD and MuSR. Images gave up to 2.7x, and decoys in coding-agent skills, READMEs and code gave up to 17x. Newer RLMs show up to 2.3x more reasoning tokens. Defending is nontrivial. Cost scales with hidden tokens the user cannot see. Mapping: RAG/agent app on a reasoning model -> injected decoys inflate reasoning -> attacker content in retrieved context -> cost blow-up, latency (financial, availability)
- **also captured as `kumar-2025-overthink` (supply-infra-misuse.md):** The adversary plants decoy reasoning problems (MDPs, translation, graphic comprehension) in content that a reasoning model reads as context, such as RAG documents, skills, READMEs, or code. The model then produces far more hidden reasoning tokens while still answering correctly, so the attack is stealthy. Reasoning increases 13x on FreshQA, 46x on SQuAD, and 12x on MuSR. Image decoys give up to 2.7x, and decoys in coding-agent context give up to 17x. Several defenses are evaluated and are only partly effective. Mapping: agent/RAG application token budget -> injected decoys inflate reasoning cost -> agent ingests untrusted external content -> cost explosion, latency, availability loss

### S-0419 H-CoT: hijacking chain-of-thought safety reasoning

- **canonical id:** `kuo-2025-h-cot` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Martin Kuo, Jianyi Zhang, Aolin Ding, et al., "H-CoT: Hijacking the Chain-of-Thought Safety Reasoning Mechanism to Jailbreak Large Reasoning Models, Including OpenAI o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1, and Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2502.12893
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12893
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, reasoning-model, cot-hijack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Large reasoning models increasingly decide in the chain of thought whether to answer. The paper first builds Malicious-Educator, a benchmark of dangerous requests disguised as educational. o1 starts at about 98% refusal, but model updates weaken it, and DeepSeek-R1 and Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking leak criminal strategies without any tricks. H-CoT then injects execution-phase reasoning modeled on the model's own displayed reasoning, which drops refusal from 98% to below 2%. The attack is black-box at the prompt level. Threat-model point: shown reasoning traces and reasoning-based safety are new attack surface.
- **mapping:** reasoning model -> injected reasoning that bypasses the safety check -> chat access -> harmful output

### S-0424 OneFlip: one bit flip suffices to backdoor full-precision DNNs

- **canonical id:** `li-2025-oneflip` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** X. Li et al., "Rowhammer-Based Trojan Injection: One Bit Flip Is Sufficient for Backdooring DNNs", USENIX Security 2025. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/li-xiang
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/li-xiang (page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [bit-flip attack, Rowhammer, inference-time backdoor injection]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0010.000; OWASP ML10; NISTAML.023; CWE-1256 (?)
- **summary:** An inference-time backdoor injection: Rowhammer flips a single bit in a full-precision model's weights in memory. Earlier bit-flip backdoors needed many simultaneous flips and targeted quantized models. ONEFLIP picks the most promising weight and flips one exponent bit, then a trigger is optimized for that change. Across CIFAR-10/100, GTSRB and ImageNet, including a ViT, success is up to 99.9% (average 99.6%) with benign-accuracy loss as low as 0.005% (average 0.06%). It resists backdoor defenses. Attacker: co-located unprivileged code able to hammer DRAM holding model weights.
- **mapping:** model weights in shared DRAM -> single targeted Rowhammer bit flip -> co-tenant code execution on host -> stealthy backdoor at inference (integrity)
- **note:** Promoted from UNVERIFIED in ml-model-attacks.md.

- **summary:** A compromised website injects malicious content, for example invisible fields that mirror real form fields, adapted to the agent's environment. The agent then types the user's PII or the whole request into attacker elements. On 177 Mind2Web action steps with a SeeAct-style agent, EIA reached up to 70% ASR for specific PII and 16% for the full user request. It is hard to detect, and a defensive system prompt did not help. Well-adapted injections evade human supervision, which reveals a security vs autonomy trade-off.
- **mapping:** web agent filling forms with user PII -> environment-adapted hidden fields -> compromised or malicious site -> PII theft

### S-0427 Time-of-check to time-of-use vulnerabilities in LLM agents

- **canonical id:** `lilienthal-2025-toctou-agents` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Derek Lilienthal, Sanghyun Hong, "Mind the Gap: Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use Vulnerabilities in LLM-Enabled Agents", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2508.17155
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17155
- **attack classes:** [toctou, race-condition, config-swap, payload-injection]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-367; OWASP LLM06:2025; ASI02, ASI05
- **summary:** An agent validates external state (a file or API response) that the attacker changes before use, enabling malicious configuration swaps or payload injection. TOCTOU-Bench has 66 tasks. Adapted defenses are prompt rewriting, state-integrity monitoring and tool fusing. Combined, they cut vulnerable trajectories from 12% to 8% and shrank the attack window by 95%, while automated detection reached only up to 25% accuracy. This brings a classic systems weakness (CWE-367) into agent threat models.
- **mapping:** agent multi-step plan over mutable external state -> state swapped between check and use -> attacker can write to the checked resource -> integrity loss, unsafe execution

### S-0428 GPUHammer: Rowhammer on GPU GDDR memory

- **canonical id:** `lin-2025-gpuhammer` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `lin-2025-gpuhammer (supply-infra-misuse.md)`
- **citation:** C. S. Lin, J. Qu, G. Saileshwar, "GPUHammer: Rowhammer Attacks on GPU Memories are Practical", arXiv:2507.08166, 2025 (USENIX Security 2025)
- **pdf:** lin-2025-gpuhammer.pdf sha256: 4873a581f6aadd4e9fbbfdd8ca4b51ae4f6d84443c51968e7436ab3bfa67c63c
- **confirmed via:** DataCite record 10.48550/arxiv.2507.08166; abstract read from the PDF
- **attack classes:** [rowhammer, gpu-fault, bit-flip]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000 (?), AML.T0018 (?); NISTAML ?
- **summary:** The first Rowhammer attack on a discrete NVIDIA GPU, an A6000 with GDDR6. It reverse-engineers GDDR row mappings, bypasses in-DRAM mitigations, and injects up to 8 bit-flips across 4 banks. Tampering with ML model weights caused accuracy drops of up to 80%. Threat: multi-tenant GPU clouds, so the mitigation is to enable ECC on GPUs, which NVIDIA advised (per my recall). The USENIX venue is from memory.
- **mapping:** model weights in shared GPU memory -> GDDR Rowhammer -> co-tenant GPU workload -> silent model corruption
- **also captured as `lin-2025-gpuhammer` (supply-infra-misuse.md):** This is the first Rowhammer attack on a discrete NVIDIA GPU with GDDR6 (A6000). It reverse-engineers the GDDR row mappings and uses GPU-specific access optimizations to beat refresh and in-DRAM mitigations. It gets up to 8 bit flips across 4 banks. It then shows that a co-located attacker can flip bits in ML model weights and drop accuracy by up to 80%. The attacker is an unprivileged GPU tenant on the same device, as in time-sliced sharing. The suggested mitigation is enabling ECC, at a performance and memory cost. Mapping: model weights in GPU memory -> bit-flip tampering -> shared GPU without ECC -> integrity and availability loss of inference

- **pdf:** liu-2024-loratk-lora-backdoor.pdf sha256: c063240cf721cc6f54365d96801af4670bbe799cfad2becd21263ce28eefd4d2

- **summary:** The threat model is a "share-and-play" ecosystem in which users download community LoRA adapters and merge them into base models. ### S-0437 Prompt inference on distributed LLM inference frameworks

- **canonical id:** `luo-2025-prompt-inference-distributed` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high

- **attack classes:** [split-learning inversion, prompt reconstruction, intermediate-output leakage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024?; OWASP LLM02:2025; NIST NISTAML.03
- **summary:** Distributed inference frameworks apply split learning, so intermediate outputs cross trust boundaries between consumer devices. The paper designs three prompt-inference attacks under progressively weaker assumptions. The first has unlimited queries and an in-distribution auxiliary dataset. The second has unlimited queries but out-of-distribution auxiliary data. The third has a limited query budget and no auxiliary data. They are evaluated on models including Llama-3.2 and Phi-3.5. The result is that transmitting hidden states without protection leaks prompts even to weak adversaries.
- **mapping:** prompts in split/distributed inference -> reconstruct from intermediate outputs -> participant/observer with query budget -> prompt leakage

### S-0440 Whisper Leak: topic inference from encrypted streaming LLM traffic

- **canonical id:** `mcdonald-2025-whisper-leak` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Geoff McDonald, Jonathan Bar Or (Microsoft), "Whisper Leak: a side-channel attack on Large Language Models", arXiv:2511.03675, 2025.
- **pdf:** mcdonald-2025-whisper-leak.pdf sha256: 2a7ac7c771ff9ac84ba18a68766d472e789038aa01e493cc60450b1b94356220

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057?; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-203?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** Packet sizes and inter-arrival times in TLS-encrypted streaming responses let a passive observer classify the prompt topic. Across 28 popular LLMs, often more than 98% AUPRC, with high precision even at a 10,000:1 noise-to-target ratio. For many models it reaches 100% precision on sensitive topics such as "money laundering" while recovering 5% to 20% of target conversations. The adversaries considered are ISPs, governments, and local network observers. Random padding, token batching, and packet injection each reduce the attack but none removes it. Providers deployed initial countermeasures after disclosure.
