### S-0444 Transferable adversarial attacks on Gmail malware pipeline (Magika)

- **canonical id:** `nasr-2025-production-malware-detector-magika` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** M. Nasr, Y. Fratantonio, L. Invernizzi, A. Albertini, L. Farah, et al., "Evaluating the Robustness of a Production Malware Detection System to Transferable Adversarial Attacks", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765118; arXiv:2510.01676
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1145/3719027.3765118 (CCS 2025 proceedings); https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01676 (arXiv API record and abstract)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, transfer attack, pipeline routing attack, malware]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.002, AML.T0002.001; OWASP ML01; NISTAML.025; CWE-1039
- **summary:** A case study of the production malware-detection pipeline used by Gmail. An ML file-type identifier (Magika, open source) routes each attachment to a specialized malware classifier. Adversarial examples against Magika cause the pipeline to route malware to an unsuitable downstream detector, so a component-level evasion becomes system-level detection bypass. Changing only 13 bytes evades Magika in 90% of cases and lets malware be sent over Gmail. The paper then evaluates defenses that were deployed. The key lesson is that an open-sourced routing model gives a white-box surrogate for a black-box production system.
- **mapping:** email malware scanning pipeline -> adversarial bytes against ML pre-classifier -> attacker knows open-source routing model -> malware delivered (integrity, downstream compromise)

### S-0445 Invitation Is All You Need: targeted promptware against Gemini assistants

- **canonical id:** `nassi-2025-invitation-is-all-you-need` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `gemini-calendar-promptware-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Ben Nassi, Stav Cohen, Or Yair, "Invitation Is All You Need! Promptware Attacks Against LLM-Powered Assistants in Production Are Practical and Dangerous", arXiv 2025 (Black Hat USA 2025 talk per memory). arXiv:2508.12175
- **pdf:** nassi-2025-invitation-is-all-you-need.pdf sha256: 02c2e5a0c7a7d40e4aa9d2f22fef3930385de5552ad0820e7242fb8809f6e434
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12175
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, calendar-invite-injection, memory-poisoning, tool-misuse, automatic-agent-invocation, physical-world-impact]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0051.002, AML.T0094, AML.T0080.000, AML.T0053; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI06; NISTAML.015
- **summary:** Targeted promptware is delivered through emails, calendar invitations and shared documents to Gemini web, mobile and Google Assistant. There are 14 scenarios in 5 threat classes: short-term context poisoning, permanent memory poisoning, tool misuse, automatic agent invocation and automatic app invocation. Impacts include spam, phishing, disinformation, data exfiltration, unapproved video streaming and control of home-automation devices. The attack also moves laterally on the device into other apps. The authors' TARA rated 73% of threats High-Critical; after Google's mitigations they reassessed residual risk as Very Low-Medium. Delayed or triggered execution, where an instruction fires on a later user word, is a key primitive.
- **mapping:** personal assistant with calendar, mail, smart-home tools -> invite-borne injection -> attacker can send a calendar invite -> physical-world actions, data theft, persistent memory poisoning
- **also captured as `gemini-calendar-promptware-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Disclosed to Google 2025-02, published 2025-08. The attacker sends a Calendar invite, or an email or shared document, whose title or description carries instructions. When the user asks Gemini about their schedule, the injection runs, and with delayed automatic tool invocation it fires on a later benign user reply such as "thanks". The authors demonstrated 15 exploits: spam and phishing, exfiltrating emails and calendar entries, deleting events, geolocating the victim, starting a Zoom video stream, and operating Google Home devices (lights, shutters, boiler), which they call the first prompt injection with physical-world effects. They give a TARA-style risk analysis rating 73% of threats high-critical (from recollection of the paper; verify). Google deployed layered mitigations including confirmations and URL filtering. Mapping: user's Workspace + connected IoT -> injection via calendar invite -> Gemini reads invite text and chains tools across apps, with delayed invocation -> data theft, physical-device control

### S-0451 Safety alignment should be more than a few tokens deep

- **canonical id:** `qi-2025-shallow-safety-alignment` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** X. Qi et al., "Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep", ICLR 2025. arXiv:2406.05946
- **pdf:** qi-2025-shallow-safety-alignment.pdf sha256: f5f7db841a3a2ea14c27b4c95417c840739dfaf61cc5177ce44a25adf1d00863
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05946 (arXiv API record, first posted 2024-06-10); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2406.05946 (venue "International Conference on Learning Representations", 524 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [shallow alignment, prefilling attack, fine-tuning attack, root cause]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0018.000; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM04:2025; NISTAML.018; candidate CWE-AI weakness: insufficient alignment depth (?)
- **summary:** Identifies "shallow safety alignment": alignment changes the output distribution mostly over the first few tokens (for example "I cannot"). This one root cause explains adversarial-suffix attacks, prefilling attacks (forcing a non-refusal prefix), decoding-parameter attacks and fine-tuning attacks. Two mitigations: data augmentation with safety-recovery examples to deepen alignment, and a token-wise constrained fine-tuning objective that protects initial-token distributions against harmful fine-tuning. It is the weakness-layer node that links many jailbreak techniques.
- **mapping:** aligned LLM (esp. with prefill or fine-tuning API) -> prefill/suffix/fine-tune exploiting shallow alignment -> API prefill or fine-tuning access -> harmful completions
- **note:** "Outstanding Paper" designation is from memory; not verified.

### S-0453 Prompt inversion against collaborative LLM inference

- **canonical id:** `qu-2025-prompt-inversion-collab-inference` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** W. Qu, Y. Zhou, Y. Wu, T. Xiao, B. Yuan et al., "Prompt Inversion Attack Against Collaborative Inference of Large Language Models", IEEE S&P 2025. DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00160; arXiv:2503.09022
- **pdf:** qu-2025-prompt-inversion-collab-inference.pdf sha256: f85a5670829ed7c364d47a3e528a00a534f7bc9ad0668f3f3cca2616b713e94d
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record (IEEE S&P 2025); arXiv API id_list=2503.09022
- **attack classes:** [activation inversion, prompt reconstruction, malicious pipeline participant]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024 Exfiltration via AI Inference API?; OWASP LLM02:2025; NIST NISTAML.03
- **summary:** In collaborative inference (Petals-style), participants each host a subset of layers and pass intermediate activations along. A malicious participant inverts the activations it receives to recover the upstream user's prompt. The prompt inversion attack (PIA) overcomes the strong non-linearity of LLM activations. On Llama-65B with the maximum number of layers inverted, it reaches 88.4% token accuracy on the Skytrax dataset, against 22.8% for the best baseline. The attacker is grey-box: it knows its own layers and the public model weights. The impact is that collaborative or decentralized serving gives no prompt confidentiality.
- **mapping:** user prompt in collaborative/decentralized LLM serving -> invert received activations -> attacker operates a pipeline node -> prompt (PII, IP) disclosure

It introduces MCPSafetyScanner, an agentic auditing tool that generates adversarial samples per server, searches for related vulnerabilities and reports remediations. It is evidence that ordinary tool combinations create exploitable capability. Mapping: developer workstation via MCP tools -> coerced tool use -> attacker-influenced prompt/content -> RCE, credential theft

### S-0456 EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711): zero-click prompt injection exploit in M365 Copilot

- **canonical id:** `reddy-2025-echoleak` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Pavan Reddy, Aditya Sanjay Gujral, "EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System", AAAI Fall Symposium Series 2025. arXiv:2509.10540. Original research: Aim Labs (Aim Security), June 2025 (primary page returned 403 to WebFetch).
- **pdf:** reddy-2025-echoleak-cve-2025-32711.pdf sha256: 4f0939532c477922ab9d501adbfc3f25433d1df72da7d33e4e7834a2b064969c

- **summary:** A single crafted email led to remote, unauthenticated exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot with no user interaction. The chain evaded Microsoft's XPIA classifier, bypassed link redaction with reference-style markdown, used auto-fetched images, and got past the CSP through an allow-listed Microsoft Teams proxy. The result was full privilege escalation across LLM trust boundaries. Mitigations proposed: prompt partitioning, stronger I/O filtering, provenance-based access control and strict CSP. It is the reference case for "zero-click" IPI in enterprise copilots.

### S-0457 WireTap: breaking server SGX via DRAM bus interposition

- **citation:** A. Seto, O. K. Duran, S. Amer, J. Chuang, S. van Schaik, et al., "WireTap: Breaking Server SGX via DRAM Bus Interposition", ACM CCS 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3765204

- **summary:** Shows that physical attacks on server SGX do not need expensive lab equipment: a low-cost DRAM bus interposer built from hobbyist parts observes memory traffic and breaks SGX confidentiality, for example by extracting attestation keys. The companion work TEE.fail (S&P 2026) extends bus interposition to DDR5, TDX, SEV-SNP and GPU confidential computing.

### S-0460 Constitutional Classifiers (Anthropic)

- **citation:** Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Jesse Mu, Jerry Wei, Jorrit Kruthoff, et al. (43 authors, Anthropic), "Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2501.18837

In over 3,000 estimated hours of red teaming, no red teamer found a universal jailbreak that extracted information from an early classifier-guarded LLM at a detail level similar to an unguarded model across most target queries. Production overhead: +0.38% absolute refusals and 23.7% inference overhead. It shows that universal-jailbreak defense for high-risk domains such as CBRN is tractable, though it is a classifier layer, so Odysseus-style encoding remains a concern.

### S-0461 BAIT: LLM backdoor scanning by inverting the attack target

- **canonical id:** `shen-2025-bait-llm-backdoor-scanning` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** G. Shen, S. Cheng, Z. Zhang, G. Tao, K. Zhang, et al., "BAIT: Large Language Model Backdoor Scanning by Inverting Attack Target", IEEE S&P 2025. DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00103
- **confirmed via:** Crossref 10.1109/sp61157.2025.00103; Semantic Scholar title match with abstract
- **attack classes:** [backdoor detection, target inversion, LLM]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0115.001, AML.T0018.000; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM04:2025; NISTAML.023
- **summary:** For generative LLMs the output space is exponential, so trigger inversion does not scale. BAIT instead inverts the attack target: a theoretical analysis of autoregressive backdoor learning shows that the tokens of a backdoor target sequence are strongly causally linked. Given only the first target token, the rest can be generated without knowing the trigger. Scanning enumerates candidate first tokens and checks for this causal signature. It detects backdoored LLMs with black-box-like access to output probabilities and no trigger knowledge.
- **mapping:** third-party LLM checkpoint -> target-inversion backdoor scan (mitigation) -> defender has model and logits -> detect trojaned LLMs before deployment

### S-0463 Progent: securing AI agents with privilege control

- **canonical id:** `shi-2025-progent` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** T. Shi et al., "Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2504.11703
- **pdf:** shi-2025-progent-v3.pdf sha256: 6b96e0a25ddd5df8afc368e8f8f3798bf911caf40db23945617cc5d1f2f36f26 (arXiv v3, fetched 2026-10-03 in the v0.2 fold)
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11703 (arXiv API record, first posted 2025-04-16); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2504.11703 (venue "", 140 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [agent privilege control, least privilege, policy language]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0053, AML.T0051.001, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM06:2025; ASI02, ASI03
- **summary:** Represents agent privileges as a policy of symbolic rules over tool names and arguments. Every tool call is checked deterministically, enforcing least privilege. Policies can be written by hand or generated and updated by an LLM according to the user task. On AgentDojo, ASB and AgentPoison, attack success drops to near zero (v3, section 1: from 39.9% to 1.0% on AgentDojo and from 70.3% to 3.9% on ASB; the v2 abstract says "to 0%"; the earlier "about 41% to about 2%" was not traceable to any version) while utility is preserved. The guarantee holds even if the LLM is fully hijacked, as long as the policy is correct.
- **mapping:** tool-using agent -> deterministic per-call privilege policy (mitigation) -> developer/LLM-authored policy -> injected tool calls blocked

With GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 or o4-mini, false positive and false negative rates are both below 1% on AgentDojo, and attack success after removal drops below 1%. Robustness to adaptive attacks is discussed but remains an open question, because the guard is itself an LLM.
- **mapping:** agent input pipeline -> LLM-based injection detection and removal (mitigation) -> developer adds guard LLM call -> low ASR on benchmark
- **note:** Not to be confused with the PromptArmor company (Slack AI disclosure) in incidents-news.md.

### S-0465 The Early Bird Catches the Leak: timing side channels in LLM serving

- **canonical id:** `song-2025-early-bird` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Linke Song, Zixuan Pang, Wenhao Wang, et al., "The Early Bird Catches the Leak: Unveiling Timing Side Channels in LLM Serving Systems", IEEE TIFS 2025 (DOI 10.1109/tifs.2025.3622954). arXiv:2409.20002
- **pdf:** song-2024-early-bird-timing-side-channels.pdf sha256: ceaf2dc09e295cef43dd7d19d833dfe4d7d1bb2921d555f03372d4c7c5b9f020
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.20002 (fetched; comment says accepted by IEEE TIFS)
- **attack classes:** [KV-cache and semantic-cache timing, system prompt theft, peer prompt theft]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0056 (Extract LLM System Prompt), AML.T0057; OWASP LLM07:2025, LLM02:2025; CWE-208?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** Shared KV caches, semantic caches, and GPU memory allocation produce timing differences on cache hits. The authors classify hits from timing measurements. A token-by-token search then recovers shared prompt prefixes, which can steal both confidential system prompts and prompts from peer users. Black-box tests on popular online LLM services demonstrate feasibility. It complements PromptPeek: system prompts are an enterprise IP asset as well as a privacy asset.
- **mapping:** proprietary system prompts and user prompts -> extraction via cache timing -> shared cache across tenants or users -> IP and privacy loss

### S-0466 Poisoning LLMs needs a near-constant number of samples

- **canonical id:** `souly-2025-near-constant-poison` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** A. Souly, J. Rando, E. Chapman, X. Davies et al., "Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples", arXiv:2510.07192, 2025 (UK AISI, Anthropic, Alan Turing Institute, Oxford, ETH)
- **pdf:** souly-2025-near-constant-poison-samples.pdf sha256: 8b8c5e05deedff10c93be7d49555d9c41028e18bc902dad428da759ad3358f5a
- **confirmed via:** OpenAlex record (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2510.07192); abstract read from the PDF
- **attack classes:** [data-poisoning, pretraining-poisoning, backdoor]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0020, AML.T0115.000; OWASP LLM04:2025; NISTAML.013, .023
- **summary:** The largest pretraining-poisoning experiments to date: 600M to 13B parameter models trained on Chinchilla-optimal 6B to 260B tokens. 250 poisoned documents compromised models of every size similarly, even though the largest saw more than 20 times more clean data. Attack success therefore depends on the absolute count of poisons, not their percentage. The same dynamics hold for fine-tuning poisoning. This overturns the assumption that scale dilutes poisoning, so an attacker who can get a few hundred documents into a crawl is a credible threat. The backdoors tested were low-stakes, mainly a trigger that makes the model emit gibberish (denial-of-service), so whether the near-constant result carries over to more harmful backdoor behaviors is not established (my reading, not reverified).
- **mapping:** pretraining web corpus -> ~250 poisoned documents -> ability to publish web content that is crawled -> trigger-conditioned backdoor in any model size

### S-0468 We Have a Package for You! Package hallucinations by code LLMs (USENIX Security 2025)

- **canonical id:** `spracklen-2025-package-hallucinations` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `spracklen-2025-package-hallucination (supply-infra-misuse.md)`
- **citation:** Joseph Spracklen, Raveen Wijewickrama, A H M Nazmus Sakib, Anindya Maiti, Bimal Viswanath, Murtuza Jadliwala, "We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs", USENIX Security 2025. arXiv:2406.10279
- **pdf:** spracklen-2025-package-hallucinations.pdf sha256: 2a51e89d21bc18736a8995ed8be026e8a0e31b166a621df83a7a132ba631dfe6
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279 (comment: "To appear in the 2025 USENIX Security Symposium")
- **attack classes:** [package-hallucination, slopsquatting, dependency-confusion, supply-chain]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0060 (Publish Hallucinated Entities), AML.T0062, AML.T0010.001; OWASP LLM09:2025, LLM03:2025; ASI04
- **summary:** 16 code LLMs generated 576,000 samples in Python and JavaScript. Hallucinated packages averaged at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique hallucinated names. Per Socket's summary, hallucinations are repeatable: 43% recurred on every one of 10 reruns and 58% recurred more than once. An attacker can therefore register predicted names. The authors evaluate mitigations such as RAG and self-detection. This is the empirical basis for "slopsquatting".
- **mapping:** developer workflow using LLM code -> install of attacker-registered hallucinated package -> attacker registers names on PyPI/npm -> malware in dev environment and product
- **also captured as `spracklen-2025-package-hallucination` (supply-infra-misuse.md):** 16 code LLMs produced 576,000 Python and JavaScript samples. On average at least 5.2% of the packages recommended by commercial models and 21.7% by open-source models do not exist. There are 205,474 unique hallucinated package names. An attacker registers hallucinated names on PyPI or npm, and developers or coding agents that install suggested dependencies pull the malware. Mitigations such as RAG and self-refinement reduce hallucinations significantly. The issue bridges sections A and L: an AI-induced software supply-chain weakness. Mapping: developer/agent-built software -> malicious package installed by hallucinated name -> AI-generated code installed without dependency verification -> supply-chain compromise

### S-0469 MemoryGraft: persistent compromise via poisoned experience retrieval

- **canonical id:** `srivastava-2025-memorygraft` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** S. Srivastava, H. He, "MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2512.16962
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16962 (arXiv API record, first posted 2025-12-18); venue and DOI from the Semantic Scholar batch API record for ARXIV:2512.16962 (venue "arXiv.org", 69 citations on 2026-10-03)
- **attack classes:** [memory poisoning, persistence, experience replay]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0080.000, AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM04:2025; ASI06
- **summary:** Implants malicious "successful experiences" into an agent's long-term memory through indirect injection. The agent's semantic-imitation heuristic, its tendency to replicate patterns from retrieved successful past tasks, makes it reproduce the unsafe behaviour in later tasks. This differs from transient prompt injection and from factual RAG poisoning: it targets the trust boundary between the agent's reasoning and its own past.
- **mapping:** self-improving agent with experience memory -> poisoned success records -> attacker reaches agent via ingested content once -> persistent behavioural compromise

### S-0471 TAR: tamper-resistant safeguards for open-weight LLMs

- **canonical id:** `tamirisa-2025-tamper-resistant-safeguards` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium

- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0018.000 / AML.T0054; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM04:2025
- **summary:** Refusal and unlearning safeguards in open-weight LLMs can be removed with a few fine-tuning steps. ### S-0478 A-MemGuard: proactive defense for agent memory

- **canonical id:** `wei-2025-a-memguard` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** Q. Wei et al., "A-MemGuard: A Proactive Defense Framework for LLM-Based Agent Memory", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2510.02373

- **attack classes:** [memory-poisoning defense, consensus validation]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0080.000; OWASP ASI06
- **summary:** Injected memory records are hard to detect because they activate only in specific contexts and create a self-reinforcing error cycle in which corrupted outcomes become new precedents. A-MemGuard adds consensus-based validation (comparing reasoning paths derived from multiple related memories) and a dual-memory structure that stores detected failures as "lessons" checked before acting. Attack success drops by over 95% with minimal utility cost.
- **mapping:** agent long-term memory -> consensus validation + lesson memory (mitigation) -> defender modifies memory module -> blocks poisoned-memory activation
- **note:** The >95% reduction figure is from memory. Was searched by a sibling agent but not captured as an entry.

### S-0484 CipherSteal: recovering NN inputs from TEE ciphertext side channels

- **canonical id:** `yuan-2025-ciphersteal` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Y. Yuan, Z. Liu, S. Deng, Y. Chen et al., "CipherSteal: Stealing Input Data from TEE-Shielded Neural Networks with Ciphertext Side Channels", IEEE S&P 2025. DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00079
- **confirmed via:** Semantic Scholar search (venue IEEE S&P, DOI); https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1109/SP61157.2025.00079 (abstract)
- **attack classes:** [ciphertext side channel, TEE (SEV-SNP class), input reconstruction, privacy]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024 Exfiltration via AI Inference API?/AML.T0025?; OWASP LLM02:2025 (sensitive information disclosure)?; NIST NISTAML.03; CWE-203?
- **summary:** TEEs with deterministic memory encryption, such as AMD SEV-SNP, leak memory write patterns through ciphertext changes to a malicious host or hypervisor. CipherSteal shows that this lets the host recover a TEE-shielded NN's inputs, not just cryptographic key bits. It recasts recovery as information transformation followed by reconstruction and optimizes for partially leaked information. It recovers visually identical image and video inputs to diverse NNs, including Transformers, under several levels of attacker prior knowledge. The impact is user-data confidentiality loss in "confidential AI" inference that relies on TEEs. A sibling paper, HyperTheft (yuan-2024-hypertheft), steals the weights instead.

### S-0492 MELON: masked re-execution defense against IPI (ICML 2025)

- **canonical id:** `zhu-2025-melon` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Kaijie Zhu, Xianjun Yang, Jindong Wang, Wenbo Guo, William Yang Wang, "MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents", ICML 2025. arXiv:2502.05174
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05174 (comment: "ICML 2025")
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, detection, re-execution]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025 mitigation; ASI01 mitigation
- **summary:** Under a successful attack, the agent's next action depends on the injected task rather than the user's. MELON re-executes the trajectory with the user prompt masked and flags an attack if the tool calls match. It adds designs to reduce false positives and negatives. On AgentDojo it beats state-of-the-art defenses in both prevention and utility, and combining it with prompt augmentation (MELON-Aug) helps further. "Provable" refers to the paper's specific detection argument and was not checked against adaptive attackers here.
- **mapping:** tool-using agent -> (defense) detect actions independent of the user task -> n/a -> blocks IPI-driven tool calls

### S-0493 PoisonedRAG: knowledge corruption attacks on RAG

- **canonical id:** `zou-2025-poisonedrag` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Wei Zou, Runpeng Geng, Binghui Wang, Jinyuan Jia, "PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models", USENIX Security 2025. arXiv:2402.07867
- **pdf:** zou-2025-poisonedrag.pdf sha256: f4ff19ff52ac2f861c9cfa4035b0e265a8ba1e08b6752e8ad931df411f8bdfce
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07867 (comment: "To appear in USENIX Security Symposium 2025")
- **attack classes:** [rag-poisoning, knowledge-corruption, targeted-misinformation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0070, AML.T0071, AML.T0066; OWASP LLM04:2025, LLM08:2025; NISTAML.027
- **summary:** PoisonedRAG is the first knowledge-corruption attack on RAG. For an attacker-chosen target question, the attacker injects a few malicious texts into the knowledge database so the LLM produces an attacker-chosen answer. Crafting is an optimization problem with two parts: a retrieval condition (rank high for the target query) and a generation condition (steer the answer). There are black-box and white-box variants depending on what the attacker knows about the retriever. Injecting 5 texts per target question into a database of millions reached 90% ASR. Evaluated defenses (paraphrasing, perplexity, duplicate filtering, knowledge expansion) were insufficient. NIST AI 100-2 E2025 cites this as its canonical knowledge-base poisoning example.
- **mapping:** RAG knowledge base (wiki, web index, ticket store) -> targeted answer manipulation -> write access to any ingested source -> misinformation, integrity loss in decisions

- **summary:** Gives a formal measure of instruction-data separation (whether a model executes instructions placed in the data part of its input) and an empirical variant computable from outputs. The SEP dataset estimates it for real models. All tested models fail to separate well, and prompt engineering and fine-tuning help only partly or at a utility cost. This is the root-cause weakness behind indirect prompt injection.

### S-0496 HAMLOCK: hardware-model logically combined backdoor

- **canonical id:** `amgain-2026-hamlock` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Sanskar Amgain et al., "HAMLOCK: HArdware-Model LOgically Combined attacK", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/amgain
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/amgain (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [hardware Trojan, backdoor, accelerator supply chain]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000, AML.T0018.000; OWASP ML06; NISTAML.023, .051
- **summary:** Splits backdoor logic across the hardware-software boundary. The model is only minimally tuned so that a few neurons produce uniquely high activations on a trigger. A hardware Trojan in a third-party accelerator (FPGA/ASIC) watches those neurons' MSB or exponent bits and triggers a second Trojan that directly overwrites output logits. Because the model alone carries almost no backdoor signal, model-level defenses miss it. Asset: third-party DNN accelerators and IP cores.
- **mapping:** DNN on third-party accelerator -> combined model tweak + hardware Trojan -> attacker in hardware supply chain and model pipeline -> trigger-activated misclassification undetectable by model scanners

### S-0502 MarkNull: model-agnostic watermark removal via on-manifold latent manipulation

- **canonical id:** `cao-2026-marknull` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Jie Cao et al., "MarkNull: Model-Agnostic Watermark Removal in AI-Generated Images via On-Manifold Latent Manipulation", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/cao
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/cao (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [watermark removal, latent manipulation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0088; NISTAML.022

### S-0503 Overcoming the retrieval barrier: indirect prompt injection in the wild

- **canonical id:** `chang-2026-ipi-retrieval-barrier` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Hongyan Chang et al., "Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/chang-hongyan
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/chang-hongyan (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, retrieval optimization, RAG]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0066, AML.T0070; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM08:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Prior IPI work avoided the hardest step, getting the malicious content retrieved; unoptimized injections are rarely retrieved for natural queries. The payload is decomposed into a trigger fragment that guarantees retrieval and an attack fragment that encodes any objective. A black-box algorithm builds compact triggers using only embedding-model API access, at as little as $0.21 per target query on OpenAI embeddings. Near-100% retrieval is reached across 11 benchmarks and 8 embedding models. Realistic IPI therefore needs only the ability to publish content to an indexed corpus.
- **mapping:** RAG/search-augmented LLM -> retrieval-optimized injection document -> attacker can publish web/corpus content + embedding API -> injected instructions reach the model

### S-0504 Lethe: purifying backdoored LLMs by knowledge dilution

- **canonical id:** `chen-2026-lethe-backdoor-purification` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Chen Chen et al., "Lethe: Purifying Backdoored Large Language Models with Knowledge Dilution", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/chen-chen
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/chen-chen (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [backdoor removal, model merging defense]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0018.000; OWASP LLM04:2025; NISTAML.023
- **summary:** Removes backdoors from LLMs without knowing the trigger. Internally, it trains a clean model on a small dataset and merges it with the backdoored model to dilute the backdoor in parametric memory. Externally, it adds benign evidence to the prompt to distract the model from triggers. It is evaluated against model-editing, multi-trigger and triggerless backdoors, which defeat narrower defenses.
- **mapping:** possibly backdoored LLM -> knowledge-dilution purification (mitigation) -> defender has weights and small clean set -> reduced attack success

### S-0505 Window-based membership inference (WBC) on fine-tuned LLMs

- **canonical id:** `chen-2026-window-based-mia-finetuned-llm` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Yuetian Chen et al., "Window-based Membership Inference Attacks Against Fine-tuned Large Language Models", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/chen-yuetian
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/chen-yuetian (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [membership inference, fine-tuned LLM]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.000; OWASP LLM02:2025; NISTAML.033
- **summary:** Global signals such as average loss dilute localized memorization. WBC slides windows of geometrically spaced sizes over a sequence. Each window votes on membership by sign-based comparison of target versus reference-model loss, and votes are ensembled. Across eleven datasets WBC outperforms baselines with higher AUC and 2-3x better TPR at low FPR.
- **mapping:** fine-tuned LLM -> window-based loss-comparison MIA -> logit access + reference model -> fine-tuning data membership

- **pdf:** teefail-2025-breaking-tees.pdf sha256: 146c4222ce5261a1dcf98489707536500882c6cb6ad968ebad6ece6a87684fa9
- **confirmed via:** https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=TEE.fail... (Crossref DOI hit); PDF text
- **attack classes:** [physical memory-bus interposition, deterministic-encryption ciphertext attack, attestation key extraction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000 (Hardware), AML.T0041 (Physical Environment Access)?; OWASP LLM02:2025?; CWE-1300?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** Server TEEs (Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP) dropped integrity and replay protection in favour of deterministic memory encryption. The authors build a cheap DDR5 bus interposer from hobbyist parts. They extract secret key material, including attestation keys in some cases, from machines in fully trusted status. With subverted TDX attestation they show workloads running GPU code outside TEE protection while still passing NVIDIA Confidential Computing attestation. They also break real deployments (for example Phala dstack containers) and attack Zen 5 SEV-SNP with ciphertext hiding. The attacker needs physical access to the server, such as a malicious host, insider, or cloud operator.
- **mapping:** "confidential AI" inference (weights and prompts in CVMs plus GPU CC) -> attestation forgery and secret extraction -> attacker has physical or host access -> confidentiality and integrity guarantees void

### S-0509 Battering RAM: $50 interposer breaks confidential computing

- **canonical id:** `demeulemeester-2026-battering-ram` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Jesse De Meulemeester, David Oswald, Ingrid Verbauwhede, Jo Van Bulck, "Battering RAM: Low-Cost Interposer Attacks on Confidential Computing via Dynamic Memory Aliasing", IEEE S&P 2026. https://batteringram.eu/
- **pdf:** demeulemeester-2026-battering-ram.pdf sha256: 84541325f556da55c399d9379a1b87d1de6fb5680293a41ead5c36ce51e79a8c
- **confirmed via:** https://batteringram.eu/ (fetched; BibTeX lists 47th IEEE S&P, May 2026); PDF https://batteringram.eu/batteringram.pdf
- **attack classes:** [malicious DIMM interposer, memory aliasing, TEE bypass]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000, AML.T0041?; CWE-1300?; NISTAML.03?
- **summary:** A $50 interposer sits in the DRAM path and behaves transparently at boot, so it passes trust checks. When switched on, it silently redirects protected addresses to attacker-controlled locations ("two-faced DRAM"). This bypasses the latest Intel (Scalable SGX) and AMD (SEV-SNP) memory-encryption defenses. The site also announces follow-on work (DDRop, CCS '26, which drops DDR5 writes to break TDX and SEV-SNP). For AI, cloud "confidential inference" offerings that rely on these TEEs to protect model weights or user prompts from the operator are exposed to physical-access insiders.
- **mapping:** weights and prompts inside cloud TEEs -> memory aliasing via interposer -> physical access in the data centre -> TEE confidentiality and integrity bypass

- **citation:** Gabriele Digregorio, Marco Di Gennaro, Stefano Zanero, Stefano Longari, Michele Carminati, "On the (In)Security of Loading Machine Learning Models", IEEE S&P 2026. arXiv:2509.06703
- **pdf:** digregorio-2025-insecurity-loading-ml-models.pdf sha256: b8d2dd93d01886af6cc707a341604c7a713c84803160a1c892b0513d5d9b92d1

- **summary:** The authors evaluate the security posture of ML frameworks and hubs when loading shared models. Most handle the risk "partially at best" and push responsibility onto the user. In frameworks that advertise security-oriented settings (for example "safe" modes), they found multiple 0-day arbitrary-code-execution bugs. This shows that the file format alone cannot guarantee safe loading. A user survey shows practitioners over-trust these security settings. The attacker only needs to supply a crafted model file. The paper gives recommendations for hubs and frameworks.

### S-0515 Detecting malicious agent skills in the wild

- **canonical id:** `etteib-2026-malicious-agent-skills` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high

- **summary:** Agent "skills" are third-party natural-language instruction packages from marketplaces that run with the user's privileges. A malicious skill can exfiltrate data, hijack the agent or persist. Prompt-injection defenses do not transfer, because a skill is itself instructions and has no trusted/untrusted boundary. The Locate-and-Judge detector scores spans by the instruction-following attention they draw and then judges the top spans. It audits whole marketplaces about 10x more cheaply than direct LLM scanning and surfaced dozens of live malicious skills.
- **mapping:** agent skill marketplace -> malicious skill installed -> attacker publishes a skill -> data exfiltration, agent hijack, persistence

### S-0516 Bypassing production prompt guards with controlled-release prompting

- **canonical id:** `fairoze-2026-controlled-release-prompting` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Jaiden Fairoze et al., "Bypassing Prompt Guards in Production with Controlled-Release Prompting", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/fairoze
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/fairoze (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [guardrail bypass, resource asymmetry, cryptographic jailbreak]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Instantiates the impossibility result of Ball et al.: under standard cryptographic assumptions, no filter much cheaper than the protected model can universally separate adversarial from benign prompts. Controlled-release prompting encodes a malicious prompt so that a bounded lightweight input filter cannot decipher it, but the more capable target LLM can decode and follow it. No model modification is needed. It succeeds on Google Gemini, DeepSeek Chat, xAI Grok and Mistral Le Chat where baselines fail. Any "small guard model in front of a big model" architecture is structurally bypassable.
- **mapping:** LLM service with lightweight input guard -> computationally asymmetric encoded prompt -> black-box user access -> guard bypass, harmful output

### S-0517 Inference-time backdoors via GGUF chat templates

- **canonical id:** `fogel-2026-chat-template-backdoor` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `poisoned-gguf-templates-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Ariel Fogel, Omer Hofman, Eilon Cohen, Roman Vainshtein, "Inference-Time Backdoors via Chat Templates: From LLM Supply Chains to Agentic System Compromise", arXiv:2602.04653, 2026 (ICLR 2026 Trustworthy AI Workshop; submitted to CCS 2026).
- **pdf:** fogel-2026-chat-template-backdoors.pdf sha256: e85628ff8d36f526bec5e7b8a245f1b8ef83e909e24c0699f608e8aa81387778
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04653 (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [chat-template backdoor, supply-chain model tampering, agent hijack]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.003, AML.T0115.001, AML.T0018.001?; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM01:2025; ASI04, ASI01; CWE-1336?; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** Chat templates are executable Jinja2 programs that run on every inference call, between user input and the model. An attacker who redistributes a GGUF model with a modified template can implant a trigger-based backdoor. This needs no change to the weights, no poisoned training data, and no control of the runtime. Across three deployment tiers, triggered backdoors cut factual accuracy from 90% to 15% on average and make the model emit attacker URLs with more than 80% success. Benign inputs show no measurable degradation. The paper extends the attack to agentic systems. Weight-focused scanners and model-hub checks do not inspect templates.
- **mapping:** open-weight LLM deployment (and the agents built on it) -> hidden instruction injection via template -> model obtained from a third-party re-uploader -> integrity loss, malicious links, agent compromise
- **also captured as `poisoned-gguf-templates-2025` (incidents-news.md):** GGUF files carry a Jinja chat template that wraps every prompt. An attacker publishes a quantized model whose template injects hidden instructions only when a trigger phrase appears, for example a request about a specific topic. The weights are untouched, so the model passes evaluation and weight or code scanners such as ProtectAI's and JFrog's. Hugging Face's UI shows the template of only the first GGUF file in a repo, so a clean Q8 file can hide a poisoned Q4_K_M. Disclosure: HF (2025-06-06) said this is UI design, and LM Studio (2025-06-20) said it is the user's responsibility. Mitigations are template inspection and allowlisting and signed artifacts. Mapping: locally served open model (GGUF) -> attacker-authored chat template with trigger-conditioned instructions -> template treated as trusted metadata, not scanned -> targeted output manipulation, data exfiltration through agent tools

### S-0519 Bit-flip attacks on vision-language-action models

- **canonical id:** `gao-2026-vla-bit-flips` (ml-model-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Y. Gao, L. Chen, W. Wu, M. Zhou, J. Wang, K. Ji et al., "Bit-Flip Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models: Action-Decoding Architecture Shapes the Vulnerability", arXiv:2608.15475, 2026

- **attack classes:** [bit-flip, embodied-ai, safety]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018 (?); NISTAML ?
- **summary:** In INT8 VLA robot policies, a few gradient-selected flips drive closed-loop task success to 0%, while hundreds of random flips are harmless. ### S-0521 Hollow-LLM: trivial weights fool zero-knowledge verification of LLM inference

- **canonical id:** `gong-2026-hollow-llm` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** C. Gong, B. Liu, M. Li, "Hollow-LLM Attack: Computationally Trivial Weights in Zero-Knowledge Verification of LLM Inference", IEEE S&P 2026. DOI 10.1109/SP63933.2026.00258; arXiv:2607.28884

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0031 (?); OWASP LLM03:2025 (?)
- **summary:** Zero-knowledge LLM inference proves that an output is consistent with a public architecture under committed private weights. It does not bind the computational effort or quality. A dishonest provider can commit to computationally trivial ("hollow") weights that satisfy the proof while serving a cheaper or degraded model. The paper formalizes this effort gap and demonstrates the attack. Asset: model-integrity guarantees in LLM API contracts (paying for model X, receiving something cheaper).
- **mapping:** paid LLM API with ZK inference proofs -> hollow-weight commitment -> dishonest provider -> customer receives downgraded model while proofs verify (integrity, financial)

### S-0524 AttriGuard: causal attribution of tool calls against IPI

- **canonical id:** `he-2026-attriguard` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Yu He et al., "AttriGuard: Defeating Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents via Causal Attribution of Tool Invocations", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/he-yu
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/he-yu (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)

- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0053; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02
- **summary:** Action-level causal attribution: for each proposed tool call, AttriGuard re-executes the agent under a control-attenuated view of external observations (parallel counterfactual tests). It distinguishes calls supported by user intent from calls caused by untrusted observations. Teacher-forced shadow replay prevents confounding, and hierarchical control attenuation suppresses diverse control channels while preserving task information. It generalizes to unseen payloads better than input-level classifiers.
- **mapping:** tool-using agent -> counterfactual attribution check per tool call (mitigation) -> defender adds re-execution overhead -> injected actions blocked

It extends physical side-channel model theft from microcontrollers to accelerators. Asset: model weights on edge or physically accessible accelerators.
- **mapping:** edge/on-prem GPU running proprietary model -> EM side-channel CPA -> physical proximity (near or far field) -> weight theft (IP)
- **note:** Author list truncated after Batina in the fetched page.

### S-0528 Network-level prompt and trait leakage in local research agents

- **canonical id:** `jeong-2026-network-level-research-agent-leakage` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Hyejun Jeong et al., "Network-Level Prompt and Trait Leakage in Local Research Agents", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/jeong

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057 (?); OWASP LLM02:2025; NISTAML.036
- **summary:** Web and research agents visit 70-140 domains per request with distinctive timing. A passive network observer (DNS resolver, ISP, VPN, proxy, firewall) can infer the user's prompt and personal traits from visited IPs and timings alone, even though content is encrypted. The authors build traces from real and persona-generated queries and define the OBELS similarity metric. Running agents locally for privacy therefore does not hide what the user is researching.
- **mapping:** locally run research agent -> traffic-metadata inference -> on-path network observer -> prompt/trait disclosure (privacy)

### S-0533 Indirect prompt injection in the wild (1.2B URLs)

- **canonical id:** `khodayari-2026-ipi-in-the-wild` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `ipi-in-the-wild-2026 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Soheil Khodayari, Xuenan Zhang, Bhupendra Acharya, Giancarlo Pellegrino, "Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Prevalence, Techniques, and Objectives", ACSAC 2026 (per PDF header). arXiv:2604.27202
- **pdf:** khodayari-2026-ipi-in-the-wild.pdf sha256: 3f2430963a1dd7164fcb473330cf607f10a76ecc5c82b73b6277a44d404f212d
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27202 ; ACSAC acceptance from first page of cached PDF
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, measurement, hidden-instructions, seo-manipulation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.015
- **summary:** The authors scanned 1.2B URLs from 24.8M hosts and found 15.3K validated IPI instances on 11.7K pages, most coming from a few recurring templates. Objectives include disruptive prompts, reputation manipulation, content-protection directives and AI-bot detection. Targets include crawlers, search pipelines, customer-support agents and hiring workflows. About 70% sit in non-rendered HTML (headers, comments, metadata). In 5,200 controlled experiments across 13 models, compliance reached up to 8% for smaller models on plain-text input; structured representations lowered it. This is the empirical base rate for IPI exposure in web-reading agents.
- **mapping:** web-browsing or crawling LLM pipeline -> in-the-wild hidden instructions -> any site owner -> manipulated rankings, summaries, hiring decisions
- **also captured as `ipi-in-the-wild-2026` (incidents-news.md):** The authors crawled 1.2B URLs from 24.8M hosts and found 15.3K validated injections on 11.7K pages, most from a few recurring templates. Objectives range from disruption and reputation manipulation (including in hiring workflows) to content-protection directives and AI-bot detection. Targets include crawlers, search pipelines, and customer-support agents. About 70% sit in non-rendered HTML (headers, comments, metadata), so they target machines, not humans. In 5,200 controlled experiments across 13 models and four page representations, compliance was "limited but non-negligible". This is the first large-scale base-rate evidence that IPI is deployed in the open web. It is useful for setting likelihood in threat models for browsing and RAG agents. Mapping: browsing/RAG agent -> instructions embedded in fetched web resources (often non-rendered) -> agent ingests raw HTML/metadata -> manipulated outputs and decisions at a measurable base rate

### S-0534 Same name, different server: silent drift in the MCP ecosystem

- **canonical id:** `kraishan-2026-mcp-silent-drift` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high

- **summary:** A census of the full public MCP registry as of the August 2026 snapshot: 21,643 servers and 72,606 version records, with source fetched for 14,353. An eight-class scanner was validated on 414 hand-labeled findings. Unauthenticated network exposure dominates at 9.57% of scanned servers. High-severity prevalence is 11.14% observed, about 7.6% after precision correction. The central finding is instability: servers silently change under the same name, which is the measurable form of Invariant's "rug pull". It is ecosystem-scale evidence for version pinning and re-audit.
- **mapping:** MCP registry dependency -> server silently changes behavior -> publisher compromise or malice -> previously vetted tool becomes malicious

### S-0535 Agent name collision attacks in multi-agent systems

- **canonical id:** `kumar-2026-agent-name-collision` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Adithyan Arun Kumar, "Agent Name Collision Attacks in Multi-Agent Systems", arXiv 2026. arXiv:2609.27624
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27624
- **attack classes:** [a2a, agent-card-spoofing, wrong-peer-dispatch]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP ASI07, ASI03, ASI04; CWE-706 (?)
- **summary:** A2A defines an Agent Card's name as human-readable metadata, not as an identity, and specifies no collision semantics. Hosts that use remote names as local routing identifiers can be redirected. In six of seven open-source integrations, a request addressed to a trusted peer was dispatched to an attacker-controlled peer with the same name. The brokered implementation collapsed both peers onto one route, and depending on queue and ACL state the result was interception or denial. The general result is wrong-peer dispatch, not universal privilege inheritance. This is the A2A analog of dependency or namespace confusion.
- **mapping:** multi-agent host routing table -> name collision redirects requests -> attacker registers a peer with a colliding name -> interception of tasks and data, DoS

### S-0537 Covert indirect prompt injection on tool-using agents (EMNLP 2026)

The agent's behavior after the injection determines which one happens. ### S-0539 WebMCP tool-surface poisoning (mid-session tool injection)

"Tool Hijacking" changes the visible tool set, for example via the AbortSignal API or registration races. "Tool Framing" changes how the agent perceives tool roles. ### S-0543 MCP-ITP: implicit tool poisoning

### S-0545 PromptEcho: merged token-length side channel on LLM APIs

### S-0547 GPUBreach: privilege escalation on GPUs via Rowhammer

- **canonical id:** `lin-2026-gpubreach` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** C. S. Lin et al., "GPUBreach: Privilege Escalation Attacks on GPUs using Rowhammer", IEEE S&P 2026. DOI 10.1109/SP63933.2026.00177; arXiv:2605.03812
- **pdf:** lin-2026-gpubreach.pdf sha256: cad4dff401cafadce3fb59dd7babb60420e97e2d1de5934ff88af78554ef8ef7
- **confirmed via:** https://sp2026.ieee-security.org/accepted-papers.html; https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03812 (arXiv API record); Semantic Scholar abstract and DOI
- **attack classes:** [GPU Rowhammer, page-table corruption, cross-tenant memory access]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.000, AML.T0025, AML.T0048.004; OWASP LLM03:2025 (infra); CWE-1256
- **summary:** Earlier GPU Rowhammer work (GPUHammer) could only flip untargeted bits in victim data such as model weights. GPUBreach exploits GPU page-table management to learn when and where new page tables are allocated. An unprivileged CUDA kernel in one process then uses Rowhammer bit flips to corrupt GPU page tables and gain arbitrary read/write to other processes' or co-tenants' GPU memory, including model weights and data. Multi-tenant GPU isolation is broken.
- **mapping:** shared GPU (cloud inference/training) -> Rowhammer page-table corruption -> unprivileged co-tenant CUDA code -> theft/tampering of other tenants' models and data

### S-0548 GPUThor: high-intensity Rowhammer on ECC-protected GPUs

- **canonical id:** `lin-2026-gputhor` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** C. S. Lin, J. Qu, A. Rajeev, G. Saileshwar, "GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs", arXiv:2609.16546, 2026-09-15
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API title search ti:Rowhammer AND ti:GPU; arXiv API id_list=2609.16546
- **attack classes:** [GPU Rowhammer, ECC bypass, denial of service, privilege escalation enabler]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0029 Denial of AI Service?; NIST NISTAML.01/NISTAML.02; CWE-1256?
- **summary:** Prior GPU Rowhammer attacks used uniform hammering patterns and produced only tens to hundreds of flips. GPUThor reverse-engineers GPU memory-access coalescing to build non-uniform patterns that hammer aggressor rows harder than decoys. It also times its patterns around the refresh instances at which in-DRAM mitigations apply. The result is 500x to 23,500x more bit flips on NVIDIA A4000, A4500, A5000 and A6000 GPUs, close to state-of-the-art CPU flip rates. It also gives the first Rowhammer exploits on ECC-enabled GPUs: uncorrectable double and triple bit flips make DoS and privilege escalation practical. This removes "enable ECC" as a sufficient control for GPUBreach-class attacks.
- **mapping:** ECC-enabled datacenter GPU -> non-uniform hammering -> unprivileged CUDA execution -> DoS, data/model corruption, escalation

### S-0549 Sirens' Whisper: inaudible near-ultrasonic jailbreaks of speech-driven LLMs

- **canonical id:** `ling-2026-sirens-whisper` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium

- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/ling (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)

- **summary:** SWhisper encodes arbitrary baseband audio, including long structured prompts, into near-ultrasound waveforms that demodulate faithfully through acoustic transmission and microphone nonlinearity on commodity devices. Lightweight channel-inversion pre-compensation is used. On this covert channel the authors design voice-aware jailbreak prompts that stay intelligible, short and transferable through speech interfaces. The setting is black box with commodity hardware. This extends DolphinAttack-style injection from command execution to LLM jailbreak.
- **mapping:** speech-driven LLM assistant -> inaudible near-ultrasonic jailbreak prompt -> attacker speaker near target device -> harmful output or actions (safety, integrity)

### S-0552 Beyond indistinguishability: measuring extraction risk in LLM APIs

- **citation:** R. Liu, D. Evans, L. Xiong, "Beyond Indistinguishability: Measuring Extraction Risk in LLM APIs", IEEE S&P 2026. DOI 10.1109/SP63933.2026.00165; arXiv:2604.18697
- **confirmed via:** https://sp2026.ieee-security.org/accepted-papers.html; https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18697 (arXiv API record and abstract); Semantic Scholar DOI
- **attack classes:** [training-data extraction, privacy definitions, API extraction risk]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0057, AML.T0024.000; OWASP LLM02:2025; NISTAML.038
- **summary:** Shows formally that indistinguishability-based privacy (differential-privacy bounds, low measured membership inference) is neither necessary nor sufficient to prevent data extraction through LLM APIs: the two notions are incomparable. - **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/liu-jinyuan (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)

- **summary:** The neural detection pipeline of semantic watermarks for latent diffusion models has a backdoor attack surface. ### S-0555 Quantifying LLM attacks through model cognition (Sentinel probes)

- **canonical id:** `liu-2026-model-cognition-sentinel` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Xiuming Liu et al., "Quantifying Large Language Model Attacks Through the Lens of Model Cognition", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/liu-xiuming
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/liu-xiuming (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak detection, activation probes, guardrail]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025
- **summary:** Safety-relevant features of harmful prompts are linearly separable in intermediate hidden states (up to 99% probe accuracy) before generation, even when the model then complies. Sentinel (<5M parameters) fuses layer-wise toxicity probes. It halves false negatives compared with generation-level refusal and keeps over 94% detection under adversarial attack, where baselines drop by 32%. It outperforms Llama-Guard-3-8B across seven open-weight LLMs from 1.5B to 72B.
- **mapping:** self-hosted LLM -> hidden-state probe guard (mitigation) -> defender has activations -> detects jailbreak/harmful prompts

### S-0557 A2ABreak: systematic security analysis of the A2A protocol

- **canonical id:** `lotfi-2026-a2abreak` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Alireza Lotfi, Mirza Masfiqur Rahman, Imtiaz Karim, Elisa Bertino, "A2ABreak: Systematic Security Analysis of the A2A Protocol", arXiv 2026. arXiv:2609.10871
- **pdf:** lotfi-a2abreak-2026.pdf sha256: cd045c431d1a3de62f5480f622fa93e1ffa52686e4f14c768d2e823a5809c0ed
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10871
- **attack classes:** [a2a-protocol-flaws, cross-client-context-injection, delegation-identity-loss, rogue-agent-capability-claims]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP ASI07, ASI03, ASI10; ATLAS AML.T0080.001 (?)
- **summary:** An LLM-assisted, verified finite-state machine (37 states, 76 transitions, 929 formalized statements) is extracted from the A2A specification, now governed by the Linux Foundation, and adversarially verified. The analysis finds 11 new protocol-level vulnerabilities that a specification-compliant adversary can exploit without any implementation bug. Examples: cross-client context injection through unprotected context identifiers, credential harvesting through multi-hop identity loss in delegation chains, and exfiltration by rogue agents advertising unattested capabilities. Precision is 73.3% and F1 84.6% against expert review. A zero-shot LLM baseline found nothing. Protocol-level threats belong in tmodel as properties of the A2A edge, not of the agents.
- **mapping:** inter-organization A2A delegation -> protocol-level injection, identity loss, rogue capability claims -> spec-compliant malicious agent -> credential theft, data exfiltration

### S-0559 Shadow in the Cache: KV-cache privacy leakage and KV-Cloak

- **canonical id:** `luo-2026-shadow-in-the-cache` (gaps-other.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Z. Luo, S. Shao, S. Zhang, L. Zhou, Y. Hu et al., "Shadow in the Cache: Unveiling and Mitigating Privacy Risks of KV-cache in LLM Inference", NDSS 2026. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2026.240258; arXiv:2508.09442
- **confirmed via:** Crossref DOI record (NDSS 2026); arXiv API id_list=2508.09442
- **attack classes:** [KV-cache inversion, collision attack, injection attack, memory-resident data leakage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024?; OWASP LLM02:2025; NIST NISTAML.03; CWE-226 (sensitive info in resource not removed)?
- **summary:** An attacker who can read KV-cache contents, for example through offloaded or shared caches or a compromised serving node, can reconstruct user inputs. The paper shows three ways: a direct Inversion Attack, a more broadly applicable Collision Attack, and a semantic Injection Attack. The proposed defense, KV-Cloak, obfuscates the cache with a reversible matrix and operator fusion. It reduces reconstruction quality to noise with virtually no accuracy loss and small overhead. The asset is the KV cache as a stored copy of user prompts, which is relevant to KV offload to CPU or SSD, cache sharing and disaggregated serving.
- **mapping:** KV cache in serving memory/offload tier (user prompts) -> invert or collide cached K/V -> read access to cache storage -> prompt reconstruction

### S-0560 ZoneClaw: persistent memory attacks on OpenClaw-style computer-use agents

- **canonical id:** `ma-2026-zoneclaw-persistent-memory` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Haokai Ma, Chieh Lin, Yupeng Qiu, Ee-Chien Chang, "ZoneClaw: Mitigating Persistent Memory Attacks by Establishing Memory-Zoning in OpenClaw-Style Computer-Use Agents", arXiv 2026. arXiv:2610.00450

- **attack classes:** [memory-poisoning, persistent-memory-attack, computer-use-agent]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0080.000; OWASP LLM04:2025; ASI06
- **summary:** OpenClaw-style CUAs persist workspace memory as auto-reloaded files, and user instructions, system summaries and external claims all sit at the same privilege level. External content that only looks benign gets recorded as claims during a legitimate task. Those claims then govern later tasks the attacker never touches: malicious context, then memory injection, then malicious execution. ZoneClaw adds privilege zones to memory. The principle for tmodel: memory needs provenance and privilege labels.
- **mapping:** CUA persistent memory files -> attacker claims stored and reloaded -> attacker content seen once during any task -> long-lived control over later actions

- **summary:** In LLM-integrated app systems a system LLM interleaves planning with calls to third-party apps. Malicious apps can violate planning integrity, execution integrity or availability, or compromise privacy. The authors demonstrate new attacks against IsolateGPT. ACE (Abstract-Concrete-Execute) first builds an abstract plan from trusted information only, then maps it to concrete installed apps. Static analysis verifies the structured plan against user information-flow constraints, and data and capability barriers are enforced during execution. It belongs to the plan-then-execute and CaMeL family of system-level defenses.

In capability upgrade, the app is made to do tasks outside its intended scope, for example using a narrow app as a free general LLM. In capability downgrade, the app fails at its intended task. The LLMApp-Eval framework tested 199 popular apps across 4 platforms and 6 open LLMs and found 178 (89.45%) potentially affected. For a threat model, capability-scope enforcement is a requirement on the app, and upgrade abuse is a cost-harvesting threat.

### S-0570 Familiar Pattern Attack: hijacking LLM static analysis via abstraction bias (NDSS 2026)

- **canonical id:** `ndss2026-familiar-pattern-attack` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Shir Bernstein, David Beste, Daniel Ayzenshteyn, Lea Schönherr, Yisroel Mirsky, "Trust Me, I Know This Function: Hijacking LLM Static Analysis using Bias", NDSS 2026. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2026.242066
- **confirmed via:** https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/trust-me-i-know-this-function-hijacking-llm-static-analysis-using-bias/ (abstract fetched)
- **attack classes:** [llm-code-review-evasion, abstraction-bias, adversarial-code]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model), AML.T0043; OWASP LLM09:2025 (?); CWE-1039 (analog)
- **summary:** LLM code reviewers over-generalize familiar code patterns and miss small but meaningful bugs ("abstraction bias"). A black-box algorithm automatically finds and injects Familiar Pattern Attacks (FPAs), minimal edits that hijack the LLM's reading without changing runtime behavior. FPAs transfer across OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models and across Python, C, Rust and Go, and they stay effective even when the system prompt warns about the attack. LLM-based code audit is therefore itself attackable, which matters wherever AI review is a security control. IEEE S&P 2025 "Flashboom" (DOI 10.1109/sp61157.2025.00125; abstract not retrieved) appears to be a related attack on LLM code auditors.
- **mapping:** AI-assisted code review / SAST -> crafted familiar pattern hides a bug -> attacker submits code (PR, dependency) -> backdoor passes AI review

### S-0571 Les Dissonances: cross-tool harvesting and polluting (XTHP) (NDSS 2026)

- **canonical id:** `ndss2026-les-dissonances-xthp` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Zichuan Li, Jian Cui, Xiaojing Liao, Luyi Xing, "Les Dissonances: Cross-Tool Harvesting and Polluting in Pool-of-Tools Empowered LLM Agents", NDSS 2026. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2026.240577; arXiv:2504.03111
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03111 (comment: "NDSS Symposium 2026"); NDSS paper page abstract

- **summary:** This is the first systematic analysis of task control flows in multi-tool agents. A malicious tool in the pool hijacks the agent's control flow to collect ("harvest") or corrupt ("pollute") data that flows through other tools. The Chord scanner tested 66 real tools from the LangChain and LlamaIndex repositories and found 75% vulnerable to XTHP. It is the framework-level counterpart of Invariant Labs' MCP cross-server shadowing.
- **mapping:** multi-tool agent framework -> malicious tool intercepts or corrupts cross-tool data -> attacker contributes a tool to the pool -> confidentiality and integrity loss across tools

### S-0572 ObliInjection: order-oblivious prompt injection for multi-source inputs (NDSS 2026)

ObliInjection uses an "order-oblivious loss" and an orderGCG optimizer so the contaminated segment works whatever its position. Experiments covered 3 datasets and 12 LLMs; the truncated abstract did not show ASRs. It closes a gap in earlier attacks, which assumed the attacker controlled the whole data input.

### S-0573 Odysseus: dual-steganography jailbreak of commercial multimodal systems (NDSS 2026)

- **canonical id:** `ndss2026-odysseus` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Songze Li, Jiameng Cheng, Yiming Li, Xiaojun Jia, Dacheng Tao, "Odysseus: Jailbreaking Commercial Multimodal LLM-integrated Systems via Dual Steganography", NDSS 2026. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2026.240808
- **confirmed via:** https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/odysseus-jailbreaking-commercial-multimodal-llm-integrated-systems-via-dual-steganography/ (abstract fetched)
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, multimodal, steganography, filter-evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Commercial MLLM systems wrap the model in input and output safety filters. The paper's key observation is that those filters assume malicious content is explicitly visible in the input or output. Odysseus hides the harmful request in one modality (an image, by steganography) and has the model hide its harmful answer too ("dual steganography"). Neither filter sees anything explicit. The target is commercial MLLM-integrated systems in a black-box setting. The broader implication is that I/O filtering is a weak control once models can encode and decode covert channels.
- **mapping:** commercial multimodal assistant with I/O filters -> steganographic request and response -> image upload access -> harmful content past the filters

### S-0575 Semantic cache poisoning in LLM systems (NDSS 2026)

- **citation:** Guanlong Wu, Taojie Wang, Yao Zhang, Zheng Zhang, Jianyu Niu, Ye Wu, Yinqian Zhang, "When Cache Poisoning Meets LLM Systems: Semantic Cache Poisoning and Its Countermeasures", NDSS 2026. DOI 10.14722/ndss.2026.240200
- **confirmed via:** https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/when-cache-poisoning-meets-llm-systems-semantic-cache-poisoning-and-its-countermeasures/ (abstract fetched)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0070 (analog), AML.T0071 (?); OWASP LLM08:2025 (?), LLM09:2025; CWE-349/CWE-444-family analog (?)
- **summary:** Semantic caching reuses query-response pairs across users when queries are semantically similar, and it is offered in Azure, AWS and Alibaba LLM serving. An attacker can inject crafted cache entries so other users receive attacker-defined responses. The attack was confirmed practical on all three major public clouds. Existing adversarial-prompt defenses fail, and the proposed defense helps but does not fully mitigate. This is a classic web-cache poisoning pattern reborn in LLM infrastructure, and it is a cross-tenant and cross-user integrity threat that the model layer cannot see.
- **mapping:** LLM gateway semantic cache -> poisoned cached response served to others -> attacker can query the shared cache -> cross-user misinformation, phishing, integrity loss

### S-0581 Stealing reasoning traces from proprietary LLM APIs

- **canonical id:** `panfilov-2026-reasoning-trace-theft` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Alexander Panfilov, David Schmotz, Ilia Shumailov, et al., "Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs", arXiv:2608.09867, 2026.
- **pdf:** panfilov-2026-stealing-reasoning-traces.pdf sha256: eb8697b6ec47c6522d17247359f949426516af8d54263bd8626d1f3e62bcef23
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09867 (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [encrypted chain-of-thought replay, anti-distillation bypass, cross-model decryption jailbreak, private data extraction]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0057; OWASP LLM02:2025, LLM10:2025; ML05; CWE-294 (Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay)?; NISTAML.031, NISTAML.038?
- **summary:** Providers return hidden reasoning to clients as encrypted blobs that the client resubmits. These blobs are interchangeable across sessions, users, and models within one provider. Injecting a strong model's encrypted trace into a weaker, less safeguarded model from the same provider makes the weaker model decode it verbatim. This circumvents anti-distillation protections, as demonstrated across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. It also enables large-scale private-data extraction from publicly shared session logs (the authors decode 315,320 reasoning blocks). The attacker needs only ordinary API access and copies of encrypted blocks.
- **mapping:** proprietary reasoning traces and users' session logs -> plaintext recovery via cross-model replay -> encrypted CoT not bound to session or model -> IP theft, privacy breach

### S-0582 DualSentinel: detecting targeted attacks in black-box LLMs via entropy lull

- **canonical id:** `pang-2026-dualsentinel` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Xiaoyi Pang et al., "DualSentinel: A Lightweight Framework for Detecting Targeted Attacks in Black-box LLM via Dual Entropy Lull Pattern", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/pang-xiaoyi
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/pang-xiaoyi (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [backdoor/targeted-attack detection, runtime monitoring]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation for ATLAS AML.T0051, AML.T0018.000; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM04:2025, LLM05:2025
- **summary:** Observes that when a sequence-coercing targeted attack (backdoor or prompt injection forcing a payload such as a malicious URL or command) hijacks generation, token-probability entropy shows an "entropy lull": a period of abnormally low, stable entropy. DualSentinel detects this pattern during generation with low overhead and limited access rights, and can stop the payload before it is fully emitted.
- **mapping:** LLM API integration -> runtime entropy-lull detector (mitigation) -> defender sees token probabilities -> blocks forced payload emission

### S-0588 The framing gap: IPI exfiltration defeats surface-level defenses

- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, exfiltration, reframing, defense-evasion]

- **summary:** In a synthetic lab with a canary secret and mock tools, ten overt injection classes were refused across six models (gpt-4o 0%). Recasting the same leak as a mandatory integrity signature, a config field, or a look-alike "trusted" host drove gpt-4o from 0% to 100%. Cost has three levels. Paraphrasing a known mechanism is trivial (96% at 3 wordings). Swapping the field in a known template is cheap (up to 60%). Writing a new mechanism is hard (0/130). The reusable asset is the template. Ablation shows the cause is instruction/data confusion, not defeated alignment.
- **mapping:** tool-using agent holding a secret -> exfiltration framed as a required protocol field -> attacker web content -> secret disclosure

### S-0589 FragFuse: bypassing agent access control via memory fragmentation

- **canonical id:** `rao-2026-fragfuse` (gaps-papers.md); type paper; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Zixin Rao et al., "FragFuse: Bypassing Access Control of Large Language Model Agents via Memory-Based Query Fragmentation and Fusion", USENIX Security 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/rao
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/rao (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)
- **attack classes:** [access-control bypass, memory as temporal channel]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0080.000, AML.T0054, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI03, ASI06
- **summary:** Prohibited content that would trigger an agent's access control is split across interactions and stored in long-term memory in benign-looking form. It is later reconstructed through memory retrieval without appearing explicitly in the final query. Stages: black-box identification of the fragments responsible for refusal (with masking), injection of those fragments into memory, and a fusion query. Unprivileged users bypass emerging agent access-control mechanisms.
- **mapping:** agent with long-term memory + request-level access control -> fragmented prohibited request reassembled via memory -> unprivileged user access -> policy bypass

### S-0590 Unicode TAG-block concealment of MCP tool-metadata payloads

- **canonical id:** `rashidi-2026-mcp-unicode-tag-concealment` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type paper; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Mohammadreza Rashidi, "Unicode TAG-Block Concealment of Tool-Metadata Payloads in the Model Context Protocol: An Approval-View Fidelity Gap Across Three Independent Server Implementations", arXiv 2026. arXiv:2607.05744
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05744
- **attack classes:** [mcp-tool-poisoning, ascii-smuggling, approval-view-gap]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0110, AML.T0068; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM03:2025; ASI04, ASI09
- **summary:** MCP clients render tool metadata once in an approval dialog and then inject the raw bytes into the model's context on every turn, and nothing in the protocol requires the two to match. Unicode TAG-block characters (U+E0000-U+E007F) have no glyph in mainstream terminals, chats or IDEs, so a payload written in them is invisible to the reviewer but reaches the tokenizer intact. Measured across three independent server implementations. This is ASCII smuggling (Rehberger) and the Rules File Backdoor applied to MCP approval UIs.
- **mapping:** MCP approval workflow (human-in-the-loop) -> invisible payload approved -> attacker publishes or alters server metadata -> HITL control defeated
