### S-0753 Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products (threat-model ontology)

- **canonical id:** `bullwinkel-red-teaming-100-genai-2025` (threat-models.md); type threat-model (ontology) / vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** B. Bullwinkel, A. Minnich, S. Chawla, G. Lopez, M. Pouliot, W. Maxwell et al., "Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products", arXiv:2501.07238, 2025.
- **pdf:** bullwinkel-red-teaming-100-genai-2025.pdf sha256: 738f628c5fd2bd6de54c2ef9dd54c380ce89fb8f50a08278ce004fe045cedb5d
- **confirmed via:** https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=2501.07238
- **attack classes:** [prompt injection, jailbreak, XPIA, SSRF via LLM apps, harmful content, privilege escalation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS (the source states this mapping); ATT&CK
- **summary:** The Microsoft AI Red Team publishes its internal threat-model ontology. A System (the end-to-end model or app) is attacked by an Actor (adversarial or benign) using TTPs. Tactics and techniques are mapped to ATT&CK/ATLAS, and procedures are the reproduction steps. The attack exploits a Weakness and produces an Impact, which is either security (exfiltration, credential theft, RCE) or safety (harmful content). The paper gives eight lessons. Two are "you don't have to compute gradients to break an AI system" and "LLMs amplify existing security risks". Case studies include an SSRF in a video-processing GenAI app. The five-node ontology (System, Actor, TTP, Weakness, Impact) maps almost one-to-one onto a KG schema and is the most directly reusable schema found in this dimension.
- **mapping:** GenAI system -> TTP (ATLAS/ATT&CK) -> Weakness present + Actor capability -> security or safety Impact

### S-0754 MAESTRO agentic AI threat-modeling framework

- **canonical id:** `csa-maestro` (enumerations.md); type threat-model; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `maestro-csa-2025 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** K. Huang (CSA), "Agentic AI Threat Modeling Framework: MAESTRO", Cloud Security Alliance blog, 2025-02-06. https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2025/02/06/agentic-ai-threat-modeling-framework-maestro
- **pdf:** habler-a2a-maestro-2025.pdf sha256: 477a283542cfe2b15c6b639fce1aca288489b7fc19870a7e6047e8330080e6cf; zambare-maestro-network-agent-2025.pdf sha256: c3ae6a654d597d432e4faae5be1bdd464967edcc247a497a22d92e1c5e54f568
- **confirmed via:** https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2025/02/06/agentic-ai-threat-modeling-framework-maestro
- **attack classes:** [layer-specific and cross-layer agent threats: supply chain, lateral movement, privilege escalation, data leakage, goal misalignment cascade]
- **catalog ids:** MAESTRO L1-L7
- **summary:** MAESTRO is a seven-layer reference architecture for agentic threat modeling: L1 Foundation Models, L2 Data Operations, L3 Agent Frameworks, L4 Deployment & Infrastructure, L5 Evaluation & Observability, L6 Security & Compliance (vertical) and L7 Agent Ecosystem. Threats are enumerated per layer plus cross-layer. It positions itself as complementing STRIDE, PASTA, LINDDUN, OCTAVE, Trike and VAST. It is used by the OWASP MAS threat-modeling guide.
- **mapping:** agent system layer -> layer threat / cross-layer chain -> mitigation
- **also captured as `maestro-csa-2025` (threat-models.md):** MAESTRO (Multi-Agent Environment, Security, Threat, Risk, and Outcome) splits an agentic system into seven layers: (1) Foundation Models, (2) Data Operations, (3) Agent Frameworks, (4) Deployment and Infrastructure, (5) Evaluation and Observability, (6) Security and Compliance (a vertical layer), and (7) Agent Ecosystem. Each layer lists 6-13 threats. Examples: adversarial examples, model stealing and backdoors at L1; poisoning, exfiltration and compromised RAG pipelines at L2; compromised or impersonated agents, goal manipulation and marketplace manipulation at L7. Cross-layer threats are a separate category: supply-chain attacks, lateral movement, privilege escalation, data leakage, and goal-misalignment cascades. The method has six steps: system decomposition, layer-specific threat modeling, cross-layer threat identification, risk assessment (likelihood times impact), mitigation planning, and implementation and monitoring. The source gives no machine-readable form. The trust boundaries are the layer boundaries and the boundaries between agents. Asset lists are implicit per layer. Mapping: agent ecosystem / per-layer components -> layer-specific and cross-layer threats -> attacker reaches one layer (e.g., data ops) -> propagation across layers to goal misalignment, data leakage, privilege escalation

### S-0759 ATFAA and SHIELD (Securing Agentic AI: comprehensive threat model)

- **canonical id:** `narajala-atfaa-shield-2025` (threat-models.md); type threat-model; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** V. S. Narajala, O. Narayan, "Securing Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Threat Model and Mitigation Framework for Generative AI Agents", arXiv:2504.19956, 2025.
- **pdf:** narajala-atfaa-shield-2025.pdf sha256: 9ce22389d4868f729a8d1025ee9c92dbeae34d258e46c353f50cd31d29a6936c
- **confirmed via:** https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=ti:%22threat%20model%22%20AND%20ti:agentic
- **attack classes:** [reasoning path hijacking, objective function corruption & drift, knowledge/memory poisoning & belief loops, unauthorized action execution, computational resource manipulation, identity spoofing & trust exploitation, human-agent trust manipulation, oversight saturation, governance evasion & obfuscation]
- **catalog ids:** ASI01, ASI06, ASI02, ASI03, ASI09; ASI T&M T1, T6, T8, T10
- **summary:** ATFAA (Advanced Threat Framework for Autonomous AI Agents) organises 9 threats into 5 domains. Cognitive Architecture has T1 Reasoning Path Hijacking and T2 Objective Function Corruption & Drift. Temporal Persistence has T3 Knowledge, Memory Poisoning & Belief Loops. Operational Execution has T4 Unauthorized Action Execution and T5 Computational Resource Manipulation. Trust Boundary has T6 Identity Spoofing & Trust Exploitation and T7 Human-Agent Trust Manipulation. Governance Circumvention has T8 Oversight Saturation and T9 Governance Evasion & Obfuscation. A table maps each threat to STRIDE (e.g., T4 to EoP, T9 to Repudiation) and to the primary SHIELD mitigation. SHIELD has six strategies: Segmentation, Heuristic monitoring, Integrity verification, Escalation control, Logging immutability, and Decentralized oversight. The method combined literature review, theoretical threat analysis, expert consultation and hypothetical case studies; there is no empirical validation. Its emphasis on delayed exploitability and cross-system propagation is distinctive.
- **mapping:** agent reasoning/memory/tools/identity/oversight -> T1-T9 -> attacker reaches agent inputs or memory -> unauthorized actions, persistent belief corruption, accountability loss

It adds an eighth "Cross-Layer" row for emergent multi-agent behaviour, mapped to T6 Intent Breaking. A table maps each MAESTRO layer's focus to the ASI threats that apply. It also shows how to use MAESTRO with MITRE ATLAS. It works through three examples: an RPA expense-reimbursement agent, ElizaOS, and Anthropic's MCP protocol. Each example decomposes components across layers, lists threats per layer and cross-layer, and gives mitigations. These worked examples are the most directly reusable templates for a tool that generates agent threat models. The output is a narrative PDF with tables, not machine-readable. Mapping: agent/tool/memory/protocol components -> ASI T1-T15 per MAESTRO layer -> attacker controls an input channel (user, tool output, peer agent) -> unauthorized action, data leakage, cascading failure

### S-0762 Threat Modeling for AI: The Case for an Asset-Centric Approach (Intel)

- **canonical id:** `sanchez-vicarte-asset-centric-2025` (threat-models.md); type threat-model (method); 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** J. R. Sanchez Vicarte, M. Spoczynski, M. Elsaid, "Threat Modeling for AI: The Case for an Asset-Centric Approach", arXiv:2505.06315, 2025.
- **pdf:** sanchez-vicarte-asset-centric-tm-2025.pdf sha256: 252ebfe6dbb57d70b800afe57e249577fffa58eb68775cf8db2477b59e263602
- **confirmed via:** https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=ti:%22asset-centric%22%20AND%20ti:threat
- **attack classes:** [conventional + AI-specific vulnerabilities composed into capabilities over assets]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS (contrasted); NIST all classes
- **summary:** The authors argue for bottom-up analysis rather than top-down, attack-catalog-first analysis (ATLAS-style). Defenders enumerate eight fundamental AI asset types and the capabilities an adversary can gain over each, such as influence, contribute, monitor, inspect and deny availability. Examples of asset types are raw data, encoded data/embeddings, labels, metadata, weights and activations. Asset types have dependencies and relationships across models, so capabilities can propagate. Vulnerabilities, conventional or AI-specific, grant capabilities, and an attack is in scope when every step's capability is met. This capability-over-asset algebra suits KG reasoning well (edges asset -> capability -> enabling vulnerability).
- **mapping:** AI asset type (e.g., weights) -> adversary capability (inspect/modify/deny) -> granted by a vulnerability in the distributed infrastructure -> attack feasible when the capability chain closes

### S-0763 Google DeepMind: An approach to technical AGI safety and security

- **canonical id:** `shah-2025-gdm-agi-safety-security` (gaps-other.md); type threat-model; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** R. Shah, A. Irpan, A. M. Turner, A. Wang, A. Conmy et al. (30 authors), "An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security", arXiv:2504.01849, 2025
- **pdf:** shah-2025-gdm-agi-safety-security.pdf sha256: 8f6b9fb28658ae812e379ae4435193af727d7ecf0882a02b820f55ad90f16bf3
- **confirmed via:** arXiv API id_list=2504.01849
- **attack classes:** [misuse, misalignment, mistakes, structural risks; access control, monitoring, weight security]
- **catalog ids:** ASI10 (rogue agents), ASI03?; NIST NISTAML.04
- **summary:** The paper names four risk areas: misuse, misalignment, mistakes and structural risks. It focuses technical work on the first two. Against misuse, the strategy is to identify dangerous capabilities proactively, then apply robust security (including model-weight protection), access restrictions, monitoring and model-level safety mitigations. Against misalignment it proposes two lines of defense. The first is model-level: amplified oversight and robust training. The second is system-level: monitoring and access control that limit harm even if the model is misaligned, treating the model as a potential insider threat. Interpretability, uncertainty estimation and safer design patterns support both, and the parts combine into AGI safety cases. The "misaligned model as untrusted insider" framing maps onto ASI10 (rogue agents) and gives a system-security control set.
- **mapping:** AI system with dangerous capabilities -> misuse by threat actor, or misaligned model acting as insider -> weak access control/monitoring -> severe harm

### S-0764 Frontier AI Risk Management Framework in Practice (SafeWork-F1)

- **summary:** This report applies the E-T-C analysis (deployment Environment, Threat source, enabling Capability) from the Frontier AI Risk Management Framework v1.0, SafeWork-F1. It covers seven areas: cyber offense, biological and chemical risks, persuasion and manipulation, uncontrolled autonomous AI R&D, strategic deception and scheming, self-replication, and collusion. Red lines (intolerable thresholds) and yellow lines (early warnings) define green, yellow and red zones. All evaluated recent frontier models sit in the green or yellow zones, and none crosses a red line. No model crosses the yellow line for cyber offense or uncontrolled AI R&D. Certain reasoning models sit in yellow for self-replication and for deception and scheming. Most models are yellow for persuasion. Yellow cannot be ruled out for bio/chem. This is a Chinese-lab counterpart to the US frontier frameworks, and E-T-C is a ready-made triple for KG precondition modelling.
- **mapping:** frontier model deployment -> (environment, threat source, enabling capability) -> threshold crossing -> zone-dependent controls

Section 3 covers risk management: technical and institutional challenges, risk-management practices, technical safeguards and monitoring, open-weight models, and societal resilience. For a company threat model, the "cyberattacks" and "AI-generated content and criminal activity" sections give the evidence-graded state of AI-as-attacker-tool. The "technical safeguards and monitoring" section gives the evidence on whether controls work. I read only the table of contents and front matter.

### S-0769 Agent Security is a Systems Problem

- **canonical id:** `christodorescu-agent-security-systems-2026` (threat-models.md); type threat-model (position + principles); 2026; confidence high
- **RPT-0009 overlap:** also logged in research/0009-sagai/sources.md
- **citation:** M. Christodorescu, E. Fernandes, A. Hooda, S. Jha, J. Rehberger, K. Chaudhuri et al., "Agent Security is a Systems Problem", arXiv:2605.18991, 2026.
- **pdf:** christodorescu-agent-security-systems-2026.pdf sha256: eb02d189389663de9e0b4a315ca9f33b07fa1b2e32b23972ea245273134bbadf
- **confirmed via:** https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=ti:%22agent%20security%22%20AND%20ti:%22systems%22
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, data exfiltration, unauthorized tool actions (11 real-world attacks analysed)]
- **catalog ids:** ASI01, ASI02, ASI03; LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025
- **summary:** The position is that the model must be treated as an untrusted component, with security invariants enforced at the system level, because model robustness alone is insufficient. The paper gives a generic agent security architecture and core principles. Two are provable separation of instructions and data (analogous to NX bits and prepared statements) and least-privilege sandboxing with verifiable policy generation. It conjectures that model-based instruction/data separation will always be evaded by persistent attackers. It maps 11 real-world agent attacks to violated principles. It is useful as a rule base: a threat model should flag any design where an untrusted-data path reaches a privileged tool without a system-level policy check.
- **mapping:** agent runtime (LLM untrusted) -> principle violations -> untrusted data reaches the context + privileged tool -> exfiltration, unauthorized action

### S-0776 Threat model and defense architecture for prompt injection in multi-agent systems

- **canonical id:** `paul-2026-mas-prompt-injection-threat-model` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type threat-model; 2026; confidence high

- **summary:** The paper enumerates 14 attack vectors in 4 categories: direct (3), indirect via tool outputs (4), inter-agent message passing (4) and cascading through the orchestrator (3). Against a 6-agent production-representative system, 67% of agents were vulnerable to at least one scope violation despite system-prompt guardrails, and indirect injection via tool outputs succeeded 43% of the time. Four architectural defenses cut overall injection success from 31.2% to 4.2%. Message signing with provenance reduced inter-agent injection 91%. Boundary I/O sanitization reduced indirect injection 78%. Role-scoped tool privileges eliminated privilege escalation. Inter-agent anomaly detection caught 84% of cascading attempts. A ready-made attack-vector and control matrix for tmodel.
- **mapping:** multi-agent system -> 14 injection vectors -> various entry points -> scope violation, privilege escalation, cascade
- **also captured as `paul-mas-prompt-injection-tm-2026` (threat-models.md):** The paper enumerates 14 injection vectors in 4 categories and tests them against a 6-agent production-representative system. 67% of agents were vulnerable to at least one scope violation despite system-prompt guardrails, and indirect injection via tool outputs succeeded 43% of the time. Four architectural defenses, including message signing with provenance tracking, cut overall injection success from 31.2% to 4.2%. It is very recent (September 2026), 6 pages and not peer-reviewed, so treat it as low-to-medium evidence. ### S-0787 The Dual LLM pattern

- **canonical id:** `willison-2023-dual-llm-pattern` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type framework; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Simon Willison, "The Dual LLM pattern for building AI assistants that can resist prompt injection", simonwillison.net, 2023-04-25. https://simonwillison.net/2023/Apr/25/dual-llm-pattern/
- **confirmed via:** https://simonwillison.net/2023/Apr/25/dual-llm-pattern/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, privilege-separation]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025/LLM06:2025 mitigation; ASI01/ASI02 mitigation
- **summary:** A Privileged LLM sees only trusted user input and can call tools. A Quarantined LLM processes untrusted content and has no tools, so it is assumed it may "go rogue". A non-LLM Controller passes untrusted outputs to the Privileged LLM only as symbolic variables ($VAR1), never as raw text. Willison listed the weaknesses himself: UX cost, social engineering of the user into copy-pasting, and chaining risks. It is the conceptual ancestor of CaMeL and of the 2025 design-patterns paper. In threat-model terms it introduces an explicit trust boundary between privileged control flow and untrusted data.
- **mapping:** tool-using assistant -> (defense) untrusted data isolated from the privileged planner -> n/a -> prevents IPI-driven tool calls

- **summary:** The report identifies 38 distinct attack vectors for stealing model weights. It defines attacker operational-capacity tiers from opportunistic criminals to top nation-state operations, and estimates whether each tier could execute each vector. It proposes graded security levels (SL1 to SL5) with benchmark controls, for example centralised weight storage, reduced access, insider-threat programs, and confidential computing. It is the main structured threat model for the "model weights" asset and maps directly to an asset -> attacker tier -> vector -> control schema for the tool.

- **also captured as `rand-securing-model-weights-2024` (threat-models.md):** The asset is frontier model weights. The report defines five attacker operational-capacity categories: OC1 amateur attempts, OC2 professional opportunistic efforts, OC3 cybercrime syndicates and insider threats, OC4 standard operations by leading cyber-capable institutions, and OC5 top-priority operations by the top cyber-capable institutions. It lists about 38 attack vectors in 9 categories. Each vector has real-world precedents (Appendix A) and expert-estimated feasibility per OC level. It defines security levels SL1-SL5, each meant to defeat the vectors that are feasible for OC1-OC5 respectively, with benchmark security measures per level. Google DeepMind's FSF v3 explicitly aligns its "security level N" with RAND, and Anthropic's ASL-3 Security Standard scopes in a similar set of attacker groups. Its vector-by-capability feasibility matrix is a ready-made attacker-capability model that can be encoded as KG edges (vector -> feasible-for OC). Mapping: model weights (+ training infra) -> 38 theft vectors -> attacker capability OCn -> weight exfiltration, which enables misuse or removal of safeguards

### S-0796 UK AISI Frontier AI Trends Report

- **canonical id:** `aisi-2025-frontier-ai-trends` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type framework (government evaluation synthesis); 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** UK AI Security Institute, "Frontier AI Trends Report", 2025. https://www.aisi.gov.uk/frontier-ai-trends-report

- **attack classes:** [offensive cyber capability trends]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0016.002; NISTAML.04
- **summary:** The report synthesises AISI testing of more than 30 frontier systems. In cyber, models complete apprentice-level tasks 50% of the time on average, up from just over 10% in early 2024. In 2025 AISI tested the first model that could complete expert-level tasks needing more than 10 years of human experience. The length of cyber tasks models can complete unassisted is doubling roughly every eight months. Autonomy results: hour-long software tasks at more than 40% success, against under 5% in late 2023. Self-replication evaluations went from 5% to 60% success between 2023 and 2025.
- **mapping:** n/a (capability trend) -> time-varying attacker capability parameter -> AI-enabled adversaries -> rising likelihood over time

### S-0798 Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy v2.2 (ASL-3 Security Standard)

- **canonical id:** `anthropic-rsp-v2-2-2025` (threat-models.md); type framework (frontier safety; attacker scope for weight security); 2025; confidence high

- **attack classes:** [model weight theft; misuse/jailbreak of deployed models]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0054
- **summary:** The ASL-3 Security Standard requires being "highly protected against most attackers' attempts at stealing model weights". The groups in scope are hacktivists, criminal hacker groups, organized cybercrime, terrorist organizations, corporate espionage teams, internal employees, and state-sponsored programs that use broad-based, non-targeted techniques (not novel attack chains). The ASL-3 Deployment Standard covers jailbreak-driven misuse. The policy notes that red-teaming tests may be impossible to pass if weights are released or if unmoderated fine-tuning access is given. The attacker-group list is directly comparable to RAND OC1-OC3/OC4.
- **mapping:** model weights -> theft by in-scope actor groups -> non-novel attack chains -> catastrophic misuse risk

### S-0799 Design patterns for securing LLM agents against prompt injections

- **canonical id:** `beurer-kellner-2025-design-patterns` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type framework; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `beurer-kellner-design-patterns-2025 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** Luca Beurer-Kellner, Beat Buesser, Ana-Maria Creţu, Edoardo Debenedetti, Daniel Dobos, et al. (14 authors; IBM, Invariant Labs, ETH Zurich, Google, Microsoft and others), "Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections", arXiv 2025. arXiv:2506.08837
- **pdf:** design-patterns-prompt-injection-2025.pdf sha256: c202a240f8f03c93cfafd157f218ec790c9e503beeaf80e229fb5e1645ab7f9c
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837 ; pattern names verified in cached PDF text
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection-defense, design-patterns]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025 mitigation; ASI01, ASI02 mitigation
- **summary:** Six principled patterns give provable resistance to prompt injection by limiting what untrusted input can affect: Action-Selector, Plan-Then-Execute, LLM Map-Reduce, Dual LLM, Code-Then-Execute and Context-Minimization. The paper analyzes the utility and security trade-offs of each and gives case studies. Each pattern can be a named control node in tmodel, mapped to the agent capability configurations it makes safe. The organizational affiliations listed are from memory.
- **mapping:** LLM agent architecture -> (defense) constrained flows from untrusted input to consequential actions -> n/a -> IPI cannot trigger unauthorized actions
- **also captured as `beurer-kellner-design-patterns-2025` (threat-models.md):** The paper gives principled design patterns that make agents provably resistant to prompt injection, with utility/security trade-offs and case studies. The patterns, as recalled and not re-verified from the PDF, include action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute and context-minimisation. Each pattern constrains whether untrusted input can influence which tools are called. For a threat-model tool this is the mitigation side: each pattern removes specific edges from the agent's data-to-action graph. Mapping: agent tool-calling loop -> prompt injection -> untrusted data reaches the planner -> pattern breaks the path

### S-0801 Cisco Integrated AI Security and Safety Framework

- **canonical id:** `cisco-ai-security-framework-2025` (enumerations.md); type framework; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `cisco-ai-security-framework-2025 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** A. Chang, T. Saade, S. Mendapara, A. Swanda, A. Garg, "Cisco Integrated AI Security and Safety Framework Report", arXiv:2512.12921, 2025.
- **pdf:** cisco-ai-security-framework-2025.pdf sha256: eab096683fb01df730263a0f9045360067fdec3e028c5d0d63d23b6b80031fc7
- **confirmed via:** http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=2512.12921 ; local PDF text
- **attack classes:** [goal-hijacking, data-theft, communication-compromise, system-manipulation, sabotage/integrity-loss, supply-chain-compromise, privilege-escalation, multi-agent prompt injection, MCP threats, harmful content (25 categories)]
- **catalog ids:** OB-001..019; AITech-x.y; AISubtech (112)
- **summary:** This is a four-level, ATT&CK-like taxonomy with stable ids: 19 Objectives (OB-001 to OB-019, for example OB-001 Goal Hijacking, OB-004 Communication Compromise, OB-009 Supply Chain Compromise, OB-014 Privilege Escalation), 40 Techniques (AITech-x.y, for example AITech-1.1 Direct Prompt Injection, AITech-1.3 Multi-Agent Prompt Injection, AITech-9.2 Detection Evasion), 112 Subtechniques, and Procedures. It adds an MCP threat taxonomy of 14 threat types in four groups (injection/interpretation 3, tool integrity 3, data exfiltration/access 4, execution/payload 4), an AI supply-chain taxonomy, and a 25-category harmful-content taxonomy in 5 groups. It explicitly integrates security and content safety. Table 1 claims that ATLAS has no multi-agent/tool coverage; that claim is out of date, since ATLAS has had agentic techniques since 5.0.0 (2025-09). It is vendor-authored, and no public machine-readable release was found.
- **mapping:** AI system (model, agent, MCP, supply chain) -> objective -> technique/subtechnique -> procedure -> security or safety harm
- **also captured as `cisco-ai-security-framework-2025` (threat-models.md):** This is a lifecycle-aware taxonomy with four levels: 19 objectives (attacker goals, ids like OB-004), 40 techniques, 112 subtechniques and procedures. Objectives are grouped into three risk groups: common manipulation threats, data-related threats, and downstream threats and impact risks. It positions itself as unifying the partial views of MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI 100-2 and the OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10s, and integrates safety harms with security. This is the successor lineage to the Robust Intelligence AI security taxonomy, which Cisco acquired; the RI page itself could not be fetched. The report mentions machine-readable expression (STIX-like); whether a published JSON exists was not confirmed. Mapping: AI lifecycle component -> objective/technique/subtechnique -> attacker procedure -> security or safety harm

It notes that NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 do not yet cover MCP in detail. Mapping: MCP servers/agents/data -> injection, supply chain, role overstep -> attacker controls content or a server package -> exfiltration, privilege escalation

### S-0806 Google: An introduction to Google's approach for secure AI agents

- **canonical id:** `google-2025-secure-ai-agents` (gaps-other.md); type framework; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** S. Díaz, C. Kern, K. Olive, "Google's Approach for Secure AI Agents: An Introduction", Google, May 2025. https://research.google/pubs/an-introduction-to-googles-approach-for-secure-ai-agents/
- **pdf:** google-secure-ai-agents-2025.pdf sha256: ad61f1b34e326130be37fb60f0a29d39626d700db8b0a57cdf5597ba510431c1
- **confirmed via:** cached PDF text (google-secure-ai-agents-2025.pdf, pre-existing in cache without an entry)
- **attack classes:** [rogue actions, sensitive data disclosure, prompt injection, misalignment]
- **catalog ids:** ASI01, ASI02, ASI03; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM06:2025
- **summary:** The paper names two key agent risks. Rogue actions are unintended, harmful or policy-violating actions, caused by malicious input such as prompt injection or by misalignment and misinterpretation. Sensitive data disclosure is unauthorized revelation of private information. It states three core principles: (1) agents must have well-defined human controllers, (2) agent powers must have limitations, and (3) agent actions and planning must be observable. Its hybrid defense-in-depth combines deterministic runtime policy enforcement with reasoning-based defenses such as adversarial training and guard models. It complements the SAIF entries already present.
- **mapping:** agent with tools and user data -> injected or misaligned plan -> missing deterministic policy layer -> rogue action or data disclosure

### S-0808 Agents Rule of Two (Meta)

- **canonical id:** `meta-2025-agents-rule-of-two` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type framework; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `meta-agents-rule-of-two-2025 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** Meta AI, "Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security", Meta AI blog, 2025-10-31. https://ai.meta.com/blog/practical-ai-agent-security/
- **confirmed via:** https://ai.meta.com/blog/practical-ai-agent-security/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection, agent-capability-composition, design-rule]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0053; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI03
- **summary:** Within a session an agent should have at most two of three properties: [A] processing untrustworthy inputs, [B] access to sensitive systems or private data, [C] changing state or communicating externally. If all three are required, a human in the loop or another reliable validation is mandatory. The rule is inspired by Chromium's "Rule of 2" and Willison's lethal trifecta, and Meta presents it as a supplement to least privilege and defense in depth, not a replacement. Its C is broader than the trifecta's "external communication" because it also covers state changes, so it addresses integrity as well as exfiltration. It is directly encodable as a tmodel rule over agent assets.
- **mapping:** agent session capability set (A,B,C) -> prompt-injection-driven harmful action -> all three present without supervision -> confidentiality or integrity loss
- **also captured as `meta-agents-rule-of-two-2025` (threat-models.md):** Until prompt injection can be reliably detected, an agent in one session must satisfy at most two of three properties: [A] processes untrustworthy inputs, [B] has access to sensitive systems or private data, [C] can change state or communicate externally. It is inspired by Willison's lethal trifecta and Chromium's "Rule of 2". Meta says it is not sufficient on its own, and that it does not address hallucination, agent errors or over-privilege. As a threat-model rule it is a three-boolean check on any agent node, so it is trivially encodable. Mapping: agent session -> prompt injection -> A and B and C all true -> exfiltration/state change

### S-0811 NIST AI 800-1 (2nd public draft): managing misuse risk for dual-use foundation models

- **canonical id:** `nist-ai-800-1-ipd2` (gaps-other.md); type framework; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** U.S. AI Safety Institute (NIST), "Managing Misuse Risk for Dual-Use Foundation Models", NIST AI 800-1 Second Public Draft, January 2025. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.800-1.ipd2.pdf
- **pdf:** nist-ai-800-1-ipd2.pdf sha256: 362c24f9cfc1e3ba4e0756a49654eaacf3837e963fbd6ff20fe5fcefe06d3b82
- **confirmed via:** PDF downloaded from the URL (objectives read)
- **attack classes:** [misuse enablement, unauthorized model access/weight theft, safeguard red-teaming]
- **catalog ids:** NIST NISTAML.04; ATLAS AML.T0048?
- **summary:** The draft is organized by objectives. Objective 1 is to identify potential misuse risk: anticipate capabilities (1.1), create threat profiles (1.2) and conduct risk assessments (1.3). Objective 2 is to plan to manage misuse risk: map capabilities to mitigations (2.1) and set an organizational plan (2.2). Objective 3 is to protect the model from unauthorized access: assess misuse risk from actors gaining access (3.1) and maintain sufficient security practices (3.2). Objective 4 is to measure misuse risk: capability evaluations (4.1) and red-teaming safeguards (4.2). Objective 5 is to mitigate misuse risk before deployment: proportionate safeguards (5.1) and assessment with safeguards in place (5.2). Later objectives cover post-deployment and transparency. Practice 1.2's "threat profiles" is a direct analogue of the tool's threat-model output. This draft is the status as of 2025-01, and whether a final was published was not checked.

### S-0820 The lethal trifecta for AI agents

- **aliases merged:** `willison-lethal-trifecta-2025 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** Simon Willison, "The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication", simonwillison.net, 2025-06-16. https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/
- **confirmed via:** https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, data-exfiltration, agent-capability-composition]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02; NISTAML.039
- **summary:** An agent that combines (1) access to private data, (2) exposure to untrusted content and (3) the ability to communicate externally can be made to steal that data. LLMs cannot reliably tell where an instruction came from, so any attacker text that reaches the context can issue commands. The post cites exploited products including Microsoft 365 Copilot, the GitHub MCP server, GitLab Duo, ChatGPT, Bard, Amazon Q and Slack. Willison argues guardrails will not reliably protect, recommends avoiding the combination altogether, and points to design patterns and CaMeL. For tmodel this is a capability-composition rule that can be checked mechanically: flag any agent asset holding all three capabilities.
- **mapping:** agent (private data + untrusted input + egress) -> injected exfiltration -> attacker content reaches the context -> confidentiality loss
- **also captured as `willison-lethal-trifecta-2025` (threat-models.md):** An agent that has access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally can be made to exfiltrate data by injected instructions. The post lists products with documented exploits of this shape, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub's MCP server, GitLab Duo, ChatGPT/Operator, Bard/NotebookLM/AI Studio, Amazon Q, GitHub Copilot Chat, Slack AI, Mistral Le Chat, Grok and the Claude iOS app. These are links to researcher write-ups that other RPT-0014 agents should verify individually. The mitigation is to avoid the combination, since guardrails at about 95% effectiveness are insufficient against adversaries. Mapping: private data + untrusted content + egress channel on one agent -> injected exfiltration -> attacker can place content the agent reads -> confidentiality loss

### S-0821 The Promptware Kill Chain

- **canonical id:** `brodt-2026-promptware-kill-chain` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type framework; 2026; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `promptware-kill-chain-2026 (incidents-news.md)`, `promptware-kill-chain-2026 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** Oleg Brodt, Elad Feldman, Bruce Schneier, Ben Nassi, "The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt Injections Gradually Evolved Into a Multistep Malware Delivery Mechanism", arXiv 2026. arXiv:2601.09625
- **pdf:** promptware-kill-chain-2026.pdf sha256: 9dc29042de217a72b60d5f95538b4eb5232354bcab12962e32c91161f4b524ae
- **confirmed via:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09625

- **summary:** The paper argues that prompt injection has evolved into "promptware", a malware execution mechanism. It proposes a seven-stage kill chain: Initial Access (prompt injection), Privilege Escalation (jailbreak), Reconnaissance, Persistence (memory or retrieval poisoning), Command and Control, Lateral Movement, and Actions on Objective. Of 36 studies and incidents analyzed, at least 21 traverse four or more stages. This is directly reusable as the stage dimension of an attack-path model in the tmodel KG, and it lines up with ATT&CK and ATLAS tactics.
- **mapping:** LLM-powered app ecosystem -> multi-stage promptware campaign -> initial injection channel -> persistent compromise, lateral spread, data or physical impact

It analyzes 36 studies and real incidents against production LLM systems and finds at least 21 that cross four or more stages. It argues for defense-in-depth at every stage. This is the most direct bridge from the incident log above to a threat-model structure. Recommended as a KG schema candidate for chaining incident steps. Mapping: any LLM-integrated app -> multi-stage promptware -> untrusted content reaches model with tools/memory -> full kill-chain outcomes
- **also captured as `promptware-kill-chain-2026` (threat-models.md):** The paper reframes prompt injection as "promptware", a malware execution mechanism, with a seven-stage kill chain. Across 36 studies and incidents, at least 21 documented attacks span four or more stages, which supports the claim that the multistage threat model is not merely theoretical. It reviews countermeasures per stage. The stage list works as a tactic axis for sequencing agent threats in attack trees and graphs, and is comparable to ATLAS tactics. Mapping: LLM app/agent -> 7-stage chain -> injection foothold via untrusted content -> persistence, lateral movement, data theft

### S-0829 MCP specification: Security Best Practices

- **canonical id:** `mcp-spec-security-best-practices` (threat-models.md); type standard (protocol security considerations); n.d.; confidence high
- **citation:** Model Context Protocol, "Security Best Practices" (specification, draft basic). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/security_best_practices
- **confirmed via:** URL above (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [confused deputy via MCP proxy (static client ID + DCR + consent cookie), token passthrough/audience validation failure, SSRF via OAuth metadata discovery (cloud metadata, DNS rebinding), state-handle hijacking, local MCP server compromise (malicious startup commands, DNS rebinding to localhost), OAuth authorization URL injection (javascript: XSS, shell command injection), stdio proxy privilege escalation, OAuth mix-up, localhost redirect URI impersonation, scope over-granting]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-441, CWE-918, CWE-79, CWE-78, CWE-352; ASI03, ASI04; ATLAS AML.T0083
- **summary:** This is the protocol's own threat model, with explicit preconditions and MUST/SHOULD mitigations. Example: the confused-deputy attack needs all of a static client ID, dynamic client registration, a third-party consent cookie and no per-client consent. The mitigation is per-client consent storage, exact redirect-URI matching and a single-use `state`. For SSRF, a malicious server populates `resource_metadata` or `authorization_servers` URLs pointing at 169.254.169.254 or localhost. Mitigations are HTTPS-only, blocking private IP ranges, egress proxies and DNS pinning. Local servers run with the client's privileges, so one-click configuration must show the full command and sandbox it. Its precondition lists map directly to the tmodel "precondition" field.
- **mapping:** MCP client/proxy/authorization server -> confused deputy/SSRF/token misuse/local RCE -> listed vulnerable conditions -> account takeover, credential exfiltration, host compromise

### S-0830 MSRC Vulnerability Severity Classification for AI Systems

- **canonical id:** `msrc-ai-severity-classification` (enumerations.md); type standard; n.d.; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `msrc-ai-severity-classification (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** Microsoft Security Response Center, "Vulnerability Severity Classification for AI Systems" (AI bug bar). https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/aibugbar
- **confirmed via:** https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/aibugbar
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection, input-perturbation, membership-inference, attribute-inference, training-data-reconstruction, property-inference, model-theft, input-extraction]
- **catalog ids:** MSRC AI classes
- **summary:** This is the severity rubric used for Microsoft's AI bug bounty. Under "Inference Manipulation" it rates Prompt Injection and Input Perturbation from Critical/Important down to content-related. Under "Inferential Information Disclosure" it covers Membership Inference (Moderate/Low), Attribute Inference, Training Data Reconstruction and Property Inference (Important to Low), Model Theft (Critical/Important/Low) and Input Extraction (Important/Low). Content-related issues (CBRN, election integrity, CSEAM and others) are in or out of scope, but they receive no severity. No version or date is shown. It is one of only two vendor-published, severity-graded AI vulnerability class lists found; the other is 0DIN.
- **mapping:** AI service -> vuln class -> impact scope -> severity
- **also captured as `msrc-ai-severity-classification` (threat-models.md):** This is a severity rubric for AI vulnerabilities reported to MSRC. Inference manipulation ranges from Critical (zero-click exploitation that leads to data exfiltration or privilege abuse) down to Low. Inferential information disclosure is split by target: training data, model architecture/weights, or prompt/input. Severity scales with how the targeted data is classified; theft of highly confidential model components is Critical. Content-safety issues are rated in scope or out of scope rather than by severity. The assumed attacker uses legitimate inference interfaces with crafted inputs, at different levels of user interaction. This is a vendor-defined C/I rating scheme that a threat-model tool can reuse to score impact. A publication date could not be confirmed (the page did not state one in the fetch). Mapping: AI service inference interface -> prompt injection / inferential disclosure -> attacker with API or user-channel access -> exfiltration or privilege abuse (Critical) down to Low

- **catalog ids:** ?
- **summary:** This report moves from a threat taxonomy to an ontology for secure AI. Its sections are: formal expression of the ontology, an alternative mathematical approach, relationship to other work, and hierarchies and relationships. It extends ETSI's TVRA risk method to AI, covering effects on risk impact and likelihood. The threat landscape is described through threat dimensions, attacks as instances of a threat agent, adversarial goals (confidentiality versus integrity and availability), and threat modelling: attacker objectives, an attack surface spanning data acquisition and curation, implementation, deployment and humans, and a trust model. A final section on "AI and SAI ontology" uses nouns, verbs, adverbs and adjectives. The KG phase must align with or reuse this standards-body ontology. No entry existed in the corpus.
- **mapping:** (ontology) threat agent -> attack instance -> adversarial goal -> attack surface -> TVRA impact and likelihood

### S-0839 EU AI Act Article 15 (accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity)

- **canonical id:** `eu-ai-act-art15` (enumerations.md); type standard; 2024; confidence high (text); medium (application dates)
- **citation:** Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 15. https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/15/
- **confirmed via:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/15/
- **attack classes:** [data-poisoning, model-poisoning, adversarial-examples/model-evasion, confidentiality-attacks, model-flaws, feedback-loop-bias]
- **catalog ids:** Art. 15(5) classes; ~ NISTAML.013/.011/.022/.03; ATLAS AML.T0020/T0018/T0015/T0024
- **summary:** For high-risk systems, Art. 15(5) requires that "the technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws". Art. 15(4) adds resilience and mitigation of feedback loops for continuously learning systems. This five-item list is the only legally binding AI attack enumeration found. It omits prompt injection, agents and supply-chain code execution, which harmonized standards (prEN 18282) are expected to fill. The fetched page states that high-risk obligations apply from 2027-12-02 (Annex III) and 2028-08-02 (Annex I). These dates differ from the original 2026-08-02 in the 2024 text, consistent with a later postponement; the amending act was not verified here.
- **mapping:** high-risk AI system (EU market) -> listed attack class -> legal obligation -> compliance evidence

### S-0844 BSI: Evasion attacks on LLMs, countermeasures in practice

- **canonical id:** `bsi-2025-evasion-attacks-llm-countermeasures` (gaps-other.md); type standard; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** BSI (Federal Office for Information Security), "Evasion Attacks on LLMs – Countermeasures in Practice", v1.0, 2025-11-06. https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/KI/Evasion_Attacks_on_LLMs-Countermeasures.pdf
- **pdf:** bsi-evasion-attacks-llm-countermeasures.pdf sha256: 0790e86a8db2115bd415d80b99b57e868fee85ff8d983397f4e55ac458fdb5d1
- **confirmed via:** BSI AI publications page (fetched; lists the document); PDF text (document history: v1.0, 6 November 2025)
- **attack classes:** [inference-time evasion: direct/indirect prompt injection, jailbreak, steganographic payloads, memory injection, MCP abuse, code-agent weaponization]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI06; ATLAS AML.T0051, AML.T0080.000 AI Agent Context Poisoning: Memory?; NIST NISTAML.018 (prompt injection)?
- **summary:** BSI uses "evasion" for inference-time manipulation that makes an LLM behave in unwanted ways, which includes prompt injection. Chapter 2 covers attack mechanism, attack steganography, entry points, and the attacked component and attacker position. Three case studies follow: spyware injection into LLM long-term memory (Rehberger), private-repository access through MCP (Milanta et al.), and weaponizing code agents (Karliner, 2025). Chapter 3 groups countermeasures under named codes: SPTE (secure prompt engineering), guardrails and filtering, SFF (safe file and filesystem), LPP (least privilege), other design patterns, CLI (context locking and isolation between instructions and data), and MFT (model alignment). There is an overview matrix, an integration walkthrough for a basic LLM system, secure design patterns, and a practitioner checklist in Chapter 6. This is control-level material with ids that the KG can use directly.
- **mapping:** LLM application component (memory, files, tools) -> evasion/prompt-injection entry point -> attacker position (user, document, tool) -> countermeasure code (SPTE/LPP/CLI/...)

Predecessor TS 104 223 V1.1.1 (2025-04). https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/304200_304299/304223/02.01.01_60/en_304223v020101p.pdf

- **summary:** This is the first European Standard (EN) for AI cybersecurity. It turns the UK Code of Practice into 13 principles with "shall/should" provisions across five lifecycle phases. Secure Design covers P1 awareness, P2 design for security, P3 evaluate threats and manage risks, and P4 human responsibility. Secure Development covers P5 identify/track/protect assets, P6 infrastructure, P7 supply chain, P8 document data/models/prompts, and P9 testing and evaluation. Secure Deployment covers P10 end-user communication, Secure Maintenance covers P11 updates/patches and P12 monitoring, and Secure End of Life covers P13 data and model disposal. P3 requires threat modeling of AI-specific attacks. It cites the OWASP AI Exchange and the ATLAS mitigations as informative references. Other ETSI SAI outputs in 2026 include TS 104 033 (AI computing platform security), TS 104 158-1/-2 (incident reporting) and TS 104 275 (deepfake harm prevention, 2026-09).
- **mapping:** AI system lifecycle phase -> principle provision -> required control/evidence

### S-0851 EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice: Safety and Security chapter

- **canonical id:** `eu-gpai-code-2025-safety-security` (gaps-other.md); type standard; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** European Commission / AI Office, "The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice", published 2025-07-10; Safety and Security chapter PDF https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/118119
- **confirmed via:** https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai (fetched); chapter PDF fetched and text extracted (43 pp)
- **attack classes:** [systemic risk, model theft/unauthorized release, insider threats incl. (self-)exfiltration, serious incident reporting]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0048.004?; ASI10; NIST NISTAML.031
- **summary:** The chapter applies only to providers of GPAI models with systemic risk under AI Act Article 55. Its commitments include: (1) a Safety and Security Framework; (2) systemic risk identification, with risk scenarios; (3) analysis, covering model-independent information, evaluations, modelling, estimation and post-market monitoring; (4) acceptance determination; (6) cybersecurity protection, where Measure 6.1 defines a Security Goal naming threat actors including non-state external threats and insiders, and Measure 6.2 applies the mitigations in Appendix 4; (7) Model Reports; (8) responsibility allocation; and (9) serious-incident reporting. Appendix 4 covers general mitigations, protection of unreleased parameters, hardening interface access, insider threats "including in the form of (self-)exfiltration or sabotage", and more. The chapter cites the RAND Securing AI Model Weights report. Measure 9.3 timelines include a serious cybersecurity breach, "including the (self-)exfiltration of model weights", to be reported within 5 days, critical-infrastructure disruption within 2 days, and death within 10 days. Commitment 6 exempts models no more capable than an open-weight model. This is the operative EU security obligation for frontier-model weight theft.
- **mapping:** GPAI model weights and infrastructure -> theft, insider sabotage, self-exfiltration -> Security Goal mismatched to threat actors -> systemic risk; reporting within 5 days

- **summary:** The spec defines how agent clients authorise to MCP tool servers. A protected MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server and the MCP client is an OAuth 2.1 client acting for the user. It builds on draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-13, RFC 8414 (AS metadata), RFC 7591 (dynamic client registration), and RFC 9728 (protected resource metadata). Its security section names the agent-specific identity threats: token audience binding and validation, token theft, authorization-code protection, open redirection, the confused-deputy problem, and access-token privilege restriction. This is the closest thing to a standard for "OAuth for agents" and gives concrete control nodes for the KG.
- **mapping:** agent-held delegated tokens -> confused deputy, passthrough, theft -> MCP servers accept tokens not issued for them -> unauthorised actions on user resources

### S-0855 NIST Adversarial ML taxonomy (2025 edition)

- **canonical id:** `nist-ai-100-2-e2025` (ml-model-attacks.md); type standard; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `nist-ai-100-2-e2025 (enumerations.md)`, `nist-ai-100-2-e2025 (threat-models.md)`, `nist-ai-100-2-e2025-genai-section (llm-agent-attacks.md)`
- **RPT-0009 overlap:** also logged in research/0009-sagai/sources.md
- **citation:** A. Vassilev, A. Oprea, A. Fordyce, H. Anderson, X. Davies, M. Hamin, "Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations", NIST AI 100-2 E2025, March 2025. DOI 10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025
- **pdf:** nist-ai-100-2-e2025.pdf sha256: 4811fb6ad73f9c9121843ab77e029b5adc6f2c86d33c2fc5b2099ef133847646
- **confirmed via:** https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025 (resolves to https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-2e2025.pdf); Crossref record 10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2025; v0.2 fold: author list verified 2026-10-03 against the title page of the cached PDF (Vassilev, Oprea, Fordyce, Anderson, Davies, Hamin)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, poisoning, backdoor, model-poisoning, energy-latency, model-extraction, reconstruction, membership-inference, property-inference, prompt-extraction, data-extraction, prompt-injection, supply-chain, misuse]
- **catalog ids:** NIST AI 100-2 is itself the catalog; ATLAS cross-references are partial
- **summary:** The reference US-government taxonomy. It splits attacks on Predictive AI from attacks on Generative AI and organizes each by attacker objective: availability, integrity, privacy, and (for GenAI) misuse. It characterizes each attack by capability (training-data control, model control, testing-data control, label limit, source-code control, query access, resource control) and by knowledge (white, gray, black box). The 2025 edition gives every attack a stable identifier (NISTAML.0xx, see the catalog key) and adds GenAI supply-chain, indirect prompt injection and agent sections. Mitigations are listed per class, together with their known limits, for example the trade-off between robustness and accuracy and the difficulty of evaluating defenses. It is the best single crosswalk target for a threat-model tool's attack vocabulary.
- **mapping:** any AI asset (data, model, API, RAG, agent) -> NISTAML class -> attacker capability and knowledge -> availability / integrity / privacy / misuse violation
- **also captured as `nist-ai-100-2-e2025` (enumerations.md):** This is the US government's reference AML taxonomy, split into a Predictive AI (PredAI) tree and a Generative AI (GenAI) tree. Attacks are classified by stage of learning (training vs deployment), attacker goal (availability, integrity, privacy, plus GenAI misuse), capability (training-data control, model control, testing-data control, label limit, source-code control, query access, resource control) and knowledge (white, grey or black box). E2025 introduced stable ids: - Top-level violations: NISTAML.01 availability, .02 integrity, .03 privacy, .04 misuse and .05 supply chain. - Leaves: .011 model poisoning, .012 clean-label poisoning, .013 data poisoning, .014 energy-latency, .015 indirect prompt injection, .016 IPI availability attacks, .017 time-consuming background tasks, .018 prompt injection, .021 clean-label backdoor, .022 evasion, .023 backdoor poisoning, .024 targeted poisoning, .025 black-box evasion, .026 model poisoning (integrity), .027 misaligned outputs, .031 model extraction, .032 reconstruction, .033 membership inference, .034 property inference, .035 prompt extraction, .036 leaking information from user interactions, .037 training data attacks, .038 data extraction, .039 compromising connected resources and .051 supply-chain model poisoning. In total there are 30 distinct ids (5 top-level and 25 leaves). Some leaves appear under several goals; for example .018 appears under availability, integrity, privacy and misuse. Section 3.5 covers agent security only briefly. The document cites ATLAS mitigations (AML.M0000-M0004) but provides no id-level crosswalk to ATLAS, OWASP or CWE. The CSRC page notes a known error on page x to be fixed in a future revision. No E2026 edition was listed as of the fetch. Mapping: model lifecycle stage (training data, model, deployment API, RAG/tools) -> NISTAML leaf -> attacker capability + knowledge -> availability/integrity/privacy/misuse violation
- **also captured as `nist-ai-100-2-e2025` (threat-models.md):** Included here for its attacker-model axes, which a threat-model generator needs. The axes are: attacker goals (availability breakdown, integrity violation, privacy compromise, plus misuse enablement for GenAI); attacker capabilities (training-data control, model control, testing-data control, label limits, source-code control, query access, resource control); attacker knowledge (white, gray, black box); and lifecycle stage (training versus deployment). The author list is from memory; confirm from the PDF title page in the next pass. Other RPT-0014 agents cover its attack catalog in detail. Mapping: model/data/API -> attack class -> attacker capability + knowledge -> availability/integrity/privacy/misuse
- **also captured as `nist-ai-100-2-e2025-genai-section` (llm-agent-attacks.md):** GenAI part: section 3.3 Direct Prompting Attacks [NISTAML.018] with information extraction [NISTAML.038] and prompt extraction / system prompts [NISTAML.035]. Section 3.4 Indirect Prompt Injection [NISTAML.015], subdivided into availability [NISTAML.016, .017 time-consuming background tasks], integrity [NISTAML.027], which explicitly includes knowledge-base poisoning (PoisonedRAG, Phantom), Neural Exec execution triggers, jailbreaking via IPI and injection hiding, and privacy [NISTAML.039 compromising connected resources, NISTAML.036 leaking user interactions]. Section 3.5 Security of Agents cites the U.S. AISI/CAISI agent-hijacking work but has no id. Section 3.6 lists benchmarks (JailbreakBench, AdvBench, HarmBench, StrongREJECT, AgentHarm, Do-Not-Answer, TrustLLM, AgentDojo, Garak). Training-time GenAI attacks are [NISTAML.037]. Gaps: no separate ids for MCP or tool poisoning, multi-agent propagation, memory poisoning, computer-use attacks or denial of wallet. Mapping: n/a (standard)

### S-0858 C2PA Content Credentials technical specification (v2.2 to 2.4)

- **canonical id:** `c2pa-2026-content-credentials-spec` (gaps-papers.md); type standard; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, "Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification", versions 2.2-2.4. https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.2/specs/C2PA_Specification.html ; current index https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.4/index.html
- **confirmed via:** https://c2pa.org/specifications/ (redirect notice to 2.4, fetched 2026-10-03); https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.2/specs/C2PA_Specification.html (table of contents incl. 9.2 Hard Bindings, 9.3 Soft Bindings, fetched)
- **attack classes:** [content provenance, manifest binding, soft binding (watermark/fingerprint)]
- **catalog ids:** mitigation standard for ATLAS AML.T0088; NIST AI 100-4 context
- **summary:** The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity specification defines cryptographically signed provenance manifests ("Content Credentials") attached to assets. Assertions record actions (including AI generation), ingredients and claims. Hard bindings are cryptographic hashes; soft bindings are watermarks and fingerprints, accessed via a Soft Binding API, used to re-associate stripped manifests. The site also publishes Security Considerations, Harms Modelling and AI/ML guidance. The current version is 2.4 (c2pa.org/specifications redirects there). Threats relevant to the KG: manifest stripping, re-signing with untrusted certificates, and soft-binding attacks from the watermark-removal and forgery literature.
- **mapping:** media provenance chain -> manifest stripping, forged/untrusted signing, soft-binding removal or forgery -> attacker re-encodes or edits media -> provenance loss or false provenance
- **note:** Threats listed are the reviewer's synthesis, not text from the spec; read the C2PA Security Considerations document for normative threat lists.

- **attack classes:** [agentic tool misuse, access control violation, cascading failures, orchestration exploitation, identity impersonation, memory/context manipulation, critical systems interaction, supply chain, untraceability, goal/instruction manipulation]
- **catalog ids:** AIVSS Core Risks <-> ASI01-ASI10
- **summary:** AIVSS is the only published AI-specific vulnerability scoring scheme found, and it is a CVSS overlay rather than a replacement. It requires a CVSS v4.0 base score ("Practitioners should not use CVSS v3.1"). An agentic uplift is then computed as AARS = (10 - CVSS_Base) x (Factor_Sum/10) x ThM, where ThM is a threat multiplier based on exploit maturity. The final score is AIVSS = (CVSS_Base + AARS) x Mitigation_Factor. Factor_Sum sums ten Agentic Risk Amplification Factors, each scored 0, 0.5 or 1: Execution Autonomy, External Tool Control Surface, Natural Language Interface, Contextual Awareness, Behavioral Non-Determinism, Opacity & Reflexivity, Persistent State Retention, Dynamic Identity, Multi-Agent Interactions and Self-Modification. The ten Core Risks are mapped to ASI in Appendix B. The project site lists an SSVC calculator and a Python reference calculator with seven domain profiles. The scores are explicitly ordinal. Status is pre-1.0.
- **mapping:** vulnerability in agentic system -> CVSS 4.0 base + architecture amplification factors -> severity for prioritization

### S-0865 Arcanum Prompt Injection Taxonomy (Haddix)

- **canonical id:** `arcanum-pi-taxonomy` (enumerations.md); type catalog; n.d.; confidence high

- **summary:** This is the most granular open prompt-injection enumeration, with four orthogonal dimensions verified in taxonomy.json: 27 intents (PIT-I-NN, what the attacker wants), 70 techniques (PIT-T-NN, how the model is manipulated), 63 evasions (PIT-E-NN, obfuscation past filters) and 12 inputs (PIT-N-NN, where the payload enters), for 172 nodes in total. Each node has an id, title, description, examples, aliases to OWASP, ATLAS and NIST, and a delivery class. It is practitioner-sourced (red-team practice), not peer-reviewed. The four-dimensional structure (intent x technique x evasion x channel) matches the KG need better than single-axis lists.
- **mapping:** LLM input channel (PIT-N) -> technique + evasion -> attacker intent (PIT-I) -> impact

### S-0867 ATLAS AML.CS0004: camera hijack attack on facial recognition (Shanghai tax system)

### S-0868 Inadequate Detection or Handling of Adversarial Input Perturbations

- **canonical id:** `cwe-1039` (enumerations.md); type catalog; 2018; confidence high
- **citation:** CWE Content Team (MITRE), "CWE-1039: Inadequate Detection or Handling of Adversarial Input Perturbations in Automated Recognition Mechanism", CWE 3.1, 2018-03-29 (renamed and updated since). https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1039.html
- **confirmed via:** https://cwe-api.mitre.org/api/v1/cwe/weakness/1039 ; NVD record https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2025-26644
- **attack classes:** [evasion, adversarial-examples, biometric-spoofing]
- **catalog ids:** AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model), AML.T0043 (Craft Adversarial Data); OWASP ML01:2023; NIST NISTAML.022/.025; AVID S0403; SAIF riskModelEvasion
- **summary:** This is the oldest AI weakness in CWE, at Class abstraction, ChildOf 693 and 697. It covers ML recognizers (image, audio) that fail to detect inputs crafted to be classified as another concept. Its single observed example is CVE-2025-26644, a Windows Hello biometric authentication spoof via adversarial perturbation. NVD published it 2025-04-08 with CVSS 3.1 5.1, and it is one of the few NVD records that carries an AI-specific CWE. The attacker is inference-time and usually needs black- or grey-box query access, plus physical presentation for biometrics.
- **mapping:** ML-based authenticator/classifier -> adversarial input misclassified -> attacker can present crafted input -> authentication bypass, detection evasion

### S-0872 Failure Modes in Machine Learning (Microsoft / Berkman Klein)

- **canonical id:** `microsoft-failure-modes-ml-2019` (enumerations.md); type catalog; 2019; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `kumar-failure-modes-ml-2019 (threat-models.md)`
- **citation:** R. Shankar Siva Kumar, D. O'Brien, K. Albert, S. Viljoen, J. Snover, "Failure Modes in Machine Learning Systems", arXiv:1911.11034, 2019; also Microsoft Learn https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/engineering/failure-modes-in-machine-learning
- **pdf:** kumar-failure-modes-ml-2019.pdf sha256: 19cff0fe3df7e9345c2d0060274f8e3155828ac7108d34694f4c198dc3d0c5be
- **confirmed via:** http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=ti:"failure modes in machine learning" ; local PDF text
- **attack classes:** [perturbation, poisoning, model-inversion, membership-inference, model-stealing, reprogramming, physical-adversarial-example, malicious-ML-provider, supply-chain, backdoor, exploit-software-dependencies, reward-hacking, side-effects, distributional-shift, natural-adversarial-examples, common-corruption, incomplete-testing]
- **catalog ids:** ~ ML01-ML10:2023; ATLAS AML.T0015/T0020/T0024.*/T0018/T0010
- **summary:** This is the earliest practitioner taxonomy that puts intentional and unintentional failures in one table. It has 11 intentional failure modes. These are (1) perturbation, (2) poisoning, (3) model inversion, (4) membership inference, (5) model stealing, (6) neural net reprogramming, (7) adversarial example in physical domain, (8) malicious ML provider recovering training data, (9) attacking the ML supply chain, (10) backdoor ML and (11) exploit software dependencies. It has 6 unintentional modes: reward hacking, side effects, distributional shifts, natural adversarial examples, common corruption and incomplete testing. Each mode is tagged with the violated property (C/I/A) and given a scenario. It was built with input from 23 external partners and later became the basis of Microsoft's SDL AI/ML bug bar.
- **mapping:** ML system -> failure mode -> adversary vs design flaw -> C/I/A/safety violation
- **also captured as `kumar-failure-modes-ml-2019` (threat-models.md):** This taxonomy splits failures into intentional ones (caused by an adversary) and unintentional ones (a system that is correct by design but produces unsafe outcomes). For each intentional failure it records whether it violates confidentiality, integrity or availability, and gives the attacker's goal. It underlies the Microsoft threat-modeling guide, the bug bar and the later agentic failure-modes taxonomies. Its two-axis split (security versus safety, intentional versus unintentional) is a candidate top-level classifier for KG threat nodes. Mapping: ML model/data -> intentional or unintentional failure -> adversary or environment -> C/I/A violation

### S-0873 ATLAS AML.CS0000: evasion of a deep-learning detector for malware C&C traffic

- **canonical id:** `atlas-cs0000-palo-alto-c2-evasion` (gaps-other.md); type catalog; 2020; confidence high
- **citation:** MITRE ATLAS case study AML.CS0000 (Exercise, 2020; Palo Alto Networks AI Research Team). https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0000
- **confirmed via:** local ATLAS data v6.0.0 (raw/atlas-2026.09.yaml, case-studies and relationships)
- **attack classes:** [evasion, proxy model, ML-based NIDS bypass]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0000.001, AML.T0002.000, AML.T0005, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0042, AML.T0015; ML01
- **summary:** The team rebuilt a URLNet-style C&C traffic detector from a public paper and about 60 million HTTP headers, reaching about 99% TPR and 0.01% FPR as a proxy. They crafted evasive samples by removing header fields that C&C traffic does not use, then queried the target until it was evaded; crafted packets were scored benign with over 80% confidence. The attacker uses grey-box knowledge from public research.
- **mapping:** ML-based network detector -> proxy-model-guided evasion -> public research and query access -> C2 traffic undetected

### S-0886 CWE-1426 Improper Validation of Generative AI Output

- **canonical id:** `cwe-1426-genai-output-validation` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type catalog; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `cwe-1426 (enumerations.md)`
- **citation:** MITRE CWE, "CWE-1426: Improper Validation of Generative AI Output", added CWE 4.15 (2024-07-16). https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1426.html
- **confirmed via:** https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1426.html (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [improper-output-handling, agent-tool-misuse]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-1426; OWASP LLM05:2025, LLM06:2025; ATLAS AML.T0077, AML.T0053
- **summary:** This weakness covers products that do not validate generative AI output against security, content or privacy policy before using it. The entry notes that in agent settings, unvalidated output can trigger tool calls that write files, create databases or run code. Mitigations: run AI components in non-privileged environments, use semantic comparators and external guardrails, and train on negative examples. Observed example: CVE-2024-3402, where a ChatGPT GUI failed to sanitize model output and the result was XSS. The entry points to CWE-77/94/116 as the usual root causes behind apparent "AI output" bugs.
- **mapping:** LLM output -> injection into a downstream interpreter (HTML, shell, SQL, tool call) -> output passed without validation -> XSS/RCE/data destruction
- **also captured as `cwe-1426` (enumerations.md):** The product invokes a generative AI component "whose behaviors and outputs cannot be directly controlled" but does not validate outputs against the intended security, content or privacy policy. It is ChildOf CWE-707 (improper neutralization) and was the first entry submitted by the AI WG itself. The observed example is CVE-2024-3402, a ChatGPT GUI that validated inputs but not model output, which led to stored XSS. Its typical threat-model role is the second half of a prompt-injection chain, where the model becomes a confused deputy whose output reaches a browser, shell, SQL engine or template renderer. Mapping: downstream interpreter (browser, shell, DB, template engine) -> attacker-influenced model output executed -> output not encoded/validated -> XSS/SQLi/RCE, policy violation

### S-0887 CWE-1427 Improper Neutralization of Input Used for LLM Prompting

- **canonical id:** `cwe-1427-llm-prompt-neutralization` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type catalog; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `cwe-1427 (enumerations.md)`
- **citation:** MITRE CWE, "CWE-1427: Improper Neutralization of Input Used for LLM Prompting", added CWE 4.16 (2024-11-19). https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1427.html
- **confirmed via:** https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1427.html (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [direct-prompt-injection, indirect-prompt-injection]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-1427 (parent CWE-77); ATLAS AML.T0051; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018/.015
- **summary:** CWE-1427 is the weakness behind prompt injection. A product builds LLM prompts from external data in a way that the model cannot tell developer instructions apart from user or third-party content. The entry names RAG and external APIs as typical routes for untrusted data. Listed consequences cover confidentiality (reading application data), integrity, and access control (privilege escalation that depends on what the LLM is integrated with). Its parent is CWE-77 (command injection). Mitigations are input sanitization, separating user input from system prompts, guardrails or supervisors on output, and fine-tuning; the entry rates their effectiveness as moderate to high. Observed examples: CVE-2023-32786 (prompt injection in a framework leading to SSRF), CVE-2024-5184 (system prompt disclosure in an email-analysis product), CVE-2024-5565 (code execution in a text-to-SQL library), and CVE-2024-48746 (code execution in a BI dashboard).
- **mapping:** prompt-assembly code -> injection of attacker instructions -> untrusted text concatenated into context -> SSRF/RCE/data disclosure in connected systems
- **also captured as `cwe-1427` (enumerations.md):** This is the base-level weakness for prompt injection: "the product uses externally-provided data to build prompts provided to LLMs, but the way these prompts are constructed causes the LLM to fail to distinguish between user-supplied inputs and developer provided system directives". It is ChildOf CWE-77 (command injection), and its alternate term is "prompt injection". The observed examples are all chains where the injection leads to a classic impact. CVE-2023-32786 (LangChain SSRF via prompt injection), CVE-2024-5184 (EmailGPT service-logic takeover), CVE-2024-5565 (Vanna text-to-SQL RCE via its prompt-driven visualization) and CVE-2024-48746 (NL component of a BI dashboard leads to code execution). The CWE AI WG minutes of 2026-06-12 record "extensive proposed changes" to CWE-1427 by Kurt Seifried (CSA) with "mixed" WG responses, so the entry may be revised in CWE 5.0. No capability or access is implied. The weakness exists whenever untrusted text reaches the prompt without an enforced boundary, which covers both direct (user) and indirect (retrieved document, tool output) channels. Mapping: system prompt + prompt-assembly code -> injected instructions override developer intent -> attacker text reaches context window (user turn, RAG chunk, tool result, file name) -> data exfiltration, unauthorized tool calls, RCE via downstream sink

### S-0888 CWE AI Working Group and CWE 5.0 pipeline

- **canonical id:** `cwe-ai-working-group` (enumerations.md); type catalog; 2024; confidence high (primary minutes); medium on the CWE 5.0 date, since it is a target date
- **citation:** CWE Program, "CWE AI Working Group" (formed 2024; GitHub repo created 2024-07-12), minutes 2026-06-12 and slides 2026-06-26. https://github.com/CWE-CAPEC/AI-Working-Group
- **confirmed via:** https://cwe.mitre.org/community/working_groups.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWE-CAPEC/AI-Working-Group/main/meeting_minutes/20260612-CWE-AI-Working-Group-Meeting-Minutes.pdf ; meeting_slides/CVE-CWE-AI-WG-260626-new-entry.pptx
- **attack classes:** [prompt-injection, special-token-injection, retrieval-injection, workflow-logic-injection, human-approval-bypass, context-isolation, MCP-config-injection, package-hallucination]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-1426/1427/1434/1039; future CWE 5.0 ids unknown ("?")
- **summary:** The WG is a forum of CWE and CVE stakeholders that meets biweekly, with Steve Christey Coley (MITRE) and Erick Galinkin among the leads. Its mission is "to identify and address gaps in the CWE corpus where AI-related weaknesses are not adequately covered". Per the 2026-06-26 slides, CWE 5.0 is "to be released in October" 2026, with "support for AI-specific lifecycles" and the "goal: significant increase in AI coverage". Active new-entry submissions include the following. "Improper Isolation of Task-Relevant Context" (Sasha Romanosky, RAND, CDR #204). "Improper Isolation of Executable Logic in AI/ML Workflow Definitions" (CDR #183). "Improper Neutralization of Reserved Special Tokens in AI Instruction Streams" (Sentry, CDR #173). "Improper Control of Learned Representation Stability" (Kurt Seifried, CSA, CDR #179). "Bypass of Human Authorization Controls" (Kodem Security, CDR #174). Likely modifications rather than new entries include "Cross-Model Scripting (XMS)" (to be folded into CWE-79), "Improper Neutralization of Configurations Used for MCP Client", and "Improper Neutralization of Retrieved Content Used in AI Prompt Construction". Deprioritized items are "Insufficient Input Validation in Generative AI Applications" and "Bias in AI Models", the latter questioned as a security weakness. The WG's stated framing is that "most/all AI-related submissions are too low-level to have their own entry" and that "CWE doesn't make separate entries for 'where the bad input came from'". In other words, CWE will not split prompt injection by channel (RAG vs email vs file name). The WG is also reviewing RAND's draft inclusion-criteria paper, "A Structured Approach to Identifying and Characterizing AI Vulnerabilities". The minutes say CVSS discussions declined to score "output manipulation alone".
- **mapping:** n/a (governance of the enumeration); informs which KG weakness nodes will gain stable CWE ids in Oct 2026

### S-0889 MIT AI Risk Repository (Slattery et al.)

- **canonical id:** `mit-ai-risk-repository` (enumerations.md); type catalog; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** P. Slattery, A. K. Saeri, E. A. C. Grundy, J. Graham, M. Noetel et al., "The AI Risk Repository: A Comprehensive Meta-Review, Database, and Taxonomy of Risks From Artificial Intelligence", arXiv:2408.12622 (v3), 2024-2025; database v4 (Dec 2025). https://airisk.mit.edu/
- **pdf:** slattery-2024-mit-ai-risk-repository.pdf sha256: 8f3559ee5c4621a7cd72281daa0b28377dd2bde20f243598d6910ae50e396765
- **confirmed via:** https://airisk.mit.edu/ ; http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=2408.12622 ; arXiv PDF
- **attack classes:** [AI system security (subdomain 2.2), privacy compromise (2.1), cyberattacks/weapons (4.2), fraud/scams (4.3), multi-agent risks]
- **catalog ids:** domain ids 1.1-7.x
- **summary:** This is a meta-review database of risks extracted from published frameworks. The arXiv v3 abstract reports 74 frameworks and 1,725 risks; the website says "1,700+" risks and "Version 4" (December 2025), which added a multi-agent subdomain. There are two taxonomies. The Causal Taxonomy classifies by entity (human/AI), intent and timing (pre/post-deployment). The Domain Taxonomy has 7 domains and 24 subdomains: (1) Discrimination & toxicity, (2) Privacy & security, (3) Misinformation, (4) Malicious actors & misuse, (5) Human-computer interaction, (6) Socioeconomic & environmental and (7) AI system safety, failures & limitations. It is licensed CC BY 4.0. Its finding that human decisions cause about 38% of risks and AI systems about 42% is a useful prior for STRIDE-like actor modeling. The limitation for security is that all technical attacks on AI collapse into one subdomain (2.2 "AI system security"), so it cannot serve as an attack enumeration. It is applied to AIID incidents as the "MIT" taxonomy.
- **mapping:** risk statement -> domain/subdomain + causal (entity, intent, timing) -> governance coverage check

### S-0893 Insecure Setting of Generative AI/ML Model Inference Parameters

- **canonical id:** `cwe-1434` (enumerations.md); type catalog; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** L. Wong (MITRE) and AI WG "New Entry" subgroup, "CWE-1434: Insecure Setting of Generative AI/ML Model Inference Parameters", CWE 4.18, 2025-09-09. https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1434.html
- **confirmed via:** https://cwe-api.mitre.org/api/v1/cwe/weakness/1434 ; cwec_v4.20.xml

- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM09:2025 (Misinformation); NIST NISTAML.027 (misaligned outputs, loosely); ATLAS ? (no direct technique)
- **summary:** The product relies on a generative model "configured with inference parameters that produce an unacceptably high rate of erroneous or unexpected outputs", for example temperature or sampling settings. Its status is Draft. It is ChildOf CWE-440 and CWE-665, CanPrecede CWE-684, and PeerOf CWE-691. The entry was developed by the AI WG new-entry subgroup between February and August 2025. It is the first CWE to treat output reliability as a weakness, a position the WG later generalized: "output matters when it guides or changes system behavior in security-relevant ways" (2026-06-12 minutes, discussing package hallucination).
- **mapping:** model-serving configuration -> high-variance output used for decisions -> no bounds on sampling -> integrity loss in downstream decisions, package-hallucination squatting
