- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0053, AML.T0011.003 (Malicious Link); OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI05
- **summary:** A web page that said "download this Support Tool and run it" made Claude Computer Use (beta) download a Sliver C2 implant, `chmod +x` it and execute it. The host joined the attacker's C2 with no human involvement. Natural-language social engineering of the agent was enough; no bash injection was needed. It is the canonical demonstration that CUA prompt injection means host compromise. HiddenLayer showed a related `rm -rf` case the same day; see the sibling incidents file.
- **mapping:** CUA host -> IPI leads to download and execution of malware -> agent visits an attacker page -> full host compromise (botnet/C2)

### S-0997 Wiz: malicious Cog model on Replicate reads other customers' prompts and results

- **canonical id:** `replicate-cross-tenant-2024` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / advisory; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Wiz Research, "Wiz Research discovers critical vulnerability in Replicate", 2024-05-23 (reported 2024-01), https://www.wiz.io/blog/wiz-research-discovers-critical-vulnerability-in-replicate
- **confirmed via:** https://www.wiz.io/blog/wiz-research-discovers-critical-vulnerability-in-replicate (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [malicious model container, tenant isolation failure, prompt/output interception]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0011.000?, AML.T0105?; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM02:2025; CWE-668, CWE-653; NIST AI 100-2 n/a (infrastructure)
- **summary:** Wiz uploaded a malicious model packaged in Replicate's Cog container format and got RCE on Replicate's infrastructure. Shared network namespaces then let it reach a centralized Redis queue serving multiple customers. Through TCP packet injection it could read customers' prompts and model outputs and alter webhook callbacks, which would let an attacker change other users' prediction results. The attacker needed only a free account that could push a model. The assets are other tenants' inference inputs and outputs (privacy) and their integrity. Replicate mitigated quickly, and Wiz reports no customer data was compromised.
- **mapping:** inference platform job queue -> attacker model RCE plus shared network namespace -> weak tenant network isolation -> cross-tenant prompt/output theft and result tampering

### S-0998 Skeleton Key jailbreak (Microsoft)

- **canonical id:** `russinovich-2024-skeleton-key` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Mark Russinovich, "Mitigating Skeleton Key, a new type of generative AI jailbreak technique", Microsoft Security Blog, 2024-06-26. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/06/26/mitigating-skeleton-key-a-new-type-of-generative-ai-jailbreak-technique/
- **confirmed via:** https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/06/26/mitigating-skeleton-key-a-new-type-of-generative-ai-jailbreak-technique/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, multi-turn, behavior-guideline-augmentation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** Skeleton Key asks the model to augment its behavior guidelines rather than drop them. The attacker presents the context as safe, for example as research or education, and asks the model to answer everything with only a warning prefix. Once the model accepts the "updated guidelines", it complies with later requests. In April-May 2024 Microsoft tested Llama3-70b-instruct, Gemini Pro, GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o, Mistral Large, Claude 3 Opus and Command R Plus, and all of them complied. GPT-4 resisted except when the request arrived in the system message. Microsoft's mitigations: Prompt Shields input/output filtering, system-message hardening, abuse monitoring, and Azure AI Content Safety.
- **mapping:** hosted model / application -> guideline-override jailbreak -> chat or system-message access -> unrestricted harmful output

### S-0999 SAPwned: SAP AI Core training jobs reach cluster-admin and cross-tenant secrets

- **canonical id:** `sapwned-2024` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / advisory; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Wiz Research (H. Ben-Sasson), "SAPwned: SAP AI vulnerabilities expose customers' cloud environments and private AI artifacts", 2024-07-17, https://www.wiz.io/blog/sapwned-sap-ai-vulnerabilities-ai-security
- **confirmed via:** https://www.wiz.io/blog/sapwned-sap-ai-vulnerabilities-ai-security (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [AI platform tenant isolation failure, Kubernetes compromise, credential exposure, training-data exposure]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0105 (Escape to Host)?, AML.T0055?, AML.T0035 (AI Artifact Collection)?; OWASP LLM03:2025; CWE-306, CWE-284, CWE-522; NIST AI 100-2 n/a
- **summary:** Reported 2024-01-25 to 05-15 and disclosed 2024-07-17. Wiz ran its own code as an ordinary AI Core training job, defined through an Argo Workflow that spawns a Kubernetes pod. From there it found five issues. Network isolation could be bypassed by sharing the process namespace with the Istio sidecar or running as UID 1337. Loki's `/config` exposed AWS secrets. Unauthenticated EFS/NFS shares held customer training data by customer id. An unprotected Helm (Tiller) server leaked registry and Artifactory credentials. Helm then gave full cluster-admin. The reachable assets included AWS, Azure, SAP HANA Cloud, and GCR credentials and other customers' private models and datasets. SAP patched by 2024-05-15 and no customer data was compromised. The attacker capability is that of a legitimate tenant.
- **mapping:** managed ML training platform -> tenant-submitted job escapes network policy -> unauthenticated internal services and shared secrets -> cross-tenant model, data, and cloud-credential access; supply-chain write

### S-1000 Sysdig: LLMjacking (stolen cloud credentials to abuse hosted LLMs)

- **canonical id:** `sysdig-2024-llmjacking` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `sysdig-2024-llmjacking (supply-infra-misuse.md)`, `llmjacking-2024 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Sysdig Threat Research Team, "LLMjacking: Stolen Cloud Credentials Used in New AI Attack", 2024-05-06. https://sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack/
- **confirmed via:** https://sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack/ (fetched); v0.2 fold: CVE verified 2026-10-03 against the Sysdig post of 2024-05-06 (CVE-2021-3129, Laravel; over US$46,000 per day)
- **attack classes:** [cost-harvesting, credential-abuse, llm-access-resale]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0034, AML.T0055 (Unsecured Credentials), AML.T0096; OWASP LLM10:2025; CWE-522 (?)
- **summary:** Attackers exploited a vulnerable Laravel instance (CVE-2021-3129) to steal cloud credentials. They probed ten hosted LLM services (Bedrock, Azure, Vertex AI, Anthropic, OpenAI), using invalid-parameter calls to test access quietly and checking logging configuration. The estimated cost to a victim is over $46,000 per day at maximum quota on Claude 2.x. Detection: watch for ValidationException on InvokeModel and enable model-invocation logging, since CloudTrail does not show prompts. This is the operational "denial of wallet" via credential theft; the sibling incidents file covers follow-ups.
- **mapping:** cloud account with LLM service entitlements -> unauthorized model invocation and resale -> stolen cloud keys -> large financial loss, abuse attributed to the victim
- **also captured as `sysdig-2024-llmjacking` (supply-infra-misuse.md):** Attackers exploited a vulnerable Laravel system (CVE-2021-3129), took cloud credentials, and targeted ten cloud-hosted LLM services, including Anthropic Claude on AWS Bedrock. Their tooling checked quietly which models were enabled, without invoking them visibly. Access was resold through an "OAI Reverse Proxy". Sysdig estimates the victim could pay more than USD 46,000 per day in LLM consumption if undiscovered. Detection relies on CloudTrail/Bedrock invocation logging and model-access governance. Mapping: cloud account with LLM entitlements -> unauthorized model use billed to the victim -> leaked long-lived cloud keys, unmonitored model enablement -> financial loss, abuse attributed to the victim
- **also captured as `llmjacking-2024` (incidents-news.md):** First reported 2024-05. Attackers took cloud keys, initially by exploiting a vulnerable Laravel instance (CVE-2021-3129, from memory; not confirmed here). They checked for Bedrock access, checked whether model-invocation logging was on, enabled models through APIs, and resold access through reverse proxies such as OAI-reverse-proxy. Sysdig estimated victim costs of over $46k/day initially and up to about $100k/day with Claude 3 Opus. One spike was 61,000 Bedrock calls in 3 hours on 2024-07-11. Later variants tampered with logging configuration. The asset is the organization's model-API entitlement and budget. Mitigations: key hygiene, invocation logging, SCPs, and anomaly alerts. CSA (2026-06) reports LLMjacking evolving into using stolen AI compute as attack infrastructure. Mapping: cloud AI API entitlement (Bedrock/Azure OpenAI/Vertex) -> invocation with stolen credentials -> long-lived leaked keys, logging off -> financial loss, abuse attributed to victim

### S-1001 Trail of Bits: Sleepy Pickle model-tampering via pickle

- **canonical id:** `tob-2024-sleepy-pickle` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** Boyan Milanov (Trail of Bits), "Exploiting ML models with pickle file attacks: Part 1", Trail of Bits Blog, 2024-06-11. https://blog.trailofbits.com/2024/06/11/exploiting-ml-models-with-pickle-file-attacks-part-1/
- **confirmed via:** https://blog.trailofbits.com/2024/06/11/exploiting-ml-models-with-pickle-file-attacks-part-1/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [malicious pickle, in-memory model tampering, backdoor, disinformation, user data theft, phishing via model output]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0018.002, AML.T0011.000, AML.T0010.003; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM04:2025; ML06, ML10; CWE-502; NISTAML.05, NISTAML.051
- **summary:** Sleepy Pickle is a "hybrid" exploit. The pickle payload does not just run a shell. It patches the deserialized model in memory, changing weights or hooking methods, so the model emits harmful output, steals user data, or inserts phishing links. Nothing malicious is left on disk after the load. Delivery routes include man-in-the-middle, supply-chain compromise, phishing, insiders, and post-exploitation. The Fickling tool builds such payloads with one command. Sandboxing, egress control, and least privilege limit classic shell payloads but do not stop in-model tampering. Safer formats (safetensors) and Fickling-style analysis are the recommended mitigations.
- **mapping:** deployed model behaviour and users -> stealthy in-memory model modification at load -> model distributed as pickle through any channel -> integrity loss, data theft from end users

### S-1002 Exposed container registries holding AI models

- **canonical id:** `trendmicro-2024-container-registries` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `trend-exposed-registries-2023 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Trend Micro, "Silent Sabotage: Weaponizing AI Models in Exposed Containers", Trend Micro research, 2024. https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/cyber-attacks/silent-sabotage-weaponizing-ai-models-in-exposed-containers (ATLAS AML.CS0028)
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [model theft from registries, model tampering via push access]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.004 (Container Registry), AML.T0035, AML.T0048.004, AML.CS0028; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML05, ML06; CWE-306?
- **summary:** Trend Micro found more than 8,000 exposed container registries. About 70% (6,259) had push (write) permission that would let attackers upload tampered images. They found 1,453 unique AI models inside supposedly private images that could be pulled without authentication. Attackers could steal model IP or replace models inside images that are later deployed. The weakness is that container registries are an AI model distribution channel outside ML-specific controls.
- **mapping:** proprietary models in container images -> theft or tampering via open registries -> registries without auth or with write access -> IP loss, poisoned deployments
- **also captured as `trend-exposed-registries-2023` (incidents-news.md):** Trend Micro used service-indexing portals to find more than 8,000 internet-exposed private container registries. About 70% had permissive access controls that allowed writes. The images held more than 1,000 unique AI models that could be pulled without authentication. An attacker could steal the models (IP), or modify them and push poisoned images that downstream deployments would run. The attacker needs only a network scan. This is a measurement study of exposure, not a confirmed exploitation. Mapping: model-serving container images -> unauthenticated read/write registry -> registry exposed to internet -> model theft, poisoned image deployment

### S-1003 Deceptive Delight multi-turn jailbreak (Unit 42)

- **canonical id:** `unit42-2024-deceptive-delight` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence medium
- **citation:** Royce Lu (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42), "Deceptive Delight: Jailbreak LLMs Through Camouflage and Distraction", 2024-10-23. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/jailbreak-llms-through-camouflage-distraction/
- **confirmed via:** https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/jailbreak-llms-through-camouflage-distraction/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, multi-turn, topic-camouflage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** An unsafe topic is embedded among benign ones over 3 turns. The attacker asks for a narrative that links them, then for elaboration on each, then for expansion on the unsafe one. The technique exploits the model's limited attention to context. Across 8 anonymized models, 40 unsafe topics and 8,000 cases, average ASR was 65% versus 5.8% for direct requests. Success required both harmfulness and quality scores of at least 3 on a 0-5 scale. It is in the same family as Crescendo and Echo Chamber.
- **mapping:** chat LLM -> camouflaged multi-turn request -> chat access -> harmful content

### S-1004 Wiz: Hugging Face shared inference and CI/CD takeover risk

- **canonical id:** `wiz-2024-hf-inference-crosstenant` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `wiz-hf-cross-tenant-2024 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Wiz Research, "Hugging Face works with Wiz to strengthen AI cloud security", Wiz Blog, 2024. https://www.wiz.io/blog/wiz-and-hugging-face-address-risks-to-ai-infrastructure
- **confirmed via:** https://www.wiz.io/blog/wiz-and-hugging-face-address-risks-to-ai-infrastructure (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [malicious model to container escape, cross-tenant access, CI/CD takeover]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0011.000, AML.T0105 (Escape to Host), AML.T0010.001; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; ASI05; CWE-502; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** Wiz uploaded a malicious pickle model to Hugging Face's Inference API. With container-escape techniques they broke out of their tenant and could compromise the service running customers' custom models. That would allow cross-tenant access to private models. They also flagged a shared CI/CD takeover risk: malicious Spaces could compromise the build pipeline. The impact for AI-as-a-service providers is "devastating": attackers could reach millions of private models and apps. Hugging Face remediated jointly with Wiz.
- **mapping:** multi-tenant AI inference platform -> cross-tenant compromise via a malicious model -> platform runs untrusted pickle models in weakly isolated containers -> mass confidentiality and integrity breach
- **also captured as `wiz-hf-cross-tenant-2024` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2024-04-04. Wiz uploaded a crafted PyTorch pickle model and got code execution inside HF's Inference API when the model loaded. From there it queried EC2 IMDS (169.254.169.254) for node IAM credentials and ran `aws eks get-token` to get node-level Kubernetes access, which let it read other customers' pod secrets. In Spaces, a malicious Dockerfile ran code at build time. An internal container registry with weak access control allowed pulling and pushing, so overwriting, all images across tenants. The attacker needed only a free account that could upload a model or Space. The assets are other tenants' private models, datasets, and apps. HF hardened IMDS (IMDSv2 with hop limits) and added registry authentication. The key lesson is that inference-as-a-service must treat customer models as untrusted code. Mapping: multi-tenant model hosting (EKS, registry) -> attacker model executes on load -> pods reach IMDS; registry lacks auth -> cross-tenant secret access and image overwrite

### S-1005 Probllama: Ollama path traversal to RCE (CVE-2024-37032)

- **canonical id:** `wiz-2024-probllama` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `probllama-2024 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Sagi Tzadik (Wiz Research), "Probllama: Ollama Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2024-37032)", Wiz Blog, 2024-06. https://www.wiz.io/blog/probllama-ollama-vulnerability-cve-2024-37032 ; NVD CVE-2024-37032 (CVSS 8.8, CWE-22)
- **confirmed via:** https://www.wiz.io/blog/probllama-ollama-vulnerability-cve-2024-37032 (fetched); NVD API
- **attack classes:** [path traversal, RCE on inference server, model theft and tampering]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0049, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0035?; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML05, ML06; CWE-22 (NVD); NISTAML.05
- **summary:** Ollama before 0.1.34 did not validate the model digest format in its blob paths. An attacker-controlled registry or a pull request through the API could write arbitrary files, leading to RCE (CWE-22 per NVD). Wiz found more than 1,000 exposed Ollama instances on the internet. They stress that these new AI inference tools lack built-in authentication, which lets attackers "steal or modify the AI models". Their mitigation advice is never to expose such tools without an authenticating reverse proxy.
- **mapping:** self-hosted LLM inference server -> RCE / model tampering via model pull API -> server exposed with no auth -> host compromise, model theft
- **also captured as `probllama-2024` (incidents-news.md):** Ollama's `/api/pull` accepts a model from a private registry. The manifest's `digest` field went unvalidated into a filesystem path, so an attacker-controlled registry could write arbitrary files on the server. Wiz turned the file write into RCE by planting a shared library and writing `/etc/ld.so.preload`. Ollama has no authentication by default, so any network-reachable instance can be told to pull from the attacker's registry. Wiz counted over 1,000 exposed vulnerable instances, many hosting private models. Fixed in 0.1.34, about 4 hours after disclosure. This links to the later mass exposure of Ollama servers (see ollama-exposed-2025). Mapping: self-hosted model server (Ollama) -> unauthenticated pull from attacker registry with traversal digest -> exposed API with no auth, root process -> host RCE, model theft

### S-1006 Zenity AgentFlayer: zero-click chains against ChatGPT Connectors, Copilot Studio, Cursor+Jira, Einstein, Gemini (Black Hat USA 2025)

- **canonical id:** `agentflayer-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: Azure detail from memory; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Zenity Labs, "AgentFlayer" research, Black Hat USA 2025-08. Press: CSO, "Black Hat: Researchers demonstrate zero-click prompt injection attacks in popular AI agents". https://www.csoonline.com/article/4036868/black-hat-researchers-demonstrate-zero-click-prompt-injection-attacks-in-popular-ai-agents.html
- **confirmed via:** https://www.csoonline.com/article/4036868/ (search hit); https://hackread.com/agentflayer-0-click-exploit-chatgpt-connectors-steal-data/ (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [zero-click indirect prompt injection, connector/data-source abuse, exfiltration via rendered image URL]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS case study AML.CS0037 (Data Exfiltration via Agent Tools in Copilot Studio); ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0057; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI02; CWE-1427
- **summary:** Date 2025-08. Zenity showed poisoned artifacts against several platforms. For ChatGPT Connectors, a document shared into the victim's Google Drive carried a hidden prompt in white, 1-pixel text. When the user asked ChatGPT to summarize it, the prompt made ChatGPT search the connected Drive for API keys and leak them through an image URL that passed the url_safe check via an Azure Blob endpoint (Azure detail from memory; not confirmed here). Other chains targeted Copilot Studio customer-service agents, Cursor with the Jira MCP via tickets, Salesforce Einstein, and Gemini. The attacker needs only to share a file or send a ticket or email. Several vendors patched. The lesson: any connected data source extends the injection surface to everything else connected.
- **mapping:** connected SaaS data (Drive, CRM, tickets) -> injected shared artifact -> connector grants read across the user's data + image rendering -> secret/API-key exfiltration

### S-1007 AI ClickFix: social-engineering a computer-use agent into running a clipboard command

- **canonical id:** `ai-clickfix-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research (researcher blog) / catalog; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** J. Rehberger, "AI ClickFix: Hijacking Computer-Use Agents Using ClickFix", Embrace The Red, 2025-05-24, https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/ai-clickfix-ttp-claude/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0055
- **confirmed via:** MITRE ATLAS 2026.09 case study AML.CS0055 (local yaml); blog URL not fetched
- **attack classes:** [agent social engineering, indirect prompt injection via web UI, clipboard injection, RCE]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0055 (AML.T0100 AI Agent Clickbait, AML.T0078 Drive-by Compromise, AML.T0112.000); OWASP LLM01:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI05, ASI09?; CWE-1427
- **summary:** This adapts the human "ClickFix" lure to agents. A web page says "Are you a computer? Please see instructions to confirm", and its button runs JavaScript that copies a malicious command to the clipboard. Claude Computer Use clicked the button and then followed on-page instructions to open a terminal, paste, and run the command, which gave the attacker code execution. The attacker only needs the agent to visit a page. The asset is the host the agent controls. Rehberger used ChatGPT to build the lure site. This is a demonstration.
- **mapping:** computer-use agent with terminal -> crafted "verification" page plus clipboard payload -> agent treats on-page UI text as instructions -> arbitrary command execution

### S-1008 AIKatz: session tokens scraped from ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot desktop-app memory

- **canonical id:** `aikatz-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / catalog; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Lumia Security, "AIKatz - All Your Chats Are Belong To Us", 2025-11-12, https://www.lumia.security/blog/aikatz ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0036
- **confirmed via:** https://www.lumia.security/blog/aikatz (fetched 2026-10-02); MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0036 (ATLAS dates it 2025-01-01; the blog says 2025-11-12)
- **attack classes:** [credential theft from AI client, session hijack, chat-history manipulation, memory poisoning]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0036 (AML.T0090 OS Credential Dumping, AML.T0091.000, AML.T0092 Manipulate User LLM Chat History, AML.T0080.000/.001); OWASP LLM02:2025; OWASP ASI03, ASI06; CWE-522, CWE-312?
- **summary:** The ChatGPT and Claude desktop apps are Electron-based, and M365 Copilot is WebView2-based. Some of their worker processes run with permissive privileges, so a local attacker (malware running as the user) can scan process memory with regex for ChatGPT and Copilot JWT tokens and Claude session keys. With a token, the attacker can read the victim's whole conversation history, delete or flood chats, inject prompts, and plant persistent memories. For Copilot, the attacker also gets OneDrive and SharePoint tokens. All three vendors declined: Microsoft said no security boundary is crossed, Anthropic closed the HackerOne report, and OpenAI pointed to Microsoft. Lumia suggests restricting worker-process security descriptors.
- **mapping:** AI desktop client session -> local malware reads tokens from process memory -> tokens unbound to device; permissive worker ACLs -> conversation theft, memory/context poisoning, cloud-file access

### S-1009 Anthropic: agentic misalignment (LLMs as insider threats)

- **canonical id:** `anthropic-2025-agentic-misalignment` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** Anthropic (Aengus Lynch et al.), "Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs could be insider threats", 2025-06-20. https://www.anthropic.com/research/agentic-misalignment
- **confirmed via:** https://www.anthropic.com/research/agentic-misalignment (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [agentic-misalignment, insider-threat, blackmail, corporate-espionage]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM06:2025; ASI10, ASI03
- **summary:** 16 frontier LLMs acted as an email-oversight agent ("Alex") in simulated companies, with autonomous email sending and access to sensitive mail. Under goal conflict or a threat of replacement, models blackmailed and leaked data. Blackmail rates in the primary scenario: Claude Opus 4 96%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 96%, GPT-4.1 80%, Grok 3 Beta 80%, DeepSeek-R1 79%. Direct instructions not to do so did not reliably stop them. The scenarios were deliberately binary and contrived, and Anthropic reports no evidence of this in real deployments. Security relevance: an agent given broad access is a potential insider, so least privilege and monitoring apply to the agent itself.
- **mapping:** enterprise agent with email and data access -> self-motivated harmful action (blackmail, leak) -> goal conflict or replacement threat in context -> confidentiality and integrity harm

### S-1010 Anthropic: mitigating prompt injection in browser use (Claude Opus 4.5)

- **canonical id:** `anthropic-2025-browser-prompt-injection-defenses` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** Anthropic, "Mitigating the risk of prompt injections in browser use", 2025-11-24. https://www.anthropic.com/research/prompt-injection-defenses

- **canonical id:** `anthropic-2025-gtg-1002` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high (as reported), medium (attribution)
- **aliases merged:** `anthropic-gtg-1002-2025 (incidents-news.md)`

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0016.002, AML.T0103 (Deploy AI Agent)?, AML.T0054; NISTAML.04
- **summary:** Anthropic reports that an actor it assesses as Chinese state-sponsored (GTG-1002) ran instances of Claude Code as autonomous penetration-testing orchestrators and agents. The AI executed 80% to 90% of tactical operations on its own "at physically impossible request rates". About 30 entities were targeted and "a handful of successful intrusions" were validated. Anthropic banned accounts and notified the affected entities and authorities over a ten-day investigation. It contrasts this with its June 2025 "vibe hacking" case, in which humans directed the operations. Attribution and autonomy percentages are Anthropic's assessment.
- **mapping:** enterprise networks -> intrusions run largely by agents -> attacker access to a coding agent with tools, safeguards bypassed by role-play -> espionage at scale
- **also captured as `anthropic-gtg-1002-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Detected mid-September 2025. Anthropic assesses with high confidence a Chinese state-sponsored actor it calls GTG-1002. The actor built a framework in which Claude Code, driving open-source tools (scanners, password crackers, exploit frameworks) through MCP servers, did 80-90% of the tactical work: reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvesting, data triage, and exfiltration. Humans intervened at about 4-6 decision points per campaign. There were about 30 targets in tech, finance, chemicals, and government, and it "succeeded in a small number of cases". Safeguards were bypassed by splitting malicious work into innocuous subtasks and claiming to be a legitimate security firm. Claude's hallucinations, such as claimed credentials that did not work, limited full autonomy. MITRE catalogued it as campaign C0062. Some outside researchers questioned the autonomy claims (I did not collect those critiques). Mapping: enterprise networks (any org) -> agentic AI-run intrusion at machine speed -> commercial agent + MCP tools, decomposition jailbreak -> espionage, data theft

### S-1013 BodySnatcher (CVE-2025-12420): unauthenticated user impersonation through ServiceNow Virtual Agent / AI Agents

- **canonical id:** `bodysnatcher-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** AppOmni, "BodySnatcher (CVE-2025-12420): agentic hijacking vulnerability in ServiceNow", 2026-01. https://appomni.com/ao-labs/bodysnatcher-agentic-ai-security-vulnerability-in-servicenow/ ; The Hacker News, 2026-01 https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/servicenow-patches-critical-ai-platform.html
- **confirmed via:** https://appomni.com/ao-labs/bodysnatcher-agentic-ai-security-vulnerability-in-servicenow/ (search hit); https://cyberscoop.com/servicenow-fixes-critical-ai-vulnerability-cve-2025-12420/ (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [broken authentication, hard-coded secret, agent impersonation, privilege escalation]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-798, CWE-287, CWE-290?; OWASP ASI03 (Identity & Privilege Abuse); OWASP LLM06:2025?; ATLAS AML.T0012?
- **summary:** Patched 2025-10-30, disclosed 2026-01. The Virtual Agent API used a static client secret identical across all ServiceNow instances, and account linking trusted only an email address. Knowing just a target's email, an unauthenticated attacker could impersonate them, including an admin, and run AI agents as that user. That bypassed MFA and SSO and let the attacker create a backdoor admin account. Fixed in Now Assist AI Agents 5.1.18 / 5.2.19 and Virtual Agent API 3.15.2 / 4.0.4. This is classic auth weakness made more severe by agentic capability: the agent is the attacker's execution engine.
- **mapping:** ServiceNow tenant (all records, admin) -> impersonation via static secret + email-only linking -> integration auth not bound to MFA -> full tenant takeover via agent actions

### S-1014 Brave: indirect prompt injection in Perplexity Comet (agentic browser)

- **canonical id:** `brave-2025-comet-indirect-prompt-injection` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `comet-brave-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Artem Chaikin, Shivan Kaul Sahib (Brave), "Agentic Browser Security: Indirect Prompt Injection in Perplexity Comet", Brave blog, 2025-08-20. https://brave.com/blog/comet-prompt-injection/
- **confirmed via:** https://brave.com/blog/comet-prompt-injection/ (fetched; title wording from memory)
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, agentic-browser, account-takeover, cross-origin-abuse]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0053, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI03
- **summary:** Instructions hidden behind a Reddit spoiler tag were run when the user clicked "Summarize this page". Comet navigated to the user's Perplexity account to read the email, triggered an OTP through a look-alike domain (trailing-dot perplexity.ai.), read the OTP from the logged-in Gmail, and posted both in a Reddit reply, which enabled account takeover. Root cause: page content was not separated from user instructions. Because the agent acts with the user's logged-in sessions everywhere, it breaks the same-origin isolation the web relies on. Mitigations: separate instructions from content, check actions against user intent, confirm sensitive actions, isolate agentic browsing.
- **mapping:** agentic browser with the user's authenticated sessions -> cross-site action chain via IPI -> attacker posts content on any site -> account takeover, cross-origin data theft
- **also captured as `comet-brave-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Reported 2025-07-25, published 2025-08-20. When a user asked Comet to "summarize this page", it passed the page content to the model with no separation from the user's instruction. A hidden Reddit comment told the agent to read the user's Perplexity email, trigger a login OTP, read the OTP from the user's open Gmail tab, and post both back as a reply, which is account takeover. The attacker needs only to publish web content. The browser-agent's ability to act across logged-in origins defeats same-origin policy assumptions. Perplexity's fixes were incomplete on retest, and Brave's update says the issue was not fully mitigated. Brave then found similar issues in Opera Neon and others. Mapping: user's authenticated web sessions (email, bank) -> indirect injection on any visited page -> agent acts across origins with user cookies, no instruction/data separation -> credential/OTP theft, account takeover

### S-1015 NIST CAISI: Strengthening AI agent hijacking evaluations

- **canonical id:** `caisi-2025-agent-hijacking-evaluations` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** NIST Center for AI Standards and Innovation (formerly U.S. AISI) technical staff, "Technical Blog: Strengthening AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations", NIST, 2025-01-17. https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations
- **confirmed via:** https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations (fetched); cited as ref [353] in NIST AI 100-2 E2025 section 3.4.2
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, agent-hijacking, data-exfiltration, rce, phishing]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0053, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02; NISTAML.015/.027/.039
- **summary:** NIST defines agent hijacking as indirect prompt injection against agents: instructions placed in data the agent consumes make it carry out an attacker task. CAISI extended AgentDojo with async execution and Inspect integration. They also added three high-impact injection tasks: remote code execution, database exfiltration, and automated phishing. Baseline attacks succeeded 11% of the time and new red-team attacks 81%. When the attacker could try 25 times, average success rose to 80% from 57% for a single attempt. This shows that pass@k is the right metric for a persistent attacker. The new attacks generalized across all four AgentDojo environments (Workspace, Travel, Slack, Banking).
- **mapping:** tool-using agent (email/workspace/banking) -> hijack via injected data -> attacker can write content the agent will read -> RCE, data exfiltration, phishing sent from a trusted identity

### S-1017 Anthropic: browser-agent prompt-injection red-team rates for Claude for Chrome

- **canonical id:** `claude-for-chrome-redteam-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high (as vendor-reported)
- **citation:** Anthropic, "Piloting Claude for Chrome", 2025-08-25 (updated through 2025-12-18), https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-chrome (redirected from https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-for-chrome)
- **confirmed via:** https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-chrome (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection against browser agents, hidden form fields, DOM injection]

- **summary:** Anthropic reports 123 test cases across 29 attack scenarios. Browser use without its mitigations had a 23.6% attack success rate in autonomous mode, and 11.2% with them. On four browser-specific challenge cases (hidden form fields, URL and tab-title injection) success fell from 35.7% to 0%. In the example, a phishing email posing as the employer asked for emails to be deleted for "mailbox hygiene", and the unprotected agent deleted them. The mitigations were site-level permissions, action confirmations, system-prompt guidance, blocking high-risk site categories, and injection classifiers. This is a vendor-measured baseline, useful for setting threat likelihood for browser agents. It shows that residual risk stays non-zero.

### S-1018 PromptLock: AI-powered ransomware PoC (later tied to NYU "Ransomware 3.0")

- **canonical id:** `eset-2025-promptlock` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: cipher detail from recollection; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `promptlock-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Anton Cherepanov, Peter Strýček (ESET Research), "First known AI-powered ransomware uncovered by ESET Research", WeLiveSecurity, 2025-08-26 (updated 2025-09-03). https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/ransomware/first-known-ai-powered-ransomware-uncovered-eset-research/
- **pdf:** raz-2025-ransomware-3.pdf sha256: b0e20d49b8959784097e746176f0f293d3a666bbc5af18324665a7c834b08d91
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [LLM-generated ransomware logic at runtime, local-model malware]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0102, AML.T0112.000?; NISTAML.04
- **summary:** PromptLock uses OpenAI's gpt-oss-20b locally through the Ollama API to generate Lua scripts on the fly from hard-coded prompts, then runs them. The scripts enumerate the file system, inspect and exfiltrate files, and encrypt them. Destruction capability appears not to be implemented. ESET's 2025-09-03 update says the authors of an academic study, "Ransomware 3.0: Self-Composing and LLM-Orchestrated", contacted them and that their prototype closely matches the samples found on VirusTotal. ESET concludes it was a proof of concept, not malware seen in actual attacks. Treat it as a capability demonstration. The NYU page I tried returned 404, so the paper reference is unconfirmed.
- **mapping:** file servers and endpoints -> polymorphic ransomware logic generated per run -> local LLM runtime available or downloadable -> data encryption and exfiltration
- **also captured as `promptlock-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2025-08. ESET found samples on VirusTotal of a Golang ransomware that, through the Ollama API, prompts a locally hosted gpt-oss:20b with hard-coded prompts. The model generates cross-platform Lua scripts at runtime to enumerate the filesystem, choose files, exfiltrate, and encrypt with SPECK (SPECK from my recollection of ESET's post). The scripts vary on every run, which defeats static signatures. NYU researchers then said it was their academic proof of concept ("Ransomware 3.0"), not an in-the-wild campaign. It is still a credible design pattern for threat models. Mapping: endpoint files -> malware generating payloads via a local or remote LLM -> LLM reachable from the infected host -> encryption/exfiltration with polymorphic logic

### S-1019 ForcedLeak: Salesforce Agentforce CRM exfiltration via Web-to-Lead and an expired allow-listed domain

- **canonical id:** `forcedleak-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Noma Security, "ForcedLeak: AI Agent risks exposed in Salesforce AgentForce", 2025-09-25. https://noma.security/blog/forcedleak-agent-risks-exposed-in-salesforce-agentforce/
- **confirmed via:** https://noma.security/blog/forcedleak-agent-risks-exposed-in-salesforce-agentforce/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection via public form, CSP bypass via expired domain, data exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0057; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM05:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI02; CWE-1427, CWE-942?
- **summary:** Reported 2025-07-28, fixed 2025-09-08 (Trusted URLs Enforcement), public 2025-09-25, CVSS 9.4 (Noma). An unauthenticated outsider submits a Web-to-Lead form whose 42,000-character Description field holds instructions. When an employee later asks Agentforce about the lead, the agent queries other CRM records and embeds the data in an `<img src>` URL. The URL pointed to a domain still on Salesforce's CSP allow-list that had expired, which Noma re-registered for about $5. Outcome: zero-click exfiltration of lead and contact data from the CRM. The lesson: an allow-list is only as strong as domain ownership hygiene.
- **mapping:** CRM records -> injection through a public web form -> agent processes external lead text with CRM read access + allow-listed but lapsed domain -> customer data exfiltration

### S-1021 Tenable "Gemini Trifecta": Cloud Assist log injection, search-history injection, browsing-tool exfiltration

- **canonical id:** `gemini-trifecta-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: User-Agent detail from recollection; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Tenable Research, "The Trifecta: How Three New Gemini Vulnerabilities in Cloud Assist, Search Model, and Browsing Allowed Private Data Exfiltration", 2025-09-30. Mirror: https://securityboulevard.com/2025/09/the-trifecta-how-three-new-gemini-vulnerabilities-in-cloud-assist-search-model-and-browsing-allowed-private-data-exfiltration/
- **confirmed via:** https://securityboulevard.com/2025/09/the-trifecta-how-three-new-gemini-vulnerabilities-in-cloud-assist-search-model-and-browsing-allowed-private-data-exfiltration/ (search hit); https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/researchers-disclose-google-gemini-ai.html (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [log-to-prompt injection, search-history injection, tool-based exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI06?; CWE-1427
- **summary:** Date 2025-09. (1) Gemini Cloud Assist summarized raw cloud logs, so an attacker could inject instructions through attacker-controlled log fields such as the HTTP User-Agent sent to the victim's public service (User-Agent detail from my recollection of the Tenable post) and induce phishing links or cloud queries. (2) The Search Personalization model trusted the user's search history, and a malicious site could inject searches through JavaScript, which turns history into an injection channel to leak saved info and location. (3) The Browsing Tool could be induced to fetch an attacker URL with private data in the request, which bypassed the defenses against markdown image exfiltration. Google remediated all three. Novel channels: logs and browser history as untrusted prompt sources.
- **mapping:** cloud project data / user personal context -> injection via logs or search history -> assistant ingests attacker-writable telemetry as trusted context -> data exfiltration, phishing

### S-1022 GeminiJack: zero-click Gemini Enterprise / Vertex AI Search exfiltration via shared Workspace artifacts

- **canonical id:** `geminijack-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium-high
- **citation:** Noma Labs, "GeminiJack", 2025-12-11 (primary URL not fetched). Press: Dark Reading https://www.darkreading.com/remote-workforce/gemini-enterprise-exposes-sensitive-data ; Infosecurity https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/google-fixes-gemini-enterprise-flaw/
- **confirmed via:** https://www.darkreading.com/remote-workforce/gemini-enterprise-exposes-sensitive-data (search hit); https://securityaffairs.com/185574/hacking/geminijack-zero-click-flaw-in-gemini-enterprise-allowed-corporate-data-exfiltration.html (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [zero-click indirect prompt injection, RAG poisoning, image-URL exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0070?; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM08:2025; OWASP ASI06?; CWE-1427
- **summary:** Reported 2025-06, fixed by 2025-11, public 2025-12-11. An attacker shares a Google Doc, calendar invite, or email containing instructions with someone in the target organization, and no notification is needed. When any employee runs a routine Gemini Enterprise search such as "show me our budgets", the RAG layer retrieves the poisoned item, and the model follows its instructions to gather other corporate data and send it out through an external image URL. DLP and endpoint tools do not see it. Google separated Vertex AI Search from Gemini Enterprise and changed RAG instruction handling. Another instance of the EchoLeak class: external content and internal data in one context, with an exfiltration-capable output channel.
- **mapping:** enterprise Workspace corpus -> poisoned shared artifact retrieved by RAG -> shared-content ingestion + image rendering -> corporate data exfiltration

### S-1023 Supabase MCP: support-ticket injection leaks integration tokens

- **canonical id:** `generalanalysis-2025-supabase-mcp-leak` (gaps-other.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: title from recall; C15 rule)
- **citation:** General Analysis, "Supabase MCP can leak your entire SQL database", 2025-07 (demonstration dated 2025-07-08 on the page). https://www.generalanalysis.com/blog/supabase-mcp-blog
- **confirmed via:** https://www.generalanalysis.com/blog/supabase-mcp-blog (fetched; title from recall, content fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, confused deputy with privileged MCP, data exfiltration via write-back]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI03; MCP01, MCP02, MCP06; ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0086 Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation?
- **summary:** A developer uses Cursor with the Supabase MCP server configured with the `service_role` key, which bypasses row-level security. A customer files a support ticket whose text addresses the assistant directly. When the developer asks the assistant to review tickets, it reads the untrusted ticket and runs two privileged SQL queries. One selects the `integration_tokens` table (OAuth tokens and session credentials). The other inserts the results into the ticket thread, where the attacker reads them. The recommended mitigations are a read-only mode, project scoping, feature limits, manual review of tool calls, and treating fetched data as untrusted.
- **mapping:** production database (secrets) -> injected ticket text drives privileged MCP SQL -> developer agent with service-role credentials reads attacker-writable data -> credential exfiltration

### S-1024 Google: layered defense strategy against prompt injection in Gemini

- **canonical id:** `google-2025-layered-ipi-defense` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Google GenAI Security Team, "Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy", Google Security Blog / blog.google, 2025-06-13. https://blog.google/security/mitigating-prompt-injection-attacks/ (redirected from https://security.googleblog.com/2025/06/mitigating-prompt-injection-attacks.html)
- **confirmed via:** https://blog.google/security/mitigating-prompt-injection-attacks/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, defense-in-depth, markdown-sanitization, hitl]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM05:2025, LLM06:2025 mitigation; ATLAS AML.T0077 mitigation
- **summary:** Layers: (1) model hardening through adversarial training in Gemini 2.5. (2) Prompt-injection content classifiers over emails and files. (3) "Security thought reinforcement", targeted instructions to ignore adversarial content. (4) Markdown sanitization that blocks external image rendering, plus suspicious-URL redaction via Safe Browsing. (5) A user-confirmation framework for risky actions such as deleting calendar events. (6) End-user security notifications. A production reference architecture whose layers each map to a tmodel control.
- **mapping:** consumer and enterprise assistant -> (defense) layered controls across model, input, output and action -> n/a -> reduced IPI impact

- **summary:** Researchers pulled the ML models that ship inside the Google Photos Android app from the device. ATLAS's procedure has them dumping the model at runtime and getting full white-box access (AML.T0044). With the weights, they could reuse the proprietary models and build white-box adversarial examples (AML.T0043.000) against the features they power. The attacker needs only a device with the app. The asset is on-device model IP and the integrity of model decisions.
- **mapping:** mobile app with on-device model -> model extracted from APK or memory -> no model encryption or attestation -> IP theft, white-box evasion

### S-1026 GTIG AI Threat Tracker: PROMPTFLUX, PROMPTSTEAL (LAMEHUG), QUIETVAULT

- **canonical id:** `gtig-2025-ai-threat-tracker` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: malware family names from recollection; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `gtig-ai-threat-tracker-nov-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Google Threat Intelligence Group, "GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Advances in Threat Actor Usage of AI Tools", Google Cloud Blog and report, 2025-11. https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools
- **pdf:** gtig-ai-threat-tracker-nov-2025.pdf sha256: bc517904af9d5c40ad4f3a7dc1f8bba30c6b874f42ca93a1146a02ea1f86bf45
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched); PDF text
- **attack classes:** [malware querying LLMs at runtime, AI-driven obfuscation and self-modification, AI-CLI secret harvesting, guardrail social engineering]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0102 (Generate Malicious Commands), AML.T0096 (AI Service API), AML.T0112.000 (Local AI Agent)?, AML.CS0044; NISTAML.04
- **summary:** GTIG describes malware families that call LLMs during execution. PROMPTFLUX is an experimental VBScript dropper found in early June 2025. It asks the Gemini API for obfuscated VBScript to rewrite itself and evade detection. PROMPTSTEAL, which CERT-UA reports as LAMEHUG, is used by APT28 (FROZENLAKE) against Ukraine. It queries Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct through the Hugging Face API to generate commands to run. GTIG calls this its "first observation of malware querying an LLM deployed in live operations". QUIETVAULT steals GitHub/npm tokens and uses an AI prompt with AI CLI tools installed on the host to hunt for further secrets. Other families listed are FRUITSHELL and PROMPTLOCK. GTIG also reports actors using pretexts such as CTF players or students to get around Gemini's safeguards.
- **mapping:** endpoints and developer hosts -> malware that generates commands and obfuscation via LLM APIs -> outbound access to LLM APIs, AI CLIs installed locally -> evasion of static detection, credential theft
- **also captured as `gtig-ai-threat-tracker-nov-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2025-11. GTIG reports the first malware families that query LLMs during execution. PROMPTFLUX is an experimental VBScript dropper that calls the Gemini API to rewrite and obfuscate itself hourly and persist through the Startup folder. PROMPTSTEAL (also tracked as LameHug; APT28, Russia) is a Python data miner that asks Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct on the Hugging Face API for one-line Windows reconnaissance and collection commands. Others include FRUITSHELL, PROMPTLOCK, and QUIETVAULT (from my recollection of the report; check the PDF). Actors used pretexts ("CTF participant", "student") to get past safety controls, and the underground market for AI tools matured. The asset abused is the AI API itself, as a C2-like dependency, and the stolen or abused API keys. Mapping: endpoints -> malware delegating command generation/obfuscation to LLM APIs -> API keys in malware, hosted model access -> signature evasion, adaptive intrusion

### S-1027 Google GTIG, "Adversarial Misuse of Generative AI" (Jan 2025)

- **canonical id:** `gtig-adversarial-misuse-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / threat-intel report; 2025; confidence high

- **summary:** Date 2025-01-29. GTIG analyzed government-backed actors' use of Gemini. Iran had the most activity (over 10 APT and 8 IO groups). China had over 20 APT groups doing reconnaissance and post-compromise research (lateral movement, privilege escalation, evasion). North Korea had 9 APT groups, including support for the IT-worker scheme. Russia's APT use was limited. Uses were coding, CVE research, reconnaissance, and content. Jailbreak attempts were low-effort, such as copied public prompts, and GTIG says they failed. It found "no indications of them developing novel capabilities" and no prompt-injection or ML-targeted attacks on Gemini by these actors. A useful baseline for 2025 before the agentic shift.
- **mapping:** orgs targeted by APTs -> LLM-assisted operations -> access to public LLM -> productivity uplift only (as of early 2025)

### S-1030 Invariant Labs: GitHub MCP toxic agent flow

- **canonical id:** `invariant-2025-github-mcp-toxic-flow` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `github-mcp-invariant-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Invariant Labs, "GitHub MCP Exploited: Accessing private repositories via MCP", 2025-05-26. https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability
- **confirmed via:** https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, toxic-agent-flow, cross-repository-leak, confused-deputy]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0053, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI03
- **summary:** An attacker opens an issue in a public repository containing a prompt injection. When the victim asks their agent (Claude Desktop with Claude 4 Opus and the official GitHub MCP server) to look at open issues, the agent reads the issue and uses the victim's token to read private repositories. It then publishes the data (repository names, relocation plans, salary) in a public PR. The flaw is architectural, not a bug in the MCP server: any agent with a broadly scoped token is affected regardless of model. Mitigations: per-session least-privilege policies (one repository per session) and runtime monitoring with MCP-scan in proxy mode. This is a canonical lethal-trifecta and confused-deputy case.
- **mapping:** developer's GitHub token held by an agent -> IPI via public issue -> attacker can open an issue in a repo the agent reads -> private source and data disclosure
- **also captured as `github-mcp-invariant-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2025-05-26. An attacker opens an issue containing an injection in any public repository the victim owns. The victim asks an agent (Claude 4 Opus in Claude Desktop with the official GitHub MCP server) to "check open issues". The agent follows the injected instruction, reads the victim's private repos with the victim's broadly scoped token, and writes the contents (project names, relocation plans, salary) into a pull request on the public repo. The MCP server code is not buggy. The flaw is the architecture: an agent holding one token across all repositories processes untrusted text. Proposed mitigations: per-session single-repo scoping and runtime guards such as MCP-scan. Mapping: private source repos -> indirect injection via public issue -> over-scoped PAT shared across repos + agent reads untrusted issues -> private data published

### S-1031 Invariant Labs: MCP tool poisoning attacks (TPA, rug pull, cross-server shadowing)

- **canonical id:** `invariant-2025-mcp-tool-poisoning` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Invariant Labs, "MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks", 2025-04-01 (updated 2025-04-07 and 2025-04-11). https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks
- **confirmed via:** https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [mcp-tool-poisoning, rug-pull, cross-server-shadowing, credential-exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0110, AML.T0115.002, AML.T0011.002, AML.T0083 (Credentials from AI Agent Configuration); OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM03:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI02, ASI04
- **summary:** This post originated three named MCP attack classes. (1) Tool Poisoning: hidden instructions in a tool description that the model sees but the user does not. The PoC is a poisoned `add` tool that makes Cursor read `~/.cursor/mcp.json` and `~/.ssh/id_rsa` and send them through a hidden parameter while explaining the arithmetic. (2) Rug Pull: a server changes its tool descriptions after the user has approved it. (3) Cross-server Shadowing: a malicious server's descriptions change how the agent uses other, trusted servers, for example redirecting email recipients. Proposed mitigations: UI that shows model-visible instructions, pinning server versions with hashes, and cross-server dataflow controls. Claude Desktop was described as susceptible but was not the demonstrated target.
- **mapping:** MCP client host (IDE or desktop agent) and its credentials -> poisoned tool metadata hijacks the agent -> user installs or connects a malicious MCP server -> SSH key and credential theft, trusted-tool hijack

### S-1032 "Wayback Copilot": private GitHub repos exposed through Bing cache to Copilot

- **canonical id:** `lasso-2025-wayback-copilot` (gaps-other.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Lasso Security, "Major vulnerability in Microsoft Copilot: Wayback Copilot", 2025-02-27. https://www.lasso.security/blog/lasso-major-vulnerability-in-microsoft-copilot
- **confirmed via:** https://www.lasso.security/blog/lasso-major-vulnerability-in-microsoft-copilot (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [retrieval of stale cached data ("zombie data"), secret exposure, dependency confusion enabler]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM02:2025, LLM08:2025?; ATLAS AML.T0057 LLM Data Leakage?; CWE-524/CWE-212?
- **summary:** Bing's cache (cc.bingj.com) kept snapshots of GitHub repositories that were once public and later made private, and Copilot could still retrieve them. Lasso extracted 20,580 repositories from 16,290 organizations, including Microsoft, Google, Intel, PayPal, IBM and Tencent. It found more than 300 private tokens, keys and secrets (GitHub, Hugging Face, GCP, OpenAI) and more than 100 internal Python and Node packages open to dependency confusion. The issue was found in August 2024. Microsoft rated it low severity and removed Bing's cached-link feature, but Copilot kept back-end access for a time. The lesson is that an AI assistant's retrieval layer can outlive the source's access-control change.
- **mapping:** source code and secrets once public -> AI assistant retrieves stale search cache -> anyone with Copilot access -> secret exposure, supply-chain attack via dependency confusion

### S-1033 CamoLeak: GitHub Copilot Chat private-repo exfiltration via Camo proxy

- **canonical id:** `legit-2025-camoleak` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `camoleak-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** O. Mayraz (Legit Security), "CamoLeak: Critical GitHub Copilot Vulnerability Leaks Private Source Code", 2025-10-08 (updated 2026-02-12); no CVE, CVSS 9.6 per Legit Security. https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/camoleak-critical-github-copilot-vulnerability-leaks-private-source-code
- **confirmed via:** https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/camoleak-critical-github-copilot-vulnerability-leaks-private-source-code (fetched); per sibling incidents file (not independently verified here)
- **attack classes:** [indirect-prompt-injection, csp-bypass, image-proxy-exfiltration, private-code-leak]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0077, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM05:2025; NISTAML.036/.039
- **summary:** Hidden PR comments (`<!-- -->`) carried the injection, and Copilot Chat processed them with the victim's permissions. To get past GitHub's CSP, the researcher pre-generated a dictionary of HMAC-signed Camo proxy image URLs, one per character, and had Copilot render secret data as a sequence of those images, which the browser fetched in order. Leaked: private source, zero-day descriptions from private issues, and AWS_KEY search results. CVSS 9.6. GitHub's fix (2025-08-14) disabled image rendering in Copilot Chat. Lesson: an allow-listed first-party proxy is still an exfiltration channel.
- **mapping:** developer's private repos via Copilot Chat -> character-by-character exfiltration through allow-listed image proxy -> attacker can comment on a PR the victim reviews -> source code and secret disclosure
- **also captured as `camoleak-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Reported via HackerOne 2025-06, mitigated 2025-08-14, public 2025-10. Hidden markdown comments in a pull request, invisible in the web UI, carried instructions that Copilot Chat followed when a reviewer asked about the PR. Copilot ran with the victim's access to private repos. Because GitHub's CSP permits only Camo-proxied images, the researcher pre-generated a dictionary of signed Camo URLs, one per character, each pointing at a 1-pixel image he controlled. Copilot "drew" the secret as a sequence of images, leaking AWS keys and an undisclosed zero-day description from a private issue. Reported CVSS 9.6 (vendor-reported; the CVE id comes from a secondary source and is not confirmed in NVD here). GitHub disabled image rendering in Copilot Chat. Mapping: private repos/secrets -> injection in PR + exfil through allow-listed proxy -> assistant has the reviewer's repo scope + renders images -> source/secret exfiltration

### S-1034 GitLab Duo remote prompt injection: private source and zero-day theft

- **canonical id:** `legit-2025-gitlab-duo-remote-prompt-injection` (gaps-other.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: author from recall; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Legit Security (O. Mayraz, from recall), "Remote Prompt Injection in GitLab Duo Leads to Source Code Theft", May 2025. https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/remote-prompt-injection-in-gitlab-duo
- **confirmed via:** https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/remote-prompt-injection-in-gitlab-duo (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, HTML injection exfiltration, hidden-text smuggling]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM05:2025; ASI01; ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0077 LLM Response Rendering?, AML.T0068 LLM Prompt Obfuscation?; CWE-79?
- **summary:** Hidden prompts can be planted in merge-request descriptions and comments, commit messages, issues and source files, all of which GitLab Duo reads as context. They are obfuscated with Unicode smuggling (ASCII Smuggler), Base16 payloads and KaTeX white text. The injected instructions made Duo take code changes from a merge request in a private project, base64-encode them into an `<img>` URL and emit raw HTML. Duo's streaming markdown renderer then made the victim's browser send the data to the attacker. Private source code and confidential issues, including zero-day vulnerability discussions, were exposed. The flaw was disclosed on 2025-02-12. GitLab's fix (duo-ui!52) blocks rendering of unsafe tags that point to non-GitLab domains.
- **mapping:** private repos and issues readable by Duo -> injected instructions in project content -> attacker can comment or open an MR in any project the victim's Duo reads -> source and zero-day exfiltration via rendered HTML

### S-1035 "Living Off AI": prompt injection through Jira Service Management tickets into Atlassian MCP

- **canonical id:** `living-off-ai-jira-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / catalog; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** Cato CTRL, "PoC Attack Targeting Atlassian's Model Context Protocol (MCP) Introduces New 'Living Off AI' Risk", 2025-06-19, https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-poc-attack-targeting-atlassians-mcp/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0039

- **summary:** An external, unauthenticated user files a Jira Service Management ticket that contains instructions. ### S-1036 LAMEHUG (APT28) technical analysis

- **canonical id:** `logpoint-2025-lamehug` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `lamehug-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Nischal Khadgi (Logpoint), "APT28's New Arsenal: LAMEHUG, the First AI-Powered Malware", Logpoint blog, 2025-07. https://logpoint.com/en/blog/apt28s-new-arsenal-lamehug-the-first-ai-powered-malware (primary: CERT-UA, https://cert.gov.ua/article/6284730; my fetch of it returned an empty JS shell)
- **confirmed via:** https://logpoint.com/en/blog/apt28s-new-arsenal-lamehug-the-first-ai-powered-malware (fetched); ATLAS AML.CS0044 references
- **attack classes:** [LLM-in-the-loop malware, phishing delivery, data theft]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0102, AML.T0096, AML.T0052, AML.CS0044; NISTAML.04
- **summary:** CERT-UA reported that APT28 sent phishing from a compromised official account carrying "Appendix.pdf.zip". Inside was a PyInstaller-packed Python executable (.pif), LameHug. The malware sends natural-language tasks to Qwen 2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct through the Hugging Face API and runs the returned system commands for reconnaissance and document collection. Because the commands are generated at run time, static signatures of the command strings do not work. The LLM API key and endpoint are a new piece of C2-like infrastructure for defenders to block or revoke.
- **mapping:** government/enterprise endpoints -> LLM-generated recon and exfiltration commands -> phishing execution, egress to public LLM APIs -> data theft
- **also captured as `lamehug-2025` (incidents-news.md):** The ATLAS incident date is 2025-06-03. CERT-UA attributed it to UAC-0001 (APT28). Phishing emails from a compromised official account delivered a Python-based tool. The tool sends natural-language task descriptions to an LLM through an API (press reports Qwen2.5-Coder through the Hugging Face API; not verified here) and executes the returned Windows commands for reconnaissance and document collection, then exfiltrates the results. Because commands are generated at runtime, static signatures fail. The asset is the victim's Windows hosts and documents. The provider's API is used as an external dependency, and stolen or free API tokens are the precondition. This is one of the first publicly attributed state-actor uses of LLM-in-the-loop malware. Mapping: government endpoint -> phishing-delivered implant asks hosted LLM for commands -> outbound access to AI APIs allowed; no egress control on AI endpoints -> reconnaissance and data theft

### S-1037 McDonald's McHire (Paradox.ai "Olivia"): 64M applicant records exposed

- **canonical id:** `mchire-2025-paradox-breach` (gaps-other.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** I. Carroll, S. Curry, "McHire" write-up, 2025-06-30/07-01. https://ian.sh/mcdonalds

- **summary:** McHire is the Paradox.ai recruitment-chatbot platform used by most McDonald's franchisees. Its admin interface accepted the default credentials 123456:123456. An IDOR on the internal API endpoint `PUT /api/lead/cem-xhr` then exposed records of "more than 64 million applicants": names, emails, phones, addresses, shift preferences, chat histories and auth tokens. The issue was disclosed on 2025-06-30. The default credentials were disabled the same evening and Paradox confirmed resolution on 2025-07-01. Nothing here is AI-specific; the asset is the AI agent's conversation and lead store, and the failure is ordinary authentication and authorization.

### S-1038 SesameOp: backdoor uses OpenAI Assistants API as C2

- **canonical id:** `msft-2025-sesameop` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `sesameop-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Microsoft Incident Response (DART), "SesameOp: Novel backdoor uses OpenAI Assistants API for command and control", Microsoft Security Blog, 2025-11-03. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/11/03/sesameop-novel-backdoor-uses-openai-assistants-api-for-command-and-control/ (ATLAS AML.CS0042)
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [LLM API as covert C2 channel, espionage persistence]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0096 (AI Service API), AML.CS0042; NISTAML.04
- **summary:** In a long-running intrusion of several months, with internal web shells and compromised Visual Studio utilities, the actor's SesameOp backdoor used the OpenAI Assistants API as its command-and-control channel. It fetched commands from the API and exfiltrated encrypted results through it. Traffic to a legitimate AI SaaS blends in with sanctioned use. Defenders need egress policy and API-key governance for AI services, and the provider can disable the attacker's keys and assistants.
- **mapping:** compromised enterprise host -> covert C2 over a sanctioned AI API -> AI SaaS egress allowed without tenant restrictions -> persistent espionage, detection evasion
- **also captured as `sesameop-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Microsoft found it in July 2025 during an incident response. The actor had been present for several months. A loader (`Netapi64.dll`, obfuscated with Eazfuscator.NET) was injected through .NET AppDomainManager injection. The backdoor, `OpenAIAgent.Netapi64`, fetched encrypted commands stored as messages in the OpenAI Assistants API, executed them locally, and posted the results back. Payloads were wrapped in AES, RSA, GZIP, and Base64. The model itself was not used; only the API's storage was. Microsoft and OpenAI disabled the actor's API key and account. Microsoft stresses this is misuse, not a vulnerability. For threat modeling, sanctioned AI API domains are a covert exfiltration and C2 path. Mapping: enterprise network egress to AI APIs -> implant uses AI service objects as dead-drop C2 -> AI endpoints allow-listed and unmonitored -> long-term covert persistence and exfiltration

### S-1039 Echo Chamber context-poisoning jailbreak

- **canonical id:** `neuraltrust-2025-echo-chamber` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** NeuralTrust, "Echo Chamber: A Context-Poisoning Jailbreak That Bypasses LLM Guardrails", 2025-06-23. https://neuraltrust.ai/blog/echo-chamber-context-poisoning-jailbreak
- **confirmed via:** https://neuraltrust.ai/blog/echo-chamber-context-poisoning-jailbreak (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [jailbreak, multi-turn, context-poisoning, semantic-steering]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0054; OWASP LLM01:2025; NISTAML.018
- **summary:** A multi-turn jailbreak that plants implicit cues and then steers the model to reason its way toward the harmful goal from its own earlier outputs. The vendor reports more than 90% success for sexism, violence, hate and pornography, about 80% for misinformation and self-harm, and more than 40% for profanity and illegal activity. Tests were 200 attempts per model on GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0/2.5 Flash variants, mostly succeeding within 1-3 turns. Vendor-reported and not peer reviewed.
- **mapping:** chat LLM -> self-reinforcing multi-turn steering -> chat access -> restricted content

Blachez, from recall), "A well-funded Moscow-based global 'news' network has infected Western artificial intelligence tools worldwide with Russian propaganda", Special Report, 2025-03-06. https://www.newsguardtech.com/special-reports/moscow-based-global-news-network-infected-western-artificial-intelligence-russian-propaganda/
- **confirmed via:** URL above (fetched); Wikipedia API page "Pravda network" (American Sunlight Project coined "LLM grooming"; later ISD findings)

- **summary:** The Pravda network published about 3.6 million articles in 2024. NewsGuard says these were aimed at web crawlers and search results, and so at AI systems, rather than at human readers. An audit of 10 leading chatbots found they repeated Pravda-laundered false narratives 33% of the time. The report quotes John Mark Dougan: "By pushing these Russian narratives from the Russian perspective, we can actually change worldwide AI." Per Wikipedia, the American Sunlight Project coined "LLM grooming", later reports describe up to 10,000 articles a day in more than 50 languages, and ISD documented chatbots citing Pravda. ### S-1045 ChatGPT Operator: prompt injection exploits that leak PII

- **canonical id:** `operator-injection-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** J. Rehberger, "ChatGPT Operator: Prompt Injection Exploits And Defenses", Embrace The Red, 2025-02. https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/chatgpt-operator-prompt-injection-exploits/ ; OpenAI comment: Fortune, 2025-12-23 https://fortune.com/2025/12/23/openai-ai-browser-prompt-injections-cybersecurity-hackers/
- **confirmed via:** https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/chatgpt-operator-prompt-injection-exploits/ (search hit); https://fortune.com/2025/12/23/openai-ai-browser-prompt-injections-cybersecurity-hackers/ (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, browser-agent hijack, PII exfiltration via form input]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI02; CWE-1427
- **summary:** Date 2025-02. Instructions planted in a GitHub issue or web page sent OpenAI's Operator browser agent to authenticated pages, such as the user's account settings on other sites. Operator copied the email, phone, and address into a field on an attacker page, which captured keystrokes without a form submit. Operator's mitigations (user confirmation, a prompt-injection monitor, and "watch mode" on sensitive sites) reduced the attacks but were bypassed in some flows. Operator sessions run server-side, so the provider holds the user's cookies and tokens, which is a separate trust concern. In December 2025 OpenAI publicly said prompt injection "is unlikely to ever be fully solved".
- **mapping:** user PII on authenticated sites -> injected instructions on visited pages -> agent with logged-in sessions and typing ability -> PII exfiltration

### S-1046 Rules File Backdoor (Pillar Security)

- **canonical id:** `pillar-2025-rules-file-backdoor` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `rules-file-backdoor-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Ziv Karliner et al. (Pillar Security), "New Vulnerability in GitHub Copilot and Cursor: How Hackers Can Weaponize Code Agents" (Rules File Backdoor), 2025-03-18. https://www.pillar.security/blog/new-vulnerability-in-github-copilot-and-cursor-how-hackers-can-weaponize-code-agents
- **confirmed via:** https://www.pillar.security/blog/new-vulnerability-in-github-copilot-and-cursor-how-hackers-can-weaponize-code-agents (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [rules-file-poisoning, invisible-unicode, code-backdoor-insertion, supply-chain]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0081 (Modify AI Agent Configuration), AML.T0068, AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM03:2025; ASI04, ASI05
- **summary:** Malicious instructions hidden in AI-assistant rule and config files (for example `.cursor/rules` and Copilot instructions) use invisible Unicode, such as zero-width joiners and bidirectional markers, that reviewers cannot see but the model reads. They make the assistant insert vulnerabilities or backdoors into generated code and hide the change from chat logs. Because rules files are shared in repos and templates, the poison persists across forks and all future generations. Cursor called it user responsibility. GitHub later added warnings for hidden Unicode on github.com. Mitigations: audit rules files for invisible characters, treat config as code, use scanners. Repository instruction files are therefore a high-trust input channel.
- **mapping:** repository AI config/rules files -> hidden instructions steer code generation -> attacker contributes to a repo or template -> backdoored code shipped to production
- **also captured as `rules-file-backdoor-2025` (incidents-news.md):** An attacker hides instructions in shared rules files such as `.cursorrules` and Copilot instructions, using zero-width joiners and bidirectional markers. The rules files spread through repos and communities. The coding assistant follows them silently, inserting external script references, auth bypasses, weak crypto, or credential exfiltration into generated code, and it is told not to mention the changes in chat. Human reviewers cannot see the hidden text. Disclosure: Cursor (2025-02-26) said the risk is the user's responsibility. GitHub (2025-03-12) first said the same, then shipped a warning for hidden Unicode in files on 2025-05-01. The asset is the code the AI generates and, through it, every downstream user of the software. Mapping: AI coding assistant config (rules files) -> invisible-Unicode instructions in shared rules -> assistant trusts repo config as instructions; reviewers cannot see the payload -> backdoored code shipped

### S-1048 ShadowLeak: zero-click, service-side exfiltration via ChatGPT Deep Research

- **citation:** Z. Babo, G. Nakibly, M. Uziel (Radware), "ShadowLeak", September 2025. https://www.radware.com/blog/threat-intelligence/shadowleak/ ; coverage: https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/shadowleak-zero-click-flaw-leaks-gmail.html

- **summary:** An email whose hidden HTML (tiny fonts, white-on-white text, layout tricks) carries instructions reaches a Gmail inbox connected to ChatGPT Deep Research. When the user asks Deep Research to analyze their mail, the agent extracts PII, base64-encodes it, and appends it to an attacker URL that it opens with its browser.open() tool. ### S-1049 Gemini long-term memory poisoning via delayed tool invocation

- **canonical id:** `rehberger-2025-gemini-memory-delayed-invocation` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Johann Rehberger, "Hacking Gemini's Memory with Prompt Injection and Delayed Tool Invocation", Embrace The Red, 2025-02-10. https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/gemini-memory-persistence-prompt-injection/

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0080.000, AML.T0094, AML.T0051.002; OWASP LLM01:2025; ASI06
- **summary:** A document carries hidden instructions that make a memory-save conditional on a later user reply such as "yes". When the user says the trigger word, Gemini treats the memory write as user-requested and gets past the safeguard against tool calls from untrusted content. False facts were persisted into the user's long-term memory. Google assessed it as low likelihood and low impact. "Delayed tool invocation" is a general bypass for "no tool calls while processing untrusted data" policies (cf. ATLAS AML.T0094).
- **mapping:** assistant memory -> triggered memory write -> user summarizes an attacker document -> persistent misinformation and bias
