### S-1051 ReversingLabs nullifAI: broken pickle evades Picklescan

- **canonical id:** `rl-2025-nullifai` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `nullifai-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Karlo Zanki (ReversingLabs), "Malicious ML models discovered on Hugging Face platform", RL Blog, 2025-02-06. https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/rl-identifies-malware-ml-model-hosted-on-hugging-face
- **confirmed via:** https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/rl-identifies-malware-ml-model-hosted-on-hugging-face (fetched); also ATLAS AML.CS0031 in atlas.yaml
- **attack classes:** [scanner evasion, malicious pickle, reverse shell]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0115.001, AML.T0011.000, AML.T0107 (Exploitation for Defense Evasion)?, AML.CS0031; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; CWE-502; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** RL found two PyTorch models on Hugging Face that were compressed with 7z instead of the default ZIP. This stops `torch.load()` from opening them and, likely as a result, stopped Hugging Face's Picklescan from flagging them. The pickle stream was deliberately broken after the payload, so the malicious opcodes run before deserialization fails. Picklescan relied on parsing the whole file and on a blocklist of dangerous functions, and it missed both. RL calls the technique "nullifAI". The point for a threat model is that hub-side scanning is a weak control. Loaders still execute partial pickles.
- **mapping:** ML developer host -> code execution from a corrupted pickle -> hub scanner trusted as the only control -> host compromise
- **also captured as `nullifai-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2025-02. Two Hugging Face models contained PyTorch pickles compressed with 7z rather than the default ZIP, and the pickle stream was deliberately broken after the malicious opcode. Picklescan failed or skipped them, but Python's permissive unpickler still ran the payload, a platform-aware reverse shell to a hard-coded IP, before it reached the corrupt section. This is defense evasion against the hub's security tooling. Hugging Face removed the models within 24 hours, and Picklescan was updated to handle broken files. The lesson: deny-list pickle scanning is not a security boundary. Mapping: model hub consumers -> malformed pickle evading scanner -> trust in hub "safe" scan status -> RCE on load

### S-1052 ServiceNow Now Assist second-order prompt injection via agent-to-agent discovery

- **canonical id:** `servicenow-second-order-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** AppOmni AO Labs (A. Costello), "When AI Turns on Its Team: Exploiting Agent-to-Agent Discovery via Prompt Injection", 2025-11. https://appomni.com/ao-labs/ai-agent-to-agent-discovery-prompt-injection/
- **confirmed via:** https://appomni.com/ao-labs/ai-agent-to-agent-discovery-prompt-injection/ (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [second-order prompt injection, inter-agent privilege escalation, confused deputy]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI07 (Insecure Inter-Agent Communication), ASI03, ASI01; CWE-1427, CWE-441?
- **summary:** Date 2025-11. In ServiceNow Now Assist, agents in the same team can discover and recruit each other by default, and some agents run with the privileges of the user who triggered them. A low-privileged user writes injection text into a record field. When a higher-privileged user's agent processes that record, it recruits a more capable agent to do CRUD on other records, escalate roles, or email record contents externally. This worked while ServiceNow's prompt-injection protection was enabled. ServiceNow called it expected behavior under default configuration, and AppOmni recommends supervised execution, disabling autonomous overrides, and segmenting agent teams. A key pattern for multi-agent threat models.
- **mapping:** ITSM/HR records -> injection stored in a field, executed by another user's agent, which recruits a privileged peer agent -> default agent discovery + agents acting with invoker privileges -> data exfiltration, privilege escalation

### S-1054 Malware sample with an embedded prompt injection aimed at AI malware analyzers

- **canonical id:** `skynet-prompt-injection-malware-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / catalog; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Check Point Research, "In the Wild: Malware Prototype with Embedded Prompt Injection", 2025-06, https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/ai-evasion-prompt-injection/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0043
- **confirmed via:** https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/ai-evasion-prompt-injection/ (fetched 2026-10-02); MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0043
- **attack classes:** [prompt injection against AI security tooling, detection evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0043 (AML.T0051.000, AML.T0015 Evade AI Model, AML.T0097 Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion); OWASP LLM01:2025; CWE-1427; NIST AI 100-2 direct/indirect prompt injection
- **summary:** Uploaded to VirusTotal in early June 2025 from the Netherlands. The sample, "Skynet", performed sandbox-evasion checks, collected SSH keys and hosts files, and set up an encrypted Tor proxy. It looked like an unfinished proof of concept. It embedded a C++ string telling any LLM analyzing it to ignore previous instructions and answer "NO MALWARE DETECTED". Against OpenAI o3 and GPT-4 the injection failed and the models continued their analysis. The case matters because it is the first in-the-wild attempt to target LLM-based malware triage and reverse-engineering pipelines. It defines a threat to defenders' own AI tools.
- **mapping:** SOC LLM triage/RE assistant -> analyzed artifact contains instructions to change the verdict -> analyzer passes untrusted sample content into the prompt -> false-negative verdicts (failed in this case)

### S-1056 Gemini CLI: silent code execution via context-file injection and allow-list bypass

- **canonical id:** `tracebit-2025-gemini-cli-hijack` (gaps-other.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Tracebit, "Code Execution Through Deception: Gemini AI CLI Hijack", July 2025. https://tracebit.com/blog/code-exec-deception-gemini-ai-cli-hijack
- **confirmed via:** https://tracebit.com/blog/code-exec-deception-gemini-ai-cli-hijack (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection via context files, command allow-list bypass, UI deception, credential exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI05; ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0050 Command and Scripting Interpreter?; CWE-78
- **summary:** A prompt hidden in a repository README.md, camouflaged inside GPL licence text, is loaded into context in the same way as GEMINI.md context files. Allow-list validation compared only the root command. Once a user had approved `grep`, `grep ...; <malicious payload>` ran without a new prompt. Large runs of whitespace pushed the payload out of view in the TUI, so it ran silently after the visible part. The result was silent exfiltration of environment variables and secrets while the user thought they were exploring a codebase. The flaw affected releases from 2025-06-25. It was fixed in v0.1.14 on 2025-07-25 with robust command parsing. Google's VDP first rated it P2/S4, then reclassified it P1/S1.
- **mapping:** developer workstation (env secrets) -> injected context file plus allow-list prefix bypass -> victim runs CLI agent on an untrusted repo -> silent RCE and credential theft

### S-1057 Trail of Bits: weaponizing image scaling against production AI systems

- **canonical id:** `trailofbits-2025-image-scaling-injection` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Kikimora Morozova, Suha Sabi Hussain (Trail of Bits), "Weaponizing image scaling against production AI systems", 2025-08-21. https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/08/21/weaponizing-image-scaling-against-production-ai-systems/
- **confirmed via:** https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/08/21/weaponizing-image-scaling-against-production-ai-systems/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [multimodal-prompt-injection, image-scaling-attack, hidden-text, data-exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0068, AML.T0086; OWASP LLM01:2025; ASI01
- **summary:** High-resolution images are crafted so that injected text appears only after the pipeline downscales them with nearest-neighbor, bilinear or bicubic interpolation. Users see a benign image while the model sees instructions. Affected products: Gemini CLI, Vertex AI Studio, the Gemini web interface and API, Google Assistant on Android, and Genspark. On Gemini CLI an uploaded image triggered Zapier MCP calls without confirmation and exfiltrated calendar data by email. Open-source tool: Anamorpher. Defenses: avoid downscaling or show the user the model's view, and require confirmation for tool calls initiated from image content. A preprocessing-pipeline gap that no model-level defense can see.
- **mapping:** multimodal agent preprocessing pipeline -> downscaling reveals hidden instructions -> user opens or uploads an attacker image -> tool-driven exfiltration

### S-1058 Trail of Bits: MCP "line jumping"

- **canonical id:** `trailofbits-2025-mcp-line-jumping` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Trail of Bits, "Jumping the line: How MCP servers can attack you before you ever use them", 2025-04-21. https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/21/jumping-the-line-how-mcp-servers-can-attack-you-before-you-ever-use-them/
- **confirmed via:** https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/21/jumping-the-line-how-mcp-servers-can-attack-you-before-you-ever-use-them/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [mcp-tool-poisoning, pre-invocation-injection, hitl-bypass]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0110, AML.T0011.002; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM03:2025; ASI02, ASI04, ASI09
- **summary:** Tool descriptions from `tools/list` enter the model context when the client connects, before any tool is invoked. A malicious server can therefore inject instructions without ever being called, which bypasses invocation-time consent. Examples: prefixing every shell command with `chmod -R 0666 ~;`, exfiltrating code, inserting vulnerabilities into generated code, and suppressing security alerts. Human-in-the-loop approval tends to become rubber-stamping. Mitigations: vet servers, scan descriptions, trust-on-first-use with change alerts, disable unused servers, no auto-approve.
- **mapping:** coding agent with MCP servers -> pre-invocation context injection -> malicious or compromised MCP server connected -> code exfiltration, backdoored code, disabled alerts

### S-1059 Unit 42: agent session smuggling in A2A

- **canonical id:** `unit42-2025-a2a-session-smuggling` (llm-agent-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence medium (capped from high: contains per-memory claims; C15 rule)
- **citation:** Royce Lu, Jay Chen (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42), "When AI Agents Go Rogue: Agent Session Smuggling Attack in A2A Systems", 2025-10-31. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/agent-session-smuggling-in-agent2agent-systems/
- **confirmed via:** https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/agent-session-smuggling-in-agent2agent-systems/ (fetched; title wording from memory, content fetched)
- **attack classes:** [a2a, inter-agent-injection, multi-turn, unauthorized-actions]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0080.001; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM06:2025; ASI07, ASI01, ASI03
- **summary:** A malicious remote agent exploits stateful multi-turn A2A sessions and slips covert instructions into intermediate exchanges that the end user never sees. In PoC 1 a financial assistant delegating to a malicious "research" agent leaks its system configuration, tool schemas and chat history. In PoC 2 the same setup leads to unauthorized stock trades. Mitigations: out-of-band HITL approval, context grounding to detect drift, cryptographically signed AgentCards, and exposing agent activity to the user.
- **mapping:** orchestrating agent with sensitive tools -> instructions smuggled by a remote agent -> attacker operates a peer agent the victim delegates to -> data leak, unauthorized transactions

### S-1060 Unit 42: AI Agents Are Here. So Are the Threats.

- **canonical id:** `unit42-2025-agentic-threats` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Royce Lu, Jay Chen (Unit 42), "AI Agents Are Here. So Are the Threats.", 2025-05-01. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/agentic-ai-threats/

- **attack classes:** [agent credential leakage, tool exploitation, RCE via code tools, information leakage]

The outcomes include information leakage, credential theft (exposed service tokens and secrets enabling impersonation and privilege escalation), tool exploitation, and RCE. Mitigations are sandboxing with network and syscall restrictions, least-privilege containers, DLP, audit logs, and secret managers. The authors map their findings to OWASP's Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations.

### S-1061 Unit 42: Model Namespace Reuse

- **canonical id:** `unit42-2025-namespace-reuse` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `model-namespace-reuse-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Itay Saraf, Ofir Balassiano (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42), "Model Namespace Reuse: An AI Supply-Chain Attack Exploiting Model Name Trust", 2025-09-03. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/model-namespace-reuse/
- **confirmed via:** https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/model-namespace-reuse/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [namespace hijack, model-name confusion, RCE via model deployment]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.003, AML.T0115.001, AML.T0074 (Masquerading)?; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; ASI04; CWE-494?, CWE-1357?; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** Hugging Face model ids (Author/ModelName) can be re-registered after the author account is deleted. Ownership transfers also leave the old path open. Cloud catalogs and code that fetch models by name alone will then pull the attacker's model. Unit 42 showed RCE on Google Vertex AI Model Garden and on Microsoft Azure AI Foundry this way, and reported that thousands of open-source projects reference reusable names. They disclosed to Google, Microsoft, and Hugging Face. Mitigations are version pinning by commit hash, mirroring models into trusted registries, and scanning code for model references.
- **mapping:** cloud ML deployment pipeline -> malicious model at a trusted name -> pipeline resolves models by name, not digest -> RCE in the provider endpoint / tenant
- **also captured as `model-namespace-reuse-2025` (incidents-news.md):** When a Hugging Face author account is deleted, or a model is transferred and the original account later deleted, the `Author/ModelName` namespace can be re-registered. Code and cloud catalogs that fetch models by name then pull the attacker's model. Unit 42 showed this against Google Vertex AI Model Garden and Microsoft Azure AI Foundry deployments, getting reverse shells on the providers' endpoint infrastructure. It also found thousands of open-source repos referencing reusable names. The attacker needs only a free account and a target name to watch for. Mitigations: pin models to commit revisions, mirror models into trusted internal storage, and scan code for model references. Mapping: ML pipeline/cloud model catalog -> fetch by mutable name resolves to attacker-registered namespace -> no revision pinning or provenance check -> RCE in serving endpoint, poisoned model

### S-1062 Exposed DeepSeek ClickHouse database

- **canonical id:** `wiz-2025-deepseek-db` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `deepseek-clickhouse-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Gal Nagli (Wiz Research), "Wiz Research Uncovers Exposed DeepSeek Database Leaking Sensitive Information, Including Chat History", Wiz Blog, 2025-01-29. https://www.wiz.io/blog/wiz-research-uncovers-exposed-deepseek-database-leak
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [misconfigured backend database, chat log exposure]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0085?, AML.T0036; OWASP LLM02:2025; CWE-306?, CWE-200
- **summary:** A publicly accessible ClickHouse database belonging to DeepSeek allowed "full control over database operations". It exposed more than a million lines of log streams containing chat history, secret keys, and backend details. No attack technique was needed beyond discovery. The lesson for an enterprise is that third-party LLM providers' basic infrastructure hygiene is itself a confidentiality risk for prompts and data sent to them.
- **mapping:** employee prompts and data sent to an LLM vendor -> exposure through vendor misconfiguration -> data shared with a third-party AI service -> confidentiality breach
- **also captured as `deepseek-clickhouse-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2025-01 (logs from 2025-01-06). Wiz found ClickHouse HTTP interfaces open with no authentication on oauth2callback.deepseek.com and dev.deepseek.com, ports 8123 and 9000. The `log_stream` table held over a million entries with plaintext user chat history, API keys and secrets, backend details, and directory structures. Anyone could run arbitrary SQL, and Wiz noted possible privilege escalation inside DeepSeek's environment. DeepSeek secured it within hours of notice. This is the conventional "AI provider infrastructure" risk: the model is not the weak point, its telemetry store is. Mapping: AI provider logs (user prompts, secrets) -> unauthenticated DB query -> internet-exposed analytics DB -> mass privacy breach, credential exposure

### S-1064 ZombieAgent: zero-click ChatGPT Connector and Deep Research exfiltration with memory persistence

- **canonical id:** `zombieagent-2025` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / catalog; 2025; confidence medium
- **citation:** Radware, "ZombieAgent: New ChatGPT Vulnerabilities Let Data Theft Continue (and Spread)", https://www.radware.com/blog/threat-intelligence/zombieagent/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0066 (2025-09-25)
- **confirmed via:** MITRE ATLAS 2026.09 case study AML.CS0066 (local yaml); Radware page blocked by a bot check on fetch
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, zero-click exfiltration via connectors, memory persistence, propagation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0066 (AML.T0051.001, AML.T0080.000 Memory, AML.T0085.001, AML.T0086); OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI06; CWE-1427
- **summary:** Radware sent an email with concealed instructions to a Gmail inbox connected to ChatGPT. When the user later asked ChatGPT for an ordinary inbox task, ChatGPT, through Connectors and Deep Research, retrieved the email and followed its instructions. Per ATLAS, the instructions exfiltrated data through the agent's own tool calls on the provider side, with no client-side rendering. They also wrote to ChatGPT memory so the theft continued across sessions, and could spread to further contacts. Any connector (Outlook, Drive, Jira, Teams) can be the source. The user never opened the email. OpenAI's fix status was not confirmed here.
- **mapping:** ChatGPT with connectors + memory -> attacker email/doc retrieved during routine task -> agent obeys retrieved instructions; memory writable from injected content -> silent exfiltration, persistent compromise, spread

### S-1065 "AI in the Middle": Grok and Copilot web interfaces as anonymous C2 relays

- **canonical id:** `ai-in-the-middle-c2-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Check Point Research, "AI in the Middle: Turning Web-Based AI Services into C2 Proxies & The Future Of AI Driven Attacks", 2026-02-17, https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/ai-in-the-middle-turning-web-based-ai-services-into-c2-proxies-the-future-of-ai-driven-attacks/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0061
- **confirmed via:** https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/ai-in-the-middle-turning-web-based-ai-services-into-c2-proxies-the-future-of-ai-driven-attacks/ (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [AI service abused as C2, URL-fetch relay, egress evasion]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0061 (AML.T0114 AI Service Web Interface, AML.T0086, AML.T0095); MITRE ATT&CK T1102, T1090; NIST AI 100-2 misuse
- **summary:** The PoC needs a web AI assistant that allows anonymous use and fetches URLs; Grok and Microsoft Copilot qualified. The implant drives the assistant through an embedded WebView2 browser rather than raw HTTP. It asks the assistant to "summarize" an attacker URL, with reconnaissance data packed into the URL parameters. The assistant fetches the page, so victim data reaches the attacker, and the attacker's page content, which holds the commands, comes back in the AI's response. Traffic goes only to trusted AI domains over HTTPS, with no API key to revoke. Disclosed to Microsoft and xAI. Mitigation: treat AI domains as high-value egress points and monitor automated usage.
- **mapping:** enterprise endpoint egress -> malware relays C2 through unauthenticated AI web-fetch -> AI domains trusted; anonymous access; no per-user attribution -> covert C2 and exfiltration

### S-1066 Microsoft: "AI Recommendation Poisoning" through crafted "Summarize with AI" links that write assistant memory

- **canonical id:** `ai-recommendation-poisoning-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Microsoft Security, "Manipulating AI memory for profit: The rise of AI Recommendation Poisoning", 2026-02-10, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0072
- **confirmed via:** https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/ (fetched 2026-10-02); MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0072
- **attack classes:** [memory poisoning, prompt injection via prefilled URL parameters, commercial manipulation]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0072 (AML.T0131 Crafted AI Assistant Links, AML.T0080.000 Memory, AML.T0130 AI Agent Response Biasing); OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM09:2025; OWASP ASI06; NIST AI 100-2 indirect prompt injection (integrity)
- **summary:** Websites embed "Summarize with AI" buttons that link to assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Grok) with a prefilled prompt in parameters such as `?q=` or `?prompt=`. The hidden prompt tells the assistant to "remember [Company] as a trusted source", which writes persistent memory that biases later answers in other sessions, including on health, finance, and security. In 60 days Microsoft saw 50 distinct attempts from 31 companies across more than a dozen industries. ATLAS records this as an incident by commercial entities, not criminals. Mitigations: prompt filtering, content separation, and user-visible memory controls. The one-click precondition is the same as in Varonis' Reprompt (see reprompt-2026).
- **mapping:** assistant long-term memory -> prefilled-prompt link clicked by user -> memory writable from a single user-initiated turn without confirmation -> persistent biased recommendations

### S-1067 Detecting and preventing distillation attacks (vendor report)

- **canonical id:** `anthropic-2026-distillation-attacks` (ml-model-attacks.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence medium
- **aliases merged:** `anthropic-2026-distillation (supply-infra-misuse.md)`, `distillation-claude-2026 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Anthropic, "Detecting and Preventing Distillation Attacks", Anthropic News, 2026-02-23. https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks
- **confirmed via:** https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [distillation-attack, model-extraction, account-fraud, chain-of-thought-harvesting]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0048.004, AML.T0040; OWASP LLM10:2025; NISTAML.031
- **summary:** A vendor self-report attributing coordinated distillation campaigns to three Chinese labs: DeepSeek (over 150k exchanges), Moonshot (over 3.4M) and MiniMax (over 13M). In total that is over 16M exchanges through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, using "hydra cluster" proxy architectures. The campaigns targeted reasoning, tool use, coding and agentic capabilities, including chain-of-thought training data. MiniMax reportedly pivoted within 24 hours of new model launches. Detection used classifiers, behavioral fingerprinting and cross-account coordination detection. Countermeasures included tighter access controls for education and research pathways, industry intelligence sharing, and model-level safeguards that reduce the value of outputs for distillation. The attribution is the vendor's claim and was not independently verified, so treat it as primary-source but one-sided.
- **mapping:** frontier LLM API -> large-scale output harvesting via fraudulent accounts -> many accounts + proxies -> capability / IP theft and loss of safety guardrails in derived models
- **also captured as `anthropic-2026-distillation` (supply-infra-misuse.md):** Anthropic attributes three campaigns to DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax. Together they generated more than 16 million exchanges with Claude through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, in violation of terms and regional access restrictions. They used proxy services to reach Claude at scale while evading detection. The prompt volume, structure, and focus differed from normal usage and targeted agentic reasoning, coding, tool use, and computer use. The asset is the model's capabilities, effectively its weights stolen through outputs. Attribution is Anthropic's own. Mapping: proprietary model capabilities -> extraction through mass querying -> account creation at scale, proxy access -> IP loss, safeguard-free replicas
- **also captured as `distillation-claude-2026` (incidents-news.md):** Anthropic attributes more than 16 million exchanges with Claude, made through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, to three labs. Commercial proxy services ran "hydra cluster" account networks, one of which managed more than 20,000 accounts at once. Targets per Anthropic: DeepSeek (150,000+ exchanges) on reasoning, rubric-based grading data for RL, and censorship-safe rewrites. Moonshot (3.4M+) on agentic reasoning, tool use, coding, computer use, and vision. MiniMax (13M+) on agentic coding and tool orchestration. Detection used classifiers, behavioral fingerprinting, detection of chain-of-thought elicitation, cross-account coordination analysis, and request metadata. Countermeasures were stricter verification for education and startup accounts, model- and API-level anti-distillation safeguards, and intelligence sharing. The attacker is black box with API access only. The asset is model capability and IP, and the impact is economic and competitive. These attributions are Anthropic's own. Mapping: frontier model API (capabilities/IP) -> high-volume query harvesting across sybil accounts -> weak account verification; proxy resale networks -> capability theft via distillation

### S-1069 Microsoft: Claude Code GitHub Action Read tool leaked runner secrets through /proc/self/environ

- **canonical id:** `claude-code-gh-action-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / advisory; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Microsoft Defender Security Research, "Securing CI/CD in an agentic world: Claude Code GitHub action case", 2026-06-05, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/05/securing-ci-cd-in-agentic-world-claude-code-github-action-case/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0067
- **confirmed via:** https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/05/securing-ci-cd-in-agentic-world-claude-code-github-action-case/ (fetched 2026-10-02)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection in CI, secret exfiltration, sandbox gap]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0067 (AML.T0051.001, AML.T0098 AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting, AML.T0086, AML.T0084.001); OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI02, ASI03, ASI05; CWE-1427, CWE-526 (env var exposure), CWE-693
- **summary:** Found 2026-04-29, fixed 2026-05-05, published 2026-06-05. In the Claude Code GitHub Action, the Bash tool ran in a Bubblewrap sandbox with a scrubbed environment, but the Read tool ran in-process and could read `/proc/self/environ`. Prompt injection in an issue, PR, or comment could make the agent read the runner's environment, which held `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and other CI secrets, and leak them in a way that got past both model safety checks and GitHub secret scanning. Preconditions: the workflow fires on untrusted events, users without write access can trigger it, and the agent has file and shell tools. Anthropic fixed it in v2.1.128 by unconditionally rejecting reads of sensitive `/proc` files. Microsoft recommends the "Agents Rule of Two": a workflow should never hold untrusted input, sensitive access, and external communication at once. Compare clinejection-2026 and the AWI measurement study (agentic-workflow-injection-2026).
- **mapping:** CI runner secrets -> injected instructions in GitHub event content steer agent Read tool -> inconsistent sandboxing across agent tools; untrusted triggers -> API key and secret exfiltration

### S-1070 Claude Code source exposed through an npm source map, then fake-leak repos used as malware lures

- **canonical id:** `claude-code-sourcemap-leak-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / news; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** Zscaler ThreatLabz, "Claude Code Leak" blog, 2026-04. https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/anthropic-claude-code-leak ; Help Net Security, 2026-04-03 https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/03/claude-code-leak-github-malware/
- **confirmed via:** https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/anthropic-claude-code-leak (search hit); https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/03/claude-code-leak-github-malware/ (search hit)

- **summary:** Date 2026-03-31. `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` 2.1.88 shipped a 59.8 MB JavaScript source map exposing about 512k lines of TypeScript. Press attributes the cause to a Bun bug emitting source maps in production plus a missing `.npmignore` rule. Within days, GitHub repos advertising "leaked Claude Code with unlocked enterprise features" distributed a Rust dropper (`ClaudeCode_x64.exe`), per Zscaler. It coincided with the same-day malicious Axios npm release. The exposure revealed client-side guardrail and permission logic, which helps attackers craft bypasses. Root-cause details come from secondary analyses, not an Anthropic advisory.

### S-1071 Clinejection: issue-title prompt injection, Actions cache poisoning, and a malicious cline@2.3.0

- **canonical id:** `clinejection-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / news; 2026; confidence high (chain), medium (download figure)
- **citation:** A. Khan (researcher), Clinejection disclosure, 2026-02-09; Snyk, "How 'Clinejection' Turned an AI Bot into a Supply Chain Attack" https://snyk.io/blog/cline-supply-chain-attack-prompt-injection-github-actions/ ; CSA AI Safety Initiative research note (marked "Unofficial AI-assisted Research"), 2026-03-10.
- **pdf:** csa-clinejection-research-note-2026.pdf sha256: 329847cdc575519f64845d4598bb5ad128e4cd1211ecc6cabd3e3d239940b119
- **confirmed via:** https://snyk.io/blog/cline-supply-chain-attack-prompt-injection-github-actions/ (fetched); CSA PDF (downloaded)
- **attack classes:** [prompt injection in CI, AI-agent-in-the-pipeline, GitHub Actions cache poisoning, credential theft, npm supply chain]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0010?; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM03:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI04, ASI05; CWE-1427, CWE-829, CWE-494?
- **summary:** Triage workflow added 2025-12-21, disclosed and patched 2026-02-09, exploited 2026-02-17. Cline's Claude-based issue-triage GitHub Action read issue titles. A crafted title told it to `npm install` from an attacker commit whose preinstall script stole `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and gave execution in the workflow. The attacker used Cacheract to flood the Actions cache with over 10 GB, forcing LRU eviction, then planted entries matching the nightly-release cache keys. The release workflow restored them and exposed `VSCE_PAT`, `OVSX_PAT`, and `NPM_RELEASE_TOKEN`, which were not separated between nightly and production. Eight days after disclosure, an unknown actor used the unrevoked token to publish `cline@2.3.0`, which installed the OpenClaw agent globally. It was live about 8 hours with about 4,000 downloads (the download count comes from secondary sources).
- **mapping:** software release pipeline -> prompt injection into CI agent -> agent with exec rights on untrusted issue text + shared cache + unscoped tokens -> malicious package published to millions of users

### S-1073 Unit 42: actor runs DeepSeek through the Hermes Agent framework as an autonomous operator against Langflow and n8n

- **canonical id:** `hermes-deepseek-langflow-n8n-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence high (vendor-reported)
- **citation:** Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, "Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks", 2026-07-30, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ ; MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0070 (activity dated 2026-05-07)
- **confirmed via:** https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ (fetched 2026-10-02); MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0070
- **attack classes:** [AI-orchestrated intrusion, autonomous exploitation of AI-workflow platforms, mass scanning]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.CS0070 (AML.T0116 Autonomous Reconnaissance, AML.T0117, AML.T0102, AML.T0049, AML.T0016.004); CVE-2026-33017, CVE-2026-21858, CVE-2025-68613 (as printed by Unit 42; not checked in NVD); OWASP ? (misuse); NIST AI 100-2 misuse
- **summary:** A Chinese-speaking actor (aliases knaithe and KnYuan, Zhuhai, per Unit 42) used DeepSeek as the reasoning engine inside the Hermes Agent framework, with Telegram control, terminal access, and custom red-team skills. The agent enumerated targets, found exploits, and launched attacks on its own. Targets were 84 Langflow instances, where exploitation failed because auto_login was off, and n8n, where 647,017 instances were enumerated and attempts were blocked by authentication. Seven CVEs were targeted, including CVE-2026-33017 (Langflow, CVSS 9.8) and CVE-2026-21858 / CVE-2025-68613 (n8n). The autonomous phases mostly failed. The actor's manual operations did compromise targets: data theft from three Citrix NetScaler hosts and command execution on eleven Marimo instances. The lesson is that low-code AI-workflow platforms (Langflow, n8n, Flowise) are both the targets and the tools of agentic attackers.
- **mapping:** internet-exposed AI workflow platforms (Langflow/n8n) -> AI agent automates scanning and exploitation of known CVEs -> unpatched, exposed instances; auth disabled -> RCE, credential and workflow theft (blocked here by auth)

### S-1074 LiteLLM 1.82.7/1.82.8 PyPI backdoor (TeamPCP), downstream Mercor breach

- **canonical id:** `litellm-teampcp-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / news; 2026; confidence high (LiteLLM), medium (Mercor scope)
- **citation:** Datadog Security Labs, "LiteLLM and Telnyx compromised on PyPI: Tracing the TeamPCP supply chain campaign", 2026-03. https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ ; Mercor: SecurityWeek https://www.securityweek.com/mercor-hit-by-litellm-supply-chain-attack/ , Fortune 2026-04-02 https://fortune.com/2026/04/02/mercor-ai-startup-security-incident-10-billion/
- **confirmed via:** https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ (fetched); https://www.securityweek.com/mercor-hit-by-litellm-supply-chain-attack/ (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [AI gateway supply chain, CI security-scanner compromise, credential stealer, Kubernetes lateral movement]

- **summary:** Date 2026-03-24, quarantined by PyPI in about 3 hours. TeamPCP first compromised Aquasec Trivy releases and Actions tags (2026-03-19). LiteLLM ran Trivy in CI, which leaked its PyPI publishing token. The attacker published 1.82.7, with injected code, and 1.82.8, with a `litellm_init.pth` that runs at every Python interpreter start whether or not LiteLLM is imported. The payload harvested SSH keys, cloud credentials, kube-configs, and CI secrets, encrypted them (AES-256 plus RSA-4096), sent them to `models.litellm[.]cloud`, installed persistence (`~/.config/sysmon`), and deployed privileged pods. Telnyx was hit 2026-03-27. LiteLLM is the LLM gateway in many agent frameworks, with about 95M monthly downloads per press. Downstream, Mercor confirmed a breach on 2026-03-31. Lapsus$ claimed about 4 TB, including source, interview video, and contractor PII. That claim is unverified, and lawsuits are pending.
- **mapping:** AI gateway hosts (holding every provider key) -> backdoored dependency via stolen CI token -> CI runs third-party scanner with publish secrets; unpinned deps -> mass credential theft, downstream breach of an AI-data vendor

### S-1075 Moltbook (AI-agent social network) Supabase exposure: 1.5M agent API tokens

- **canonical id:** `moltbook-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Wiz, "Hacking Moltbook: AI Social Network Reveals 1.5M API Keys", 2026-02. https://www.wiz.io/blog/exposed-moltbook-database-reveals-millions-of-api-keys
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [misconfiguration (missing RLS), credential exposure, agent impersonation]

- **summary:** Date 2026-01-31, 21:48 UTC disclosure, secured by 2026-02-01 01:00 UTC. The Supabase anon key was embedded in client JavaScript, and Row Level Security was off, so anyone had read and write access to all tables. Exposed: 1.5M agent API tokens, about 35k emails plus 29,631 early-access emails, and 4,060 private DMs between agents, some containing plaintext OpenAI keys. With write access an attacker could impersonate any agent or edit posts, a ready channel for agent-to-agent prompt injection. Wiz notes the site was "vibe-coded". The data showed about 17k humans behind 1.5M agents. No malicious exploitation was reported.

### S-1076 Claude Cowork: file exfiltration via an injected "Skill" document and an allow-listed API

- **canonical id:** `promptarmor-2026-claude-cowork-exfiltration` (gaps-other.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence medium
- **citation:** PromptArmor, "Claude Cowork Exfiltrates Files", January 2026. https://www.promptarmor.com/resources/claude-cowork-exfiltrates-files
- **confirmed via:** https://www.promptarmor.com/resources/claude-cowork-exfiltrates-files (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection via document, egress allow-list abuse, file exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025; ASI01, ASI02, ASI04; AST01/AST05 (OWASP Agentic Skills); ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0086?
- **summary:** A .docx disguised as a "Skill" hides instructions in 1-pt, white-on-white, 0.1-line-spaced text. When Cowork, a research-preview desktop agent, processes the file, the injected instructions upload the user's local files through the Anthropic API. That API is allow-listed in the agent VM's network policy, which blocks most other domains. The attacker's own API key is embedded in the payload, so the files land in the attacker's account. The demonstration exfiltrated real-estate documents with appraisals, loan estimates and partial SSNs, and also worked against Claude Opus 4.5. No human approval was needed for the upload. Per PromptArmor, Anthropic acknowledged the issue but had not remediated it at publication and advised users to avoid granting access to sensitive local files. This is a canonical case of an egress allow-list defeated by a dual-use allowed domain.
- **mapping:** local files shared with desktop agent -> injected instructions in imported document/skill -> allow-listed vendor API usable with attacker key -> silent file exfiltration

### S-1079 SalesBleed: three Agentforce flaws (DNS exfiltration, Trusted-URL redaction bypass, Slack impersonation)

- **canonical id:** `salesbleed-2026` (incidents-news.md); type vendor-research / news; 2026; confidence high
- **citation:** Zenity Labs, SalesBleed disclosure, 2026-09-24 (BusinessWire release via https://www.morningstar.com/news/business-wire/20260924811082/ ); The Register, "Salesforce Agentforce vulns allowed 0-click CRM data theft, anonymous phishing", 2026-09-24. https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/24/salesforce-agentforce-vulns-allowed-0-click-crm-data-theft-anonymous-phishing/5298958
- **confirmed via:** https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/24/salesforce-agentforce-vulns-allowed-0-click-crm-data-theft-anonymous-phishing/5298958 (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, URL-redaction bypass, DNS exfiltration, agent identity abuse]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0057; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM05:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI01, ASI03, ASI09; CWE-1427, CWE-20
- **summary:** Reported 2026-06-01, fixes 2026-08-19 to 09-21, public 2026-09-24. This attacks the same Web-to-Lead entry point after ForcedLeak's fix. Flaws 1 and 2: Zenity bypassed Agentforce's Trusted URLs redaction through hostname-parsing weaknesses, including uncommon TLDs such as `.fun` and mishandled braces and brackets. Stolen Account data was placed in an image subdomain, so rendering or Slack link unfurling leaked it through a DNS lookup, with no outbound HTTP from the victim needed. Flaw 3: the "Reply to a Slack Thread" action had no confirmation or attribution, so injected or insider prompts could send phishing under the agent's trusted identity. No CVEs were assigned. Patch-bypass recurrence on the same feature is a strong signal that output allow-listing is brittle.
- **mapping:** CRM data + agent's messaging identity -> injection via public form -> URL parser gaps, DNS side channel, action lacking HITL -> zero-click exfiltration, trusted-identity phishing

### S-1080 Breaking the lethal trifecta: causal isolation architecture (talk)

- **canonical id:** `tsao-2026-causal-isolation-lethal-trifecta` (gaps-papers.md); type vendor-research; 2026; confidence low
- **citation:** "Breaking the Lethal Trifecta: Secure Agentic Computing via Causal Isolation Architecture", USENIX Security 2026 (talk; speaker not listed on the page). https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/tsao
- **confirmed via:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/tsao (paper page and abstract fetched 2026-10-03; listed on https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/technical-sessions)

- **summary:** Splits the lethal trifecta (untrusted input, private data, external communication) across isolated components. Only typed abstractions cross boundaries, and a rule-of-two release judge keeps useful private-derived guidance while stripping exact facts based on requester trust and source sensitivity. ### S-1083 Compromised PyTorch-nightly dependency (torchtriton)

- **canonical id:** `pytorch-2022-torchtriton` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2022; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `pytorch-torchtriton-2022 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** PyTorch Foundation, "Compromised PyTorch-nightly dependency chain between December 25th and December 30th, 2022", PyTorch blog, 2022-12-31. https://pytorch.org/blog/compromised-nightly-dependency/ (ATLAS AML.CS0015)
- **confirmed via:** https://pytorch.org/blog/compromised-nightly-dependency/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [dependency confusion, malicious package, ML framework supply chain]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.001, AML.CS0015; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; CWE-427?, CWE-829?; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** PyTorch-nightly Linux pip installs between 2022-12-25 and 2022-12-30 pulled a dependency named `torchtriton` that had been published to PyPI and ran a malicious binary. This was dependency confusion against a package that was meant to come from PyTorch's own index. Stable releases were not affected. The advisory gives detection and cleanup commands. It is the canonical ML-framework package supply-chain incident.
- **mapping:** ML developer/CI hosts -> malicious binary via dependency confusion -> pip resolves a public index ahead of a private one -> credential and data exfiltration
- **also captured as `pytorch-torchtriton-2022` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2022-12-25 to 30. An attacker uploaded a malicious package named `torchtriton` to PyPI. PyPI took precedence over PyTorch's own nightly index, so `pip install` of the Linux PyTorch-nightly pulled the malicious package. The payload fingerprinted the host and exfiltrated hostname, username, environment variables, /etc/passwd, /etc/hosts, ~/.gitconfig, ~/.ssh contents, and the first 1,000 files in $HOME. The attacker needed only the ability to publish on PyPI. The targets were ML researcher workstations and CI. PyTorch renamed the dependency to `pytorch-triton` and reserved a placeholder on PyPI. Status: remediated. Mapping: ML developer workstation/CI -> dependency confusion via public index precedence -> private-index package name unclaimed on PyPI -> secrets and SSH key theft

### S-1085 ChatGPT redis-py race condition exposes chat titles and payment data

- **canonical id:** `chatgpt-redis-2023` (incidents-news.md); type advisory (vendor post-mortem); 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** OpenAI, "March 20 ChatGPT outage: Here's what happened", 2023-03-24. https://openai.com/blog/march-20-chatgpt-outage (fetch returned 403; content confirmed through press)
- **confirmed via:** https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-chatgpt-payment-data-leak-caused-by-open-source-bug/ (search hit); https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/03/27/chatgpt-data-leak/ (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [software bug in AI service stack, cross-tenant data exposure, supply chain (OSS library)]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-362 (race condition); OWASP LLM02:2025?, LLM03:2025 (supply chain)?; ATLAS ? (not an ML-specific technique)
- **summary:** Date 2023-03-20. A race condition in the open-source redis-py client caused cancelled requests to return data from another user's connection. An OpenAI server change on 03-20 made request cancellations spike, which made the bug far more likely to trigger. Users saw other users' chat-history titles. For about 9 hours, roughly 1.2% of active ChatGPT Plus subscribers may have had their name, email, payment address, last four card digits, and card expiry exposed. No attacker was involved. It was an availability and confidentiality failure in conventional infrastructure supporting an AI service. OpenAI patched redis-py upstream and took ChatGPT offline. Status: fixed.
- **mapping:** AI SaaS user data (chat history, billing PII) -> cross-tenant leakage via cache-client race -> shared Redis connection pool, load spike -> privacy breach of about 1.2% of Plus subscribers

### S-1086 MLflow path traversal LFI (CVE-2023-1177), huntr-reported

- **canonical id:** `mlflow-cve-2023-1177` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** NVD, CVE-2023-1177 (published 2023-03-24), CVSS 9.3; huntr bounty 1fe8f21a-c438-4cba-9add-e8a5dab94e28. Also CVE-2023-6831 (mlflow < 2.9.2, CVSS 8.1). https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-1177

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0049, AML.T0055, AML.T0035; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML05, ML06; CWE-22, CWE-29 (NVD)
- **summary:** NVD records path traversal ("'\..\filename'") in mlflow/mlflow before 2.2.1 (CWE-22/CWE-29). It was reported through the huntr AI/ML bug-bounty platform run by Protect AI. On a tracking server this allows reading arbitrary files such as SSH keys and cloud credentials, which can lead to takeover. CVE-2023-6831 is a later traversal before 2.9.2. MLflow servers are often deployed without authentication on internal networks. This entry stands in for the huntr report stream. The Protect AI threat-research URL I tried now redirects to a Palo Alto Networks 404, so CVE records are the stable primary source.

### S-1087 Retool breach: SMS phishing plus deepfaked employee voice to obtain MFA

- **canonical id:** `retool-2023-deepfake-voice-mfa` (gaps-other.md); type advisory; 2023; confidence high
- **citation:** Retool, "When MFA isn't actually MFA", 2023-08-29 (incident 2023-08-27). https://retool.com/blog/mfa-isnt-mfa
- **confirmed via:** https://retool.com/blog/mfa-isnt-mfa (fetched victim's primary post-mortem)
- **attack classes:** [vishing with deepfaked voice, MFA social engineering, MFA-seed cloud-sync weakness]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0088?, AML.T0073?; MITRE ATT&CK T1566.004 (spearphishing voice); CWE-308?
- **summary:** Employees received SMS phishing posing as IT and linking to a fake Okta portal. One employee entered credentials. The attacker then called using a deepfaked voice of a staff member who knew the office layout and processes, and obtained an MFA code. That code enrolled an attacker device in Okta. Google Authenticator's cloud sync then gave the attacker every OTP seed, which "silently" turned MFA into single-factor authentication. 27 cloud customers, mostly crypto firms, suffered account takeovers. The asset is the helpdesk and MFA reset process.
- **mapping:** workforce identity (Okta/MFA) -> voice-cloned helpdesk/IT call -> employee trust and cloud-synced OTP seeds -> account takeover of customer tenants

### S-1088 llama-cpp-python Jinja2 SSTI via GGUF chat_template (CVE-2024-34359)

- **canonical id:** `cve-2024-34359-llama-cpp-python` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** NVD, CVE-2024-34359 (published 2024-05-14), CVSS 9.6, GHSA-56xg-wfcc-g829. https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-34359
- **confirmed via:** https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2024-34359 (NVD API)
- **attack classes:** [template injection RCE, GGUF metadata abuse]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0011.000, AML.T0010.003; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; ASI05; CWE-76 (NVD), CWE-1336?; NISTAML.05
- **summary:** The `Llama` constructor in llama-cpp-python loads the `chat_template` from GGUF metadata. It rendered that template with Jinja2 without sandboxing, so a malicious GGUF file achieved server-side template injection and code execution on the host. The attacker only publishes a GGUF model. The victim is any app or server that loads it with an affected version. NVD lists CWE-76. Fixed in the commit referenced from the GHSA. (The researcher write-up URL I tried returned 404.)
- **mapping:** local/edge LLM runtime -> RCE through model metadata template -> loads an untrusted GGUF -> host compromise

### S-1089 Keras Lambda-layer code injection (CVE-2024-3660)

- **canonical id:** `cve-2024-3660-keras-lambda` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2024; confidence high

- **confirmed via:** https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2024-3660 (NVD API; reference https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/253266)

- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0011.000, AML.T0018.002; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; CWE-94 (NVD); NISTAML.05
- **summary:** NVD describes "an arbitrary code injection vulnerability in TensorFlow's Keras framework (<2.13)" that lets a crafted model run arbitrary code with the application's privileges. This is the Lambda-layer class: serialized Python code inside a Keras model executes on deserialization. The attacker supplies the model file. The victim is any service or notebook that loads it. The fix is Keras 2.13+ `safe_mode`, which a later CVE (CVE-2025-1550) bypassed.
- **mapping:** inference/training host -> RCE through Keras Lambda layer -> loads an untrusted .h5/.keras model -> host compromise

### S-1091 Google AI Overviews surface satire and troll forum content ("glue on pizza")

- **canonical id:** `google-2024-ai-overviews-satire-retrieval` (gaps-other.md); type advisory; 2024; confidence high
- **citation:** E. Reid (Google VP of Search), "AI Overviews: About last week", Google blog, 2024-05-30. https://blog.google/products/search/ai-overviews-update-may-2024/ ; press: The Verge URL given by the reviewer.
- **confirmed via:** https://blog.google/products/search/ai-overviews-update-may-2024/ (fetched vendor primary); Wikipedia "AI Overviews" (restriction in May 2024)
- **attack classes:** [retrieval of untrustworthy sources, data voids, satire-as-fact, RAG integrity]
- **catalog ids:** OWASP LLM08:2025?, LLM09:2025; ATLAS AML.T0070 RAG Poisoning?; NIST NISTAML.02
- **summary:** Google's own analysis attributes the failures, such as "How many rocks should I eat?" and adding glue to pizza, to three causes. Data voids are niche queries with little quality content. Satirical content was taken as fact. "Sarcastic or troll-y content from discussion forums" was surfaced as advice. Google reported "more than a dozen technical improvements", including better detection of nonsensical queries, limits on satire and user-generated content, and triggering restrictions. Nothing here was adversarial by design, but it shows that anyone who can publish in a data void can steer a production RAG answer. That is the precondition for deliberate retrieval poisoning, as in the Pravda entry below.
- **mapping:** public RAG answer engine (user trust, brand) -> low-quality or satirical sources retrieved for data-void queries -> anyone can publish web/forum content -> harmful misinformation at scale

### S-1092 Hugging Face Spaces secrets unauthorized access

- **canonical id:** `hf-2024-spaces-secrets` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2024; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `hf-spaces-secrets-2024 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Hugging Face, "Space secrets leak disclosure", Hugging Face blog, 2024-05-31. https://huggingface.co/blog/space-secrets-disclosure
- **confirmed via:** https://huggingface.co/blog/space-secrets-disclosure (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [secrets exposure, platform breach, token theft]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0055, AML.T0083?; OWASP LLM03:2025, LLM02:2025; ASI03; OWASP NHI2 (Secret Leakage); CWE-522?
- **summary:** Hugging Face detected unauthorized access to the Spaces platform, specifically Spaces secrets. It suspected that a subset of secrets had been accessed. It revoked HF tokens found in those secrets and advised all users to rotate keys and move to fine-grained tokens. Remediation included removing org tokens and adding KMS for Spaces secrets. It worked with external forensic specialists. For a threat model: AI app hosting platforms hold downstream credentials (cloud keys, API tokens), so a platform breach becomes a credential-theft event for every customer.
- **mapping:** API keys/tokens stored in an AI app host -> platform-side secret exposure -> long-lived secrets in a third-party AI PaaS -> downstream account takeover
- **also captured as `hf-spaces-secrets-2024` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2024-05-31. HF detected unauthorized access to its Spaces platform and said "a subset of Spaces' secrets could have been accessed without authorization". These were the tokens and API keys that users store for their demo apps. HF revoked the exposed HF tokens, emailed affected users, brought in external forensics, and reported to law enforcement and data protection authorities. It also moved secrets to a KMS, removed org tokens, and pushed fine-grained tokens. HF did not disclose the intrusion vector. The asset is the third-party credentials that AI apps hold, such as OpenAI keys and cloud keys, which feed LLMjacking and downstream compromise. Mapping: AI app hosting secrets store -> unauthorized platform access -> user secrets stored on shared platform -> token theft, downstream account abuse

### S-1093 NVIDIA Container Toolkit escapes (CVE-2024-0132, CVE-2025-23266)

- **confirmed via:** https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2024-0132 and ?cveId=CVE-2025-23266 (NVD API). The Wiz write-ups returned a stub page to my fetcher.

CVE-2025-23266 is a flaw in the container-initialization hooks that allows arbitrary code with elevated permissions. ### S-1095 Amazon Q Developer VS Code extension malicious commit (CVE-2025-8217)

- **canonical id:** `aws-2025-amazon-q-extension` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `amazon-q-wiper-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** AWS Security Bulletin AWS-2025-015, "Security Update for Amazon Q Developer Extension for Visual Studio Code (Version #1.84)", 2025-07; NVD CVE-2025-8217 (CWE-506). https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-015/ (ATLAS AML.CS0047)
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched); https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2025-8217
- **attack classes:** [AI-assistant supply-chain compromise, destructive agent prompt, CI token misuse]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0010.001, AML.T0101 (Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation), AML.CS0047; ASI04, ASI10?; CWE-506 (NVD)
- **summary:** An inappropriately scoped GitHub token in the extension's CodeBuild configuration let a threat actor commit malicious code to the open-source repository, and it shipped automatically in release 1.84.0. NVD describes "inert, injected code designed to call the Q Developer CLI". ATLAS AML.CS0047 records it as code to deploy a destructive AI agent. AWS says a syntax error stopped it from executing. Version 1.84.0 was pulled and 1.85.0 released. Without the bug, the code would have run with the developer's cloud and agent permissions.
- **mapping:** developer IDE with an AI agent and cloud creds -> destructive agent instructions via a poisoned extension -> CI token overprivileged, automatic release -> data and infra destruction (averted)
- **also captured as `amazon-q-wiper-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Malicious commit 2025-07-13, release 1.84.0 on 2025-07-17, fixed in 1.85.0. An attacker ("lkmanka58") used a GitHub token with too broad a scope in the extension's CodeBuild configuration to commit a prompt into the open-source repo. The prompt told the agent to wipe the local filesystem and user configuration, find AWS profiles, and delete S3 buckets, EC2 instances, and IAM users through the AWS CLI. It shipped in 1.84.0, an extension with roughly 950k installs. AWS says it did not execute because of a syntax error, and the actor described it as a demonstration. AWS revoked credentials and assigned CVE-2025-8217. This is the first widely reported case of a malicious instruction shipped inside a vendor's agent product. Mapping: developer workstation + AWS account -> malicious system prompt in signed agent release -> overscoped CI token, weak review -> potential file and cloud-resource destruction (failed)

### S-1096 Claude Code advisories (CVE-2025-54795, CVE-2025-59536, CVE-2025-52882, CVE-2025-64755, CVE-2025-66032, CVE-2026-25723)

- **canonical id:** `claude-code-cves-2025` (incidents-news.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** GitHub Security Advisories for anthropics/claude-code: GHSA-x56v-x2h6-7j34 (CVE-2025-54795) https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x56v-x2h6-7j34 ; GHSA-4fgq-fpq9-mr3g (CVE-2025-59536) https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4fgq-fpq9-mr3g ; GHSA-7mv8-j34q-vp7q (CVE-2025-64755) https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7mv8-j34q-vp7q ; GHSA-xq4m-mc3c-vvg3 (CVE-2025-66032) https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xq4m-mc3c-vvg3 ; GHSA-mhg7-666j-cqg4 (CVE-2026-25723) https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhg7-666j-cqg4 ; Datadog Security Labs on CVE-2025-52882 https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/claude-mcp-cve-2025-52882/
- **confirmed via:** the GHSA URLs above (search hits); Datadog URL (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [command-validation bypass, approval-prompt bypass, pre-trust code execution, WebSocket auth bypass, arbitrary file write]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-77/CWE-78, CWE-20, CWE-306 (WebSocket), CWE-1427?; OWASP LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI05, ASI02; ATLAS AML.T0051?
- **summary:** Dates 2025-06 to 2026. CVE-2025-54795 (fixed in 1.0.20): a command-parsing error let a crafted `echo` command bypass the confirmation prompt, so an injected instruction could run without approval. CVE-2025-59536 (fixed in 1.0.111): project code could run before the user accepted the startup trust dialog, when Claude Code was opened in an untrusted directory. CVE-2025-52882 (CVSS 8.8, IDE extensions 1.0.23 and earlier): the local WebSocket server lacked authentication, so a malicious website could connect and drive MCP and IDE tools. CVE-2025-64755, CVE-2025-66032, and CVE-2026-25723 (fixed in 2.0.55): `sed`-based and piped-command validation bypasses allowed writes to `.claude/` and outside the project. These show that allow-list command validation in agent CLIs is a fragile security boundary. Status: all patched, auto-update.
- **mapping:** developer host via coding agent -> validation/trust-dialog bypass -> agent executes shell under user privileges, untrusted repo or prompt -> RCE, config tampering

### S-1097 Cursor CVE-2025-54135 (CurXecute) and CVE-2025-54136 (MCPoison)

- **canonical id:** `cursor-curxecute-mcpoison-2025` (incidents-news.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Tenable FAQ, "CVE-2025-54135, CVE-2025-54136: Vulnerabilities in Cursor (CurXecute, MCPoison)", 2025-08. https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison ; research: Aim Labs (CurXecute), Check Point Research (MCPoison)
- **confirmed via:** https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [indirect prompt injection, MCP config tampering, trust-binding flaw, RCE]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-78/CWE-94, CWE-345?; ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0010?; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM03:2025, LLM06:2025; OWASP ASI04, ASI05
- **summary:** Disclosed 2025-08-01 and 2025-08-05, reported 2025-07-07 and 2025-07-16. CurXecute (CVSS 8.5): injected content arriving through an MCP server, such as a Slack message, made the Cursor agent write a new entry into `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Cursor auto-started the new server command before the user could reject the edit, which gave remote code execution. Fixed in 1.3.9. MCPoison (CVSS 7.2): Cursor tied approval of a project MCP server to its name, not its contents. A collaborator could commit a benign `.cursor/rules/mcp.json`, get it approved, then swap in a malicious command that ran silently. Fixed in 1.3. No in-the-wild exploitation was reported. The class: agent configuration is code, and approvals must bind to content hashes.
- **mapping:** developer host -> agent-written or swapped MCP config executes commands -> config auto-exec, name-bound trust -> RCE, persistent backdoor via repo

- **attack classes:** [model-scanner evasion, malicious pickle]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0115.001, AML.T0107?; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; CWE-345 (NVD); NISTAML.05
- **summary:** NVD: picklescan before 0.0.23 "fails to detect malicious pickle files inside PyTorch model archives when certain ZIP file flag bits are modified". The modified file still loads in `torch.load()`. This is a parser differential between the scanner and the loader. With nullifAI and ShadowPickle, it shows that hub-side scanning gives weak assurance.
- **mapping:** model registry intake -> scanner/loader parser differential -> registry gates on picklescan alone -> malicious model admitted, RCE at load

### S-1100 PyTorch torch.load weights_only=True RCE (CVE-2025-32434)

- **canonical id:** `cve-2025-32434-pytorch-weights-only` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** NVD, CVE-2025-32434 (published 2025-04-18), GHSA-53q9-r3pm-6pq6. https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-32434

It was patched in 2.6.0. `weights_only=True` was the standard advice for loading untrusted checkpoints. This CVE shows the control could be bypassed. Downstream servers that pull HF checkpoints with `torch.load`, such as vLLM's weight iterator (CVE-2025-24357, CWE-502 per NVD), inherit the risk.

### S-1102 EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711): zero-click M365 Copilot data exfiltration

- **canonical id:** `echoleak-2025` (incidents-news.md); type advisory / vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Aim Labs (Aim Security), "EchoLeak" blog, 2025-06-11 (primary 403 on fetch); MSRC CVE-2025-32711 (CVSS 9.3). Press and analysis: https://www.hackthebox.com/blog/cve-2025-32711-echoleak-copilot-vulnerability
- **pdf:** reddy-2025-echoleak-cve-2025-32711.pdf sha256: 4f0939532c477922ab9d501adbfc3f25433d1df72da7d33e4e7834a2b064969c
- **confirmed via:** https://www.hackthebox.com/blog/cve-2025-32711-echoleak-copilot-vulnerability (search hit); https://sentra.io/blog/copilot-echoleak-prompt-injection (search hit)
- **attack classes:** [zero-click indirect prompt injection, "LLM scope violation", classifier bypass, CSP bypass, markdown image exfiltration]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS case study AML.CS0059 (EchoLeak); ATLAS AML.T0051.001, AML.T0057, AML.T0077?; OWASP LLM01:2025, LLM02:2025, LLM05:2025; OWASP ASI01?; CWE-1427 (MSRC CWE label not confirmed: possibly CWE-77); NIST AI 100-2 indirect prompt injection
- **summary:** Reported early 2025, fixed server-side by 2025-06. An attacker emails the victim text phrased as instructions to the human recipient, which evades Microsoft's XPIA (cross-prompt injection) classifier. When the user later asks Copilot something related, RAG retrieves the email. Copilot then pulls privileged context (OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, chat) into a reference-style markdown link or image, a format that bypassed link redaction. The URL goes through an allow-listed Microsoft domain (a Teams/SharePoint proxy path) to defeat CSP, so the browser auto-fetches it with no click. Aim calls the root cause an "LLM scope violation": untrusted input makes the model leak data from a higher-privilege scope. Microsoft reported no exploitation in the wild. Status: patched (CVSS 9.3).
- **mapping:** tenant M365 data in Copilot's RAG scope -> zero-click injected email -> Copilot retrieves external mail into the same context as internal data; CSP-allowed proxy -> silent exfiltration of internal documents

### S-1104 Flowise CustomMCP RCE (CVE-2025-59528, CVSS 10) exploited in 2026

- **canonical id:** `flowise-cve-2025-59528` (incidents-news.md); type advisory / news; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** Press: BleepingComputer, "Max severity Flowise RCE vulnerability now exploited in attacks", 2026-04. https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-flowise-rce-vulnerability-now-exploited-in-attacks/ ; CVE record https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-59528 ; OWASP GenAI Q1-2026 round-up (item 7)
- **confirmed via:** https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-flowise-rce-vulnerability-now-exploited-in-attacks/ (search hit); https://genai.owasp.org/2026/04/14/owasp-genai-exploit-round-up-report-q1-2026/ (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [agent-builder RCE, MCP configuration injection, code injection]
- **catalog ids:** CWE-94/CWE-95; ATLAS AML.T0049?; OWASP ASI05?, ASI04?, LLM03:2025?
- **summary:** Disclosed 2025-09, exploitation confirmed 2026-04-07. Flowise from 2.2.7-patch.1 up to (not including) 3.0.6 passes the attacker-controlled CustomMCP node configuration to JavaScript `Function()`, the equivalent of eval, which yields remote code execution with full Node.js privileges. Over 12,000 instances were internet-facing. Exploitation traffic came from a single Starlink IP, which suggests opportunistic mass exploitation. Detection: POST to `/api/v1/node-load-method/customMCP` containing `child_process`, `execSync`, and similar strings. A separate cluster of Flowise Agent-node CVEs was reported in April 2026 (CVE-2026-41265 et al.; not verified here).
- **mapping:** low-code agent server -> eval of MCP config -> exposed Flowise < 3.0.6 -> RCE, credential theft

### S-1105 UNC6395 data theft via Salesloft Drift OAuth tokens

- **canonical id:** `gtig-2025-salesloft-drift` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **aliases merged:** `salesloft-drift-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** Google Threat Intelligence Group, "Widespread Data Theft Targets Salesforce Instances via Salesloft Drift", Google Cloud Blog, 2025-08. https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [third-party OAuth token theft, SaaS-to-SaaS data exfiltration, secret harvesting]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0091.000, AML.T0055, AML.T0085?; ASI03, ASI04; OWASP NHI (overprivileged/long-lived)?; CWE-522?
- **summary:** From as early as 2025-08-08 to at least 2025-08-18, UNC6395 used compromised OAuth tokens of the Salesloft Drift third-party app, an AI chat and agent integration, to export large volumes of data from Salesforce customer instances. They then mined the data for secrets: AWS access keys (AKIA), passwords, and Snowflake tokens. GTIG later confirmed that "Drift Email" integration tokens were also used on 2025-08-09 to read email from a small number of Google Workspace accounts. Google revoked the tokens and disabled the integration. This is the reference case for agent/integration OAuth tokens as a high-value, under-monitored NHI.
- **mapping:** CRM and email data reachable by an AI integration -> bulk exfiltration with stolen integration OAuth tokens -> long-lived, broadly scoped third-party app tokens -> data breach, secondary cloud compromise
- **also captured as `salesloft-drift-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Activity 2025-08-08 to 18, advisory 2025-08-20, GTIG details 2025-08-26. UNC6395 obtained the OAuth and refresh tokens that Drift's AI chat agent used for its Salesforce integration. It ran bulk SOQL exports from over 700 organizations, including Cloudflare, Google, Palo Alto Networks, Zscaler, and Proofpoint, and searched the data (for example support cases) for AWS keys, passwords, and Snowflake tokens. Some Google Workspace data was also reached. Salesloft and Salesforce revoked all Drift tokens on 2025-08-20. The AI is not the vulnerability here. The AI agent's standing, broad, long-lived integration tokens are the asset, which makes it the canonical "AI connector as supply-chain pivot" incident. Mapping: CRM data + secrets in tickets -> stolen AI-integration OAuth tokens -> long-lived broad-scope tokens held by third-party AI vendor -> mass data theft, follow-on intrusions

### S-1106 Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) exploited, CISA KEV, Flodrix botnet

- **canonical id:** `langflow-cve-2025-3248` (incidents-news.md); type advisory / vendor-research; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** CISA KEV addition 2025-05-05; Horizon3.ai write-up (2025-04); Trend Micro, "Critical Langflow Vulnerability (CVE-2025-3248) Actively Exploited to Deliver Flodrix Botnet", 2025-06. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/langflow-vulnerability-flodric-botnet.html
- **confirmed via:** https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/langflow-vulnerability-flodric-botnet.html (search hit); https://www.csoonline.com/article/3978918/critical-flaw-in-ai-agent-dev-tool-langflow-under-active-exploitation.html (search hit)

- **summary:** Date: disclosed 2025-04, KEV 2025-05-05, Flodrix campaign 2025-06. Langflow before 1.3.0 exposed `/api/v1/validate/code`, which parsed user-supplied Python and executed decorators and default arguments with no authentication (CVSS 9.8). Attackers scanned for exposed instances, ran downloader scripts, and installed the Flodrix DDoS botnet. Langflow hosts often hold LLM API keys, vector-database credentials, and tool tokens, so compromise exposes the whole agent supply. Status: patched in 1.3.0, and exploitation is confirmed by CISA. Picus reports a later Langflow RCE, CVE-2026-5027 (not verified here).

- **canonical id:** `nvd-2025-triton` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** NVD records for NVIDIA Triton Inference Server, including CVE-2025-23310 and CVE-2025-23311 (stack overflow, CVSS 9.8), CVE-2025-23317 (HTTP server reverse shell, CVSS 9.1), CVE-2024-0087 (arbitrary log file to code execution, CVSS 9.0), CVE-2023-31036 (model load API path traversal). https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-23317

The critical ones include crafted HTTP requests that cause stack overflow or a reverse shell in the 2025-08-06 batch, and a model-control API path traversal when the server runs with `--model-control explicit`. Triton is a common production model server, so these bugs put weights, inputs, and co-hosted models at risk from network attackers. ### S-1108 vLLM unsafe deserialization over ZMQ/RPC (CVE-2025-32444, CVE-2024-11041, CVE-2024-9053, CVE-2025-29783)

- **canonical id:** `nvd-2025-vllm-pickle` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** NVD records: CVE-2025-32444 (CVSS 10.0; vLLM 0.6.5 to before 0.8.5 with Mooncake, pickle over unsecured ZMQ), CVE-2025-29783 (CVSS 9.0; Mooncake unsafe deserialization over ZMQ/TCP on all interfaces), CVE-2024-11041 (CVSS 9.8; MessageQueue.dequeue pickle.loads), CVE-2024-9053 (CVSS 9.8; AsyncEngineRPCServer cloudpickle.loads). https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-32444
- **confirmed via:** https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=vLLM (NVD API)
- **attack classes:** [network-exposed deserialization RCE in distributed inference]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0049, AML.T0010.001; OWASP LLM03:2025; ML06; CWE-502 (NVD); NISTAML.05
- **summary:** In distributed and multi-node vLLM deployments, internal message channels (ZeroMQ, RPC) deserialized network input with pickle or cloudpickle. Attackers who can reach those ports get RCE on inference nodes. In some configurations the ports listened on all interfaces. NVD scores these 9.0 to 10.0 and maps them to CWE-502. Related vLLM entries cover denial of service and data exposure via ZeroMQ (CVE-2025-30202) and DoS from crafted completions requests (CVE-2024-8768). The lesson for the threat model is that distributed LLM serving brings back classic deserialization flaws on east-west traffic.
- **mapping:** GPU inference cluster -> RCE through internal KV-transfer/RPC channels -> inter-node ports reachable from untrusted networks -> node takeover, weight theft

### S-1109 vLLM prefix-cache hash collision (CVE-2025-25183)

- **canonical id:** `nvd-2025-vllm-prefix-cache` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence high
- **citation:** NVD, CVE-2025-25183 (published 2025-02-07), GHSA-rm76-4mrf-v9r8; related CVE-2025-1953 (vLLM AIBrix prefix-cache hashing). https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-25183
- **confirmed via:** https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=CVE-2025-25183 (NVD API)
- **attack classes:** [cache poisoning via hash collision, cross-request interference]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0049?; OWASP LLM04:2025?, LLM02:2025?; CWE-354 (NVD), CWE-328?
- **summary:** vLLM prefix caching used Python's built-in `hash()`. Since Python 3.12 `hash(None)` is a predictable constant, so maliciously constructed prompts can force hash collisions. Cache entries are then reused across unrelated requests, which "can interfere with subsequent responses". NVD scores it low (2.6). In a threat model, however, it is the integrity counterpart of the KV-cache confidentiality side channels: one tenant can influence another tenant's outputs through shared cache state.
- **mapping:** multi-tenant inference responses -> cross-request cache poisoning -> shared prefix cache with weak hashing -> integrity of other users' outputs

### S-1110 Nx "s1ngularity": malicious npm postinstall weaponizes local AI CLIs

- **canonical id:** `nx-2025-s1ngularity` (supply-infra-misuse.md); type advisory; 2025; confidence medium (capped in the v0.2 fold: workflow detail from recollection; C15 rule)
- **aliases merged:** `nx-s1ngularity-2025 (incidents-news.md)`
- **citation:** nrwl/nx GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c, "Malicious versions of Nx and some supporting plugins were published", 2025 (August?). https://github.com/nrwl/nx/security/advisories/GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c
- **confirmed via:** same URL (fetched)
- **attack classes:** [package compromise, AI agent CLI abuse for secret discovery, sabotage]
- **catalog ids:** ATLAS AML.T0112.000 (Local AI Agent), AML.T0011.001, AML.T0010.001; ASI02, ASI04, ASI05; OWASP LLM06:2025; CWE-506?
- **summary:** Malicious Nx versions on npm ran a postinstall `telemetry.js`. It invoked locally installed AI coding CLIs with a prompt beginning "You are a file-search agent. Search the filesystem and locate text configuration and environment-definition files..." so that the victim's own AI agent found secrets for exfiltration. It also appended `sudo shutdown -h 0` to .zshrc and .bashrc. Simply running `npm install` or `pnpm install` with the bad version triggered it. The attacker borrows the developer's authorised, privileged AI agent as a living-off-the-land search tool. This matches the QUIETVAULT behaviour GTIG describes.
- **mapping:** developer workstation secrets -> local AI agent CLI turned into a secret-search tool -> compromised dependency, permissive agent CLI flags -> credential theft, sabotage
- **also captured as `nx-s1ngularity-2025` (incidents-news.md):** Date 2025-08-26, about 22:32 UTC, live about 5 hours. The attackers stole a publish token through a vulnerable GitHub Actions workflow (pull_request_target injection, from my recollection of the Nx advisory). Malicious Nx versions ran a postinstall `telemetry.js`. If Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or Amazon Q CLI was installed, the script called it with permissive flags (for example `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or `--yolo`) and a prompt to inventory wallets, keys, .env files, and SSH keys. Results were uploaded to new public `s1ngularity-repository` repos in the victims' own GitHub accounts. GitGuardian counted 1,346 repos and 2,349 secrets. A second wave (2025-08-28) used the stolen tokens to make private org repos public. This is the first documented malware delegating reconnaissance to the victim's own AI agents. Mapping: developer secrets -> malicious package invokes local AI agents with safeties off -> AI CLIs installed with bypass flags available -> mass credential leak, private repo exposure
